summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 468, in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Kacheroo Mal, (I) the Public Analyst had reported that the sample of Kajus was adulterated due to insect infested pieces of Kajus to the extent of 21.9% and I am of the opinion that the same is adulterated due to the insect infestation of infested pieces. The Food Inspector, the P.W., 468, in the Municipal Corporation of the Delhi vs Kahroo Mal, , held that the Food Inspector had reported that "Date of Analysis: 10.1.69 Insect infested piece of Kajus: 21.9.% and I were of the opinion, that the same was adulterated due lo insect infect infested and insect infestested, it would be deemed to be unfit for human consumption and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section 2(1)(f). The Food Inspector in the Municipal corporation of Delhi vs Tek Chand Bhatia, (I.L.R. , held that in the case of food articles for which no minimum standard or purity is prescribed, the moment it is proved that a proportion of percentage of the article not being a proportion or percentage as would be covered by the rule, de minimis non curat lex is putrid, filthy, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or because it is insect infuated or on account of any other cause." The Food Inspector also held that the same being adulterated due to infestation of the article for human consumption was a correct statement of the law. The respondent filed a revision before the High Court which dismissed the revision. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The true meaning of section 2 (ia) (f) has been brought out in Municipal Corporation Delhi vs Tekchand Bhatia, (supra) and the conclusion that 'it would not be necessary in such a case to prove further that the article was unfit for human use. [401C D] 1.2. The true interpretation of section 2 of the Act has been brought to in Municipal Corporation, Delhi vs TekChand Bhatia, (AIR 1988 Delhi, referred to. 1.3. The true scope of section 2 is that the article must be unfit for personal consumption because it consists wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid, disgurbing, rotting, decomposed, disgacerated, disgecting, rotating, rotten or decomeased animal or any vegetable substance or that it is insects infested or on account Of any other cause. To fall under that sub clause an article of food must be unfit to human consumption because it consist wholly or in parts of any filthy or putrid, Disgusting or rotten, rotten. . or insect infective infested or diseased animals or vegetable substance. To fall within that sub clause, an article of Food must be unfit For bringing the case within the mischief of this sub clause, and it would not be possible in such a situation to prove further, that the article of food was unfit for personal use. [409D E] 1.4. The true intention of the legislature is to bring the case within its purview.

The appellant was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The foodgrains found in his possession were also ordered to be forfeited to the State. The foodgrains were sold. The appellant appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge, Santhal Parganas, Dumka and his revision in the High Court was summarily dismissed. The defence of the appellant was that he was an agriculturist and that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands he had taken on lease from various parties. The defence was that he had stored foodgrains above the permitted quantities for a wholesale dealer, and that the grains were grown by the appellant on the lands him had taken on rent from various parties, and that he had taken the lease from various persons. The defence did not accept the evidence of the witnesses on the ground that they were interested in the appellant. The Sessions Judge rejected the documentary evidence on the ground, that they wereinterested in the appellant and that the presumption under paragraph 3(2) could not be drawn. The defence, before the High Court, was that he is an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law because the presumption under para 3(2), could not be raised. The defence raised by the appellant was rejected by the High Court. The appellant contended that he was a agriculturist and that he was not liable under the law, because the presumption in his case cannot be drawn. Held, that the presumption in the case cannot be raised. It is obvious that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there, because storage has reference to "business as a dealer and that is the essence of the Order. In the present case, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it is obvious that subsection (2) speaks of storage of for sale as an dealer although the word "carrying on the business" is not there, Because storage has reference only to "business" as a dealer. But in the present case the appellant produced receipts and proved by oral evidence that he was the next door neighbour and had a "soft corner for him". The presumption under section 3(2)(a) could not, therefore, be drawn.

The defendant was a monthly tenant in respect of the land described in schedule to the plaint. The defendant was a tenant from month to month under him and the tenan cy was determined by a notice to quit. The defendant 's tenancy was determined by the notice to quit, and the suit was, in fact one for ejectment of a lessee on the expiration of the period provided for in the lease. The defendant made a strenuous endeavour before the High Court to establish that as the Patta of 1913 as well as the Kabuliyat of 1924 were both invalid and inoperative, he was never a tenant in respect Of the land in suit and no tenancy could be created by the two payments of rent, inasmuch as the Receiver had no authority to receive them. The High Court, however, held that the defendant was a ' monthly tenant ' under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The defendant ' s tenancy was one from month to year since its inception in 1924. The defendant admitted in his written statement that payment to the Receiver had the same effect as payment to the plaintiff. The defendant also admitted in his evidence that payment to and acceptance of rent by the Receiver had been received by the Receiver. [277 D] (2) The defendant admitted that payment to him had the same affect as payment to him. The defendant did not acquire any permanent right in the land by prescription or otherwise and that by reason of the payment of rent on 8th March, 1925, and 16th March, 1926, the defendant became a tenant from year to month under the provision of section 116, Transfer of Property act. [277 E] (3) The defendant was not a tenant from the month to month since its inception. The defendant, therefore, was not a ' monthly tenancy under section 116, or Transfer of Property Ac tory Act. [277 F] (4) The defendant did make a strenuous effort before the High court to establish that the tenancy was one for one year and when he accepted rent again in 1926, such acceptance amount ed to his assenting to the defendant 's continuing in possession is evidenced by acceptance of rent from him in the year 1926.

The appellant assessee, a firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards, and the Income tax Officer, after giving the assessee an opportunity of being heard, passed an order of assessment on the basis of the material on record, and the assessee was directed to produce the documents on the date of hearing. The assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of assessment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the omission of Section 137 did not make any difference and that the ban on the courts as contained in the repealed Section 137 of the 1961 Act, even in respect of the documents filed in the assessment proceeding after April 1, 1964, for assessment years 1964 66 onwards, and that the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under Section 138(1)(b) had no relationship to the power of the court to summon that record. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court fell in error in holding that the omission in Section 137 did make any difference. [501G] 1.2 The High Court was right in holding that after the repeal of Section 137 of 1961 Act by Act V of 1964, there is no longer any impediment left in the way of a court to summon the production of documents from the income tax authorities after April 1. 1964 relating to assessment proceedings for 1964 65 onwards and that the sanctity attached to an Order of the Commissioner under Section 138 (1)(b), has no relevance to the exercise of powers by a court to summoning the production of the documents from the Income tax authorities after March 1, 1964 relating to the assessment proceedings for 1963 65 onwards. [502C] 1.3 The High Court, therefore, fell in error by holding that the failure of the legislature to make any difference or that the ban imposed on the courts under Section 137 continued to remain in force by virtue of the provisions of Section 138 (2) and after 1967 by Section 138 (3) of the Act even in respect to the documents filed by an assessee before the income tax authority after April 1 1964 for assessment years 1963 65 onwards and the Commissioner of Income Tax has the authority to furnish or cause to be furnished the sought for information, if he was satisfied that there were no circumstances justifying its refusal. [503D] 1.4 The High Court erred in holding that since after the repeal, there was no longer any difficulty left in the matter of a court of law to summon the produce of documents from income tax authorities, even after April 1., 1964 relating to assessments relating to the period 1964 65 onwards. The finality attached to the order of the Income tax Tribunal under Section 138 of the Act is, thus restricted to the cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the Section is called for by any person other than a court of Law. [504E] 1.5 The High Court also fell in error. [505B] 1.6 The finality attached under Section 138 does not affect the powers of the courts to require the production of assessment records or the disclosure of any information therefrom to it, in a case pending before the court when the court, by a judicial order, requires the production of such record, considered relevant by it for decision of a case pending pending before it. [506C] 1:7 The finality attached with the order of Commissioner under Section138(1)(a) of the 1961 Income Tax Act, 1961, is, thus, restricted to the case where the information or information etc. is called for, by any person, other than a Court of law by a judicial Order.

The appellant was married to Seinaba and he made a gift of his properties including immovable property to Seinha on April 7, 1944 by a registered deed. Mammotty died on May 3, 1946 without leaving any issue. The appellant 's mother, who was the guardian of his minor wife, filed a suit for possession of the property on the ground that the gift was not valid. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the gift by the husband to his minor wife to be valid must be accepted on her behalf by a legal guardian of her property under the Muhammadan Law, that is to say by the father or his executor. HELD : (i) The gift was by a registered document no question in this behalf can arise. [560 G] (ii) The gift did not necessarily fail merely because possession was not handed over to the minor 's father or guardian and the donor could nominate a person to accept the gift on behalf of his minor daughter. [560 D] (iii) The gift by a father to his minor grandson when the father was alive, without delivery of possession to the father, was not delivered to Sein Dutta but to her mother, the first appellant, and she accepted the gift on the behalf of her minor wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him, for after the celebration of marriage a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father was living. [560 E] (iv) The gift in the present case did not necessarily fall merely because possession is not handed over but to her father or guardian. [560 F] (v) The gift, by a father, to his minor grandsons when the father is alive, was completed ordinarily by the acceptance of the guardian of the property of the minor Wilayat ul Mal. [560 C] (vi) The gift is by a registered instrument no question in that behalf can arise, and the completion of the gift for his benefit is the sole consideration. Mammottty was living at the time of the gift in the house of his mother in law and was probably a very sick person though not in marzulmaut. His minor wife who was also living at the place of her mother in law was capable under Muhammadan law to accept the gifts on behalf of her mother who had attained majority and had lived in her care where the husband was also residing. [560 A B] (vii) The gift does not necessarily fail simply because possession was handed over to a minor who has no guardian of the properties in existence. [560 B] (viii) The gift must be completed by delivery of the property to and acceptance by any person in whose control the minor is at the time. [560 H] (ix) The gift cannot be completed by the delivery of the gift to the minor. [560C] (x) The gift actually made was by a deed which was registered and handed over by Mammotti to his mother in Law and accepted by her on behalf of 'the minor. [561 D] (xi) The gift made by Mammottee to his mother was not delivered by Sein Dutta and to her mother in Law. [561 E] (xii) The gift could not be completed by delivering the deed to his mother, who had attained discretion and had lived at her mother 's house and in her care when the husband was himself the guardian.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration and governance of Hindu Religious and Charitable Institutions and Endowments in the State of Madras. Section 76(1) provides for the better administra tion and governance of the Hindu Religious and charitable institutions and Endowments in their State. Section 76 provides for the levy of contribution which was of the nature of a tax and not a fee. The Act does not contemplate separate rules to be made in respect of each religious institution likely to obtain the benefit of services rendered by the State for which the contribution is to be levied. Under section 76(2) of the Act audit fee is not to be prescribed by rules. the Commissioner has to determine, having regard to the facts and circumstances of each case, the fee (being not more than the maximum prescribed) for meeting the cost of audit of the institution. That im.plies that the Commissioner has not determined the audit fee under section 76(1). The Commissioner has to form an estimate of the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of the accounts of each religious endowment. The Commissioner has also to form an estimates of the reasonable costs which may be incur in making an efficient audit of the account of each religious endowments. The Commissioner had to form an estimated estimate of the cost which may he incurred in making the effective audit of accounts of each of the religious endowment. That im is sufficient to say that the amount demanded is not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred for auditing the accounts. The Commissioner, therefore, proceeded to observe "It is sufficient to mean that until such rule was made no contribution could be demanded" and proceeded to observe that "it is sufficient to mention that the amount demand made of the petitioners ' temple for the payment of a sum of Rs. It was not the case of the respondents that the Commissioner had not determined the annual audit fee under Section 76(2). It was not their case that the Commissioner was not determined the Audit fee under section76(2). The High Court was of the view that the Commissioner did not determine the audit fee. The High Court, however, held that the Commissioner 's order was set aside and it was directed that the case be remanded to the High Court for disposal according to law and in the light of the observations made in this judgment. The High court, however, directed that the cases be remanded to High Court for deciding the case according to law. The High ' Court, however held that the demand for levy of contribution was Premature, and that audit fee demanded by the Commissioner was without jurisdiction. The High, Court, however. held that the audit fee demanded was Premature and that audit fees demanded by the commissioner was without jurisdiction and was "on that account without competence or authority of law". The High Court also held that the order passed by the High Court was without jurisdiction, and that the demand was Premature. The High Courts, however, took the view that under the Act the Government had to make under section 100 rules applicable to each temple separately and prescribing the method for determining contribution find no support in the provisions of the Act or its scheme. The High courts, however, proceeded on the ground that the Commissioner having not determined the correct cost of auditing the accounts of the temple, and proceeded to hold that the demand made of Rs. 1,00,000 was without jurisdiction under section 76 (2).

The appellant was charged with committing contempt of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appellant 's petition under section 19 of the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the High court. The High court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant contended that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right under section 19. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the High Court affecting the right of the party aggrieved. The order or decision must be Such that it decides any bone of contention which may be appealable to this Court under section 19, and that it decides certain bone of contention raising before the High court affecting the right. [508B C] Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court, ; , referred to. The order of the Supreme Court in Baradakata Mishra vs OrissaHigh Court, ; and Baradakanda Mishra vs Orissa State, ; , relied on. The order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further, does not decide anything against the alleged contemner and cannot be appealed against as a matter Of right under section 20. [509C D] Baradkanta Mishra vsOrissa High Court, , referred to and relied on. In the instant case, the order or the order of dismissal passed by the High Court dismissing the appellant ' s petition under section 20 of the Act does not decide any question. The order is not appealable under section 19 because it does not decide something against the alleged contemnor and cannot be Appeal against as a right under section19. [510E F] Baradikanta Mishra vs State of Orissa, ; , distinguished.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another in the Court of the Magistrate, First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) of the . The Magistrate convicted him under section 6 (1 A) and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment. The High Court upheld the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the amendment was not covered by the words " wireless telegraphy apparatus " in section 6(I A) of Act XVII of 1933, and that the words " telegraphy apparatus" in section 6 (I A) were comprehensive enough to take in " wireless telegraphic transmitter " and that the amendment did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the amending Act of 1949. Held, that the amendment made in the year 1952 as the said amendment was unnecessary and redundant. Section 6 (1A) of the Act continued to be on the statute book even after the amending Act was repealed by Act XLVIII of 1952, and that it was in force when the offence was committed by the appellant. The words " telegraphary apparatus" in the section did not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. The words were comprehensive enough enough to take into account the words used in the Act, but not the content of that Act. The words ' telegraphary apparatus ' in section 6 of the Act did not prohibit possession of a Wireless apparatus. The language of the relevant words in section 6 did not prohibit, the possession of an wireless apparatus. Therefore, it cannot be said that section 6 (i A) of The Act continued to remain on the statute books even after the amendment of 1949.

The appellant, a son of Adwaita, was the wife of Aghore Nath Roy, a son, of Adwaitta, the former managing Shebait of the debutter estate. On the 28th August, 1941, the deities represented by some of the Shebaits filed two applications under section 36(6) (a) (ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for the reopening of the two compromise decrees mentioned in Schedules Ka, Kha and Ga. The applications were dismissed by the Subordinate Judge, on the ground that the appellant was a mere benamidar for her husband Aghore in respect of the purchase of Ga Schedule properties in court sale, and also that the Kobala executed by the Chakrabortys in her favour on July 26, 1940, was a fictitious transaction. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to prove that the Kubala executed by her in favour on July 28, 1940, on July 26. 1940, was fictitious transaction. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The decreeholders, therefore, must be deemed to be the purchasers of these properties within the meaning of clause (b) of section 36(2). [163 D] (ii) The decree holders, therefore, should be deemed to have been the purchasers of the properties within the ambit of the provisions of section 36 (2). [164 D] (iii) The decreeholder, therefore, was entitled to have the two compromise decree reopened and on the passing of the new instalment decrees to have the properties, which were in possession of the real decreeholder. [164 D E] (iv) The decree holder, therefore, could not be said to be the purchaser of these properties. [164 E] (v) The decree debtors, therefore, were entitled to have two compromise decrees reopened and on passing of the fresh instalment decrees to which the appellant was entitled, they must be deemed not to be the owners of these properties, within the meaning Of clause (b).

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The company had its registered office at Bombay. The company transferred its shares to the appellant company. The company applied for leave under Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The application was rejected by the City Civil Court. The appellant company then applied for leave to appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the document in question amounted to a transfer of the decree that was expected to be passed in the pending suit, that as the decree was not in existence at the date of the document it operated as an agreement to transfer the decree when it would be passed, that such an agreement could be enforced by a suit for specific performance as contemplated by Order XXI, r. 16 of the Civil Procedure Code. HELD: (i) The provisions of Order XXI, Rule 16 contemplate the actual transfer by an assignment in writing of a decree after it is passed and that while a transfer of or an agree ment to transfer a decree that may be passed in future may, in equity, entitle the intending transferee to claim the beneficial interest in the decree after it was passed, such equitable transfer does not render the transferee a transferee of the decree by assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI rule 16 of Code of Civil procedure. [1405 D] (ii) The provisions Of Order XXI, rules 16 contemplate the delivery of possession of the property to the transferee of the property. The transfer in writing of the property does not entitle the intending purchaser to claim the benefit of section 146 if the provisions of that section can be availed of by him. [1406 E] (iii) The provisions in Order XXI, Rules 16 contemplate the physical transfer by an assignee in writing of an order after it is made and that while the transfer of or agree ment to transfers a decree that might be passed in subsequent suit, that may be made in future may in equity, disentitle the intending transferee of the suit to apply for execution of the decree to the Court which passed it. [1407 E F] (iv) The provisions contained in Order XXI Rule 16 contemplate actual transfer by assignment in words of words of words in a decree after the word 'decree ' and that while in a transfer of a decree that can be passed in later suit, the transferee of a decree, that may, in justice and equity, entitle him to claim the equitable interest in the suit after it is executed, such equitable transfers does not render a transferee a transferee or of the decree itself by assignment in ink within the meaning Of Order XXI Rule16. [1408 F G] (v) The provisions relating to execution of a decree at the instance of a transferee by assignment in a writing within the expression 'decree ' in Order XXI rule16 of the Code, enables the transferee of his decree to execute it in the same manner and subject to the same conditions as an application for execution made by the decree holder. [1409 G] (vi) The provisions regarding execution of a decrees at the instance o of a transferee, by assignment in letter or by operation of law and enables such transferee to apply for execute the decree to a Court which passed the decree. [1410 E] (vii) The provisions under Order XXI Rule 17 contemplate the actualtransfer by an assignment of a decree which may be passed at the instance by a transfer in writing or by operation or law and enables the transferee to apply to execute it, in the same way and subject to such conditions as an applica tion for execution made in the suit.

The petitioner alleged that the Railway in this country were owned by the Railway and on account thereof, adequate safety security protection to the passenger and their properties are not available. In view of the recent pronouncements of this Court no objection has been raised in the counter affidavit and we have not been called upon to adjudge the locus standi of the petitioner to maintain an action like this. The petitioner has maintained that he may every citizen of this country for the matter of that, is entitled to demand that the State shall provide adequate facilities and create and maintain an environment in which the right to move freely and carry on any business or profession would both be practicable and feasible. The petitioner, however, has maintained that the Railway is owned by the Government and on behalf of the Government, adequate safety protective protection to the people and their properties was not available. It is true that this is worked out also in the Railways and, as quickly as possible, classification conforming to this is introduced. But this means that accident have to be stopped, attack on, the persons of passengers and ping on their property had to stop. This means that accidents had to be avoided and attack on the people of the passengers or prying on the property has to stopped. The obligation imposed by the Railways Acts and the Rules thereunder must be complied within. It is necessary to point out that this is working out also in this country, and as quickly as practicable, classification conforming with this is introduced.] [727B] 1.8 The quality of a service should improve and. We hope that early steps shall be taken to implement in a phased manner the improvements referred to in the counter Affidavit and in our decision. [728C] 1:9 The quality of work should improve.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. They were the owners in possession of certain lands. The appellants filed applications for restoration of their lands on the ground that the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961. The applications were made in time under Regulation 21 of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations, 1958. The applications for restoration were made in the prescribed time under Regulation 20 of the Jagirs Abolition Act. The applications filed on May 6, 1961 were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal of the appeals and hence the applications for restoration made by the appellants in all the four cases were within 30. The applications of restoration were made within 30 days from the receipt of order of dismissal. The applications made on May 6 1961 were within time under Regulation 22 of the Bombay Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The applications dated May 6,1961 were within 30 and were within 30 respectively of the receipt. The applications in all the three cases were well within the period of limitation prescribed by Regulation 21. The applications on May 6. 1961 were well within time under Regulations 19(1) and 19(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The applications to restore the appeals were made in accordance with Regulation 21 of Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulation, 1958. In the applications for restoring the appeals filed on May 7, 1961, the appellants contended that since the orders passed in the appeals were not received by them, the restitution applications filed on April 9, 1961 were beyond 30 days of receipt of the orders of dismissal and hence the application for restoration was made in time. Held, that the Tribunal committed an error of law in dismissing the applications of restoration made by appellants in all four cases. The appellant 's case was that Telibandha was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy as early as 1857 by Dinanath Sao himself and later in the year 1896 when a partition took place between his descendants who were up till that time living jointly, all the coshares not only re affirmed the dedication made by DinanathSao of this village of Telibandha but also themselves dedicated the village Telibandha to the deities in this temple by accepting the award made by the Panchas. The appellant 's suit was dismissed by the trial court. The High Court agreed with the Trial Court that dedication by Dinanath Guo was dedicated to Shri Ramchandra Swamy temple and that no trust was created thereby. The High court agreed with the trial court that dedication by the Panch Faisla was made in favour of the appellant as the manager on behalf of the deities for this property. The High ' Court agreed with this finding and held that the dedication by Dinnath Sao was not proved. The High. Court agreed with that finding. The High, Court agreed with both the Trial Court and the Trial Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of appellant that the dedication of the village Telabandha had not been proved but disagreeing with the Trial court, it held that there was no absolute dedication of the Village for the purpose of the temple by the Panch 116 Faisla Award of 1896 and no trust was established thereby. Held, that the document (the Panch Faisala) clearly and unambiguously shows an .absolute dedication of the property to Shri Ramchandra Swami temple, set aside the judgment and decree of the High Court and send the case back to the High Court for disposal of the appeal after deciding the other issues in the suit that require to be decided for its proper disposal.

The appeal is against the order of the High Court. The appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the AvadhBar Association. There were three charges against the appellants. The first charge was that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar. The second charge was that the Chief Judge was acting in the dis charge of administrative power under clause 14 of the U.P. High Court 's Amalgamation Order, 1948 in a most casual manner under the control of the Allahabad High Bar quite unbecoming of the office which he held. The High Court discharged the notices. The High court discharged the notices and held that contemners Nos. 1 & 2 were guilty of contumacious conduct, and the High Court gave the ground that they were responsible for the passing of the resolution. The High ' Court further held that contemners No. 1 &2 were guilty of criminal contempt. The High Curt also held that contemners nos. 1 & 3 were guilty of wilful disobedience of Court 's order. The High Courts held that contemners no. 1 & the Chairman, action Committee of the Faizabad Bar were guilty of Contempt of Court. The High, Court held that contemners were guilty of contempt as contemner No. 2 was. The High. Court further held: (1) that contemners Nos, 1 & 2 are guilty of contuma fidelity conduct, and (2) that contemners nos, 1 &2 are guilty of criminal Contempt. The matter becomes clear when the High Court said "we do not propose to punish contemners Nos.1 & 2 for the contumacious conduct of which we have adjudged them guilty though we express our disapproval of that conduct and hope that the indiscretion will not be repeat ed". The matter becomes evident when the High court said "we did not propose to be punish contemners Nos." 1 & 2 for contumacious conduct for which we have graded them guilty though they were not inclined to proceed against the appellants". The High Court did not wish to proceed against them.

The appellants were the owners of a joint movable and immovable properties. The appellants filed an application before the Sub Judge for registration. The Sub Judge dismissed the application and did not direct return of the award holding that the limitation for the registration of the award had already expired. The appellants preferred an appeal before the High Court. The High Court ordered that the arbitrators ' application dated 14th of August, 1978 should be kept pending and be heard when the injunction order was vacated. On the question whether the limitation for registration of the Award had already expired, HELD: The order made by the Sub Judge directing the arbitrators to keep the award in the custody of the court was wrong and without jurisdiction, but no arbitrator could be compelled to disobey the order of the court and if in compliance or obedience with court of doubtful jurisdiction, he could not take back the award from the custody of court to take any further steps for its registration then it cannot be said that he has failed to get the award registered as the law required. [690C] In the instant case admittedly the award was in the court of the learned Munsif from 28th January, 1978 to 24th November, 1983 the award was filed in the court pursuant to the order of this Court directing maintenance of status quo and 20th of December, 1982 was the date of the order of injunction. The award was made on 28th of November, 1977 and before the expiry of the four months from 28th November, 1977 the award was made in the custody. The award as it was in the custody was filed in court pursuant to order of the High Court on 24th of June, 1985. The award, therefore, was in the possession of the court. [691D E] In the facts and circumstances of the case, however, the parties are directed to pay and bear their own costs.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent gave notice to the appellant to vacate the premises on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises to the sub tenants and that he had waived his right in regard to the prohibition against sub tenancy and the provision in section 13(1)(e) was for the protection of his rights which he was entitled to waive. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent had waived his rights in regard to prohibition against sub tenant and the provision of section 13(2) was for protection of his right which he was entitle to waive. Held, that the respondent 's suit for ejectment was not brought for the enforcement of the agreement which recognised sub letting but he asked the Court to enforce the right of eviction which flows directly from an infraction of a provision of the Act which prohibits it. The respondent 's right to sue for ejectment on a ground of subletting being a personal right for his benefit, the landlord must be taken to have waived it as by an express contract he had allowed the tenant to sub let and consequently he could not evict the appellant under section 13(l)(e) of the Act. The respondent had waived the statutory rights enacted for the benefit of the appellant and the provisions in section 13 of the Act were not intended to be in conjunction with section 15 of the Act and section 23 of the Contract Act.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 to be committed by Madan Lal, one of the prosecution witnesses. The prosecution case was that the appellants were charged with criminal conspiracy to commit the offence of cheating punishable under section 120B of the Indian. Penal Code for having dishonestly or fraudulently misappropriates or otherwise converts for his own use any property entrusted to him or under his control as a public servant or allows any other person to be, or to be likely to be concerned in any proceeding or business transacted or about to be transacted by him or having any connection with the official functions of himself or of any public servant to whom he is subordinate, or from any person whom he knows to be interested in or related to the person so concerned, or (c)if he habitually accepts or obtains or agrees to accept or attempts to obtain from any person for himself or for any other person, any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. The appellants were charged for criminal conspiracy under section 5 (2) of Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 1955, to have been committed by Madan lal, one of them, and the other by one of the accused. The prosecution alleged that the appellants had been charged under section 5 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act, and the appellants were convicted under section 120 A of the Indian Indian Penal Code. The appellants contended that the offence as defined in section 5(1) of the Act was not based solely on the presumption and that it could come into play only when there was no offer to give an acceptance of a bribe by a public servant. Held, that the intention of the Act, was to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and that it can come into play even when there is no offer to pay an d acceptance of a gratification by a public Servant. The offence as defined by section 5(4) of the Indian Act was not one of bribery and the offence as contemplated in section 5 (1) of Prevention Of Corruption (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1956, was not one which was covered by section 5 (4) of Prevention Corruption Act, but was one which was not covered by section 7 (1) (d) of the General Clauses Act. The offence was one which could be committed by a public officer only for the purposes of Chapter IX of the Indian Police Act. The appellants had been convicted under section 5 and under section 5. The offence of criminal conspiracy was one which had been committed by the appellants. The appellants could not be said to be a public servant for the purposes Of Chapter IX of Indian Police Act, and it could not be stated of them that he was interested in giving or attempting to give any bribe for hushing up the case.

The appellant Bank of Saurashtra (the Bank) had pledged oil tins and pledged oil tin and the surety was discharged to the extent of the value of security. The surety was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. The surety 's surety 's bond was executed by the principal debtor in favour of the Bank. The surety gave personal guarantee on the specific understanding and with the full knowledge of the Bank that the principal debtor had offered two securities, one the pledge of oil tins, and another personal guarantee of the surety. The surety also agreed to give personal guarantee on behalf of the surety and with the knowledge of the bank that the principal borrower was offering another security, namely, pledge of goods. The surety agreed to give security on the specific terms and conditions of the contract of guarantee. The sureties gave personal guarantee of Rs. 20,000 to the Bank. On the basis of the said agreement, the surety was paid Rs. 20 lakhs. The surety offered two securities on the specific condition that the principal creditor shall offer two securities, One the pledge of goods to be kept under the lock and key of the Bank to be supervised by the Bank 's employee and secondly, the personal guarantee of surety. The sureties agreed to give two securities on behalf of them to be kept Under the lock and keys of the Bank and endorsed by the surety to the Bank, Ext. 81, and the letter of guarantee Ext. 31 executed by the surety in favour of Bank as also the bond executed by the Principal debtor in favour thereof. The surety, however, did not give personal guarantee to the Bank on the specific promise of the surety, but only gave personal guarantee to him on the specific assurance that the principal debt shall be discharged to the tune of the value. The surety did not give any personal guarantee on his behalf. The surety however, did so. The surety filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368 04 P. from the surety. In the suit, the surety pleaded that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal debtor pledging oil tins as and by way of security for the advance and, therefore, two securities were offered, namely, pledged oil tIns and another personal guarantees of the surety; and the personal guarantee executed by the guarantor in favour of The Bank Ext. 81 executed by the creditor in favour of 'the surety ' in favour of, the Bank, all on September 16, 1957, constituted one composite transaction and they evidence that the principal Debtor had offered two security, one the pledged oil touts and another personal Guarantee of the surety on the specific agreeing condition that the surety shall offer two security, namely pledge of goods, and the personal Guarantee of ' the surety. On appeal by the surety, the High Court held that the surety having lost one security, namely the pledged goods, the surety would not be discharged from the obligation undertaken under the letter of Guarantee. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The surety is entitled to restitution. [83C] 2. The surety would not, therefore, be discharged from his obligation undertaken under a letter of guarantee. [83D] 3. The surety in good faith contracted to offer personal guarantee on a specific understanding and to the full knowledge and with the complete knowledge of the Court that the principal guarantor was offering another personal security, namely; pledge of goods and the goods were to be in the custody of the creditor Bank. [83E] 4. The surety had given personal guarantee on it the specific understanding that the principal buyer was offering another Security, namely, guarantee of goods. [83F] 5.

The appellant was the son of Amritrao. The land in suit was allotted to the appellant. The appellant was the grandson of Amritrao, and the land in suit were allotted to the share of the appellant. In 1943, the appellant was the daughter of Amritrao and the land was allotted to her. The appellant 's father was the son. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the land in the suit. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that (1) the lands in suit were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for 91 years to be rendered by the patel and the grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government; and (2) the grant was made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag and not by the sovereign authority and neither the Inam Rules nor the provisions of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900 applied. Held, that the grant was not a service grant and no question of a claim of a share in the emoluments of office fell even for consideration, not to speak of decision. The grant was not made by the Ruler of the State of Bombay, but was made by way of emoluments for 91 year to be rendered to the patelki inam. The grant, therefore, made by the jagir of Nawabag, was not a grant of land burdened with service. The grant made by the Jagir of Nawabag was not a " service grant" and no question was of a claim in a share in emoluments of office fallen even for consideration.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was a member of the Hindu undivided family. The family of the appellant was governed by the Hindu Law of inheritance and inheritance. The appellant was a member in the family of the respondent. The respondent was a member. The family was governed by Hindu Law. The appellant 's father was a member and was governed by a Hindu law. The family consisted of two members, namely, the respondent and the respondent. On the question whether the respondent was a coparcener, HELD : (1) The respondent was not a coparcener. The respondent had not acquired a right by birth in the property held by his father. The respondent 's father had settled down in Madras. The respondent did not acquire a right by inheritance. The respondent could not have acquired a right under the Hindu Law. [234 D] (2) The respondent had acquired a right to the property held in the property by his father, a right expressly saved by section 3 of the Act. [234 E] (3) The respondent could have acquired a property by birth, if he was not a member of his family. The respondent, therefore, could not have purchased a right by the appellant by inheritance. [234 F] (4) The respondent ' s father had settled in Madras and then in Bangalore sometime between 1928 and 1930, and as a large part of the,state was situate in Madras. He had settled down amidst Hindus according to Hindu law not only in matters of succession and inheritance but also in matters of their property including the Hindu concept of coparcenary and survivorship. [234 G] (5) The respondent did have a right by descent in the property owned by him. The respondent having been born in Madras had already acquired a right in the property holding by his father a right expressly conferred by section 3. [234 C] (6) The respondent having acquired a right expressly by section 3, the appellant could not have sold the property by inheritance. He could not have transferred the property by sale. [234 B] (7) The respondent acquired a right of inheritance by birth, and the respondent could not be said to have acquired a vested right by birth.

The appellants are manufacturers of fabrics of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage. It has, however, been held that the retrospective effect given by section S I will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the , and, therefore, the retrospective effect of section S I would be subject to section 12B of the . The appellants are manufacturers in the manufacture of fabrics of various types. In the process of weaving the same into fabrics, yarn was obtained at an intermediary stage. It was, however, held that the yarn which is produced at an intermediate stages in the mill of the appellants and subjected to the integrated process of weaving, the same into fabric, will be liable to payment of excise duty. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the retrospective retrospective effect given to section S I of the Finance Act, 1982, is subject to the provision of sections 11 A and 11B, of the , as amended by the Finance Act 1982. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The definition of "place of removal" in section 2(1) of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1982 is the production or manufacture of goods and not removal. The definition of the expression "place of manufacture" in section 3 of the Act is the production, manufacture or manufacture of the excisable goods. The definition is not required to be made and, in our view, cannot be made of the place of manufacture or production of the excisable product. [707E] 1.2 The definition of 'place of removal ' in section 2 of the Finance Bill, 1982, does not, in any manner, indicate that it is only when the goods are removed from the factory it will be removal and when the excisable goods manufactured or cured or if such excisable goods are used in the manufacture or production or manufacture thereof, the said goods will be deemed to have been removed from the place or premises immediately before such consumption or utilization. It has been already noticed that the specification that has to be made by the Collector is of any premises appurtenant to the place of manufacturing or production of excisable goods. [708B] 1.3 The specification that has been made by the collector is of any premise appurtenant to the factory, it is not required that the manufacturer should specify such premises for the purpose of collection of excise duty, but, rule 9 does not, anywhere, indicate that the specification is not required. [709C] 1.4 The specification is not necessary to be made of a place of manufacture and production of the goods. In the instant case, the appellants are liable to pay excise duty on the yarn after it is sized for the purpose for weaving the same in an integrated process for weaving the said fabrics into fabrics. Be that as it may, as the appellants are not liable to pay any excise duty on yarn after it was sized for for the purpose, of weaving the said same into fabrics. [710E] 1:5 The definition of place of removal' in section 2 (1) of Finance Bill, 1981, does not indicate that it was only when the excisable commodity is taken outside the factory it would be removal and if the excisable goods are consumed in the same place, this cannot be done without payment of excise duties at the place and in the manner prescribed. [711B] 1:6 The specification that have to be made is of any place of manufacture, or production or manufacturing of the excisable article. The specification is made not required to make the place of production or manufacture or production thereof.

The appellant was charged with the offence of cheating punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellant was a public servant and was entrusted with the duty of maintaining a high standard of integrity and to maintain a high standard. The appellant was charged under section 5 (2) of Prevention of Corruption act, 1947 and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution alleged that the appellant had committed the offence of criminal misconduct under section 5 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act, and section 161, Indian Penal Code, and section 5(1)(d) of the Act. The appellant pleaded that the appellant did not pay the money to the appellant in repayment of the loan by him to Russel Nathaniel and his wife expressed their reluctance to send Miss Eylene with him to the police station and therefore the appellant was guilty of gross abuse of his official position on the part or the appellant and that the conviction of the appellant under section 5 was not justified. The trial court accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant of the charged framed against him and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo rigorous rigorous imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 161, I.P.C. and to two years rigorous imprisonment under section 161 of Indian Penal Code and to two year rigorous imprisonment under s. 161, Indian. The High Court maintained the conviction of appellant under section 161 and sentenced him and to pay fine of Rs, 5001 or to both. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The appellant was guilty for grossly abusing his position as a police officer and extorted money from Russel Nathiiel and his son also a gold ring from Roshan Lal. The appellant in his official capacity as a police Officer was expected to maintain a low standard of integrity, and to uphold the maintenance of law. Instead they proved facts that there was a gross abuse of the official position on his part or the Appellant and in the circumstances of the case they were satisfied that the sentence imposed was not excessive. [655 C] (2) The appellant had obtained money from Rushare Nathaniel handed over the currency notes to the appellant who put them in the left side pocket of his trousers. The appellant proved facts that he was guilty of grossly abusing his official position as a public servant within the meaning of section 5(I)(d) Of the Prevention of corruption Act and thereby obtained for himself a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, and the charge under that section was established. [656 D] (3) The appellant in the official capacity as the police officer was expected to keep a high standard and to uphold maintenance of law and to uphold his maintenance maintenance of law, [656 E] (4) The appellant grossly abused his position as public servant and extorted amount from Russel. Nathaniel was expected to maintaining a high standards of integrity and To uphold the maintenance and maintain the maintenance of public order. Instead them proved facts that they were not guilty of grossly abused his official position, favour or disfavour to any per son. The appellant had been guilty of grossly misusing his position as an police officer and had obtained for himself an valuable thing or monetary advantage, and he had also a gold chain from Roshan Lal, and also a gold security from Roshan Lal to Roshan Lal. [657 E] (5) The appellant having obtained money from the Russel Naniiel and his daughter, and also the gold ring from the Roshan Lal, the appellant in his private capacity as a public officer was expected, to maintain a higher standard of integrity.
