The appellant was prosecuted for the offence of having accepted illegal gratification as a motive or reward for doing an official act and showing in the exercise of his official functions to obtain a pecuniary advantage for himself punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special Judge acquitted the appellant. The High Court held that the sanction accorded in this case was not a valid sanction. Held, that the sanction was not a proper sanction. The sanction was not valid. The sanction itself and the evidence of the witnesses showed that the papers placed before him were relevant to the only question before him whether he should or should not accord his sanction to the prosecution of the appellant. Held, further, that the sanctioning authority was not a competent authority to grant the sanction. The sanctioning authority was a competent authority and the sanction accorded was not a invalid one. The sanction accorded was a valid sanction and the evidence was of the opinion that the sanction granted was not a genuine one. The sanctioning officer was a competent officer and the sanction was a valid one. The authority granting the sanction was competent to grant the same. The sanction, therefore, clearly showed that the sanctioning officer had applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the sanction granted by him was not a legal one. The papers placed before the sanctioning authority apparently gave him the necessary material upon which he decided that it was necessary in the ends of justice to accord his sanction. The papers which were placed before him apparently gave him a necessary material upon whom he decided that they were relevant to. accord his sanction and were relevant to his only question before he whether he should accord his sanction for the prosecution of his appellant.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenants under section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The tenant contended that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and for reconstruction. The Rent Controller held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction of tenants. The High Court dismissed the revision petitions. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant landlord that the landlord had only a life interest in the premises and that it was inherent in such a life interest that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14(I)(b) as grounds for eviction of a tenant by demolition of the property for the purpose of reconstruction. HELD: (1) The landlord is defined under section 2(6) as follows: " 'Landlord ' includes the person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a building whether on his own ac count or on behalf of himself and others or as an agent, trustee, executor, administrator, receiver or guardian or who would so receive the rent or be entitled to receive, the rent, if the building were let to a tenant". [275 D] (2) The expression landlord is defined in section 2(7) as follows " "Landlord ' include the person who receives or is entitled, to receive the rents of a building, whether on his personal ac count or not, as an agent; trustee, executor administrator, receiver, or guardian or whose would so receive, the rents or be entitled, to receiving the rent, If the building were rented to a tenant, the landlord would be entitled to evict the tenant on the ground of demolition and reconstruction. [275 E] (3) The expression 'landlord ' is defined under the Act as follows: 'Landlord " includes the person receiving or is entitle to receive the Rent Rent Rent Rent and the tenant is entitled to get the rent. [275 F] (4) The expression "landlord" is defined under Section 2(6). The definition of the expression "landlord is defined under s 2(6), as follows: "( "landlord" includes the person whose rent is payable or payable or payable to the landlord, whether on behalf of or on behalf or another, or on behalf, or on his behalf, or as an Agent, trustee, receiver or receiver, trustee or who would, so receive the rents or are payable to the tenant". [276 B] (5) The expression tenant is defined under sec. 2(6)(b) to mean a person who is paid or is entitled under a decree or order of a court or other authority to receive the amount of rent or to receive the same rent, whether on the own ac count, or on the behalf of another or on behalf. The expression "tenant" is defined in sec. 2 (6) as follow: " "Land Landlord" includes a person who has been receiving or is payable to the owner, whether on or behalf of another, or as a trustee, trustee, trustee or receiver or guardian, or who would be entitled, under a decree of court or other person, to receive or receive the rent, whether the building were letting to a tenant." [276 C D] (6) The expression landlords is defined under Sec. 2(7). The definition is defined under that section as follows: (7) "Landlord" includes the persons who are receiving or is liable to receive the income of a building or a building, either on his own or on behalf and who are entitled to receive or is entitled for receiving the rent or is entitled on behalf or on behalf by or another, to receive rent, if, the building were so let to a tenants.

The appellant decree holder filed a suit for recovery of possession of the suit land. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The decree holder filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: The definition of the intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, is bhumidhari property. Rights in it are part of bhumidhari rights. Rights in them are part of the bhumidhari rights, execution should have proceeded against trees in groves and the view taken by the execution court, that there is a distinction between, trees and a grove and grove land, should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench). [712B C] The contention is well settled, under the general law, that trees, before they are cut, form parts of 'land '. [712C] The contention of the respondent decree holder that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in. section 6 of the Act in the State of Uttar Pradesh, new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 18 of the Act, read with section 73 of the , so that nothing more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee. The uncut trees are deemed to be parts of the 'land ' and the view of the execution court that there is no distinction between, tree and a grove is always included in the whole.

The appellants were charged with an offence under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The trial court convicted accused 2 to 4 for an offence under section 302 IPC and awarded sentence of rigorous imprisonment for two years each. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in recording a conviction against the appellants for an offence punishable under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC without a specific charge having been framed against him as envisaged by law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The conviction of all the appellants for the offence under Section 324 IPC is not permissible. That apart, according to the medical evidence, none of the accused persons individually had been charged for the substantive offence of murder under Section 302/149 IPC. The injuries caused by them according to the postmortem report were on vital part of the body, though some of the injuries caused by blunt weapons were grievous in nature. The injuries on the deceased had been caused by all the four appellants and that the death had occurred due to multiple injuries which were found sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. [89D E] 1.2. The injuries inflicted by them according the postmortem report, were on vital parts of the body though some of them were grievous in character. The injuries attributed to them were not found to be sufficient in the normal course of nature. The medical evidence also shows that the injuries sustained by them were not sufficient in the general course of nature, to cause death of the deceased. [89E F] 1.3. The injuries sustained by the deceased had not been found sufficient in ordinary course of type to cause death and the death had happened due to multiple injury which were found insufficient in the ordinary Course of nature to causing death. [90F] 1.4. The injuries were on vital portion of the body. The injuries had been caused with the intention to cause death, and the death has occurred due to several injuries which were not on any vital part of body, though any of the injuries were grievous in gravity. [90G] 1.5. The injuries alleged to have been caused by the appellants according to the autopsy report were on any vital parts of body, although some of the Injuries caused by blunt weapon were grievous in Nature. [90E] 1.6. The injuries found on the deceased having been caused by blunt injuries were on any important part of the bodies, though some were grievous in shape. The injuries, therefore, fall under Section 326 IPC and convicted them for the said offence, and sentenced them to suffer rigorous rigorous imprisonment for a period of three years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ each. [90H; 91A] 1.7. The conviction and sentence of all the accused for the offence of murder punishable under Section 324/149 IPC is not sustainable. That apart the conviction of all of the appellants for offence under Section 325 IPC is not justified. That apart according to the Medical evidence, none other of the accused appellants individually had been charge sheeted for an offence of murder of Suku or were sufficient in the Ordinary course of nature for causing death of Suku. Medical evidence is clear on this aspect of the case and it is not possible to say that the injuries inflicted by the first appellant with the chopper were inflicted with the intention of causing death of the Suku or was sufficient in the extraordinary course of nature of nature to Cause death. [91G H; 91A B] 1.8.

The assessee company was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69. The assessee company claimed that it was not following any particular method of accounting regularly in the past years, that it was the Indian Company which was finally filing the returns of income on behalf of the assessee by incorporating the figures as per its profit and loss account, that the Indian Company was not aware of the assessee 's system of accounting in regard to royalty and that, therefore, it had committed a mistake in filing the returns for the assessment year 1967 68 and 1969 69. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal held that the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash basis for 1967 68 and that the Indian company was not aware that the IndianCompany had credited to the assessee in its books for the relevant years (accounting year for the Indian Company). The High Court in appeal held that the assessee was not maintaining any particular method or method of accounting in respect of royalty and that the alleged statement in the returns relating to the assessment years 1968 69 and 1968 69 was an incorrect statement made by the Indian Company, which was not aware about the true state of affairs relating to the assessee ' 's accounts. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The method of accounting adopted by the assessee for the relevant accounting years is really irrelevant. [105D] 1.2 The method of accounts adopted by the Income Tax Officer for the relevant assessment years is really relevant. [105E] 1.3 The method of Accounting adopted by the appellant for the relevant relevant accounting years was really irrelevant. In the circumstances, the method of accounting adopting by the assessee in the books of the Indian Company does amount to its receipt by the assessee and is accordingly taxable and that it is immaterial when did it actually receive it in U.K. Section 145 of the Act and Section 5(2)(b) governs it irrespective of the fact whether it maintains its accounts on cash basis or mercantile basis. [105F] 1.4 The method of account accounting adopted by it for the relevant year is really irrelevant and is therefore immaterial when did the assessee actually receive it. [105G] 1.5 The method of computation adopted by the Revenue for the relevant previous years is really immaterial. [105H] 1.6 The method of computing the income tax payable by the assessee is really irrelevant when did it really receive it in the U.K., Section 145 of Income Tax Act is relied upon by the assessee to say that the method of computation of income tax payable is binding upon the department; on that basis it is immaterial whether it maintains the accounts on cash or mercantile basis or mercantile foundation. [105A] 1.7 The method of calculation adopted by the Department for the relevant tax years is really material. In the instant case, the method adopted by the department for the relevant Assessment years is really crucial. In the case of a non resident assessee like the petitioner clause (a) of sub section (2) of Section 5 has no application whatsoever and that Section 5(1)(b) applies to it irrespective of whether it maintains their accounts on cash. [105B] 1.8 The method of calculating the income tax paid by the assessee by way of royalty and making an entry to that effect in its own books at Coventry is really irrelevant, and that it was immaterial when did not actually receive it, but the assessee firm was a debtor in respect of that amount and unless the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt, clause (a), cannot apply.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the statement of the approver was not corroborated in material particulars and qua the appellant. HELD : (i) The statement of the appellant was not corroborated by the approver 's story because the knife was got prepared by accused No. 1 and hi, motive to commit the murder because of the suspicion he had about his wife having a liaison with the deceased. The time gap between the preparation of the knife and murder is great and it is possible in such circumstances that the appellant might have cemented and not proceeded with the commission of the offence. [534 B] (ii) The evidence of the approver and the testimony of the approver were sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of the first accused upon which the conviction was based. [535 C] (iii) The evidence on record showed that the appellant was telling a story which in its general outline was true, and it was easy for him to work into the story matter which is untrue. [536 E] (iv) The evidence showed that the approver 'Shanker 's evidence was sufficiently corroborated for his conviction. [537 F] (v) The evidence in the present case showed that the witness was telling a version which in its ordinary outline was true and it was impossible for him to have cemented. [538 B] (vi) The evidence was sufficiently corroboration for the conviction.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and section 21 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on July 8, 1961 a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.W. Chaudhury did not challenge the findings of the High Court on questions of fact but the argument was put forward that upon the findings recorded by the High Court the appellant could not be convicted of the charges because he was not a "public servant" within the meaning of section 5(3) of the Act. Held, that the appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21, cl. (12) of section 21, Indian Penal Code and section 2, Prevention of Corruption act. The appellant was an employee in the service of the State Government and he was therefore a "public Servant" within the definition of that section. The appellant could not therefore be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning Of section 21, Penal Code in view of the language of section 81 of the . The appellant was a person performing duties immediately auxiliary to those of the Works Manager who was an officer of the Government and the duties which he performed were immediately auxiliary to that those of the Engineer who was the lead of the office. The appellant, therefore, could not be deemed to have been a public servant under the section. The words "public servant ' include every officer in the Service or pay of a local authority or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of a Government company as defined in s 617 of the .

The appellant was convicted for contravening cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Declaration of Stock Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. He was further convicted for contravening section 3 of the Bombay Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and sentenced under section 3 of that Act to rigorous imprisonment of six months and to fine of Rs, He was also convicted for contravening sections 3 and 4 of the Maharashtra Prevention of Food adulteration Act, 1954. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant in respect of contravention of cl. 3. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The order of the High Court maintaining the order of forfeiture is not legally valid because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to. the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. [274E] (ii) The rule is contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the Defence of India Act provides that "the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder or any order made under any such rule shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act or in any instrument having effect by virtue of any enactment other then this Act. [275E] (iii) The rule was contrary to an established practice of law. The rule is not contrary to an earlier existing act. The rule was not contrary to the law contained under section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, but it lays down that "the provision of this Act shall have effect effect notwithstanding anything contained in any law other than this". The rule is therefore contrary to an old act. [275F] (iv) The rule does not matter that section 43 of Defence of India Rules provides that "The provisions of this section shall have effect " notwithstanding anything inconsistent with therewith contained in this Act or, in any instrument, having effect by way of any enactment, other than this." The rule is inconsistent with an existing act. [276F] (v) The rule cannot be challenged in a court of law.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge, Allahabad, for the murder of one Hari Singh. The Sessions Judge acquitted the appellant. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the only inference which arises from the fact that violet gave the particular shout was that by so doing, she intended to facilitate the murder of Kunwar Singh, Section 107 of the Penal Code which defines abetment provides to the extent material that a person abets the doing of a thing who "Intentionally aides, by any act or illegal omission, the doing of that thing. " Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The court which acquitted the appellant was justifiably influenced by the consideration that though at the earliest stage he had asked that an identification parade be held, the demand was, opposed by the prosecution and the parade was there fore not held, that by so do, he intended to facilitate murder of Kunwar singh. [219D] 2. The court below was not impressed by his evidence. [220C] 3. The circumstance that Shri Ram had voluntarily accepted the risk of being identified, in a parade but was denied that opportunity was an important point in his favour. [221D] 4. The circumstance of Shri Ram was undoubtedly true and was not sufficient to sustain the conviction of Shri Ram. [222D] 5. The circumstance, that Shri Ram was a party to the murderous design, was real and valuable. The circumstance was that Shri Ram, along with Ram Chandra, had moved an application before the Additional District Magistrate (Judicial) who was conducting the committal proceedings that he was not known to the witnesses and therefore he should be put up for being identified in an identification parade. The circumstance did not justify the inference that he was a party in the murderous plan.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34, of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted accused 2 under section 302, read with section 149, and convicted him under section 302. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The conviction of accused 2 under s. 302 read with s. 34, of Indian Penal Code, though the trial court or even the High Court in appeal may be able to come to the conclusion that the acquittal of some of the persons named in the charge and tried will not necessarily meet displace the charge under section 149 because along with the two or three persons convicted were others who composed the unlawful assembly but who have not been identified and so have not been named. [682 C] (ii) The judgment of the High Court cannot be sustained. The judgment of acquittal of accused 2, 3 and 4 is set aside. [690 C] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the acquittal was bad in law. [691 B] (iv) The judgment cannot be sustained on the ground that the said finding was read in the context of the whole judgment. [692 C] (v) The judgment is set aside and the appeal is allowed. [693 C] (vi) The judgment and order of the High court are set aside. The appeal is allowed and the appeal of the appellant is allowed. The appellant is acquitted. [694 D] (vii) The judgment under appeal is set aside, and the appeal filed by the appellant is dismissed.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of iron and steel products, was granted a licence for import of iron and Steel products. The licence holder transferred the same in favour of M/s Metalic Metal Indus tries. The licence was transferred in favour of the petitioner on 11th May, 1983. The licence holders transferred the same to M/s Industrial Cable India Ltd., Rajpura. The licenceholder transferred the same. The petitioner transferred the same, in favour of another company. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the customs authorities were right in taking the view that the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods should be determined according to the law prevalent on the date they were actually removed from the warehouse. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner as such has no fundamental fight to clear the goods imported except in due process of law. [638B] 1.2 The petitioner as a citizen of India has no fundamental right to clear the imported except in accordance with law. [625E] 1.3 The petitioner as an assessee has no fundamental rights to clear the same except in due course of law. The petitioner as well as the Union of India are, therefore, clearly of the opinion that the rate applicable to the import goods should be determin ed according to the laws prevalent on the day they were actually cleared from the warehouse and were in the process of being cleared, but could not be cleared because of the prohibitory orders of the Income Tax Department under section 102 of the . [638G] 1.4 The petitioner as also the Union of lndia are, therefore clearly of the view that Article 32 of the Constitution should not have been resorted to and this application does not lie under Article 32 of t he Constitution. [639G] 1:5 The petitioner as the assessee has no right to clear, the goods imported, except in due procedure of law. In a matter of this nature where liability of a citizen to pay a particular duty depends on interpretation of law and determination of facts and the provision of a particular statute for which elaborate procedure is pre scribed, it cannot conceivably be contended that enforcing of those provisions of the Act would breach fundamental right for the enforcement of which alone Article 32 of of the Constitution is attracted. [640G] 1 :6 The petitioner as appellant has no fundamental fundamental right to seek recourse to Article 32 of th e Constitution. [625G] 1.:6 The petitioner is, therefore, entitled to seek recourse under Article 32. [642C] 1:7 The petitioner as he is a manufacturer of Iron and Steel products, has no fundamental legal right to clear and the petition is not maintainable. [643D] 1:8 The petitioner as it is a manufacturer has no fundamental interest to clear the said goods on payment of duty when the goods crossed the customs barrier and were in process of being removed, but could have been cleared because of prohibitory orders of this Court under section 102. [644D] 1.9 The petitioner as assessee has no legal right to claim recourse to Article 226 of the Constitution. [ 625E] 1:10 The petitioner as citizen of India is, therefore entitled to seek resort to Article 32. The petition is not barred. [645F] 1:11 The petitioner as petitioner has no fundamental or fundamental right to do recourse to Article 136 of the Constitution, and the petition does not lie.

The appellants were the sons of the first appellant who was the son of the first respondent. The first respondent was the son. The first appellant was the son and the second appellant was the brother. The first and the second appellants were the son. In the auction sale the first appellant was declared the highest bidder. The first two appellants were the purchasers of the bungalow. The first one was the son, and the second was the son who was the managing director. The first three appellants were the brothers. The first was the son in law of the first and second appellants. The first four appellants were the joint family. The first appellants was the son but the second was his son. The second appellant was his son and the third was his son who was also the managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration. The first defendant was the son for the first time. The first plaintiff was the son as the second appellant. The first appeal was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the whole estate including the share of the sons had come to an end and consequently in an auction sale the share of sons did not pass to the auction purchaser; that the sale could only be challenged on proof of the debt of the first defendant which was not tainted with immorality or illegality; that the auction sale was under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code under which only " the right, title and interest of the defaulter" could be sold and therefore the right, ownership and interest of only the father could be sold; that the whole property including the share in the sons had been sold in payment of a debt binding on the family and therefore the sale in execution of the payment order could not be challenged as the sons were under a pious obligation under the Hindu law to discharge the debts of their father; that the entire estate including the shares of the sons was sold in execution of a payment order and therefore the sales in execution of payment order could only be questioned on proof of debt of the second defendant which was the right,title and interest of a father alone which could not include the share of other members of the joint family; that the first appellant had been receiving a monthly remuneration from the Bank and the properties were sold in payment to a debt binding upon the family and that therefore the sale could not be questioned as the sons had no interest left; that the appellants were not under a pious duty under the Hindu Law to discharge the debt of their father and therefore the father 's power of disposition over the son 's share had come to a end and consequently the sale in executing the payment order was not valid. Held, that the liability of the sons to discharge the dues of the father which are not tainted with the immorality and illegality is based on the pious obligation of the sons which continues to exist in the lifetime and after the death of the father and which does not come to an effect as a result of partition of the joint Hindu family property. The liability of a father, who is a managing director and whose drawing a salary or remuneration, incurred as a result thereof, continues and consequently there is merely a difference in the mode of enjoyment of the property. The petitioners in these two cases were the guardians of law and who constitute two important segments of society on whom the stability of the country depends. The Committee recommended the transfer of the petitioners in these cases, namely, Ms. Kiran Bedi, D.C.P. (North) and Jinder Singh, section I.P.C. The Committee, after considering the material available on record, recommended the transfer. The Committee also recommended the transfer to the Delhi Administration and its police officers. The Committee submitted its report to the Government. The Government, after considering all the relevant factors, recommended the transfers. The Government also issued a notification dated June 2, 1988, under section 8 B of the Act, providing that the Committee shall send a report recommending suspension of the D.C.,P. Kiran Bedi. The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of the notification dated June 3, 1988, on the ground that the Committee had not considered the material available before it and had not considered it necessary to inquire into the conduct of various police officers and others. The petitioners contended that the Committee should send a report recommended suspension of the petitioners before asking them to be cross examined at the end of the inquiry. The petitioners also contended that the committee should not have in the circumstances of the case directed the filing of a complaint against either of the petitioners for an offence punishable under section 178 I.P.,C. before asking them for getting into the witness box for being cross examined. The petitioners further contended that the report of the Committee was not a valid document and the Committee should have considered the material before it and should not have rejected the same. The petitioners, in these petitions, challenged the validity and legality of the notification on the ground of violation of principles of natural justice. The petitioners submitted that the Committee was in a position to consider the material available and the material available at the end and to take into consideration all the aspects of the case. The petitioners relied on the report of a Committee which was not considered by the Committee. The petitioners urged that the Committee ought not have considered the materials available before it, and should not be asked to get into the witness examined for being cross examine till the end of inquiry. The respondents contended that the procedure adopted by the Committee was discriminatory and violative of principles of Natural Justice. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 8 B. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners have filed these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The orders of the Committee directing the filing of the complaints and the criminal proceedings initiated against the petitioners before the Metropolitan Magistrate pursuant to the complaints filed on behalf of the Committee should be quashed and we accordingly quash the said orders of the committee and also the criminal proceedings. [501G] 2. The orders passed by the Committee directing filing of the complaint and the criminal proceeding initiated against the petitioner before the Metropolitan Magistrates pursuant to the complaint filed on behalf by the Committee should also be quashed and the criminal action initiated against the appellants before the Metropolitan magistrate pursuant to the Complaints filed on behalf Of the Committee should he quashed and we hereby quash the said order of the Committee and also the Criminal proceedings. [525B] 3. The orders directing the filing and filing of the criminal proceedings pursuant to the criminal proceedings against the petitioners after the complaint filed by the Committee shall be quashed and We accordingly quash the aforesaid orders of the High Court and also the civil proceedings. [401C] 4. The Committee should have examined the conduct of the various police officers, and in particular among others Ms. Kiran Mehta, D. C.P. and Jinder singh, section I., Incharge Police Post, Tis Hazari.

The petitioners, who are seven in number, challenged as unconstitutional and ultra vires the provisions of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, the Rajasthan Passengers & Goods Taxation Rules, 1959, and a notification issued under R. 8. A notification issued under r. 8 of the Rajasthan Goods Taxation Rules 1959, was challenged as it was beyond the competence of the State Legislature to enact the Act. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act in the guise of taxing passengers and goods, taxes really the income of the petitioners, or, at any rate, fares and freights, and was therefore unconstitutional. Held, that the Act was not a tax on passengers and goods and the tax was without authority of law. The Act was not one of the modes of payment of tax, but was a tax on passenger and goods, and the tax is still on passengers and passengers, though what it is to be is determined by the amount of fare or freight. The tax is still a tax on goods and goods, though what the amount of the tax is measured by the fares and freight charges. The tax, however, is still on passenger and Goods, though what is to be paid is determining by the amount, of fare or fares. The tax has been still on passengers, and goods, although what it is, to be is exempt, and is not available to the State Legislature. The tax was still on passengers or goods, though it is tobe determined from the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory, even though the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan. The tax thus is still a Tax on passengers and Goods, and the argument that it is not so, is not sound. The tax levied under the Act is still on goods and passengers, although what is to he is determinated by the amount o fare or freight, is a Union subject, and is therefore, unconstitutional.

The appellant was retrenched from the service of the respondent company on the ground that the appellant had not been paid retrenchment compensation. The appellant challenged the award in this Court. The question was whether the workmen who were retrenched were entitled to the relief of reinstatement. The Labour Court by its award directed that all the workmen shall be reinstated in service from 1st August, 1974 with full back wages, permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The appellant contended that the non availability of raw material or recurrent power shedding and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or a ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to be raised(l. The Labour court by its award held that the retrenchment was not bona fide and that the nonavailability of raw material and recurrent power shedsding and lackof profitability was an essential ingredient for the grant of relief of reinstatement to the extent of full wages or a Part of it ? Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question in controversy which fairly often is raised in this Court is whether the Labour Court in the facts and circumstances of the case was justified in awarding full back wages. Once leave against relief of reinstatement was rejected, the order of the Labour Court holding that retrenchment was invalid and it was motivated and the relief of reinstate must follow, has become final. [569D E] 2. The only limited question is whether the workmen concerned did not have any opportunity of explaining why their services should not be terminated and, therefore, reinstatement was held to be the appropriate relief and Act aside the order of reinstatement. [569E] 3. The only question is whether in appropriate cases the Court may, in the spirit of labour and management being partners in the industry, direct scaling down of back wages with some sacrifice on management 's part too. [569G] 4. The only restricted question is whether it is an exceptional case for departing from the normal rule. [569H] 5. The only only limited question in controversy is whether the termination of service is bad and the relief for reinstatement must follow, have become final. The only point is whether the workman was entitled to the benefit of reinstatement effective from the day on which the workman was deprived of his livehood, and it is wholly undeserved. [569C] 6. The only issue is whether the retrenchment of workmen was invalid for the reasons found by the Labour Court and the workman were 567 entitled to the reliefs of reinstatement effective. [569F] 7. The only relevant question is whether there was any loss caused to the appellant consequent on the refusal of workmen to be paid full back wages and whether the non availability was a mere device or a rule to torment of the workmen by deprive them of their livinghood, the actual reason being the inability of the workmen.

The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge, Mahasu under section 302 Indian Penal Code for committing the murder of his wife Churi. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the confession recorded during the investigation of a case by a second class magistrate not specially empowered was admissible in evidence under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and that the statement recorded during the course of the investigation of the case could not be put in evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: (1) The statement recorded during investigation of a criminal case by a first class magistrate not specifically empowered was admissible under section 164. [14C] (2) The statement was recorded by the magistrate and was signed by the accused. In this case, the evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that the accused was with Churi deceased in the house when she was murdered. The evidence on record established beyond any manner that the police was aware of the murder of Churi deceased before the visit of the accused to the house of Shri Mahajan. [14D] (3) The statement of the accused that he was taken by the rolice to the police post from the bazar cannot be accepted because there was nothing to show that the police were aware of the crime before the visit. The evidence of the accused establishes beyond any doubt that the deceased was recovered after the accused had visited the house of the accused. The evidence also establishes beyond any reasonable doubt that the relations of the accused with the deceased, ts would be shown hereafter. were strained would, in the absence of any cogent explanation by him, point to his guilt. [14E F] (4) The statement made by the accused that the accused had gone to see film show at Kotkhai, which had been arranged by the Publicity Department, according to Head Constable Bhag Singh PW, lasted from 7 to 8 30 p.m. while the intimation which was given by Mangat Ram PW 10 to the police regarding a murderer having come to the residence of Shri Mahajan was entered in the daily diary at 10.50 p.m., cannot be accepted. [14G H] (5) The statement given by the accused to a police officer cannot be accepted as evidence under section 162 of the Code. [14H] (6) The statement is recorded by the Magistrate and is signed by the complainant. The accused would have also in that event gone and made a report to the police. The version of the accused, that he was taking by the rosters to the police Post from the bazaar cannot be accepted since there is nothing to show, that the police knew of the murder. Had Joginder been the son of the accused and the fact that the relations between the accused with deceased, tS would be shown hereinafter. were strained will, in the light of the evidence on the record, establish beyond any manner, of doubt that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with him without the child. [14A B] (7) The statement, therefore, cannot be accepted, because there is nothing on record to show that any police was aware that the murder of the deceased was committed during his absence. Had Joginder was the son of accused, the accused would have had a natural affection for the child and it is difficult to believe that he would had insisted upon Churu staying with him with without the child, and it is impossible to believe that she would have insisted on Churi stayingwith him without the son.
