The appellant No. 1 is a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil) having secured 69.96% marks in the qualifying examination thus in all 99.46 marks out of 150.23 marks out of 100.23 marks in the competitive examination thus in both the appellants were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3 were excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court. The Tribunal by its order dated 24th May, 1990 dismissed the petition and the appellants aggrieved against the aforesaid decision have approached this Court by grant of special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The selection was made according to the rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. However, the Rules are clearly in violation of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C.R., 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State of Punjab & Ors., J.T. On a direction given by this Court on 4th September, 1991 the record of the marks awarded to the selected candidates it is clear that a large number of candidates have been selected though they had secured very high marks in the viva voce out of 50 marks kept for this purpose. Thus it is an admitted position that if the marks for interview were kept even at 15% of the total marks, the appellants before us were bound to be selected and a large number Of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appellants, before us were found suitable in all other respects according to the Rules. [418C D] 1.2 The selection was thus made according to rules of 1973. [419D] 1.3 The selection was therefore made according to law and practice. [420F] 1.4 The selection was accordingly made according to Rules of 1973 and the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [421F] 1:5 The selection was not made according to any rules of 1973 or this practice is consistently followed for last 17 years. [422F] 1 :6 The selection was also made according to rule of 1973 and it was consistently followed for this last 17 years, and there is nothing to show that any malafide was in the matter or of the impugned selection. [423F] 1.:7 The selection was done according to the procedure laid down by this Court in the above referred cases and in case the marks for vivavoce were kept even in 15% of total marks, both the appellants before this Court were bound to get selected and a small number of selected candidates would had gone much lower. In view of the fact that the result of the impugned appointments was declared in 1987 and the selected candidates have already joined the posts, the appellants in the present case were bound to have been selected on the basis of marks secured by them in interview, calculated on the basis Of converting the same to 15% of their total marks.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court, on reference, held that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge of conspiracy against the appellants. The High court, however, held that there was direct evidence of the prosecution and the prosecution had not established the complicity of Sadanand in the murder of the Collector. The High, however, acquitted the appellants. Hence the appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. In dealing with a case against an accused person, the Court cannot start with the con fession of a co co accused person; it must begin with other evidence adduced by the prosecution and after it has formed its opinion with regard to the quality and effect of the said evidence, then it is permissible to turn to the confession in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the said other evidence. [457C D] 2. The confession may be regarded as evidence in that generic sense because of the provisions of section 30, the fact remains that it is not evidence as defined by section 3 of the Act. The result, therefore, is that in dealing with a criminal case against an an accused person the Court cannot commence with the con tention of a coaccused person; it should begin with other other evidence adduced in by the prosecution, and after it had formed its opinionwith regard to the Quality and effect of such evidence, then the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [458D] 3. The confession is not substantive in evidence against other accused persons in that trial. In the instant case, Sadanand had been called and he had also confessed to his guilt. The prosecution has further led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadanand at the jail, enforcement of rules became slack and there was a regular flow of food from outside. This type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav, being a follower, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that she was bribing the jail officials for meeting Sadanand and he had confessed to his innocence. [459C D] 4. The prosecution had further led evidence in the case to show that before the arrival of the Sadanand at his jail, enforcement was slack and the fact of that they were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. [460E] 5. The confession made by a co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence. [413D] 6. The confession, of a co coaccused is not substantive piece of evidence against other coaccused persons in the said trial. In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law.

The appellants were employed in the same company. The company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The company had been paying the highest wages in the comparable concerns revised them. The company made comparison with concerns which were not comparable. The Tribunal took into account comparable concerns in the same industry and provided wage scales on the same lines so that, so far as manufacturing concerns in the present appeals are concerned, there will be equality in the matter of competition. The Tribunal did not consider the total effect of the increase it was granting in basic wage and dearness allowance together as it should have done, for the purpose of finding out whether the total pay packet in the appellants ' concerns can bear comparison with the total wage packet of the concerns with which the Tribunal had compared the appellants ' concern. The Tribunal, however, took into account the trend in that region and in fixing the same scale of dearness allowance for factory workmen, and fixed the same rates of dearness allowance. The Tribunal also took into account other factors in the matter. The Tribunal held that the Tribunal had not considered the total effect Of the increase it had granted in basic wage, and dearness allowance and that had made comparison with the concerns which were found not comparable. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal should have taken into account comparable industries in the same region and provided wage scale on the same line so that, while doing so, the Tribunal must have followed this pattern. Held, that the Tribunal has not merely considered what the wages for these categories in comparable concerns are, though it appears that some exemplars were filed before it but the way in which the Tribunal has dealt with the matter shows that it paid scant regard to the exemplars filed before it and did not care to make the comparison for factory workmen in the same way in which it had made comparison for factory employees in the same manner in which it has made comparison for clerical and subordinate staff. The Tribunal has not specifically considered what the wage for these categories is on the basis of the scales of wages and dearness allowance fixed by it as it should has done; but considering that wage scales fixed are less than the highest in the comparable industries though more than the lowest, it cannot be said that the total wage value fixed is abnormal or so disproportionate as compared to the total wage packets in other comparable concerns as to call for any interference with adjustments.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa, filed a suit for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof free from encumbrances and for placing the mortgaged property in his name. The trial Court held that the Rajinama executed by Shiddappa did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property, that the plaintiffs were agriculturists, that they were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking accounts the mortgages had redeemed themselves. The High Court having refused to grant leave to appeal to this Court, the mortgagees defendants 1 to 4 applied to and obtained from this Court special leave to appeal against the decision of the High Court in so far as it upheld the rejection of their claims to Annappa 's half share in the mortgaged properties. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The Rajinama and the Kabuliyat taken together evidenced a transfer of title from the mortgagors to the mortgagees and, therefore, operated to extinguish the equity of redemption not only of Shiddappa but also of Annappa. [775 E] (2) The Raj inama did not purport to file, the same on behalf of Annaappa nor had he any right to do so. [776 B] (3) The Rajama was not a complete relinquishment of his interest, but it was a complete relinquishment. [778 E] (4) The Rajasama was not the registered occupant, and the Rajinma was binding on his brother Annappa, and in this view of the matter he was binding on the brother Annaappa. [782 E] (5) The Rajma was not the sole registered occupant, but was a mere manager and karta of the joint family and that in the matter of passing the Rajinamama he had acted in that capacity and, therefore the Rajinna was binding on her brother Annappala. [768 C] (6) The Rajaniama was not an absolute relinquishment of his rights, but was an absolute relinquishment.

The respondent, a dealer in carbon paper, was assessed to sales tax at the point and at the rate of 6 paise per rupee i.e. 6 paise per rupees. The Sales Tax Officer, (Section IV), Kanpur, did not accede to the conten tions of the respondent and holding that carbon paper did not lose its character as paper even after going through certain chemical processes and that ribbon was a part of the typewriter. The respondent, however, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% and ribbon at 10%. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the levy. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that carbon paper does not lose its characteristics as paper even though after being subjected to chemical processes and the ribbon was not an accessory but an essen tial part of the printing machine. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The word 'paper ' in the common parlance means paper which is used for printing, writing or packing pur poses. [838B] (2) The word "paper" in the common dictionary means paper which a person conversant with the sub ject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. [839F] (3) The word `paper ' in common parlance means a sub stance which is used in bearing, writing or printing, or for packing, or for drawing on, or for decorating, or cover ing the walls. [840F] (4) The word is understood as meaning a sub stance, which is used as aviation petrol. [841F] (5) The word, 'paper ' is understood as a sub stance. [842F] (6) The word has not been defined either in the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 or the Rules, and as such, it has to be given the meaning which it has in 'ordinary parlance.

The appellant Mills was a sugar mill at Amroha. The respondents 1 to 4 were employed by the appellant Mills at the Sugar Mills at Amroha. On February 2, 1955, the General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents 1 to 3 from service on the ground that the management had no right to transfer the respondents 1, to 4 to the new mill. The appellant Mills challenged the order of the management before the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the management was within its rights and that as the respondents 1 and 4 had disobeyed the order of transfer and thus they were guilty of misconduct under Standing Order No. " " Held, that the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside the finding of the State Industrial Tribunal as it did not give rise to any substantial question of law within the meaning of section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The question raised was one of law, namely, whether the appellant had the right to transfer his employees from one concern to another of his in the circumstances of the case. The question was one of fact and was not one of law. The question of law involved between the parties and that raised also an important principle governing the right of an employer to transfer his employee from one concern. The question whether the appellant was the right to be transferred from one concern was really to make a new contract between them. The question that arose was one of Law, namely, the question whether the transfer from one concern could be transferred to another concern stared by him subsequent to the date of the employment. The question arose was one more question of law.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of medical and other allied products. The appellant company was a factory engaged in the manufacturing of medical and allied products. It was established in 1948. Chapter V A was inserted by section 20 of the . The provisions of the Chapter, however, have ceased to have effect on and from July l, 1973. Chapter VA was inserted by the section 20 of Act 53 of 1951. The provisions of Chapter V A were in force. Chapter V B was inserted by Act 53 of 1950. The provisions were repealed by Act 53 Of 1951. Chapter VB was inserted by Section 20 of Act No. 53 of 1951 which provided for the payment by the principal employer of a special contribution which shall be in lieu of the employer 's contribution payable under Chapter IV in the case of factories or establishments situated in areas in which the provisions of both Chapters IV and V were in force, and the payment of contribution for that purpose. The appellant 's contention was that the contribution payable under section 5 of the Act was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The appellant contended that the contribution paid under Chapter V A is a fee and it is not capable of any controversy that services and benefits are indeed meant to be and are bound to be conferred on the employees and through them on the employer, in due course, when the scheme becomes fully operative in all areas. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The contribution payable under the Act constitutes only a fee and not a tax or a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. [1088G] (2) The contribution under the Act constitute only a fee. [1087C] (3) The Government cannot go on levying employers ' contribution under section 5. When the whole Act is brought into force in the whole of India, it would not be necessary to retain this Chapter. [1090D] (4) The contribution goes to a fund known as the Employees ' State Insurance Fund which is to be utilised for the benefits to be given to the employees under the Act. the cost of these benefits will` not be met from the general revenues of the state, but will be borne entirely from the aforesaid fund only. the employers ' contribution to the fund constituted only a fee, and not a fee. The Government cannot pick out the word "tax" in section 5. [1091F] (5) The contribution is not a fee and is not a tax. [1092G] (6) The contribution paid under the Act is a fee. It is not a fees and not a fees. [1093A] (7) The contribution levied under section 5 is a fee, not a fee but a fee. In the vary nature of things, it would have been impossible for the legislature to decide in what areas and in respect of which factories the Employees 'State Insurance Corporation should be established. [1094C] (8) The contribution of the employees under section 5 constitutes only a fees and does not require any constitutional protection. [1095G] (9) The contribution does not go to a fund which is to he utilised for the benefit of the employees. [1096D] (10) The contribution to the Fund constitutes only a tax and not afee.

The petitioners are not regular employees, they do not have any specific case for absorption and regu larisation. The petitioners are being paid their daily wages in spite of their being no work for a long time. The management has throughout denied the claim and alleged that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls and paid in spite of there being no work available for them. The respondents are also running in heavy losses during the last three years and it is not possible to absorb the petitioners immediately as regular workmen. The respondents have also denied the claim of the petitioners and alleged that the petitioners have continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there is no work for them. On the clear findings in this case, this is not the position. This petition must, therefore, fail. In spite of our above conclusion, keeping in view the offer made on behalf of respondent No. 2 in the counter affidavit together with Annexure R V thereto which was reiterated at the heating before us, we direct that all the 63 daily rated workmen including the 54 petitioners herein mentioned in the aforesaid Annexure R V to the counter affidavit be given the benefit of the Voluntary Retirement Scheme framed by respondent No. 1 and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues. Subject to this direction, the special leave petition is dismissed. No costs. P.S.S. Petition dismissed. (1) The petitioners are also not regular employees. They do not have no specific job to do, they are surplus to the establish ment and merely kept on the roll on humanitarian ground. The respondents, therefore, are also running a heavy losses during their last three years.

The appellants purchased the property in question from the respondent, who was the sole proprietor of the estate. The respondent, who had purchased the property mortgaged, purchased it in 1928, and the sale was confirmed by the High Court. The appellants contended that when the sale in execution of the mortgage decree obtained by the National Agency Co. was confined to 2 1/2 as share of the purchaser, the mortgage decree was not the full owner of the property and that the co heirs were estopped from questioning the validity of the mortgage of the entire interest effected by him under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and that in conse quence the sale in favour of the appellants was not the sole proprietor or owner of the Azamabad Tea Estate and that the property in execution of that decree was not tile sole proprietor or the owner of the estate and that the suit was not barred by 0. r. 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held, that the proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial Court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on the record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale under exhibit 12(i) were held to be real, the plaintiffs would be entitled in addition to the 8 pies share decreed to them by the High court, to a further 2 as. 13 gondas share belonging to the respondent. The proper order to be passed would be to remand the matter to it for recording a further finding as regards truth of the sale.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for offences under sections 173(4) and 207A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Sessions Judge acquitted the appellant. The High Court, while dealing with the question of prejudice, held that the provisions of sections 173(1) and 207 A(3) of the Code had not been complied with and that the irregularity was curable by reference to section 537 of the Code. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of sections 172(4) & 207A(3) were not complied with, and that the defect was curable. [291 C] (ii) The provisions in section 173(4), were not complied, and that, as a necessary consequence of those omissions, the entire proceedings and the trial were vitiated. [291 D] (iii) The provisions contained in section 173 of the Code were not complied. [291 E] (iv) The provisions were introduced by the amending Act of 1955, in order to simplify the procedure in respect of inquiries leading upto a Sessions trial, and at the same time to safeguard the interests of accused persons by enjoining upon police officers concerned and magistrates before whom such proceedings are brought, to 293 see that all the documents necessary to give the accused persons all the information for the proper conduct of their defence, are furnished. The word "shall" occurring both in sub section (4) of section 173 and sub section (3) of section 207A is not mandatory but only directory, because an omission by a police officer to fully comply with the provisions of section 173, should not be allowed to have such a far reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective. [291 G] (v) The provisions have been introduced by the Amending Act of 1955 in order to safeguard the interest of accused persons, by enjoining on police officers concerned, and magistrates, before whom such committal proceedings are brought to 293 see, that all the information relating to the proper conduct and defence of the accused persons are furnished.

The appellant was the owner of a factory and was running a factory. The respondent Municipality issued a notice under section 153A of the Act requiring the appellant to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in the manner specified in the notice. The appellant contended that the existence of a nuisance of the kind mentioned in section 153A(1) of the Act was a matter for the subjective satisfaction of the respondent Municipality and beyond the scope of his enquiry. Held, that the provisions of section 153A are not attracted to the facts of the case. The provisions of section153A of the , are not attracted in the present case. The appellant could be called upon to comply with the requisition of the respondent municipality involving several lakhs of rupees as expenditure the Special Officer ought to have decided and report whether a nuisance of a kind alleged by the respondent Municipality existed. The appellant rightly contends that the provisions Of section 153A do not require to be decided. The appellant was not entitled to the relief of the petition. The appellant had no right to the relief prayed for. The appellant cannot be called uponto comply with the requisitions of the respondent. The appellant has no right to a relief prayed for in the petition. Held, further, that the Special Officer was bound to enquire into the matter and make its report both as to the existence of the nuisance and the direction as to the manner in which the effluent should be discharged. The appellant should be given an opportunity to meet the objections. The appellant is entitled to the protection of the Act.

The appellant was found in possession of railway stores which by the definition of section does not include all articles which are 'the property of a railway administration but only those which are used or intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. The appellant was convicted under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The trial court acquitted the appellant. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution must prove that the articles were being actually used or were intended to be use for the construction or operation of a railway and that the goods were in a serviceable condition. HELD: (i) The prosecution must prove the existence of a particular railway administration. In most cases the burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some, peculiarity of the goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Some evidence will have to be led to the effect that the goods of the kind were being actually use by a railway administration and that the articles belonged to any of the railways in India. [189 B] (ii) The prosecution has to prove that the goods belonged to any particular railway administration but which has been rejected or rejected for further use would be outside the definition of railway stores. In most case the burden of proving that the goods belong to any particular Railway administration it has to establish that the articles belong to a particular railway. [189 C] (iii) The prosecution is not called upon to prove that articles belonging to a particular Railway administration were the property of a Railway administration but they were used or were meant to be used for the construction, maintenance or maintenance of the railway. [190 C] (iv) The prosecution cannot prove that the items mentioned in his report were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act. [190 E] (v) The prosecution was not called upon not to prove that they belonged to any other railway administration. It was only when the burden in respect of this is discharged by the prosecution that the onus shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his possession of the same. [190 G] (vi) The prosecution could not prove that the article belonged to any specific railway administration. [190 D] (vii) The prosecution had to establish that there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. It was not called to prove that these articles belonged to a particular railways. It was merely when the burden of evidence in this respect is discharged by leading testimony about the identifying mark on the goods that the prosecution can be successfully launched against a person in unlawful possession thereof. [190 F] (viii) The prosecution should also prove that the incriminating articles belonging to the particular railway administration were the properties of a railway Administration. [190 B] (ix) The prosecution can also prove that these were railway stores in India. The prosecution must also prove that there was caused for reasonable suspicion.

The appellants were the tenants of the demised shop in Jaipur. The appellants filed a suit for ejectment of the appellants from the demised shop on the premise that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. Therein the definition of 'Tenant ' was amended by Section 3(ii) of the Amendment Act introducing to Section 3 Clause (vii) thus: "(vii) "tenant" means (a) The person by whom or on whose account or behalf rent is, or, but for a contract express or implied, would be payable for any premises to his landlord including the person who is continuing in its possession after the termi nation of his tenancy otherwise than by a decree for evic tion passed under the provisions of this Act; and (b) In the event of death of the person as is referred to in sub clause (a), his surviving spouse, son, daughter and other heir in accordance with the personal law applica ble to him who had been, in the case of premises leased out for residential purposes, ordinarily residing and in the case o f premises leased out to for commercial or business purposes, ordinarily resides and in the Case of premises leased to for residential purposes ordinarily residing and In the event o f death of the persons as is referred t o in sub clause(a), his remaining spouse, son and other heir, in accordance with t he personal law applic ation to him who has been, in, the case of residential premises to limit the rights of the heirs in the manner and to the extent provided in Sec tion 2(1) (iii). The appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in the lease hold right in the demised premises governed by the Act subject to the rights and limitations prescribed under the Act and also subject to the provisions of the Act. The appellants succeeded in September, 1966 to the estate of the tenant without any hiatus and restriction on the heritable interest of the heirs of the tenant. The appellants continued to remain in possession as on the date of the suit as statutory tenants. The appellants, by virtue of intestate succession, were entitled to remain in occupation even after determination of the contractual tenancy and no order or decree for eviction will be passed against a tenant unless any ground which entitles the landlord to get an order or decree of eviction is established. The appellants by virtue of testamentary succession under the Act, continued to remain the tenant without no hiatus, restriction on the transferable interest in the leased premises held by the tenant. They continued to remain In possession as on date of the decree as statutory tenants and continued to do the business till date of the death of their tenant without any riatus and restrictions on the heritable right held by the tenants. The heirs of the tenants were entitled to enjoy the protection of the Act, and also subject t he rights in favour of the respond ent created under section 13(1)(a) to (k) and other provi sions of the Act to inherit the status and position of the statutory tenant on his death, the LegislatUre which has created this right has thought it fit in the case. The appellants ' claim for possession was resisted by the respondent on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court reversed the decree of the trial court. Hence this appeal by the appellants. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Amending Act does not apply to the facts of the case and does not have the effect of divesting their vested rights in the lease held by the tenancy.

The appellant Board was willing to extend that scheme to all the workers except the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident Fund Scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Funds Act. The employees also contended that the services of the workmen of the appellant Board are liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not he covered by the same scheme under the Act and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. The workmen also contended that all workmen who are on Deputation and those to whose services the Employees Provident fund Act applies, should have the similar benefits and similar benefits. The workmen contended that the employees of the Board are liable only to pay gratuity and provident fund. The workmen further contended that the State Government is the financier of the Board which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4 per cent per annum. The workmen asserted that all workmen are entitled to the benefits of the Contributory Provident Fund scheme and that therefore the Board should extend the benefits of both the schemes. The workmen denied the claim and claimed that all the workmen of Board should have been given the same and identical benefits and that the same should be taken into consideration while deciding matters regarding benefits to be made available to its employees. The Industrial Tribunal held that the employees are liable to pay gratuity, provident fund and gratuity. The High Court held that the Board was not the financier and that therefore it would bring about serious injustice if they are deprived of their benefits under the Act, and such anomalies would be removed by giving the benefits under the both the schemes which are available in the following order, namely: (i) interest on bonds not guaranteed under section 66; (ii) interest on loans advanced to the Board under section 64 including arrears of such interest: (iii) interest on gratuity and provident funds is expense to be met by an employer like any other expense including wages and if the financial position shows that the burden of provident fund and pension does not result in loss to the employer that burden will have to be borne by the employer like the burden of wage structure in the interest of social justice. The High court held that the State was the financier, and that therefore, the Board should be extended the benefits of Contributory Provident Fund to all workmen other than those who are covered by the Act. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Board makes subventions to the Board for the purposes of the Act. Section 59 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948 provides that as far as practicable and after taking credit for any subventions from the State Government the Board shall carry on its operations so as not to incur a loss. Under section 66 the State Government may guarantee the payment of principal and interest of any loan proposed to be raised by the Board. Under section 67 after meeting its operating maintenance and management expenses and after provision has been made for the payment of taxes on its income and profits the revenues of the Board have to be distributed as far as they are available in that year. Under section 68 the State Government shall guarantee the payment to the Board. [63B C] 2. The contribution to the depreciation reserve is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserves. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the Board. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [63E F] 3. The contribution of the depreciation reserve was a statutory obligation.

The respondent wife filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for maintenance. The Magistrate dismissed the application filed by the respondent wife for maintenance. In revision, the High Court held that the husband having been found to be impotent, the order of the Magistrate was not a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with her husband and hence she was entitled to the grant of maintenance. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the husband had been impotent and was entitled to maintenance if he refused to live with the husband merely because her husband was impotent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The decisions referred to above in the judgment taking a contrary view must be held to be no longer good law and are hereby overruled. [707E] 1.2 The decisions referred by the High Court are not good law and they are hereby overruled [707B] 1.3 The decisions referred in the judgment in Arunachala Anandayammal vs Babu Lal Dixit, J. sounded a very pragmatic and note on this aspect of the matter and in this connection pointing out the scope of the Amendment of 1949 observed thus: "The decisions referred to in the judgment are not good legal and are hereby set aside. [708C] 1.4 The decisions referred tO have been correctly held to be not good law. [709D] 1.5 The decisions referred at the instance of the appellant in the judgment take a contrary view. [710E] 1:6 The decisions referred are not good Law and are hereby quashed. [711G] 1:7 The decisions referred above in the judgments taking a contrary decision must be held not to be good law and were hereby overruled.

The plaintiff was the owner of the suit property. The defendants were the Union of India and the State of Gujarat. The State of Saurashtra was recognised by the Union of Indian and the State Government. The State Government of Saurashtra recognised the aforesaid Resolutions dated 19th January, 1948 and 29th February, 1948. The State was then known as the State of Saurashtra. The State had recognised the ownership of the suit land and the structures vested in the Defence Ministry. The State government of Saurashtra recognised this Resolution and the State government recognised the said Resolutions. The State issued a Notification under section 3 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, on the basis of the Resolution No. 77 dated 29th February 1948. The plaintiff filed a suit for declaration of its title and for possession of the suit properties described in the plaint. The defendants claimed that the suit property was vested in the State Government on 7th July, 1952 and that the possession was handed over by the Union Government to the State Government only on 7th August, 1952 for use. The defendants denied title to the plaintiff. The Trial Court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the plaintiff had not shown possession of the property within 12 years prior to 3rd March, 1964 when the suit was filed, and that the suit was also liable to be dismissed as barred by limitation. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the vesting that wassuant to the Resolution 37 dated 19th February,1948 and Resolution 77 dated 29.2. 1948 vested in the plaintiff the land of the Parade Ground or the lands and buildings known as Rasala Lines. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Resolution No. 37 dated 19.1. 1948 was only a right or an authorisa tion to sell the land as representing the Government but not a vesting of the title itself in the Municipality. [225B] 2. The Resolution was only a legal document to show that physical possession was with the defendant but also there could not be any legal possession with the plaintiff as the title to the land was not vested in them. [225F] 3. The Resolution did not create any right or title in the suit property and the defendants had denied title of the plaintiff. [225G] 4. The Resolution had no force in the case of the plaintiff for the Parade Ground and the land in Rasala Lines or Lancer quarters it was necessary for the Court to give a finding on title of the defendant even if the defendants in possession had not pleaded adverse possession. [225A] 5. The Resolution of the State Government dated 6th May, 1952 was only a statutory document to show the title of the Municipality for the Parade ground and the land was vested and is in the possession of the Government of India. The Resolution clearly showed that possession of the land was also taken by the Government of Saurashtra. [225D] 6. The Resolution dated 19th Janu, 1948 was only an enabling document to show title of the municipality.

The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Government and was performing the duty of a metal examiner known as Chaser in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was, therefore, a public servant within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant was, therefore an officer within the meaning Of section 21(8) of the Act. The appellant, however, was not an officer of the Government. The appellant 's contention was that he was not an "officer" within the meaning o section 21(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held, that an officer in a service or pay or of the Government performing as such a public duty entrusted to him by the Government and is therefore an "officer " within the meaning ofs. 21(9), Indian Penal Code and being such public servant be fell within the definition of a public servant contained in section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act II of 1947. The appellant could not be a public servant for the purposes of the Act and could not be convicted of the offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention Of Corruption Act II Of 1947. The question for consideration before the learned Judges of the Lahore High Court was whether a person was an officer within section 21( 9) of the , Indian Penal Code, and being such a public servant be could be a public servants for the purposes Of the Act. Held, further, that an "officer in the service of or pay of Government" within the terms of section 21 of the Indian Indian Penal Code is one who is appointed to some office for the performance of some pulice duty. The true test, therefore, in order to determine whether a person is an officer of Government, is: (1) whether he is in the service, or pay of that Government, and (2) whether he was entrusted with the performance of any public duty.

The Respondent along with one Gora Lal and Sat Pal, had been granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69. The Excise and Taxation Department of the State of Punjab, Patiala Division, issued a notification under section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, for the sale of the said property. The auction in respect of the said share of the Respondent in the said property was notified for June 14,1977. The auction was notified for July 14,1977, but the Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala C. in Suit No. The contention of the Respondent was that a part of the building standing on the said plot of land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other residential house and, therefore, his said half share was exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of section 60 of Code of Civil procedure, 1908. The trial court decreed the suit but the First Appellate Court reversed the decree and dismissed the suit so far it related to the portion in which the liquor shop was situated. The Respondent then filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the second appeal holding that the portion of the building used for residence was exempt from the attachment and sale under clause (c) of proviso to sub s (1) Of section 60 of CPC. The High court also held that the portion in the said building used for residential purpose was exempt from sale under clause(ccc) Of the proviso to section 60 of Act, 1908. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Appellant that the property attached and notified for sale was exempt from attached and sale under cl. (ccc). of the proviso, while that portion in which liquor shop was situate was liable to be attached and sold in execution of a decree. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The attachment levied on, and the auction sale notified in respect of, the Respondent 's half share in the said premises were not in execution of any decree of a civil court but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorized to adopt proceedings under the said Act for recovery of revenue due to the State. [848C D] 2. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions of the said Act and the sale which was notified was also under the provisions Of the said Act. The attachment was levied under section 60, of the Code, and the sale was notified also under the provision of the said act. The attachment levying on, and auction sale notified under section 60 was also under section 61 of the Code. The attachment imposed on, and and the auction sales notified in respect thereof were also under the Provisions of the said section. [849E F] 3. The attachment under section 60 is levied under the provision, of the said Code, and, the sale which is notified is also under the said provisions of the Act. [847C D] 4. The attachment is levied under section 61 and the sale is notified under the provisions. The attachment levy levied on, or the auction sale declared under section 61 is also under section 62 of the Code and the sale has been notified also under section 63 of the Code for recovery of Revenue due to the state. [846E F] 5. The attachment, in a question, was levied under Section 61 and the sales which were notified were also under section 65 of the Code Act.

The respondent, a tenant of a house in the village of the deceased, was assessed to duty under the provisions of the Andhra Pradesh Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment on the ground that the lands in the original assessment had been undervalued in view of the glaring enhanced compensation awarded by the Civil Court, and the High Court 's decision upholding the issuance of such notice on the wrong basis was liable to be set aside. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the respondent had issued the notice on the erroneous assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to duty because the lands in question had been undervalued and required to be properly valued as at the date of the death but the basis on which it was issued was clearly unsustainable in law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court has attempted to distinguish the above decision by stating that in the instant case the res respondent had merely accepted the value of the acquired lands as determined by the Civil court and the accountable person had no objection to this course and, therefore, the respondent himself did not estimate the market value of the lands on the date of death of Rashid and as such it was not a case of mistake apparent from the record and as such the impugned notice was liable tobe quashed. [330B C] 2. The High 'Court has attempted to distinguished the above decision on the ground of mistake apparent on the record and, therefore the enhanced compensation was sought to be included in the principal value of the estate by undertaking the rectification proceedings. [330D] 3. The High, Court has attempted to distinguishing the above decision from the decision by stating, that in the present case the res Respondent had merely accepted that value of the land as determined by him in his award and the accountable persons had no objection, to this course. [330F] 4. The High Courts have attempted to distinguish this decision by stating in the instant ease that in the reassessment which was made pursuant to the impugned notice, the quantum of extra compensation decreed by the Civil Judge was included in the assessment and brought to duty. This was clearly erroneous in view of section 73A of the Act and, therefore such property had escaped assessment to duty. [330G] 5. The High courts have attempted to distinguished this decision by saying that in the first place the said property, namely, the enhanced compensation awarded was not in existence 1. at the date when the original assessment was made, it was the duty of the respondent, after scrutinising the Account filed and examining the materials produced before them, to value the estate of the deceased properly under s.36 of the Act. [330H] 6. The High. Court has attempted, to distinguish the said decision by stating the that in the second place the said properties had been undervalued. It cannot be disputed that when the original assessments were made it was the obligation of the respondent to resort to provisions of section 59 and proceed to make reassessment but such reassessment has to be done within the period of three years from the date of original assessment under section 73A. [330C] 7. The High "Court has attempted, therefore, to distinguish it by stating that the valuation for those lands adopted on the earlier occasion which was on the basis of compensation awarded by a Special Deputy Collector did not represent their correct market value which was clear from the glaring enhanced amount that was awarded by the Land Reference and, therefore it was not the case of change of opinion on his part as regards the correct valuation of the lands. [330E] 8.

The appellant was elected as a Director of the Bank from the Brehmapuri Agricultral Sales and Purchase Society. On 8.1.1987, the District Deputy Registrar of the Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur, issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors of the Bank as per the provisions of section 73FF(1) and directed him to remain present on 2.2.1987 at 11.67 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office. The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986, and he was elected on 18.8.1986 as one of the Directors of the bank from the Bre warepuri Agricultular Sales and Purchase Societies. On 8th January 1987, the District Assistant Registrar of the Cooperation Societies, Chandrapur issued a notice under section 78 (1) of Act to the appellant to show cause as to why his election should not be declared as per the provision of section 73F of the Act. The appellant 's revision petition against the order of the Assistant Registrar removing the appellant from the Committee of Directors was dismissed on 30.8.89 holding that the appellant was defaulter on 31.1.1986, on 31.3.1986, and he became defaulter under the provisions of Section 73FF(2) of the Act, and rejected the appellant 's contention that section 73FF became applicable from 6.8.86 as per the Government Notification issued on 18.4.1986, i.e. the date when he was declared elected as Director. The appellant challenged the order of removal on the ground that section 73F was applicable from 6th August 1986 as per the Govt. Notification issued on 12.5.1986 and that as he had accepted that he paid the dues on 21.10.1986 when he was elected as Director, he was defaulter under section 73FF of the Act and that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18.8,1986 to 21.10,1986 was extinguished and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. The Divisional Joint Registrar of the cooperative Societies, Nagpur, held that the appellant had already ceased to be a Director and his seat already fell vacant. The appellant preferred an appeal against that order to the Divisional Joint Registrar, who dismissed the appeal holding that the disqualification as defaulter continued after the election of the appellant and section 73FF was not attracted. The appellant then filed a revision petition under section 154 of the Act before the Divisional Joint Commissioner of the Cooperative Society, Nagpur, which was dismissed on 15.2.1988 holding that the provisions of sections 73FF and 73FF(3) of the Bombay Cooperative Societies Act were not attracted.

The respondent was in the service of the State of Maharashtra as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. After his retirement the respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. On the conclusion of the enquiry the State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Bombay. A Division Bench of that Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government 's orders dated December 4,1982 and December 4,82. The State Government ' appeal against the judgment of the High Court was dismissed by the High Court. The State of Maharashtra preferred this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The State 's power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. The State government has power to reduce the amount of Pension payable to a Government servant. [34G H] 2. The reduction of pension by 50 per percent was too harsh and disproportionate to the charges proved against the respondent. The reduction by 50 per percentage was too harsh. The reduction was too harsh to the misconduct proved against the Respondent. [34A] 3. The State should have taken into consideration the fact that the respondent had retired from service and the reduction of pension was disproportionate to the charge proved against the appellant. [34B] 4. The State has power to reduced the amount of gratuity payable to a government servant. [35C] 5. The State is entitled to take into consideration the facts and circumstances of the case.

The appellants were tenants of the premises in question. The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 3(3) of the Act was invalid in law. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the permission was invalid in view of the provisions of section 3(4) read with section 16 of the Act. HELD : (i) The order passed by the District Magistrate granting permission to the landlord to sue his tenant, was invalid in the eye of law. [642 C] (ii) The order of the District Magistrate was not a nullity in law. [613 C] (iii) The order was passed without notice to the tenant. The order was not a mere irregularity or illegality. [643 D] (iv) The order made by the District Collector granting permission to sue his tenants was invalid in that it was passed without issuing notice to the tenants. [644 E] (v) The order granting permission to prosecute the appellants was not a merely irregularity or illegality in the order passed by a District Magistrate. [645 E] (vi) The order in question was passed without hearing the appellants. [646 E] (vii) The order did not amount to a nullity in the eye. [647 A] (viii) The order dated the 5th March, 1955, was passed without giving notice to the appellants. The order did amount to a mere irregularity. [648 B] (ix) The order could not be said to be a nullity in view of section 3 of the Act, because it was passed by a person who was not a District Magistrate, the order in law could not be challenged in a civil court. [649 B] (x) The order by the District Officer granting permission to file a suit against the appellants was a nullity in that it did not amount merely to a irregularity or illegality, and it did not affect the jurisdiction of the civil court. The order passed in violation of the principles of natural justice was a nullity.

The appellant was a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission. He was convicted by the trial court under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that before making this Reference, the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of alleged misbehaviour of Shri Saini. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the President to make a reference to this Court under Article 317(1) is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article provides that the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commission can only be removed from his office on the ground of misbehaviour after the Supreme Court has on inquiry held in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under that behalf under paragraph. [629B C] 2. The power to make a Reference to this Court is not subject, to the condition of precedent that he should first have the fact examined by some another body or authority, except with the leave of this Court. [630D] 3. The power under Article 317 is not subject either to the condition or precedent that he can first have the evidence examined by some others body or authority and, secondly, whether the misconduct is of such a nature as to require his removal from the office of the Member of the Public Service Commission.[629B] 4. The power conferred by Article 317(2) is not limited to determining whether the person concerned is guilty of misbehaviour and whether the misbehaviour is of such nature as to warrant the removal of the person from his office. If a full opportunity is given to the parties to prove and rebut the facts in issue as in a regular trial. it is an idle complaint that the evidence has been examined and found upon by the Supreme Court and not by a court of first instance. The mere fact that the evidence of any particular witness is recorded by the learned Judge will not conclude the issue as regards the admissibility or relevance of that evidence. [631C D] 5. The recording of evidence will be over by September 30, 1983. In case it is not over by that date, the learned Judge may write to the Registrar of the Supreme Court for extension of time. The evidence will be transmitted to the Registrar (Judicial) of this Court immediately after the entire evidence is recorded.

The appellants were the trustees of a public temple. The endowment was a private one. The endowment consisted of two items, namely, (i) a temple, (ii) a temple and (iii) a temple. The appellants claimed that the endowment was a public one. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the endowment had been made by a private person and the deity installed in the temple was purely a family deity having nothing to do with the public. The High court also held that the temple was a public temple and the deity was a public endowment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the endowment did not confer the duty of performing all the work on the members of the public but they chose or selected only a particular person belonging to a particular community which also shows that even if the family was to become extinct, the private nature of the endowment was not to be changed. HELD: (1) The mere fact that members of the community used to come to the temple with out any hindrance also does not necessarily mean that the temple is a public temple, for members of the family or their descendants. [833 E] (2) The mere factum of worship would not determine the nature of the dedication. Some of the extracts of this document which are undisputed, in our opinion, clearly and conclusively show that the endowment is of a public nature. [834 A] (3) Where the origin of the endowment cannot be ascertained, the question whether the user of the temple by members of the Public or of the brotherhood or the Government could only be the members of that community which also showed that even if a document is available to prove the nature and origin of the dedication and the recitals of the document show that the control and management of the temple is retained with the founder or his descendants, and that extensive properties are dedicated for the purpose of the maintenance of the temple belonging to the founder himself, this will be a conclusive proof to show that the dedication was of a public character. [835 B] (4) The mere circumstance that members of a public are allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the members of a particular community who also shows that the worship by the members of his family or their ancestors is as of right that may be a circumstance which may in some cases conclusively establish that the endowment has been of a public type. [836 C] (5) The mere existence of a public endowment does not necessarily imply that the temple itself is a public one, for members or the family. [837 E] (6) The mere mere fact that member of the public are allowed, to worship by themselves would not make any an endowment public if it is proved, that the members or the Government did not make any stipulation for offerings or contributions to be made by members of his community to the temple. [838 A] (7) The mere possibility that members of his public are allowed by themselves would be a conclusive evidence to show that they were allowed to worship in the temple by way of a public trust unless it is established that the members were allowed to worshipping at the shrine of the deity.

The appellant Bank entered into certain contracts and to advance monies to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. For the purpose of carrying out the terms of the said arrangement more effectively and to secure the interest of the attorneys were desirous of appointing the Bharat Bank Ltd., as our lawful attorneys in all matters relating to the receipt of all payments under the contracts made or to be made hereafter and all monies due from us to the attorneys in any account whatever, were due from us. For the execution of the said contract the attorneys had agreed to finance the contracts and to pay the amount thereof and appropriate such receipts towards and repayment of the advances made or to become payable hereafter and all other monies due from the appellant to the attorney. The appellant Bank instituted a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur against Malhotra and Takhatmal asking for a declaration that the appellant was an assignee of the biLl and that Takhatmal had no right to attach it. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that the power of attorney dated July 13, 1946, coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948, amounts to an equitable assignment of the monies due under the bill in favour of the appellant. HELD: (i) The power of attorney coupled with the endorsements on the bill on July 19,1948 created an interest in a specific fund and was irrevocable. [757 E] (ii) The power to attorney coupled with, the endorsement on it created an interest, in a specific Fund and was irrevocable.[757 B] (iii) The power in attorney coupled with endorsement on the bills dated July 19. 1948 created an interest of a specific fund in favour of a borrower and the lender was merely authorised to act as his agent. [758 C] (iv) The power conferred by the power of Attorney coupled with the endorsed endorsement on the Bill dated July 19 1948 created an equitable assignment in favour of 'the borrower 's account and was irrevocable and irrevocable. [779 G] (v) The power under the power of the attorney coupled with a endorsement on the cheque dated July 19 in the bill dated August 19, 1948 created an Interest in a specific manner and was irrevocable; and the endorsement on that cheque was sent to and acknowledged by the military authorities. [779 C] (vi) The power by attorney coupled with an endorsement on the letter dated July 19 and the endorsement of the bill dated September 19 in the letter dated September 19, 1948 was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bill and amounted to an equitable assignmen of the fund by way of security. [779 D] (vii) The power, attorney coupled with its endorsement on the cheques dated July 19 were a clear engagement of by Malhotra to Pay the appellant Bank Out of the monies received under the bills and amounted to a equitable assignment of a specific Fund in favour of appellant. [779 E] (viii) The power conferring the power of power of attorney on the appellant coupled with the words "to present and submit supply bills for sums payable to him under the contracts directly in their own name or in payment of such bills or other amounts and to cash and to receive the amount thereof, and in repayment of the advance made or to or be made hereafter" and amounted to equitable assignment of 'the debts or fund to which the order refers. [779 F] (ix) The power that attorney coupled with his endorsement on the document dated July 19; 1948 created an equity in favour of his client in favour of him. [779 A] (x) The power was of attorney coupled to the endorsement on a bill and was irrevocable, and irrevocable.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd. The said Company had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. But that provident fund was not a recognised one. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's salary as defined in section 17 of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. But on further appeal to the Tribunal, the tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the same was exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3) (ii). The High Court answered that question in the negative and in favour of the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court by certificate. HELD: The meaning of section 17 (3) (i) is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to call into aid any of the rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High Court. [440 C] The meaning of "Profits in lieu of salary" is plain and unequivocal. Hence there was no need to called into aid any rule of construction as is sought to be made by the High court. [446 D] The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though undoubtedly that is an income. [447 E] The receipt by the assessee with which we are concerned is exempt from tax.

The Bihar Act, 1950, was enacted to provide for the regulation of the slaughter of cows and calves of cows and to provide for their regulation and control of the slaughter. The Act was passed to provide for regulation of the use of the slaughter and for matters connected therewith. The Act provided for the regulation and control by the State of Bihar and for matters incidental thereto. The Act also provided for the control of the State of Madhya Pradesh. The Act, however, provided for the prohibition of slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle. The Act further provided for the restriction of the slaughter by the State Legislature in the interest of general public and that the slaughter of buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) as long as they were as milch or draught cattle was also reasonable and valid. The Act however, provided that the slaughter was to be in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Act did not provide for the prohibition on the slaughter of calves of calves and of calves. The Act therefore did not infringe the fundamental rights under article 19(1)(g) of the petitioners. The Act thus violated the fundamental rights of the petitioners under article 19 (1)(g). The petitioners contended that the Act violated the fundamental right under article 19 of the Constitution. Held, that the Act was not constitutionally valid in so far as it prohibits the slaughter of bulls and calves and the ban on the slaughter was valid. The ban on slaughter of calve of calves was not valid. It was not necessary to apply the doctrine of severability and uphold the ban on slaughter. The entire provision banning the slaughter of buffalo, breeding bulls, and working bullocks without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness, it violated the fundamental freedom under article 19. The entire section banning the Slaughter of calves, bulls and working cattle (cattle, and buffalo) has, therefore, to be struck down.

The Company had its registered office in Nagpur in Madhya Bharat. The Company applied for a declaration that the respondent was an 'workman ' as defined for the purpose of the Standing Orders. The Company did not make a declaration under the Standing Orders but only made a declaration that it was an 'employee " within the meaning o the Central Act, and the respondent was not an 'employee. The Company filed a suit for damages for wrongful dismissal. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal the High Court held that the Standing Orders did not apply to the respondent, though he was an employee within the meaning ofs. 2(1) of the local Act, and that the remedy of the respondent was to sue the Company in damages for wrongful dismiss, and that as for amendment of the Standing Order so as to include the respondent and persons in his category, the only remedy open to the respondent was by approaching a recognised union to move in the matter. The High Court also held that the respondent did not fulfil the necessary condition of having his name and ticket number included in the departmental muster, and as the respondent did neither fulfil the necessary conditions of having his names and ticket number mentioned in the departmental roll, he was not an "employee " as defined for that purpose. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The Standing Orders apply to the Respondent and his service has been terminated in accordance with Standing Order No. (e) of Standing Order No, Standing Order No., and the mere fact of employment in the Office, Mains Department, Stores, Power House or Receiving Station of the Company was not enough to make a, 471 person so employed an 'employee" as defined for Standing Orders. [446 B] (2) The Standing Order No,. (e) and Standing Order No.(e) of the Standing order No. (f) of the standing orders do not, however, think that the case of the respondent is in any way influenced by holding that Standing Order No . Even on that construction, the failure of the Company to issue tickets will, in that view of the Standing orders themselves, including the definition clause in Standing Order No.. (e) was an essential characteristic of an employee. Standing Order No , Standing Order No ' Standing Order No ; is not an essential characteristic for an employee. [447 C D] (3) The essential content of the definition of an employee is employment in the office, Mains department, eta., of the Company either at Nagpur or Nagpur or Nagpur, and that of a workman the necessary declaration by the Company which would entitle him to a ticket under Standing Order No(e) of standing Order No. Standing Order. [448 D] (4) The essential object of the definition is employment in a Office, Main, Department, eta. of the Company whether at Nagpur or Wardha, and that is to say, that all 'workmen ' are 'employees ', but all 'workmen are not 'workmen ' for the purpose Of the Standing Orders, and the inclusion of ticket numbers in the departmental musters ' in Standing Orders cannot be an essential characteristic Of an employee. The essential content is employment in an Office, Main Department, eeta., of a Company either at Bombay or Nagpur or Wardha.

The appellant, a company owned controlled and managed by a Government Company, was started in the year 1961 65. No profit was earned at least right up to the year 1966 65 when this Project went into production. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 in respect of the year 1965 631 1966 on the plea that this Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this project went into production, and that no bonus could be granted to this Company in respect of payment of bonus under section 16 of the Act. The Tribunal held that alloy Steel Project could not be treated as a separate establishment because, under the Act, a Company is itself an establishment, so that all units of a Company like Hindustan Steel Ltd. will constitute one establishment. The Tribunal also held that alloys Steel Project could be treated as separate establishments because, under section 3(2) of the Act, the Alloy Steel Plant was a separate unit in respect of each unit and after such consolidation, profit and loss was also worked out for all the establishments together so as to find out the actual profit and loss earned or incurred by the Company itself. The Tribunal further proceededed to consider whether the Alloy steel Project could be held to be an establishment separate from Hindustan Steel Ltd., or it had to be treated as part of the main establishment owned by Hindustan Steel Ltd.. The Tribunal held, that alloy steel Project was a composite establishment in respect Of which separate accounts, separate balance sheets, profit and Loss accounts were maintained and so, no bonus was chargeable to the appellant in respect of payments of bonus under the Payment Of Bonus Act, 1964. The Tribunal, however, held that all theoy Steel Project had to be regarded as a separate unit because, under that Act, a company is itself an "establishment" so that all unit of a Company which has been in existence for a long period and has been even earning profits, so that, no bonus could have been payable until either the Project itself earned profit, or from the fifth accounting year following that year 1964 65, when this Project goes into production. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had erred in holding that merely because Alloy Steel was owned, controlled and managed, controlled and maintained by Hindustan Steel Limited, it had to he treated as a distinct establishment because, in the case of workmen of the Head Office where no separate profit and loss account was worked out and the bonus was paid on the basis of the consolidated profits of all such units. HELD: (1) The Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that simply because Alloy steel was set up bonus was paid to the employees of all the units on the basis that consolidated balance sheet is prepared for the Company in respect Of all its units and after such investigation, profit andloss statements are maintained. [696 B] (2) The Tribunal was right in holding that mere fact that alloy was owned, managed, controlled or managed by Hindustan Steel was not sufficient to hold that merely because alloy Steel was set up, bonus was paid in any year to the employees. [697 C] (3) The Tribunal had gone entirely wrong in finding that merely because the Alloy was owned controlled and maintained in respect of all its units, it had no to be treated to be a separate establishment newly set up in the year 1960 66 in view of the provision contained in section 1, sub section (2) of section 16.

The appellant sugar factory was manufacturing sugar from sugar cane. " The cess is payable by every manufacturer carrying on any industry specified in Schedule I. " The Cess is payable by each person carrying on an industry specified in column 1 of Schedule II. " The Central Govern ment has taken the view that the sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Cess Act. The High Court and the Allahabad High Court have taken the view in favour of the appellant. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The cess is leviable by every person who carries on any specified industries and every local authorities and is calculated as per the basis of Water consumed by such persons or local authority. [501C] 2. The word 'vegetable ' in the context does not attract the botanic meaning. The sugar manufacturing industry do not, therefore, come within Entry 14 of Schedule I of the Cess Act and a fortio ri the manufacture of alcohol from molasses could not be considered to be an industry within Entry 15. [502D] 3. The word "vegetable" in the context did not attract the cess. The sugar industry do not come within Entry No. 15 of Schedule 1 of the Cess Ac tation Act. [503F] 4. The word vegetable in the context do not attract the levy. The sugar manufactured by the appellant could not, therefore. come within Entry 17 of Schedule I. [504F] 5. The word `vegetable product ' means product of or made of or out of vegetable. [505F] 6. The word „vegetable products" means product of, or made of, or out of natural vegetable. [525A] 7. The word “vegetable” in the context in which the word 'vevegetable is used in Entry 15 is generally understood to mean as bringing into existence a new substance and does not mean "to produce some change in a sub stance, however minor in consequence, the change may be. The word is generally understood as bringing into operation a new substance or does not mean ' to produce some change, in a sub stand, however minor, in consequence, a change is not manufacture, and yet every change is not ' manufacture ' and yet every changed is not manufacture.
