The High Court dismissed the revision petition holding that the respondent bona fide required the premises in the premises for carrying on his business as an Advocate and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the practice was not business in the sense of business within the expression 'profession ' and that the practice in the Andhra Pradesh Act was not business. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'business ' in Section 10(2) (a)(iii) of Andhra Pradesh Buildings Act, 1960, is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice of a liberal profession like that of an Advocate or a Doctor which has nothing commercial about it. [14G] 2. The word 'business ' has to be interpreted in the context of the statute in which it occurs and not in the context in other statutory provisions. [14H] 3. The word must be interpreted in its context of the statutes in which it occur and not in a manner alien to the context of other statutes or in a manner hostile to the context in which it occurred and not in context of other statutory provisions.[14H] 4. The word may have when it occurs in other statutory provision. The word "business" in Section 10 (3) (i) is used in the wide sense so that to include any profession. [14A B] 5. The word business ' in Section 2(g) of the Act is used in wide sense so to include the practices of the profession like that in Section 10. [14C D] 6. The word is used in an inclusive sense so as not to include any business. [14D] 7. The word has to be construed in the context to the statute in the context. In Stuchbery & Ors. vs General Accident Fire and Life Assurance Corporation Ltd., ; , referred to.

The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of Rs. 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The respondent filed the suit on 16 May, 1953 against the appellant for the recovery. The appellant denied the allegation and pleaded that the respondent had deposited a sum of Rs.4,00,000 with M/s India Supplies. The respondent denied the allegation. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the use of the word 'deposit by itself occurring either in the roznamcha or in the letter dated 29 September, 1942 written by Ram Ratan Gupta would not be decisive of the question whether it was a case of deposit of the sum of Rs 4,00, 000 by the respondent with the appellant under an agreement that the same would be paid on demand. HELD : (i) The letter further shows that the terms were agreed to by the partners of the firm, namely, the partners of India Supplies and of ale respondent. 4,00.000 would not have sufficed the needs of the appellant who were then unable to pay the dues of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills. Some of the partners of a firm may have made to all or any of them or their moneys which may be in deposit with them and they shall be payable and paid in their usual course. [578 G H] (ii) The letter also shows that the term 'deposit ' by itself occurring both in the roaznamcha or the letter dated 30 September, 1942, written by Ram Rattan Gupta would not cover the advances which either party or their separate firms may have made or their moneys. [578 E] (iii) The letter shows that the words 'deposit ' were agreed to between the parties. The letter further showed that the terms of the award were agreed to and by the partners. The letter also showed that the term was agreed to by both the parties. [578 F] (iv) The letter clearly shows that the agreement was agreed to between both the parties and finally the appellant was not bankers and therefore it was improbable that the respondents who were bankers would deposit with the traders the sum of money immediately. [578 D] (v) The letter showed that the words "deposit ' were intended to be used in the sense that the award in respect of Lakshmi Ratan cotton Mills was intended to cover the advances made to Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mill. The letter shows the terms agreed to by them. [578 A] (vi) The letter stated that the terms had been agreed to by all the parties. It further shows that there were advances which were in the nature of deposit and were not covered by the award.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, dated February 28, 1986, made in exercise of powers vested under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The petitioner made an application to this Court under Article 32 in Writ Petition (Crl) No. 292 of 1986 challenging that order of detention. The petition was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of detention on the ground that the period of parole from May 15, 1986 to February 28, 1987 could not be added to the maximum period of imprison ment of the petitioner for one year as specified in the impugned order of detention passed under sub section (1) of section 3 of the COFEPOSA, and that the period from May 15. 1986 to February28, 1987 could only be added to maximum period ofatorium of the detenu. The petitioner contended that the period for which parole was granted to him could not be add ed to the maximum limit of imprison ment for one year, as specified in paragraph 2 of the writ petition. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the period during which the order of preventive detention was passed could not be included to the maximum term of imprisonment for one year. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu is in custody does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making an order of preventive Detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining authority was aware of the fact that the petitioner was already in custody and yet he was sub jectively satisfied that his order of detention became necessary. [849E F] 2. The fact of that the detenu was in custody when the order was made, yet he was satisfied that his preventive detention was necessary. [820C] 3. The fact, that the detenu has been in custody when he was in custody, does not take the away the jurisdiction and the principle enunciated by the aforesaid decision must apply. [820D] 4. The fact in the present case, there is suffi cient material to show that the detenu had confined his arguments to one point settled the writ petition as senior counsel with the allegations quoted above in paragraph 2. The Court, therefore, was right in holding that the detention order could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority had satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order of detri tion was necessary for put ting him back in jail. [820E] 5. The fact remains that after the order of the detention came to be made the petitioner was in jail for at the most one day. Charge sheet had not been submitted against him in the criminal case and he had been remanded to the judicial custody on the 27th of February, 1986 with the direction to be produced before the Metropolitan Magistrate on the 28th of February. The Court also indicated that it was not a matter of jurisdition but had to be decided on the facts of each case. [820F] 6. The fact is that the detenu, being in custody, was taken into custody. The fact was that the detenu being in custody when his order was made. Yet he was satisfied, that his preventive release was necessary. The Court then referred to the Constitution Bench decision in Rameshwar Shaw 's case (supra) and left it as a matter to be decided in every individual case on its own facts. The Court further indicated that it would not be proper to hold that summons under section 108 of the Customs Act was in existence.

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1950 53. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 22(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, to the assessee under section 34(3) of the Act. The assessee contended that the notice under section 34 was invalid as it did not comply with the requirements of section 34(1)(a) of the Income tax Act. The High Court upheld the contention of the assessee and gave its opinion that the Department ought to have issued a notice within the assessment year, and if no return was made within the time fixed by the notice, the Department should have proceeded under section 23(4) to a 'best judgment ' assessment. The assessee appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The notice under section 24(2) was served, and a return showing an income below the taxable minimum was filed. The return in answer to that notice could be filed under section 24 (1) before assessment, and for this there was no limit of time. [848 B] (ii) The notice was served, but a return showing a nontaxable income was filed. [849 C] (iii) The notice did not contain a "best judgment" assessment. The notice did contain a "reason to believe" assessment. [847 D] (iv) The notice does not contain a definite and definite statement of the facts. The notice does contain a "reasonable return" and the notice does not mention the exact nature of the information. The notice merely mentions the particulars of the income. The notice is not a "best order" assessment. It does not contain the particulars of any particular income. [846 E] (v) The notice merely states that the income is to be assessed on the basis of the return filed. The notice only mentions the particulars. The notice also does not mention that the particulars are to be furnished. The notice simply mentions the particulars and does not mention any particular income in the return. [845 D] (vi) The notice only refers to the particulars. It does mention the particulars. [856 E] (vii) The notice is a "best" assessment. There is, however, the general notice under section 23 (1) of the , which is served, and the return in the case of a person who thought that he had a taxable income and therefore a return showing the income below the tax limit could not be held, on a construction thereof, to be a return under section 24. [857 E] (viii) The notice also did not mention the particulars of income in the returns. The notice was not a " best judgment" assessment and the notice did not mention any specific income in the assessment.

The petitioners in Transfer Case No. 219 of 1988, were appointed as Directors of the nationalised bank. The petitioners in Transfer Petition No. 219/88 and C.M.P. 8572 of 1989 were appointed as directors of the nationalised Bank. The petitioners were appointed as members of the Board of Directors of the Bank. The Central Government by notification dated 23.8.1982 appointed the petitioners as Directors of a correspond ing new bank. The Central Govern ment by notification dated 22.8.1983 appointed the petitioners and the petitioners as directors of a correspond ered bank. The Board of Directors was constituted under the Act. The petitioners challenged the appointment of the petitioners as director of a correspondenc e. The petitioners contended that the Act postulates both election and nomination of members of the board of Directors and the choice between the two modes of appointment is left to the Central Government. The petitioners also contended that the provisions of the Act are ultra vires the Act. Dismissing the Transfer Petition, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The Act, by its very object, speaks of election or nomination and if election are to be construed to be the appropriate mode of choosing the representatives of the employees, appointment by nomination of one person out of the panel furnished by the representative Union of workmen or Association of non workmen, as the case may be, would not be a perfect representation in keeping with the principle of election. The mode of election or nominations must, therefore, be such as would be ideally suitable and appropriate to the banking industry and the choice of the mode is generally a matter for decision by the Central Government, and that interpretation is, in our view, wrong, and, in any case, out of harmony with the principle enshrined in Articles 19(1)(c) and 43(A) of the Constitution. The mode, of election or election must, therefore be such as to give the best form of repre sentation to every category of persons mentioned in the Act. [857E F] 1.2 The mode of appointment or nomination must, therefore. be such as will be ideally appropriate and appropriate to, the banking industry, and the choice is generally a question for decision by t the Central Government.[857F] 1.3 The mode of selection or nomination must be such as could be legitimately exercised so as to give effect to the true intent of the legislature as to the composition of the Board. [858F] 1:4 The mode of elect ment must, therefore,. be such as may be reasonably exercised so as not to give effect, to the true intention of the legislature. [859F] 1 :5. The mode and mode of election and nomination must, accordingly, be such that would be idely suitable and appropriate for the banking industry. [860F] 1.:6. The mode for election or nomination must have, therefore, been such as would not be in a perfect representation keeping with the principles of election. [861F] 1]7. The mode or mode of election must, however, be such, as would be legitimately practicable and appropriate to a banking industry and, the choice of a mode is generally one matter for decision. [863F] 1.(a) The mode of recruitment or nomination must not, therefore,, be such which would be idearily suitable and appropriate. [864F] 1(b) The mode and method of election or appointment must, therefore have to be such as should be reasonably exercised, so as to enable it to reasonably exercise its discretion in such a way as to give it the maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives. [866G] 1:6.

The assessee was imposed penalties in the sum of Rs. 1,000/ under section 220(6) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The assessee preferred appeals to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal and made an interim prayer for stay of collection of the penalties imposed. The Income tax Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Commissioner the same powers as are vested in the court under the Code of Civil Procedure when trying a suit in respect of the matters specified in the section. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the recovery proceedings as also the collection of the penalty pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. The High Court held that the Appellate Tribunal had the powers to stay the proceedings as also, the collection of penalties pending the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had the power under the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to stay the collection of tax and that the collection of penalty pending the appeals since that power is incidental and ancillary, to its appellate power. HELD: (i) The Appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power to grant stay as incidental or ancillary to its Appellate jurisdiction. [69 C] (ii) The Appellate Assistant Commissioner or the Appellate Tribunal is given the power to do all such acts, or employing such means as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. [69 D] (iii) The Appellate Tribunals must be held not to have the jurisdiction to stay the Recovery proceedings as also of the collection of taxes or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. [69 E] (iv) The Appellate Authority must be held, to have the powers to grant stay of collection during the pendency of the appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commission. [69 F] (v) The Appellate Board must be held that the power of stay by the Tribunal is not likely to be exercised in a routine manner or as a matter a matter of practice in view of section 220(5) which is confined only to the stage of pendency of an appeal before the Income tax Officer. [69 G] (vi) The Appellate 'Tribunal must be held as having the power to pass stay as incidental and ancillary or ancillary to the appellate jurisdiction. [70 E] (vii) The Appellate tribunal must be held in have the power of granting stay as incidental, or ancillary to it.

The respondent was charged with committing cognizable offences and was charged under section 7 of the Police Act with having committed cognizable offences. The respondent was charged under s. 7 of the police Act with having been guilty of dishonesty, corruption and misbehaviour in that he had on nine occasions, particulars of which were given in the charge, accepted bribes. The Superintendent of Police, after inquiry, found substantial complaints against the integrity of the respondent and recommended his transfer to the effect that the Sub Divisional Magistrate had found substantial complaints and that his general reputation for integrity was not good. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order of the dismissal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondent was not a Sub Inspector of Police at the time of the departmental trial the order of his dismissal was invalid. Held, that the departmental inquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the respondent in regard whereto the magisterial inquiry was held at an earlier stage. The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries do not affect the validity of the order of transfer. The fact of the time when the police received such complaints or that in the meantime the work of the respondent might be closely watched. The conduct of the respondent when he was officer incharge of the Police Station, Intiath, was the subject matter of (1) Civil Appeal No. The Sub Divisional Magistrate made inquiry in respect of seven of the charges which were the subject matter in the departmental trial and, therefore, it fell within the express terms of para. 486 of the Police Regulations.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Medical Service. He was promoted to supertime grade II on February 8, 1971. He was confirmed in the post of Director of Health Services on February 8. 1971. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the promotion of the appellant to supertime scale II on February 7, 1971. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was in Specialists ' grade and was senior to Dr. Sen and was not qualified for the post of Joint Director of Health Service, Manipur, and that he should have been promoted from that date. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant was in specialists ' grade. He was in Specialist ' grade and he was not qualified and, therefore, he must be considered eligible for promotion from the date on which Dr. Sen was promoted. [815E] 1.2 The appellant was not qualified to be promoted to super time grade II in February 1971. He had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists ' post. He was not qualified. Therefore, he must have been considered eligible for being promoted to super Time grade II in January 1971. [816B] 1.3 The appellant was fully qualified for being promoted as Director of Health services, Manipur. He was fully qualified to be considered for promotion to supertime Grade II in February, 1971. Therefore, the appellant was fully eligible for being considered for promotion from that date on which he claims as being eligible for promotion to Supertime grade II. [817C] 1.4 The appellant was, therefore, fully qualified for promotion to the supertime grade I in February 1971 from which date he claims as was eligible for promotion. [818D] 1.5 The appellant was a specialist ' grade. The post was converted into a specified post in supertime grade III. The post vacated by him which was in supertime scale III was offered to the appellant as and by way of promotion. The post in super time grade III was converted into an equivalent post. The post ceased to exist on February 1, 1971. [820E] 1:6 The appellant was qualified for being considered to supertime grades II in February 1972. He was, therefore fully qualified for the promotion to super time scale II in February 1973. [820B] 1:7 The appellant was entitled to be considered in the post which was deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971 on the invalidation of promotion of Dr. Sen. [820C] 1:8 The appellant was also in Specialists " grade and was junior to Dr. P. Sen and he was, therefore eligible for being appointed to that speciality and not some one who was on top of the general seniority list in Specialists" grade or general duty officers ' grade from which promotion is to be made. [820D] 1:9 The appellant was eligible for being treated as a specialist in February 1971 on the basis of his seniority in the supertime scale. He was also eligible for being posted to supertime post. [820F] 1:10 The appellant was promoted to Supertime Grade II on February 9, 1971. His refusal to accept promotion at Simla appellant was never superseded by any one junior to him in his speciality. It was implicit in this arrangement that the person to be appointed to such a post would be one who is eligible to be appointed in that speciality and the filling in of such post shall be governed by rule 8 (3). [820F G] 1:11 The appellant was rightly considered for promotion as Director of Medical Services, Manipur.

The respondent No. 1, a small holder, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 19B of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 (Act X of 628 1953) (for short the Act). The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the land inherited by him and later transferred to his sons and wife were not hit by section 10A and section 19B and section 19 B of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The gift in both the appeals fail in the face of section 19 B. [604C] (2) The gift is not hit by the ceiling set and land acquired by an heir by inheritance is saved from utilisation by the State. The gift is, therefore, saved from utilisation. [605D] (3) The gift does not affect the right of the landowner to receive rent from the tenant so settled. [606F] (4) The gift, in both the cases, does not affect either the right of ownership or the right of possession. [607F] (5) The gift by the father to the son or wife the latter had only lands within permissible limits, there was no frustration of the policy of the law. [608G] (6) The gift was not hit by Section 10A(a) of the Act because the High Court took the view that area which became surplus subsequent to April 15, 1953 was not hit under the ceiling set. [609F] (7) The scheme of the Act, according to the learned Judges, was to see that no one held in excess of the permissible area and since by the gift to the son and wife the latter has only lands within the permissible limits, the land, if among the heirs it is not, then their transfers will not be affected by the interdict of section 10 A(a) the sins of the father shall not set the teeth of the children on edge. The scheme of section 19 A is that even if the source of the excess area is inheritance, bequest of gift the capacity to own is conditioned by the permissible limit. The scheme is to see that the no one held at excess of the permitted area and since, by the gift, to the son, or wife the former had only lands outside permissible limits, it is surplus land, if amongst the heirs it was not, then his transfers will not set the light of the children.

The plaintiffs claimed the Zamindari on the death of Amarshah in 1951 and the plaintiffs claimed the other estate of Amarshih as devisees under his will. The defendants contended that the genealogical table set up by the plaintiffs was incorrect and that the genoealogical table was incorrect. The Trial Court held that the genocealogical table contained in the will of Amarshash was incorrect and the plaintiffs were entitled to the estate on the death. The High Court held that in making the order the Governor had acted in exercise of the power conferred by the Chanda Patent; that the order was contrary to the customs and the law governing the Zamindari; that the will dated December 8, 1950 set up by Amarshahah was not genuine and the plaintiffs ' suit with regard to Malguzari lands was not barred by the decision of the Compensation Officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the decision of compensation Officer regarding Malguzri lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951 had become binding and conclusive against the plaintiffs because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two months from the date thereof and the plaintiffs had been on that account not entitled to claim the compensation paid or payable in respect of the Malguzhari lands; that the decision in 1950 declaring Dayaram to be the successor on the death was not binding and conclusive and could not be reopened in a suit filed more than six years after that date and the plaintiffs could not claim the compensation payable in respect thereof; that the judgment of the Compensation officer was contrary to law and the law applicable to the case was not applicable to the facts of the case. HELD: (i) The order of the Compensation Commissioner was contrary to custom and the law of the land. The order of compensation Officer under sub section (1) shall not be subject to any appeal or revision, but any party may, within two months after the date of such order, institute a suit in the civil court to have the order set aside, and the decision of such court shall be binding on the Compensation Officer, but subject to the result of such suit, if any, the Compensation Officer shall be final and conclusive and shall not be final and binding. [319 G H] (ii) The order dated August 30, 1951 set up by respondent No. 1 was not a valid order and was not binding on the plaintiffs because the order of the Governor recognising Dayaram to be his successor on the deceased. [321 B] (iii) The order was contrary of the custom and the legal law governing the estate. The order was not a bona fide order. The order dated December 8. 1950 set up in the plaint was not a genuine order. The plaintiffs ' suit was not barred under the decision of respondent No. I. The order did not oust the jurisdiction of the Civil Court. [322 C] (iv) The order did set up by appellant No. 1 and the plaintiffs represented the true relationship between the descendants of Gangashah. The order in 1950 set up was "a fabricated will" and conferred no right or title upon the defendants. [323 C] (v) The order in question was not a mere order. The Collector had decided by his Order dated August 30. 1951 that compensation in respect of Malguzati lands was payable to Dayaram and since no suit was filed by the plaintiffs for setting aside that decision, the order became final and conclusive.

The appellants landlord filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that the standard rent was excessive and standard rent was fixed at Rs. 1,000 per month. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court took the view that the provisions of section 12 (3) (a) of the Act did not apply to the suit but that the suit was governed by the provisions contained in section 12 (2) (b) of the Bombay Rent Act. The Bombay High Court took a contrary view and held that the provisions contained therein did not apply. The Bombay view was that the dispute as to standard rent was to be raised within one month from the date of service of the notice on the tenant. The Bombay decision was affirmed by this Court in Ambalal 's case. The Bombay Municipal Corporation appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The Bombay High Courts in Ambalals 's case (supra) and in Chunilal Shivlal vs Chimanlal Nagindas took the view in Ambalaal 's Case (supra) that the dispute in regard to standard rent must be raised at the latest before the expiry of one month from date of service. The Bombay decisions are not applicable to the suit. [766 D] (2) The Bombay view is that the dispute is not limited only to a dispute raised within one months of the notice as contemplated in section 12(3) (b). The Bombay High court in Amballal Nagindass took the view contrary and held that in order to attract the applicability of section 12(2) (a), the provisions contained In sections 12 (3)(a) and (b) would apply. [767 E] (3) The Bombay decision is not applicable to a suit for eviction of rent in the instant case. [768 F] (4) The Bombay decisions were not applicable to an suit for recovery for possession of the property on the ground of a suit and if the tenant makes an application within one month of the service of the said notice on the landlord, the Court would be excluded.

The respondent company was a director of the respondent company. The respondent company was appointed as a director of a company. The company was appointed to vote and/or from time to time to appoint a special or general proxy to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Ltd. in respect of the shares held by it in the respondent company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the respondent Company. The respondent was appointed as director of the company. The directors of the respondentcompany nominated by the Aluminium Ltd., the respondent company as its managing director. The respondent Company was appointed as the managing director of the Company. The directors were appointed to vote. The respondent filed a petition under section 21 of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, read with section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1939 to 1943. The Income tax Appellate Tribunal held that the directors had a controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 2(21) of the Excess profits Tax Act, and that the directors of the company had a controlling interests in it as envisaged by section 2 (21) of that Act. The High Court answered in the affirmative the question of law referred to it. The High court answered in the negative. The question referred was: "Whether in the facts and circumstances of these cases, the Income tax Appellate tribunal was right in holding that the directors were not the shareholders of a company when such a person acquires, by purchase or otherwise, the majority of the votes carried by them. HELD: (i) The directors of a company may well be regarded as having "a controlling interest" in a company when they hold and are entered in the share register as holders of the majority of shares which, under the articles of association of the company, carry the right to vote. [193 C] (ii) The controlling interest remains vested in the Aluminium Ltd, and is at no time vested in Mr. L. G. L. Bash. [193 E] (iii) The last mentioned case was not brought to the notice of the High Court before the judgment under appeal was delivered. The facts of that case were entirely different from the facts of the case before the High Court and that decision has no manner of application to the present case. [193 G] (iv) The last one mentioned case was a case of a company which was then the appellant before the Tribunal and that decision had no manner of applying to the present appeal. [193 F] (v) The last named case was not placed before the High court before the judgment was delivered.

The respondent was an employee of the Karnataka Electricity Board. He was promoted as Accounts Superin tendent on 30th December, 1966. On 30th December 1966, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. examination. On 30.12.1966, some persons juniors to the respondent was promoted on their being denied to the respondent as he had not passed the examination. On 1st October, 1957, some persons senior to the respondent, were promoted on the basis of seniority cum merit on their having passing Part I andII of the S.,A.S Examination. The respondent opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of that Board with effect from that date. On 30st December 1966, another person junior to the Respondent was promoted on the ground that he had not been passed the examination and that in view of the later Resolution of the Board dated 5th January, 1970, it was no longer open to the respondent to rely on the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969. On 30rd December 1966, the respondent opted to join the Service under Board and ceased from that date, and therefore allowed the writ petition. The High Court allowed the writ Petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions and holding that the re spondent is exempted from passing the Departmental Examination and Kannada language test. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that in the circumstances of the case the relief to the respondent should not be denied on the ground of delay and laches. [501F] 1.2 The High Court has not been taken due note of. the Resolution dated 5th February, 1970, which was passed by the Board in pursuance of the directions of the High Court in the case of allot tees for promotion to the cadre of Accounts Superintendents as before be in sisted. The Resolution was ' passed by the board in pursuance of certain proceedings of the Government referred to in the Resolution itself. The Resolution required the passing of the examination and Kannada Language test for the purpose of earning increments and for promotion for candidates appointed after/st November, 1956. But as it is not made applicable to the allottees, it is contended that the allottees were by impli cation exempted from passing in the Departmental Examination I and Kannada languages test. The passing of the Resolution by the Board cannot have the effect of modifying a Regulation which was passed in the exercise of the powers conferred by the statute. [502F] 1:3 The resolution was not intended to cover the case of allottees and merely because the allottees were excluded from the operation of the Resolution the inference that the allottees are exempt ed from passing the examination is not justified. [503F] 1 :4 The resolution was ' passed 'by the Board in the exercise o f the powers conferred under the statute. The resolution was passed by Board in pursuance o the directions of this Court in the matter of allot tee for promotion to cadre of Accounts Superintendent as before be In sisted. the High Court by a subsequent Resolution had resolved on insisting on the passing of examination. Examination for promotion to a cadre of Accounts superintendent as before be was in sisted" the court found that it would .mean that where the passing of a S.A.,S. Examination was insisted prior to that Resolution in the case o allotees for promotion, the inference that t he allottees were exempt ed from the passing of that examination is not correct.

The petitioner 's son Suman Behera was taken from his home in police custody. The petitioner 's father was taken from police custody. He was taken from the home in police remand. The petitioner was taken from custody. The respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, was taken from him in police custody and was taken to the police station. The petitioner filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for determination of compensation. The Additional Solicitor General, however, rejected the petition. The petitioner preferred a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right, imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental rights of the citizen. [608B] 1.2 The court is the protectors of the civil liberties of the citizen, notwithstanding the right of the citizen to the remedy by way of a civil suit or criminal proceedings. Of course, relief in exercise of the power under Article 32 or 226 would be granted only once it is established that there has been an infringement of the fundamental rights, of the citizen and no other form of appropriate redressal by the court in the facts and circumstances of the case, is possible. [609C] 1.3 The court is entitled to award compensation in appropriate cases where that is the only practicable mode of redress available for the contravention made by the State or its servants in the purported exercise of their powers, and enforcement of the fundamental right is claimed by resort to Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution. [610D] 1.4 The payment of compensation in such cases is not to be understood, as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the private law but in the broader sense of providing relief by an order of making 'monetary amends ' under the public law for the wrong done due to breach of public duty, of not protecting the fundamental rights. The compensation is in the nature of compensation awarded against the wrong doer for the breach of its public duty, notwithstanding the rights available under the civil law to the aggrieved party to claim compensation under the private Law in an action based on tort. [611E] 1.5 The payment of the compensation in such a case is not tobe understood, as the same is generally understood In a civil action, for damages under Article 32 and 226 would be awarded only once it was established that there had been an infringement or the fundamental rights available to the aggrieved person where the courts found that grant of such relief was warranted. The compensation awarded is in the type of damages awarded against the wrongful doer for breach of its fundamental rights. [612D] 1:6 The payment of money in such cases are not to be construed, as it was generally understood in the civil action for compensation under the public Law. [613G] 1.7 The payment of damages in such cases may be necessary to do complete justice and enforce the fundamental rights guaranteed in the Constitution, which enable the award of monetary compensation in appropriate case, where that is, the only mode of redress. The compensation, as exemplary damages, in proceedings under Article 32, by this Court or under Article 226, would be granted once it is proved that there has had been an invasion of the fundamental fundamental rights of citizen and no others form of appropriate relief by the court.

The petitioners were convicted for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death for an offence punishable under section 302 read with section 34 Indian Penal Code. The petitioners challenged the validity of the conviction and sentence. The petitioners contended that the right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution was not an absolute right, nor indeed did it confer any right on the Press to have an unrestricted access to means of information. The petitioners also contended that the freedom of speech conferred by article 14(1)(b) of the constitution was not an arbitrary right, nor did it confer an right on the press to have an absolute access to means through information. The petitions were rejected by the President of India. The petitioners filed petitions to the President of the India for commutation of the sentence. The President of India rejected the petitions. The petitioners then filed petitions to this Court for commutation of their sentence to imprisonment for life. The petitioners prayed for a writ of mandamus or any other appropriate writ or direction directing the respondents to allow them to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga who are under a sentence of death. The petitioners were also granted a similar relief. The petitioners, who were convicted for murder, contended that the constitutional right to freedom, freedom of speech, expression conferred by Article 19(1) (a) of Constitution was not absolute right, but the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right of the Press to choose the candidates from the open market was not an unfettered right, nor was it conferred any right on them, and that the right of interviewing the prisoners right was not an unrestricted right, nor could it confer any rights on the Press, to have an unfettered unrestricted access to the means of information, and that, therefore, the right to form an opinion or opinion was not an uncontrolled right, nor does it confer any power on the Press. HELD: The right to freedom conferred by article 13(1)(c) of theConstitution is not an absolute one, nor indeed does it confer an absolute right on the citizens to have an unlimited access to means by information. The right to form a opinion or opinion is not an unfettered one, nor is it conferred any power on any authority to decide the question of the right of an interview. [1187C D] The right to be interviewed is not an arbitrary one, nor does the same confer any right upon the Press, and the security of the State, public order, decency and morality. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore, the petition should be dismissed.

The appellant was the Receiver of the estate. On the reorganisation of the Judicial Administration in Tripura, the suit was transferred to the court of the Subordinate Judge, Agartala. On the transfer of the suit to the court, the Court of the Subordinate judge transferred the suit to a court of the subordinate Judge, Agar Tripura. On the District Judge transferred the suit for recovering the amount due under the mortgage. On the question whether the surety bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the District Judge, the High Court held that the surety bond executed by the appellant was incompetent to enforce the surety bond. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the surety bonds were executed in and for the purposes of the particular proceedings which were pending before the Court of Subordinate Judge, and that the surety surety bond was executed both be the Receiver and the appellant in favour of "Sri Ramani Mohan Goswami the District Judge of Agartala his successors, successors in office and assigns". Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The surety bond is executed both bethe Receiver and the transferee of the suit and the transferee. [360 E] (2) The surety bonds are executed both be The Receiver and the transferor. [360 F] (3) The surety surety bond is a part of proceedings pending before a District Judge and on the transfer of of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond. stood validly transferred to the Court of that Subordinate Judge. [360 G] (4) The surety Bond is executed both for the purpose of the particular proceeding which were pending in the Court of District Judge. [361 C] (5) The surety agreement is a part and parcel of the proceedings.

The appellants who are dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959, filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the levy. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the transactions of supply did not result in sales and were on that account not exposed to sales tax, because steel products were supplied pursuant to the directions of the Iron and Steel Controller made under cl. 5 of the Order and not pursuant to the direction issued under cl.5 was, it said, not to dispose of or agree to dispose of any iron or steel except in accordance with the conditions contained or incorporated in the order of the Controller and that since there was liberty of contract between the parties, the transaction could be regarded as a sale. Dismissing the appeals, HELD : (1) The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U. P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants, rejecting the contention raised by the appellants. [501 B] (2) The tax payer contended that the transactions were on that date, not to disposed of or agree or dispose of or agreeing to export any iron or Steel except in accordance With the conditions contained in the order. The tax payer was under the Control Order compelled to carry out the directions of his Controller and it had no volition in the matter. The tax payee was under the control of the Controller. The taxholder contended that the supplies of sugar were made pursuant to the orders of the Controller, and no acceptance by the latter; the tax payer was Under the Control Order enjoined to carry out directions of the Controller; it had no option in the matter, and no accept by the latter. The tax was under the controlled order compelled to carryout the directions of Controller and it was had no volition In the matter. [502 C D] (3) The tax payee had no volition to the matter. It was not open to the tax payer to contend that the transactions did not result into sales and were not on that account, but subject to restrictions, the transaction would be regarded as sale. [503 D] (4) The taxholder was under the authority of the Controller to carry out his directions. The taxee was under the supervision of the Controller who had the power to carry out its directions. The levy was therefore under the control and supervision of the controller. [504 E] (5) The taxee contended that the supply of sugar was not taxable since there was no sale. [525 G] (6) The tax was leviable on the turnover of supply of wheat. The taxer contended that the sales of supply did result in sales, and were on the same account not exposed. The taxees contended that the transaction of supply did neither result in sales nor were exposed to sales Tax. [505 G] (7) The taxees were under the control, supervision and control of the controller and it had nothing to do with the supply of goods pursuant to the instructions issued under cl 5. [506 C] (8) The taxer was under the powers of the Controller under cl. 4 of the Order. The taxers contended that the contracts of supply did no result in sales. They were on that view not exposed to sale tax, because they were supplied pursuant thereto. The tax recipients contended that the goods were supplied pursuant pursuant to the order of Controller and not pursuant thereto. [507 C] (9) The tax recipients were under the Control order compelled to carrying out the directions issued under cl.(5) of the Order, and not pursuant.

The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was arrested on May 26, 1986. The report of the Advisory Board was more than three weeks after the detention which commenced on the making of the order of detention. The appellant was in custody from November 12. 1985 onwards awaiting the trial on a Charge of murder. The report was received by the Government on June 23, 1986. On June 23,1986, the appellant was released from prison on June 23. 1986. The appellant challenged the order of his detention before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant contended that the report of the advisory Board was more or less than three weeks before the detention which started on the making thereof. The High court dismissed the petition holding that the report was not made within three months of the date of detention. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The report is not made within the three months of date of detention, but it is a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the Constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date of hearing and therefore, the detention should be upheld. If a reference to an Advisory Board is to be made within three weeks, it is no answer to say, that the report though not made within two weeks, was made before the hearing of the case. If the report of such an Advisory Board was to be obtained within three months, it is not answer to say whether the report though Not made within three days, was obtained before the hearing. If the representation made by the detenu is required to be disposed of within a stipulated period, it is only a answer to say the that the report although not obtained within three days of the date, was obtained by the hearing of that case. If, the report of an advisory Board is to he obtained within three weeks of the date o f detention, it is nothing but a sufficient answer. If the Report of the advisory board is to be obtained before the expiry of three months, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it is within three months from the date of the second order of detention, and the detention should he upheld. [206E F] 2. The observation of the court to the extent that they go to support the contention of the appel lant, but we must say that in that case, the court was not confronted with the present situation at all. This implies that the question to which the Advisory Board has to apply its mind is whether on the date of its report there was sufficient cause for the detention of the person. That inquiry neces sary involves the consideration of the ques tion as to whether there was sufficient reason for the detention o f the person when the order of the detention was passed, but we see no justification for extending the jurisdiction of the Advisory board to the consideration of that question as to whether it is necessary to continue the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless the Advisory Board had reported within the period of three months that there was in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. [206H; 207A] 3. The observation that the question whether the procedural requirements are of the Constitution, and the statute has been complied with, before the date the detention order was made, is no answer. [206B] 4.

The respondent, a father of the respondent, was awarded a contract for carrying out the work of solving the dispute between the parties. The respondent, a son, filed a civil suit for damages against the petitioner and the respondent. The petitioner, who was the father of the Respondent, was the father, of the respondent. Both of them were established Vaidyas in Rajkot. They came from a well to do family. The respondent filed a civil revision application against the award and sought the judgment in terms of the award under section 17 of the (hereinafter called 'the Act '). The trial Judge rejected the objections filed beyond the period of limitation and for the reasons that (1) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the award, (2) the time for making an application to set aside the award had expired and no such application was made (3) the award was not remitted under section 16(5) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the civil revision application. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute to the arbitrator. [501C] 2. The conduct and conduct of the respondent that there was a arbitration agreement and, by signing the same, could be said to be a proper arbitration agreement in terms of section 2(a) of the , cannot be said to have been a proper arbitration contract in terms of Section 2(a). But in the present context, it is clear that the conduct of the petitioner that there was no written agreement signed by both the parties, about which there was no factual dispute, reiterated the fact that the parties have agreed to refer to the arbitration of the named arbitrator and that he made an award. This, in our opinion, in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case can certainly be construed to be a a proper arbitration Agreement in terms of s 2(a), of the Act,. But in the instant case, it is obvious that the conduct and conduct, of the parties, that there was arbitration agreement andby signing the award, it could be inferred that the parties were agreed to refer disputes in writing to the arbitrator, has made lawyers laugh and legal philosophers weep. With respect, we could not agree more in the facts and the circumstances of this case. [502D E] 3. The conduct, of parties that there is an arbitration agreement, and by signing and signing the award the same could be said, that the parties did agree to refer the disputes in writing writing to the arbitration. [503F] 4. The conduct that there was in an arbitration agreement was not a proper arbitration arrangement in terms of sec. 2(a)(i) of the . [503C] 5. The conduct or conduct of the party that there was any arbitration agreement and in signing the award thereon could be said not be a proper arbitral agreement in terms Of section 2(b) of the Arbitration Act. But in this context, it was clear that the behaviour of the parties was that there was some arbitration agreement and that by signing the arbitration award it could not be said that there was something else which could have the effect of rendering the court entirely lacking in jurisdiction in respect of the subject matter of the suit or over the parties to it.

The appellants were the mortgagees of a mortgage debt. The mortgage debt was created in the year 1939 and the mortgage debt was transferred to the appellants. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of the debt. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The appellants then filed a petition in the High Court for setting aside the decree. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the petition (exhibit 2a) dated June 2, 1939, amounted to a proceeding in execution for any of the purposes mentioned in clauses (a) and (b) of section 2(22) of the Act. HELD: (i) The order of January 30, 1937, was made under Order XXI, rule 57, as amended by the High Court. [118 A] (ii) The petition (ex exhibit 2a) was not an application at all and was certainly not a proceeding in rem. [118 E] (iii) The petition of June 2, 1938, was not an appla cation at all and could not be a proceeding in the execution. [118 F] (iv) The petition was not an applica tion at all and the respondent 's decree must be taken to have been passed "in a suit to which this Act applies. [118 G] (v) The petition in the present case was not an an application at any stage and was certainly a proceeding in executing the decree. [118 C] (vi) The petition did not amount to a proceeding within the meaning of section 2 (22) of Act.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The appellant was the karta of a joint Hindu family consisting of herself and his four brothers. The appellant, who was the Karta, was the Karta and the appellant was the sole heir of the joint family. The appellant 's widow and sons instituted O.S. No. 62 of 1954 against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April 15, 1946, were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes, and were void. The appellant instituted against his widow and sons O.S No. 63 of 1954, asking for general partition of the joint Hindu family properties and for allotment to her of the properties conveyed by the two deeds. No. 12 of 1954 and O.S Nos. 62 of 1953, against one of his sons and another person asking for damages and mesne profits for wrongful trespass on the properties. No. 13 of 1954 andO.S.No. 62 of 1955, against one another person asking O.S., No. 62/54, the appellant transferred to the appellant certain properties belonging to the joint family, and for allotment of the properties gifted by the two deed. No. 18 of 1954 and 0.S. Nos. 62/55 and 0. S. Nos. 63/54 of 1954 were filed in the High Court of Andhra Pradesh. The High Court confirmed the decree in O.S, No. 62 and decreed O.Ss. No. 63/55 and decreed O 'S. No, 63/54, and the decree for possession in respect of the properties covered by exhibit A 1 being conditional on payment by the respondents of the value of improvements made by the appellant to the properties. The High court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transfers were made by Venkatacharyulu in favour of the appellant in view of past illicit cohabitation, and that the subsequent severance of joint status in 1947 could not validate them. HELD: (i) The transfers were without consideration and were by way of gifts.
