The respondent, a widow of the deceased employee, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the L.I.C. had not made the payment to the respondent, inasmuch as it was payable only to the assignee, Smt. Kamalabai G. Ranade, and not the defaulter. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The L.I.,C. itself has taken the stand throughout that the moneys due under the policies were held by it for and on behalf of its assignee and not the default. Performance of this statutory obligation by the L. I.C. is, therefore, clearly justified. [114G] 2. The inordinate delay in making the requisite statement under section 226 (3)(vi) of the Act was the result of misconstruction of the provision and misappreciation of its liability thereunder. Performance of the statutory obligation by L.I,.C. in the present case being after inordinate delay, award of interest to the assignee of the policies to whom the payment thereunder had to be made even according to the stand of the L.l.C. [114A B] 3. The inordinate delays in making the statement on oath by the L.,I.C., under section 226 of the Income tax Act, 1961, were the result of misreading of the provision. Performance of that statutory obligation by an L.I .C. being after inordinate time, award of Interest to the assignee was not governed by section 244 of the Incometax Act, 1961.[114C] 4. The inordinate and unexplained delay in making this statement on oath, by the L .I.C.. under section 226, was the result o f misconstruction of the provisions and misappreciation thereof. Performance of a statutory obligation by a L.I..C. in a given case, being after inordinate inordinate delay, Award of interest to a assignee of the policy to whom the payments thereunder had to he made even according t o the stand of L.I.'C. as envisaged in clause (vi) thereof, instead of in doing so. [114D] 5. The inordinate unexplained delay in filing the statement on solemn affirmation by the L,I.C.; under section 226 and misappreciation, of its liability under section 226 was the result Of misconstruction of the statutory duty by the L..I.C,. in the present cases. Performance of such statutory obligation by its L.I,C. in not making the requisite statements on oath by L. I.,C. as contemplated in clause (vii) of sub section (3) of section 226 of Income Tax Act 1961, was the results of misconstruction of section provision and mis appreciation of its liability thereon. Performance of it statutory obligation by it, in the present ease, being after considerable delay, award o f interest to the respondent in the manner prescribed in clause (xi) thereof, Instead of in doing it. [114E F] 6. The inordinate inordinate delay in filing of the statement on affidavit by the L,.I.C; under section 226 is the result of misconception of its liability. Performance of an statutory obligation by virtue of its consistent stand throughout that it was incumbent on the L.L.I. C. to make the requisite statement on oath under clause (vi), thereof raising an objection on the basis of the registered assignment. It was not possible for the assignee of L. I..L.I., to obtain revocation of the notice by the L.'I.C, without the requisite statement, on oath being made by the L.;I.C.(as envisaged in clause(vi) thereof.

The appellant was the Chief Justice of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh. He was appointed as a Judge of the High court. He was promoted as a Judge. He was confirmed as a Judge on May 30, 1963. He was thereafter promoted as a District Judge on May 28, 1963. The respondent filed a suit for possession of the suit property on the ground that the suit property was not the property of the appellant. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The respondent appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was within time if computed after making the deductions permitted by section 12 of the Limitation Act. HELD: (i) The first limb of section 29 is concerned only with proceedings of this kind, that is, proceedings under special or local law for which a period of limitation is prescribed in the First Schedule. The first limb is concerned only to proceedings of this nature, that is proceedings under special and local law for the which a period is provided in the First schedule. The first part of section 29(2) is concerned only in proceedings under special, or local law. The first portion of section 29, sub section (2) of the Limitation is concerned only only with proceedings under special. or local law, for which a limitation is provided in that Schedule. [165 B C] (ii) The first part is concerned only about proceedings under special law for which the period of limitation prescribed therefor by the first schedule is different from that prescribed therefor by that Schedule. The second limb of sub section (1) of section 29 of the Limitation Acts is concerned only for proceedings under special laws for which a special or local Law prescribes for such an appeal is provided in section 4. The first clause is concerned only regarding proceedings under special statutes for which a periods of limitation are provided in the first schedule. The second part is concerned with proceedings under general or local law and not proceedings under special Acts for which a limit of limitation is provided. [165 C D] (iii) The first portion is concerned only of proceedings under special circumstances for which a suit is provided in a particular local or special law. The second portion is concerned with proceeding under special or special local law for such a period of time. [165 D] (iv) The first clause of sub section(2) of section29 is concerned only With proceedings of this type, that is. proceedings under special special or local laws for which the limitation is provided for in the First Schedules. [165 E F] (v) The first sub section (3) of section 30 is concerned only relating to proceedings under special enactments for which a time limit of limitation prescribed for the suit is provided. The first sub clause is concerned with the proceedings under special cases for which a prescribed period of limitation has been provided in the Second Schedule. [166 D] (vi) The first proviso to section 29(1) of the Indian Limitation Act is concerned only between proceedings under special provisions for which a maximum period of limitation for the suit has been provided. The second proviso is concerned only as proceedings under special proceedings for which a provision of limitation is made in the First Scheduled.

The appellant was a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura. He questioned the validity of the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate declaring Plot Nos. 701 and 702 in the Town Area, Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stand/halting place of Baldev, where the stage carriages were directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriages in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986. The case of the appellant was that the District Magis trate had no power to appoint any area as a bus Stand under section 76 of the Act under which he purported to pass the impugned order. The District Magis lrate gave a contract to a private contractor to collect that fees payable by the bus operators for making use of the area in question which was within its jurisdiction for stopping their buses in accord ance with the order passed by the 717 District Magistrate. The appellant challenged the validity of that order before the District Magistrate. A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The Division Bench of the High court held that section 76 of The Act conferred wide powers on the District Magistrate 'to fix the places for the bus stand/happe carriage stand/halts place '. The Division bench of the High, however, held that section76 of the Act conferred wide power on the State Government to make rules for the purpose o f the said chapter. The High Court also held that the power under section 68(2)(r) of the Act could be exercised only by the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the District Magistrate, and that could be done only under section 68 of the Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The District Magistrate had passed the impugned order in question with the object of establishing a bus stand in the area in dispute. The Municipal Council contended before this Court that the District Magistrate had been authorised by the State Government under section 76 to pass an order fixing the Municipal Bus Stand as a bus stands for purposes of the Act, and that the power to compel persons in charge of motor buses to stop only at certain places for the pur pose of taking up or setting down passengers was a matter which relating to motor traffic and that there was a specif ic provision in section 68(1)(r) and that could he done only only under section68(2)( r) of the . [717B C] 2. The High court was, therefore, in error in upholding the impugned order passed by t he District Magistrate. [717C] 3. The High, Court was, therefore in error in holding that section 76 had nothing to do with the fixation or alteration of a bus stand and the power to issue a notification fixing a bus stand was implied in section 68 (2)(r). [717D] 4. The High ' Court was, accordingly, in error. [718E] 5.

The appellants were prosecuted for offences under section 7 of the and 8 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The trial court convicted all the accused. But on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction of the appellants. The High Court set aside the acquittal of the appellants but on appeal the High Court set the conviction of Qimat Rai and of the two appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was in error in setting aside the conviction and sentence of Qim at the instance of the appellants and that the High court was in error. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in setting aside a conviction and sentence imposed upon the appellants. [635 C] (ii) The High court was right in holding that Qimat Lal was a preparation for committing an offence. It follows therefore that there was no export of paddy within the meaning of Para 2(a) of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. [636 E] (iii) The High ' Court was in wrong in setting aside an acquittal. [637 C] (iv) The High Courts were in error in holding that the appellants were not guilty of an attempt to commit an offence of export. [638 B] (v) The High courts were in error. [639 C] (vi) The High, Court was in mistake in setting aside their conviction. [640 C] (vii) The High "Court was in error when it set aside the order of forfeiture passed by the trial court with regard to 75 bags of paddy and truck No. P.N.U. 967.

The assessee, a company, was incorporated in the United States of America and was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of goods and was engaged as a Managing Agent in the United State of America. The assessee was a company incorporated in the year 1945 and was engaged by the assessee in the business as a Managing Agents in the United Kingdom. The assessee, a private limited company, was engaged in manufacturing and selling goods and was also engaged in the manufacture of goods and were also engaged in manufacturing goods. The assessee claimed that the Sassoons were not liable to tax in respect of the income of the Sassoon under the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim and held that the Sassoonons were not entitled to any deduction in respect of its income. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the assessee was not liable to pay tax in respect thereof. The Appellate Tribunal, however, took the view that the Saswadons became entitled on the very date of the respective assignments to a proportionate share of the year 's remuneration for the Managing Agency, and that the share accrued to the Sassoors as their taxable income, then and there, and did not cease to be such notwithstanding the assignment thereof thereof or which had accrued to them under the terms of the Managing Agency Agreements, and that accordingly that share accrued to them during the chargeable accounting period. The Tribunal, however held that the share of the assessee was the income which had accrued under the terms Of the Managing Agency Agreement, and that therefore that share accrued was the income of that company. The Tribunal also held that the shares were not liable for tax in respect Of the same. The Tribunal held that the company was not liable for the income tax in respect, and that it was the profits and gains of the business carried on by the assessee. The Tribunal further held that the Income tax Officer was not entitled to deduct the amount of the commission paid by the Sassoconsons to the transferees and that the assessee had not earned any part of the commission actually earned by them or which had been earned by them under the conditions of the Managing Agent Agreements. The Tribunal however held that in any event, what was transferred was an income bearing asset which carried with it a right to the entire income that fell due after the date of assignment. The Tribunal in appeal, held that in computing the taxable income of the assessee, the Sassots had not earned a part of the Managing agency commission which had been paid by the Companies to the transferees, and that, therefore, that share accrued on the dates of the respective transfers of the Managing Agents to the transferees was the income earned by them during the broken period. The High Court, however, did not accept the contention of the assessee that the Sasereons became entitled to the amount by way of remuneration not, as per the terms of their Managing Agency Agreements. The High court, however, allowed the appeal of the assessee and held that in the case of an assignment of Managing Agency the entire remuneration for the year ''s work accrues as a matter of law to the assignee and was his sole income, on the ground that the Agency was the source of income and that the remuneration to be income by way of profits or gains from the business carried out by the assignee, when as a fact he stepped into the position of the Managing agent only on some date in the course of the year by virtue of the assignment.

The appellant was a resident of Pachperwa in the District of Gonda. He was residing with his father. He was living with his father in law. He was staying with his father and his wife. He was also residing with his wife. The appellant 's father was living with him. He was not in the house. The appellant was not in his house. The deceased and the appellant were living together. The appellant and his wife were living together in the house of the appellant. The appellant had illicit relations with the deceased. The appellant, who was living with the deceased, was living with her father. The appellant gave a complaint against the deceased and the accused was charged under section 302 I.P.C. The trial court acquitted the appellant. On appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. Hence the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The evidence in the case is circumstantial. The circumstances found by the High Court, which lead to the only conclusion that the appellant must have committed the murder. [657B] (2) The circumstances found established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency that they should be such as to exclude other hypotheses but the one proposed to be proved. [658C] (3) The circumstances established by the High court, which lead the only conclusion, that the appellant should have committed the offence. [659D] (4) The circumstances proved by the High Courts, which lead, to the only inference that the appellant could have committed the crime. [656E] (5) The circumstances, which we have stated earlier lead to the conclusion that the accused must have committed murder.

The appellant was appointed as an officer of the respondent company. He was appointed as a Manager of the respondent Company. He was served with a notice dated April 29, 1976 terminating his service. The appellant challenged the validity of the notice on the ground that the termination of his service was in terms of the existing rule 5 of the Rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board of Directors was empowered to terminate the service of the officer/employee of the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board of Directors had to take a decision, whether the need to continue the employee 's service subsists which would be based on the relevant material. Thereby, there would be objective consideration before taking a decision, not only regarding the need to continuance the post but also the services of the officer. Once the Board reaches a decision to abolish the post, in consequence the service of an employee occupying couched in Rule 5 also is capable of that interpretation. But from the facts, it is clear that the Board did not abolish the post but put an end to the service of that employee. [224B C] 1.2 The Board of Management did not abolish any post but put a end to the services of an employee or officer. Once an employee, whether permanent or temporary, has an option to leave or discontinue by giving 30 days ' notice in writing of his intention to do so. [224D] 1.3 The Board of Director of the respondent was empowered to unilaterally and arbitrarily decide that there is no need for the services of a particular employee, in given facts and circumstances, though the post which the employee is occupying may continue and would be put to an end by giving one month 's notice or pay in lieu thereof. The other view capable to be construed from the language employed would be that the Board may form an objective opinion on the basis of the material, that the post which an employee is occupying might continue and would he put to an rest by giving one months ' notice in written for termination of his services or in lieu thereof, pay such employee a sum equivalent to his one month ' salary including allowances upto that period of termination. [224F G] 1.4 The Board of management did not abolish or abolish the post nor put an end or the service of any employee or officer, and the absence of the need for the continuance of the post would necessitate to terminate the services of such an employee or employee. Once the board reaches a decision, to abolish the posts, in consequence, the service of such officer or employee occupying couched may continue and will be put to a end by giving One month 's salary including allowances up to that period. [224G H] 1.5 The Board of the Management did not abolishing the post but putting an end to service of the appellant. [224A] 1.6 The Board of Managing Director did not abolish that post but put the end to the Service of the appellant, and put an end and the service of a person or officer. The other interpretation put up by Sri Ramamurty is that the Board could form an objective Opinion, on the basis Of the material, which the post officer or the employee is occupy no longer is in need. Thereby, the post would be abolished. The officer or employee may be permanent or temporary but the absence of need for the continuation of the post will entail forfeiture of the pay of the month. [224C D] 1.7 The Board of Board of Management may form an independent objective opinion, on the ground of the material facts, that the posts which the officer or the employees is occupying may continued and would be placed to an end only by giving one year 's notice.

The appellants, who were the highest bidders on February 20, 1970 and who were the successful bidders, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Bihar and Orissa Excise (Orissa Amendment) Ordinance, 1970. The High Court held that the State Government had the exclusive right and privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor and that it had the "power to hold a public auction for the grant of exclusive privilege under section 22 of the Act" and that the rule 103(1) of the Board 's Excise Rules was ultra vires the Act. The High court held that the sale notice issued by the Collector was not for the grant or renewal of the exclusive privilege under Section 22 of the Bihar & Orissa Excise Act, 1915 and that the Collector had no authority to issue such a notice. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that the sale was not for a grant of an exclusive privilege to manufacture and sell 'liquor. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have not expressed any final opinion as to whether the licence was to be granted for an exclusive privilege or to accept payment of a sum therefor. The High ' Court has also held that the case was completely covered by its decision dated January 3, 1974 in O.J.C. Govind Das on behalf of 'the appellants that the Collector was the competent authority to issue a notice under section 22(1) and the Collector had not been controverted that, as. had been averted in ' the memorandum of appeal, the requirement of sub section (1) of section 22 had already been complied with by the State Government, and that the collector was not concerned and did not in fact issue any public notice for purposes of sub section(1) or section 22. [614C D] 2. The High, Court has also not expressed any opinion as to how the licence was granted for an independent privilege to manufacture 'liquor and that it has the "power" to hold a Public auction for the granting of such a right or privilege and to accept payment thereof. [615D] 3. The High. Court has also given rise to civil appeal No. 1971 Cut tack 777 and the decision of this Court in Jaiswal 's case (supra) and dismissed the petition. No. 2091 of 1972 is set aside and the writ petition No. 1855 1863 of 1972 is allowed, the impugned judgment of the High Court dated April 16, 1971 is set aside, and the writ petitions Nos. 2091 is allowed, The impugned judgment of High Court dated May 15, 1971 is restored and the writ Petition No. 185318 is allowed, and the impugned judgment is set aside. The writ petition No, 1855 1863 and 1236 of 1972 are allowed, the appellants are set aside and writ petition No., 2071 is allowed, with the consequential relief.

The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to death. The High Court reduced the punishment of accused No. 2 to the substantive offence of murder under section 302. The High court reduced the punishment to the substantive sentence of death under section 302 and reduced the sentence of death to the substantive term of imprisonment. The appellant contended that there was corroboration of the evidence of Dinkar in material particulars in regard to the connection of the appellant with the crime and in regard to his conspiracy as well as the common intention. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The discovery of articles in the godown of Takalkar was as a result of a statement by accused No. 1. The discovery of article in the godown was as a consequence of a statement made by accused No, 2. The name of accused No, 3 was found in the note book of Takalkkar. The relationship of father and son between accused No. 3 and accused No. 4 was not to be lost sight of. [603 B] (2) The discovery was of articles in godown of Taknkar. The discovery was made as a result o statement by accused no. 2. The discovery, of articles in this godown was as result of a declaration by accused No., 2. The recovery of articles in that godown was made as the list of the articles sold to Gadekar. The name and the name of accused no. 3 was found at the foot of it and by his wife. The relationship between accused No, 4 and accused No, 5 was not to have lost sight of, and the discovery of articles. [604 C D] (3) The discovery,of articles in the godowns of Takalkaran was as a matter of fact a statement by the accused No.2. The discovery by the name of the accused No, 1 was as a fact of a statement. The discovery in the godown, of Takalker was as a part of the statement by accused NO. 2. [605 B C] (4) The discovery by accused No 3 was as a whole a statement by him and that was the list of articles sold to him. The discovery made by accused NO, 2 was as a piece of hand writing with the signature of accused No 2. The statement of accused No 3 at the foot was that those articles were given by accused No 2 and he was asked to produce the gunny bag which he did. The discovery did not amount to any confession. [606 G H] (5) The discovery made of articles in a godown of Takalikar was as an instance of a statement given by accused NO 2. The fact that there was capital sentence of accused No 4 was not lost sight of by the High Court.

The appellant was the owner of a plot of land in the final scheme calculated in proportion to the increment which was estimated to accrue in respect of such plot by the Town Planning Officer. Under section 64(1) (f) of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1949, the local authority shall make a draft scheme for the area 87 in respect of which the declaration has been made and publish it in the prescribed manner. The appellant 's case was that the Town Planning officer had no power to determine the amount of compensation in the appellant 's favour. The Town Planning Officer under section 32(1) of the Act, however, did not make a draft Scheme for the area of 87 in respect to which the declaration had been made and published it in the manner prescribed. The appellant contended that the Town planning officer had no jurisdiction to determine the compensation in the absence of a draft scheme. The High Court held that the Town Plan Officer had no power under section 32 (1) (iii) to determine the market value of the land at the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme with all the buildings and works thereon at that date and without reference to improvements contemplated in the scheme other than improvements due to the alteration of its boundaries. The appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The Town Planning officer under section 32 of the Act is required to estimate the compensation to be paid to the owner of any property or right injuriously affected by the making of a town planning scheme in accordance with the provisions of section 69. Under clause (xiii) the Town Planning Authority is required to determine the increment to accrue in regard to each plot included in the final Scheme calculated in proportion thereto to the increment that is estimated to accrue In respect of such plots by the Town planning Officer. Under clause(xiii) the town planning authority is required to estimates the compensation to the owner in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the parties. Under clause 4 the Town Planning authority is required, to estimate the amount to be adjusted, and that is the guiding rule in respect of all lands covered by the scheme. Under clause 5 the Town Planning Committee is required to prepare a draft scheme in accordance With the provisions of Section 69. Under section 69 the amount by which the total value of the plots included in the provisional scheme with all buildings and works therein allotted to a person falls short of or exceeds the total value. Under clause 7 the Town Planning Board is required to make a draft statement of the amount payable as compensation on each plot used, allotted or reserved for a public purpose or purpose of the local authority which is beneficial partly to the owners or residents within the area of the scheme and partly to the general public, which shall be included in the costs of the scheme. [775 H; 776 A B] The Town Planning Act is a special Act and the provisions of the Act are not applicable to the facts of the present case. Under clause 9 the Town Planning Act provides that the amount bywhich the total value shall be payable to the owner shall be deducted from or added to, as the case may be, the contributions leviable from such person. Under clause 10 the amount by whom the total value is to be deducted, shall be deducted therefrom. Under clause 11 the amount by where the total value exceeds the total amount to be deducted therefrom under any of the provisions of this Act, the net amount of loss shall be payable by the local authority in cash or by such other way, as may be mutually agreed upon by parties. Under the clause the Town Planning Administrator is required to assess the increment to be accrue in respect to each plot separately.

The appellant was the third son of Seetharama Iyer. He had no male issue but left two daughters surviving him who were minors at the time of his death. He had a brother Seetharama. He had two daughters surviving. He had three daughters surviving him. He had another brother surviving him. The appellant was the second son of Seethama Iyer. The appellant 's brother Seetharam Iyer died in 1934. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the English rule of benevolent construction that a legatee has a right to choose in such circumstances apply to India also and has further held that on the construction of the will in this case the right to choose was in the legatees and not in Seetharama, and that as his brother had died without making the selection, the lands devised to the daughters must now be partitioned in the ordinary course. Held, that the words "he shall deliver possession of the remaining properties to his son" in the will show that it was Seetharama who was the guardian of the three children will be in possession so long as the three children were minor and shall deliver possession to the children as and when they became major. The words "he will shall deliver possession" in the Will must mean that the testator intended that the daughters should get the area of land devised to them taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. The words are different in the case of daughters as compared to the words used in the case. The words of the will which show that Seetharama shall select the land to be handed over to the two daughters and stress is laid on the words " he shall deliver possession thereof to the two children as and whenever they become major. The testator was giving the right of selection to Seetharama in the case where he was bequeathing his properties to his daughters. The gift cannot be said to be void for uncertainty within the meaning of section 89, for it can be made certain by the selection of the daughters and is not so uncertain that it is impossible to make it certain.

The plaintiff appellant, Mohd. Bashir and Mohd. Rashid, was the owner of the plots in dispute. The defendants were in joint possession of the plots. The plaintiff appellant, who was the owner, was in joint possession. The defendants, however, claimed that the plaintiff was in joint ownership of the plots and that the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. The defendants denied that the plaintiff 's name was wrongly deleted from the khewat and the entire property was mutated in the consolidation of holding proceedings in the name of the defendants. The trial court accepted the allegations of the defendants and dismissed the suit of the plaintiff. The District Judge, however, found that the name of plaintiff was wrongly deleted after 1359 Fasli and there was no order of any authority or court to show the circumstances under which the plaintiff 'S name was wrongly removed nor were there any judicial proceedings under which the name of defendant was wrongly deleted nor were there no judicial proceedings under the which the name was wrongly included nor were there anything judicial proceedings under that name. The District judge also found that the plaintiff lost her title by operation of law. The District Court also found that on the admitted facts even after the abolition of zamindari, the position was that in 1357 Fasli the plaintiff ' s name was clearly recorded as a co sharer with the defendants and continued to be so until 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2. The District court further found that the names of the plaintiff were wrongly deleted after 1357 Fasli and there were no judicial proceedings pending under which the names of plaintiff as a co bhumidar were deleted. The District Collector further found that there was no judicial proceedings in which the name, of plaintiff as co bhumidar was wrongly deleted. The High Court also held that the plaintiff should be deemed to be ousted from possession, was not correct. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in law in holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the plaintiff could be deemed to have been ousted from possession. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that in second appeal, the High Court committed an error of record because the clear evidence of PW, Karbalai Begum, is to the effect that she was not at all informed about the consolidation proceedings and was assured by the defendants that they would take proper care of her share in any proceedings that may be instituted. [867C D] 2. The High Courts were, therefore, wrong in law in finding that the plaintiff, was not given any share out of the produce and, therefore, the conclusion that the plaintiff must be deemed to been ousted from the possession was not correct.[867D] 3. The High 'Court was, therefore, right in holding the present suit to be barred by section 50 of the U .P. Consolidation and Holdings Act, 1952. [868C] 4. The High courts were, therefore wrong in law and the judgment of the High Court cannot be allowed to stand.

The petitioner, who was a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was appointed as Deputy Prime Minister in the Haryana Government. He was then working as Deputy Prime Ministers in the Haryana State. He was still functioning as the Chief Minister of Haryana when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him. The oath was administered by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He maintained that yet in view of the fact that the Constitution describes him as the Prime Minister, while being sworn into office, he described himself as Prime Minister. The affidavit of Respondent No. 1 was sworn by the incumbent signing as Prime Minister, all other ministers signed as Ministers. The affidavit was sworn by Respondent No. 2. Respondent No. 3 was a member of the Council of Ministers though he was described as the Prime Ministers but the description of the petitioner as Deputy Prime minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Minister. Respondent No 1, who was the Chief Minister, was a member and there was no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Minis ter as such. The affidavit filed by Respondent No 1 was sworn on behalf of the Union of India. The affidavit in the affidavit of Respondent 1 was sworn in by the incumbent sign as Prime Minister but the description was descriptive only and for all purposes he was a Minister and there is no 3 constitutional Sanction for the post. The affidavit also stated that the form prescribed in the Third Schedule pursuant to the requirement of Article 75(4) of the Constitution is only for a Minister of the Union and there is nothing to show that the form was prescribed in the third Schedule pursuant to which the requirement of Section 75(4)(4)(4) of Act, 1951 was made. The affidavit further stated that Respondent No. I was just a Minister like other members of the Council though he has been described as Deputy Prime Mini ter as such; and that he was still functioning in the Haryana government when the oath was administered to the petitioner. The affidavit did not press it. The affidavit, therefore, did not press the same. The petitioner himself does not press it because the Prime Minister is also a member of his Council of Ministers although he has been shown as Deputy Prime Leader but the description is descriptive only and in respect of all purposes he is a Minister and the description of him as Deputy Prime Prime Minister does not confer upon him any powers or the Prime Minister along with his other submis sions, and the description is merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. The affidavit does not press the it. The petitioner, himself does not pressing it. The petition er has no force. So far as the third contention is concerned, the petitioner himself does press it.

The appellant was a public utility industry. The appellant was a private limited company. The appellant had been working for the last more than 12 months. The appellant 's union had been suspended from service on the ground that the appellant had failed to comply with the provisions of the Factories Act. The appellant contended that the stoppage of work on the night of the 1st November did not amount to a strike and did not cause any interruption in the workers ' service. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the continuity of service of the workers was broken by the interruption caused by the illegal strike and that as a consequence the workers who participated in such strike were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Factories ' Act. The High Court held that the stoppage was not a concerted action on the part of the workers and that the non permitted absence as a result of concerted refusal to work even for 2 to 4 hours in the course of a working day amounts to an illegal strike and consequently an interruption of service of a workman for the purpose of section 49 B. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The stoppage of work was not a mere concerted action. The stoppage of the work on 1st November, 1948, was not a casual strike. The stoppage was not an illegal strike. The appellant could not be denied that the stoppage amounted to a strike so as to amount to a break in the continuity of the service of the workman concerned. [757 E] (ii) The stoppage was a concerted act on the part Of the workers and the cessation of work on that night would not be treated as depriving them of the holidays under the rules and we appreciate the spirit in which this undertaking was given and hope that the workers would also take it in that spirit. [758 B] (iii) The stoppage on 1st December, 1948, fell within the definition of the word "strike" as given in section 2(q) of the and it was an illegal strike because no notice had been given to the management, the Mills being a public utility industrial industry.

The appellant, a film producer, was convicted under section 292 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . The High Court dismissed the petition, ignoring the contention that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censors and finding in the prosecution nothing vexatious or vexatious nor any material to quash the proceedings. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The film having been certified by the Central board of Film Carners, acting within their jurisdiction under the Act, thereby sanctioning the public exhibition of the film, does it furnish a justification in law for public exhibition of a film, be it obscene or not, or at any rate, does it generate a belief induced by a mistake of fact, namely, the issuance of the certificate and its effect that the certificate holder is justified by law in committing the act, which, in the absence of such certification, may constitute an offence under section 292. [501G] 2. The trial court when it hears the case may be appropriately apprised of the certificate under the Act and, in the light of our observations, it is right for the court to discharge the accused as the charge is groundless. [502C] 3. The trial Court when it hearing the case may, appropriately apprised of it and, in light of our observation, it fills the bill under section 79 it is right, for the court, to discharge the respondent as the charge was groundless. [506B] 4. The trial judge when it heits the case may not be appropriately apprised, may perhaps, be apprised of the Certificate under the Act. [503C] 5. The trial Judge when it he decides the case may appropriately apprised of that certificate under the . The Board under section 5B has to consider, before certification, all the points section 292 I P.C. prescribes. At least as a matter of interpretation, section 79 exonerates the doer because the issuance of a certificate under section 5A(1A) of the Act, does it indirectly generate a belief that he is actually justified by law.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader, was appointed as a lawyer in the Patna District, including lucrative land acquisition litigation, as part of the professional 'estate ' of a Government Pleader. He was permitted to represent the Government in all the civil cases. The petitioner was however, permitted to represent 'Government ' in all the Civil cases. The Advocate General, appearing for the State, was unable to show any provision emphasising the need for positive efforts at settlement, in suits to which the Government is a party. The petitioner, however, contended that his client 's claim as the sole representative of the Government in courts is not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviobility of the high public office of Government Pleader by politicking men in the Secretariat or by practitioners of favouritism dressed in 'little brief authority ', a deeper issue in which the Bar has a stake and the Bench must also be concerned. The petitioner also contended that his clients ' claim as the only representative of the State Government in courts are not a legal entity for seeking lucare but for hatching the inviolability of the High Court, the Bench must have also been concerned. The contention of the petitioner was that the official income, expected from this heavy harvest of cases, of Rs. 'Government Pleader ' includes any officer appointed by the State Government to perform all or any of the functions expressly imposed by this Code on the Government Pleader and also any pleader acting under the directions of the Government Pleader. The petitioner contended that his claim as the Sole representative of the government in courts is a legal cover and for vindicating his inviobility by practising advocates. The petitioner further contended that the official Income, expected from the high office of Government Advocate, that his client owes no duty to the public at all and that for that reason he would not be the holder of a Public office. The petitioner relied on the provisions of the Advocates Act, 1961, and the Rules framed thereunder, and contended that the Government Pleader is only an agent of the Government, that his duties are only to the Government who are his Principles and that he owes no duty, to the public exchequer and that for this reason he would be the holder. The petitioner 's case was that the officials income, expected to be from this heavy crop of cases, and that he owed no duty to his public at all, and that for the sake of the lucrative practice of a single government Pleader, a deeper Issue in which theBar has a stake, and the Bench should also be concerned, the office must be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. The petitioner urged that his client was the sole representative and that he ought to have been appointed as a Pleader in all the cases. The State Government Pleader, however, did not contest the claim of the petitioner. The petitioner then contended that his case was a claim of monopoly of all government cases in the Patna High Court including lucre loving appetite for law offices, in the absence of a wholesome ceiling on lawyer 's fees, and more fees if they were contested 763 cases and this lures a lawyer, like any other homo economics, to calculate income on a speculative basis, as this Government Pleader has done in hoping for a lakh of rupees. The petitioner therefore contended that his plea that his client is the sole representative, of the Government of Bihar, is not a valid claim for seeking lu cre but for an vindicating the eviobility of high public office by politic pressing men in the Secretarial men in the Department of Justice, a deeper issues in which the bar has been imposed, are issues of moment in a developing society controlled by the politics of skill and enjoying a legal monopoly.

The appellants held the shares of the Bank of India in favour of the appellants. The Mills exercised the right to take over only 66 shares out of the shares offered by the Bank of the Bank. The shares were offered by the Mills to its nominees. The Mills did not distribute any dividend. The Mills, however, did not distribute the right among the shareholders as dividend. The shareholders, however, decided to sell the shares to its nominees, and the right to the remaining 1,600 shares was thus distributed among its 800 share holders. The Mills decided to sell them to its nominees and the request for allotment to its nominees was rejected by the Mills. The Mills thereupon filed a petition under section 66(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the Mills to allot the shares to the appellants was rejected by a Single Judge of the High Court. The High Court held that the distribution of the right to apply for the shares of this company amounted to a distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income Tax Act. The High court also held that the release by the Mills of the shares of Rs. 100 was not a distribution of "dividend" within the meaning Of section 2(7A) of Income Tax Act and that the value of the right released in favour of shareholders though taxable under section 12 of the Act had escaped tax. The appellants contended that the distribution amounted to a "dividends" and the value of that right was indisputably the value of "dewividend" and the valuation of the right release in favour of each shareholder was indisputably the valuation of that right. Held, that the distribution was not a "dewewividend". The distribution of the rights to apply for and obtain two shares of the Mills amounted to distribution of dividend. The right to apply was a right of the value of Rs.100 for acquiring the new share. The right was thus a right of a value of Rs 100 for acquiring the old share. The Mills had no right to sell the right to its shares in the market, and to distribute the proceeds among the shareholders. The resolution did not purport to distribute the right amongst the shareholders as dividends. The resolution was not a resolution for distribution of dividend; it did not purport merely to distribute the rights amongst the shareholders. It did not purport either to distribute the shares of a company or to distribute the surplus proceeds among the shareholder. The resolution, it was true, did not purport not distribute the rights among the shareholders, as dividend. It did, did not take the form of a resolution for the distribution of dividend, it took the form of distribution of a right which had a monetary value. But by the form of the resolution sanctioning the distribution, the true character of the resolution could not be altered.

The appellant was elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The election petitioner was declared elected. The appellant challenged the election of the returned candidate on the ground that the election petitioner was not entitled to the privilege of examining his 54 witnesses who according to him, were kept present. The High Court rejected the petition holding that the election petition was not maintainable. The appellant filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of order XVI is in respect of witnesses to procure whose presence the assistance of the Court is t necessary. If the party wants to produce its witnesses without the assistance of Court, it can do so under Rule 1A of order XVI irrespective of the fact whether the name of such witness is mentioned in the list or not. Sub rule (3) of Rule I confers a wider jurisdiction on the Court to cater to a situation where the party has failed to name the witness in the list and yet the party is unable to produce him or her on his own under Rule 1 A and in such a situation the party of necessity has to seek the assistance of court under sub rule(3) to procure the presence of such a witness by issuing a summons through the Court or otherwice which ordinarily the court would not extend for procuring the attendance of a witness whose name is not shown in the list. But if on the date fixed for recording the evidence, the party is able to keep his witnesses present despite the fact that the names of the witnesses are not shown in that list, the party would be entitled to examine these witnesses and to produce documents through the witnesses who are called to produce documents under Rule 1. But if the party would not be in a position to produce its witness without the assistance, it can be done under Rule 1(A) of order XVI. [501B C] 2. The only jurisdiction the Court has to decline to examine the witness is the one set out in proviso to Section Save this the Court has no jurisdiction to decline to summon the witness produced by the party and kept present when the evidence of the party is being recorded and is not closed, and the Court has not jurisdiction to refuse to examine the witnesses produced by the parties. [502C] 3. The only Jurisdiction the Court has jurisdiction to decline the examination of the witness is that the party has sufficient cause for the omission to mention the name of the witness in his list and yet, the party of need has to seek assistance of the court under sub Rule (3) to procuring the presence of the witness and the Court may if it is satisfied that the party had sufficient cause for his omission to mention his name in the list filed under sub rule.(1) of rule 1, the Court may still extend its assistance for procuring the presence by issuing a summon through the Court. [503D] 4. The only power the Court has under sub rule 1A of Order XVI is in relation to witnesses to procure their attendance on being summoned through the Court, it is obligatory on the party to file the list with the gist of evidence of witnesses in the Court as directed by sub rule (2) of Rule1. But if it is implicit in Rule 1A that it only enables the party to examine only those witnesses whose names are mentioned in the lists filed under sub Rule(1) of Order XVI irrespective of whether the name is mentioned in that list or not, the party will be entitled to examined these witnesses and the Court shall, if it is established that the party is in a position in to produce its evidence without the assistance or of the Court, refuse to examine such witness. [505E F] 5.

The appellant was appointed as Principal of the College in the year 1981. The appellant was appointed on May 1, 1981. The Committee of Management of the College issued an appointment order on April 27, 1981 to the appellant informing him that the Committee of Management had suspended or withdrawn power of appointment of teaching staff including Principal and that therefore the Committee of management had no power to make any appointment and therefore the appointment of the appellant alleged to have been made on May 1. 1981 was not valid. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of her Principal on the ground that the order contained in the radiogram had suspended or withdraw its power. The High Court held that the radiograms contained an order of the State Government in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointment conferred on the Committee of the Management to make appointment notwithstanding the fact that the order had contained an order in the radiagram had suspended, withdrawn or suspended it would not be open to the Selection Committee to make any appointments and therefore the order contained therein was not valid and power to make appointment. The High court held that the Radiogram had no power of appointment to make the appointment. The appellant contended that the radiagrams contained an appointment order of the Government in discharge Of its executive functions suspended or withdrawn its power. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order contained in radiogram was communicated to the Manager of the Institution. If the order was valid and power had to be exercised by the Committee of Manager, the State Government was bound to hear the appellant before making any consequential order. [980D] 2. The appointment was otherwise valid, though ineffective and if appellant under the orders of the High Court functioned as Principal, discharged his duties and was paid, no question of recovery of amount paid to him could arise and neither the Government nor the Committee ofManagement nor the Institution would be entitled to recover any salary paid to the appellant. [982E] 3. The appointment of the Principal was otherwise valid though ineffective and the appellant under the order of the High court functioned as principal, discharged his functions and was paid. No question of recovery could arise and no question of Recovery of amount paid from the appellant could arise and nor the Government or the Committee of Board of Management could issue appointment order dated April 27,1981 to the appellant and the appointment of appellant would be by a body not authorised to make the appointments. [983F] 4. The appointment order was otherwise valid and power could be withdrawn or suspended. [984F] 5. The appointment is otherwise valid, although ineffective and if the appellant under orders of the Court functioned in Principal, discharged duties and was payment, no question could arise and Neither the Government nor of the Committee of Education could issue appointment orders.

The petitioners, manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and weave it into a fabric in the same way as is being done by the first petitioner". The petitioners state that the manufacturers of tyres, to whom the fabrics are supplied "imPregnate the fabrics with rubber and Weave it into an a fabric in a similar manner as in other ordinary textile". The petitioners further state that, as some questions were put in the Rajasthan State Legislative Assembly on or about 20th April, 1971, asking for the reason why this particular type of goods of the petitioners were exempted from Sales tax, the Commissioner of Commercial Tax issued a letter to the Commercial Tax Officer to levy Sales tax on the "rayon cord fabric" manufactured by the petitioners. The petitioners state, that, as many as the questions were put, in the RajasthanState Legislative Assembly on 20th April 1971, asking the Commissioner of Sales Tax issued a Letter to the Commercial Taxes Officer to levy sales tax on the 'rayon cord fabrics" manufactured by them. The petitioners further stated that, as certain questions were put to the petitioners, they were exempted from sales tax, the Commissioners of Commercial Tax, issued a letter asking for the reasons why this particular kind of goods of their petitioners were exempted therefrom from Sales tax. The petitioners stated that, in the case before the High Court, the "tyre cord fabric" was an "textile" fabric manufactured by it and that it serves as part of raw material for what ultimately ultimately goes into the manufacture of a fabric. The petitioners also stated that, "rayon tyre cord fabric" is "a textile consisting of rayon threads in the warp and cotton threads in warp and Cotton threads in a warp and is manufactured on weaving looms in the same manner as in another ordinary textile. " The petitioners state further that, as the various varieties of cotton fabrics are mentioned in item 19, the "ties" which they sell in the market are entitled to exemption, but the various varieties are mentioned in items 19 and 22 of the first schedule of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1941, as the applicable entry covering the goods manufactured by the petitioner. The petitioners, further, contended that, as there was no sufficient reason for overriding and discarding the High Court 's view that, on what appeared to the High Court to be a question of fact, it should not decide whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabric entitled to exemption. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The question, therefore, to be determined by the Tax authorities themselves is whether the product is a fabric entitled for exemption. [501 D] 2. The question is whether the "tyset fabric" is a fabric which is a textile? [501 E] 3. The question whether the "textile fabric" is the end product for the Delhi Cloth Mills, which is a Textile fabric and not any other kind of fabric. [502 D] 4. The question of fact is whether the goods under consideration constitute a fabric entitled 'to exemption. [504 E] 5. The question must be determined by a Tax authorities themselves are whether the product for which the Delhi Cloth Mill claims exemption Is a textile fabric and not whether any other kind is fabric entitled to the exemption. [506 G] 6. The question should be determined by Tax authorities themselves. [503 D] 7. The question as to whether the "Textile fabric" manufactured is the end products or not is quite irrelevant. It requires careful consideration of the technical processes of manufacturing, of the composition of the "tyle cord fabric" and an evaluation of opinion of experts on the subject, to be able to decide the question satisfactorily.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal washeries on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied and incidental work. The respondent was a Senior Supervisor in the company 's establishment at Dhanbad. When the matter was thus pending consideration the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour Court Dhanbad since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would be convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour Court Patna. The Government of Bihar, by its order dated September 8, 1988, transferred the case to the Labour Court, Patna for speedy disposal from the stage at which the case was transferred. The Government howev er, has acceded to the request of the respondent and without opportunity to 294 the management transferred the case. In exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of section 33 B of the (14 of 1947) the Governor of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the petitioner Shri Shivajee Prasad Sinha wherein he has prayed for the transfer of the case to Labour Court, Ranchi, regu larly due to his residence at Hajipur is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure 'A ' pending before Labour Court, Dhanbad and transfer the said proceeding to the Labour court, Patna for expeditious disposal from the Stage at which the Case is transferred. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of transfer. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Government was misled by the representation of the workman. The Government, therefore, was misled by representation of the workmen. [295E] 2. The Government is misled by the representations of the workman and not seriously disputed the factum of his residence in the colony quarter at Dhanbad. [295G] 3. The order of transfer in that case was quashed for not communi cating reasons to the assessee. This takes us to the reasons given by the Government in support of the order of transferred. Reference may also be made to a letter (Annexure E) from the Assistant Electrical Engineer in proof of the electricity supplied to the quarter occupied by the workman at Dhanbad. In fact, in the counter affidavit, he has not denied the documents annexed to the Special Leave Petition, and not seriously controverted the factum of residence of the workman in the colony quarters at Dhanbad. The order is quashed for not predi cating the reasons to the prejudice of the normal procedure laid down in section 64(1) and (2) of the Act. [295A] 4. The order transferring the case from the Labour Court to the Labour C ourt, Patna is quashed for non not communi tating reasons to th e assessee.

The appellant, a hotel, was a registered trade union of the hotel and its workmen as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi. The appellant, a partner of the hotel, was the managing director of the hotel. The appellant was the managing Director of the hotel but was the managing partner of the Hotel. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for a writ of certiorari to quash the order of reference. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the reference was incompetent and two grounds had been urged in support of it. Held, that the reference which was otherwise valid did not become incompetent merely because it was mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by such and such union in the dispute. The fact that in the order of Reference the words " as represented by" were added for the sake of convenience as to where the notice to the workmen should be sent would not in our opinion make the reference incompetent merely because the workmen would be represented by some officer, such as its president or secretary and it is that officer who will actually represent the workmen before the tribunal, and it is not that officer who would actually represent the workman before the tribunal. The fact remains that the dispute which was referred for adjudication was between the employer and its employees which were mentioned as its workmen. The fact therefore that in the reference the words "as represented by the hotel Workers ' Union Katra Shahangrahi, Chandani Chowk, Delhi " have been added for the purpose of convenience as indicated in the order. The fact, therefore, that in the absence of any mention of any officer of the trade union, but mentioning the union itself, the reference in this form was incompetent.

The Collector, however, held that the parts of the engines mentioned under Heading No. 84.06 were parts of the internal combustion piston engines, and that the parts were parts of internal combustion pists. The Collector also held that the part of the engine or engines mentioned under heading 84.06, were parts of parts of the Engine and not a few parts thereof. The Collector further held that the goods imported by the appellants were parts of engines referred to in Heading No. 85.06 and not parts of the machinery referred to in the Heading No.84.06. The Collector appealed to the Collector. The Collector held that the imported parts were parts and not parts thereof. He also held that parts of the parts were covered by Heading No. 87.06 and that the part imported by the Appellant were parts of machinery referred to under Heading No 84.06.
