Therefore, the parts mentioned under Heading no. 84.05 are excluded from the benefit of Notification. [228G H] 1.4 The Notification exempts all parts of the tractor mentioned under Heading 89.06 which include parts of machinery specified in column (2) of the Table and falling under Heading No 87.06 which also includes parts of machinery, such parts shall get the benefit under the Notification. The Notification does not, however, contain or refer to the parts of parts mentioned under heading other than Heading No. 89.06. It includes parts of the tractors mentioned under Heading 90.06 which must be all the parts constituting the engine or engine in question. [228F G] 2.1 The notification exempts also parts from the benefit under Notification. [229H] 2.2 The notification exempts parts of motor vehicles mentioned in Heading 84.04 which are included in Heading No 84,06 which are specified in column(2) of Table annexed to the Notification, irrespective of the fact that they or any or some of them have already been included under Heading 84,06. The Notification exempts further parts of the vehicles mentioned under heading 90.06. which are included within Heading No. 90.06 and which also include parts of motor vehicle mentioned under Heading 91.06. This Notification does not however, contain any or other parts thereof. [228H] 2:3 The Notification does no, however, mention the parts of engines mentioned under headings 84.06 to 84.06 not only contemplates the engine or parts thereof.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration that the right and management of the Dargah according to Muslim Law devolved on their two sons and one daughter, namely, Sayed Gaffar Sahib, Sayed Mohideen and Fathima Bee in proportion of 2:2 respectively. The defendants contended that the plaintiffs were not entitled to any right in the management or share in the offerings in the Dargah and even if they were entitled to any rights or claim the same was barred by limi tation. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was right in holding that the rights of Fathima Suraksha Bee had become barred by limitation by ouster and as such the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathima oi Bee were also not entitled to the right of management or posses sion in a Dargah and on that account they were also not entitle to any right of ownership or posses tion. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The only controversy now left to be determined is whether the High Court had right in holding the right in holding t he right of management and posses sions in a Dargah. [529G] 2.1 The only controversy left to be decided is whether the rights of the plaintiffs were specifically denied on any particular occa sion so as to put them on notice that from that date the possession of the defendants would be adverse to the inter est or rights of the appellants of Fathiman Bee. [530G] 2:2 The only controversy is whether the right of Fathil Bee to the share of the plaintiffs and on the question that females are also entitled in the right and the management of the wakf as well as the plaintiffs. [531C] 2.3 The only controversy here left to be determination is whether the courts below were right in holding in the right or claim of any share in the management of Dargah or any claim in the offerings of Dargah. [525C] 2:4 The only controversy that remains to be determined was whether the High court was right in declaring that the rights were barred by limitation. [532D] 2:5 The only controversy before this Court was whether the rights were specifically denied or not. The only question is whether the plaintiffs were claiming ouster on the basis of expressed denial of Fathmatma Bee from the fight or management of the Wakf. [533G] 2 :6 The only controversy was whether the defendants were claiming ouster of Fathim Bee from the right or title of any share of the Dargah or any claims in the offerings. This clearly goes to show that relations between Fathima pair and her brothers were cordial and as such there was no question of any knowledge to Fathimaira Bee that she was being ousted from her right or share in any of the offerings. [534G] 2(a) The only controversy then left to be determine is whether the court was right or not. [535G] 2.(b) The only question that remains to determine is whether there was any dispute now as regards the period of 27 days falling to the share or management of Dargah. The only issue is whether the defendants are claiming ouster on any particular oca sion. [536G] 2 (a) The plaintiffs were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under the Muslim Law were not entitled. They were carrying a wrong mistaken impression all throughout along that females were not entitled or entitled to any share in their offerings. [525G] 2 2.6 The only question whether females were entitled to a share in the Dargah or not is whether the Court was right or wrong in holding that females were entitled or not to any share.

The appellant was employed as a railway employee in the respondent 's railway department. He was allotted railway quarters of a suitable type and as he had refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowance. The appellant 's claim was rejected on the ground that there had been no illegal deduction from the respondent ''s wages inasmuch as the respondent had been allotted railway quarters by a suitable type, and as he refused to occupy the quarters he was entitled to the house rent allowance, and that even so, the appellant was not entitled to withhold the house rent allowances. The Authority held that the house rent Allowance claimed by the appellant was "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Authority and the Appellate Authority held that there had not been illegal deduction from his wages inasmuch as there had been illegal deduction of the house rent by the respondent '. The Appellate Authority held against the appellant. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to withhold house rent allowance as part of his wages. The appellant contended that the house Rent allowance claimed by the 1st respondent was "wages", and that the appellant had been allotted Railway quarters of a similar type and as the respondent was allotted railway quarter of a suitable kind and as he was refused to occupy them he was not liable under the rules. The High court held that the rule quoted above was inconsistent with the provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the Act and that in any event, if rule 3(i) aforesaid were to be considered as a part of the terms of the contract between the employer and the employee, section 23 of the Act prohibits an employee from entering into such a contract as has the effect of depriving him of his vested rights. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the rules which must be included in the terms of contract between the employers and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one 173 1352 of the specified places would cease to be so entitled. The rules do not make the grant in such absolute terms. Once an employee of the description given above has been offered suitable house accommodation and he has refused it, he ceases to be entitled to the House Rent Allowance and that allowance thus ceases to be "wages" under the definition in the Act.

The detenu, who was one Indru 's father, was arrested on February 18, 1980, by the Customs Officers, on the ground that he had acquired the gems in question from those persons. The detenu was arrested on March 25, 1980, and was served with a detention order, dated February 15, 1980, purporting to have been made under section 3(1) of the (for short "the COFEPOSA) by the State Government, was served on the detenus. On March 25,1980, the detenu received a letter, dated March 14, 1980 from the State Government refusing to supply the copies of the statements and documents relied upon in the grounds of detention. On April 3, 1980, the wife of the detenu, Ram Chand Bharvani, addressed a letter to the first respondent (Under Secretary to the Government of Maharashtra), requesting him to furnish the detenus with the material relied upon by the detaining authority in the grounds. On March 14,1980, a letter to him declining the request for supply of copies to the detenu, was received by the detenus on April 3,1980. On April 4, 1980, a letter was addressed to the first Respondent (Under Secretary, Home Department, to the first and the State Government requesting him to supply the detenus with material relied upon in grounds of detention, to enable them to make an effective representation. On April 5, 1980, copies were received by the detenu on April 3. On April 6, 1980, another letter was addressed by the detenu to the first respondents requesting him to make an appropriate representation. On May 2, 1980, when the detenu received the letter, the detenu replied that he had received the letter on April 3 and that he had not received the letter. On April 7, 1980, he received a letter from the State Minister declining the request of the detenu. On April 8, 1980, an order of detention, purporting to be signed by the first respondent, was served upon the detenus. The detenu received a communication from the State Secretary to the State Government on March 14, 1981, requesting him to submit the detenus with all the material relied on in the grounds, of detention. The detenu, however, received a letter on April 4, 1981, from the State Ministry requesting him to give the copies of certain statements and documents to the detenu. The detenu replied that the statements of which copies were asked for by the detenus had been incorporated in those grounds 'grounds ' which were served on the detenu, that in such a situation, the 'grounds served on the detained detenu, were more than sufficient to enable him to make a full and effective representation at the earliest. The detenu thereafter received a letter dated March 14. 1980 from the Government requesting him not to supply the copy of the statements, and documents to enable him, to make an independent representation. The detenu also received a letter addressed to the State Minister, requesting him not supply the copies and conveyed rejection of this request by a letter dated February 14, 1980. The detenu thereupon received a letter refusing to supply copies to the detenus on the ground of delay. On April 9, 1980, after a delay of more than three weeks, the copies were put in a course of communication to the detenus by the State Minister under their covering letter, dated April 3, 1981. On April 10, 1980, on the request of a detenu, the detenu was served with the detention order, purporting to had been made under Section 3(1), of the (For short "the Act"). On April 3. 1980, the detenu made a written request to the detaining authority on February 18. On April 11, 1980, again, copies were supplied.

The appellant was convicted by one of the accused persons for having committed offences under section 120B read with section 120B I.P.C. and section 120B, I.P., and section 120 B I.P, and section 120 A I.P.. The High Court held that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 was against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against the acquittal of several accused persons tried jointly. The High Court also held that the Full Bench decision of the Gujarat High Court in Beorajan 's case was not binding on it. On the question whether the Full Bench judgment of the GujaratHigh Court was correct in holding that the Full bench decision of the High Court was not binding, HELD : (i) The Full Bench decision in Rabari Ghela Jadav 's case did not militate against the maintainability or the maintainability of the joint appeal by a State against several accused persons acquitted at a joint trial. [446 B] (ii) The Full bench decision in Rabri Ghela GhelaJadav 's Case was inconsistent with Chapter XXXI of Criminal Procedure, with the result that a joint appeal to the High Court by several accused persons convicted at one trial was not maintainable. [447 C] (iii) The Full Court decision of the Bombay High Court was inconsistent with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure with the result, that a joint trial to the High court by a common order acquitting several accused persons was not maintainable, and therefore not legally prohibited. [448 D] (iv) The Full court decision of the Madras High Court in Rabari Jadav 'S case was inconsistent with section 419 of the Code on the basis of which the judgment of the High court mainly proceeds, merely lays down that the Appellate Court hearing an appeal cannot admit it only on a question of sentence and that such a restricted order of admission being invalid, the appellant would be entitled to insist that his appeal should be heard on the merits.

The appellant was a firm called O.R.M.SP. Firm which was registered under section 26(A) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed that the foreign business of the appellant was charged to tax under the 1918 Act. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim holding that in the case of business carried on in foreign territory the business as such was not assessed under section 3 of the 1918 Act but only receipt of the income in British India was assessed and it cannot therefore be held that the foreign income of the appellant is chargeable to tax under section 3. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that in view of the provisions of section 3 of 1918 Act the assessee was not entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to exemption under section 25 (3) of 1922 Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the foreign company was only taxed on remittances received from the profits of the foreign business and there was no tax on the foreign business itself under the 1918 act. HELD : (i) The assessee was entitled, to exemption under s. 25(3), with regard to the rental income from house properties owned by the foreign firm which was discontinued in the year of account. [912 D] (ii) The exemption under section 26 (3) is general. The exemption under s 25(3)(a) is general and is general. [913 E] (iii) The exemption is general. It is manifest that by section 3 of 1922 Act the charge was made on the receipt of income in British Indian and as the income received by the assessee was derived from the foreign business, it must be taken that there was an assessment to tax on the Indian business within the meaning of section 25(2) of the 1918 act.[913 B] (iv) The exemption of tax under section 25 is general. In other words, the tax is payable by an assessee but the assessment of the tax is on the basis of various heads of income derived by the assessee one of which is business. It is obvious that by section 4 of the 1918 Income tax Act the charge is made on the income of the year of assessment. It is not possible to say that the exemption under section 24(3)(b) is general in nature. [914 C D] (v) The exemption granted under section 25 of the 1922 act is general. There is no reason to restrict the condition of the applicability of the exemption under s . 25(3). [914 F] (vi) The exemption was general. The assessee was not liable to pay tax under the 1922 Act because what was taxed was the remittances received by the appellant from the foreign company and not the foreign business. [915 G] (vii) The exemption in section 25(1) is general, and is general in character. The ratio of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that there was no reason to restricting the condition of applicability of the Exemption under section 25.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said Department for the construction of the Capital Project, Bondhinagar. The contract provided that the contractor shall give notice to the Executive Engineer or his Assistant of his intention of making delivery of materials and on the materials being approved, receipt shall be granted to him by the Executive Engineer, or his Assistant. The contractor received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. At the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the Public works Department of the Govern ment of Gujarat on the September 6,1965, is in fact a works contract. " The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the transaction was a works contract and not a works contract, and that the transaction envisaged in the contract was a works Contract. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The contract in this case is a contract of sale and not a work contract. The contract in the instant case is a works contract of sale. The property in the bricks was entirely of the assessee. The essence of the contract was, therefore, the delivery of the bricks after manufacture. [163C D] Chandra Bhan Gosain`s case, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 890, followed.

The petitioner, a member of the Legislative Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir, was elected as a member of a Legislative Assembly of the State of Jammu and in the year 1975, he was elected as the President of India. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency issued on 3.12.1971 by the President of Jammu and Srinagar, on the ground that the duration of the House of the People could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of Emergency was in force under the proviso to clause (2) of Article 83 of the Constitution and since the two Proclamations of Emergency dated 3rd December, 1971 and 25th June, 1975 were either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased to be in operation by the time the House of People (Extension of Duration) Act, 1976 was passed by Parliament, the House of which the petitioner was a member, had no effect and consequently all Acts passed by the House of that People during the extended period including the Finance Act, 1976 (Act 30 of 1976) were ultra vires the constitutional Constitution. The petitioner contended that the duration for which the House of Parliament may, under clause (2), continue from the date appointed for its first meeting) in relation to the present House of the people shall, while the Proclamation of emergency issued on 3rd December 1971 and on the 25th June 1975 were both in operation, be extended for a period of one year. The petitioner also contended that the period of five years in relation to which the House was originally constituted by the President was not extended by the Proclamation of the Emergency issued on 26th June, 1977 and the Proclamation of Proclamation of Emergency dated 25th June. 1975 had ceased to operate by 26th August, 1975 because the resolutions passed by the two Houses of Parliament approving the two Pro clamations of emergency as required by clause (2)(a) of Article 352 of the Constitution as it stood during the relevant time had not been published in the official Gazette of the Government of India. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The two Proclams of Emergency were kept in force by virtue of the resolutions passed in each of the two Houses. [419D] 2. The Proclamation of Emergency of 3rd December. 1971 and on 25th June of 1975 were both both in operation. But the real question in this case is whether the two Pro clsamations of Defence of India were validly issued or not. [421E] 3. The production of the Lok Sabha Debates and of the Rajya Sabha Debates containing the proceedings of the two ProClamations of Temporary Emergency were kept open to the petitioner to contend that the two Pro Clamations of Proclamation were kept in operation by virtue of resolutions passed by Parliament until they were duly revoked by the two Procts which were issued by the Vice President acting as President of India in the year 1977. Since the two Pronsamations of Natural Justice were in force when the House of The People (Extension) Act, 1975 (Act 30 Of 1976) was passed its validity cannot be questioned. [422D] 4. The production and production of the Rajya Samity Debates and of Rajya Sabha Debates contain the proceedings of both the Houses of Parliament relating to the period between the time when the resolutions were passed in each House of the Parliament and the time when resolutions were duly adopted amounts to proof of the said resolutions. [423C] 5. The production, of the Lok Samity Debates containing the proceeding of the two House of Parliament relating To the period between 1st December, 1971 when the House was passed, in relation to that the present House was passed its valid validity cannot be challenged. [424D] 6.

The appellant was the owner of a public temple. The appellant claimed that the property belonged to the Thoguluva Thirumalayyan, the appellant 's ancestor, for a sum of Rs. 20,000/ and that the said premises were private property of the family. The Trial Court decreed the suit in favour of the appellant holding that the said property did not constitute a temple and set aside the decision of the said authorities. On appeal, the High Court reversed the said decision and held that the property in dispute was a public temple within the meaning of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The appellant thereupon filed a petition for leave to appeal to this Court. The main question in the suit was whether the property belonged exclusively to the Thuguluva Thirukoilalayyan, and that it was alienable property of the said family. The High Court reversed that decision and held in favour of appellant holding that it was incapable of valuation as it could have in either case no market value. The appellant then filed a petition in the High Court for a declaration that the said building was private property of his family and for an order setting aside the said decision. The High court reversed the decision of Trial Court and held that it was a public religious temple within the definition of the said Act. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that whether the property was a private or a public temple, it was incapable o valuation. [157 B] (2) The High court was wrong in holding that the property was the private property of that family. [157 C] (3) The High ' Court was wrong, in proceeding on that assumption. [157 D] (4) The High Courts were wrong in proceeding in on the assumption.

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the respondent company. The appellant was employed in the respondent Company. The appellant claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements at present made by the appellant. The Tribunal granted the first claim and directed that the clerical staff should be paid As. /8/ per day and the subordinate staff As. /9/ per day on all working days in lieu of tiffin arrangement which were at present made, by the appellant, the appellant should stop the re employment of retired workmen in the category of clerks above 'C ' grade. The appellant contended that the Tribunal had erred in law in making an award in respect of the cash allowance for tiffin, because he argues that it is not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tiff in its employees. Held, that the Tribunal has overlooked the fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appellant in re employing the retired personnel and, in fact, when after the award was pronounced in the proceedings of 1956 and this question was taken up for direct negotiations between the parties, the appellant agreed to consider the claim sympathetically and make a suitable provision in that behalf. The fact that the appellant was introducing a wage structure in respect of its reemployed personnel was certainly inferior to the wage structure devised for the employees of the appellant by the award , and that clearly cannot be permitted under industrial law. The fact of the matter introduces a serious infirmity in the appellant 's case as it was presented before the Tribunal by the appellant can have no material bearing in dealing with the point. The fact, that the re employment was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations, cannot be permitted to be ignored. The fact was that the re employes have made an express affidavit supporting the practices adopted by the appellants, can have no bearing in dealing With the point.

The respondent, a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund, was governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules, whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. On August 26, 1947, Browne addressed a letter to the Chief Accounts Officer communicating the sanction of the General Manager for payment of the special contribution to the provident fund to Browne in sterling in terms of r. 1413 of the Provident Fund Account Rules, whereunder payments of the provident Fund credited in his accounts in rupees were on retirement to he made in sterling and to transmit the fund in sterling to the bankers of Browne in England. The respondent, however, did not send the amount by bank draft or under the later intimation by payment to the respondent. The respondent thereupon filed a suit for recovery of the amount due from him on the ground that they represented provident fund money which by section 3 of the , was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court confirmed the order of attachment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court was in error in holding that the money in the hands of the Reserve Bank had ceased to be provident fund money and was liable to be attached. [1413 F] (2) The High court was in error by holding that the amount in the hands was exempt from attachment. [1414 F] (3) The High ' Court was in wrong in holding that by sending the two cheques to the respondent, the obligation of the Railway Administration could be discharged and not till then. [1415 F] (4) The High Courts were in error in observing that the money was discharged and the money must be deemed to have been paid out to the subscriber Browne. The order of attachment of the amount into which the two cheques drawn by the Railway Administration were converted on encashment was contrary to the terms of section 3 of . The order of attach of the amount in which the two cheque drawn by the respondent were converted on encashed was contrary to section 3 of , and the money was liable to attachment. [1515 F G] (5) The High "Court was in error, in holding that in the absence of any provision in the Provident Fund Act, the amount in question was liable to attach.

The appellant was a workman in a factory. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been guilty of misconduct. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal before the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the motivation for the termination was the suspicion which lurked in the mind of the Regional Manager that information regarding tenders was being passed on by the workman '. The Labour appellate Tribunal held that even in a case like the present the requirement of bona fides was essential and if the termination of service was a colourable exercise of the power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, the industrial tribunal would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. The Labour Court held that the motive for the termination of the services was the suspicion that the information regarding tenders were being passed on, by the workman. The Labour Tribunal also held that the action was not a disguise or cloak for dismissing the employee and the ground given that he was a cantankerous person undesirable to be retained was good. The Labour 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. HELD: (1) The Court was satisfied that the termination was a colourable exercising of the power vested in the management or as a consequence of victimisation or victimisation or unfair Labour practice practice. [417 B] (2) The power of the Court to go behind the form of the order is reaffirmed there. For instance, Vaidialingam J., speaking for the Court, observed that if the exercise of such power is challenged on the ground of being colourable or mala fide or an act of victimisation or an act or of victimisation or any unfair labour practice practice, the employer must disclose to the Court the grounds of his impugned action so that the same may be tested judicially. [418 C] (3) The power to go behind a form of the termination simpliciter may be bow fide, not colourable, and loss of confidence may be evidentiary of good faith of the employer. If the exercise of the powers is challenged on ground of being malafide or an actof victimisation or unfair trade practice, the employee must disclose to Court the grounds for his impugned action, so that the said same may be tests judicially. [518 C D] (4) The power is absolute and unfettered and is subject to the restrictions and conditions imposed by the statute. [519 E] (5) The power under the order is absolute and is subject only to the restrictions imposed by the Act.

The petitioners, who were the victims of the alleged serious breaches of duty in sanctioning permission for the conduct of the 'eye camp ', were charged with having committed serious breaches of duties in sanctioning permission to the conduct of 'eye Camp ' without ensuring a strict compliance with the conditions prescribed in the guidelines prescribed by the Government in that behalf and in not effectively dis charging the duties enjoined upon them to over see the satisfactory and safe functioning of the camp. The State Government issued a Notification dated 9.2.1988, inviting the Chief Medical Officer, Uttar Pradesh, to make a reference to the State Government for incorporation in their Revised Guidelines dated 9.3.1988. The petitioners, who had been paid a sum of Rs.5,000, were charged for having committed serious breach of duty in granting permission for the conducting of the 'Yeye camp' without ensuring a proper compliance with the condition prescribed in the Guidelines prescribed by the State Government in that respect and in not properly dis charging the duty enjoined upon them under the guidelines prescribed in the said Guidelines. The petitioners challenged the Notification on the ground that the State Government had no power to issue the Notification under section 3 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the State would approach the matter not with the spirit of a litigant in any adversy action but would look upon the proceedings as a participatory exploration for relief to the victims. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State would approach to the matter not in with the spirit o f a litigant in a adversy action But would look upon, the proceedings as an participatory explorationfor relief to the victim. These matters would have to be gone into in the criminal and other proceedings that may be pending or in the contemplation of the Government. However, the State would, however, be willing to render help to the victims within the constraints of its resources. These matters will have to be go into in the Criminal and other proceedings, that may be Pending or in the contemplated of the Government, their cases shall be considered for such benefit. [410E F] 1.2 The State would, therefore, approach the matter, not with the proposal of the Union Government for incorporation. The State would also, be willing, to render help, to the victims, within the constraints o f their resources. These matter would have to go into in a criminal and other proceeding that may be initiated or in the progress of the Government.[410B] 1.3 The State would be willing to make help to the affected victims within the limitations of its resources.[410C] 1.4 The State would pay a further sum of Rs,5,000.00 to the victims in accordance with the procedure adopted at the time of administration of the interim relief. [412D] 1.5 The amount shall be deposit ed, as was done in the matter of distribution of interim relief, with the District Judge who shall arrange to dis tribute the same in accordance with procedure adopted at that time of administration. [413E] 1.6 The amount shall, be deposit ed as aforesaid, as was made in the matter o f distribution of interim reliefs, with the State Government. The amount shall also be deposit ed. [414F] 1.7 The amount shall not be deposit ed to, as was happened in the matter. The amount, shall be deposited, as was directed in the matter, as was in the matter Of distribution of interim Relief, with the district Judge who shall ensure dis tribute to the victims.[415E] 1:8.

The petitioner No. 1 was the President of the Anom Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti. He was elected as a member of the Anam Rashtrabhatha Prachar Samity. The petitioner No. 2 was the President. The petitioner challenged the legality of the action taken by the respondent State Government under the Asom Rashtrabahasha Pra Prachar Samiti (Taking over of Management and Control) Act, 1984. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. Hence this Writ Petition. Allowing the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Act and the noti fication issued under the Act take over the management of the Anim Rashtrabha Prachar Parishad. [176G] 1.2 The Karyapalika and Byabasthapika Sabha which were in existence in 1984 when initially the action under the emergency provi sions was taken followed by the notification under the Ordinance and the Act shall be restored back and they shall take over the Management of the Samiti from the Board imme diately but it is made clear that the Karyapalika, and Bya basthapika Panchayat which were in operation in 1984 when originally the action under emergency provi ssions was taken, followed by the Notification under the Ordinance. [176H; 177A] 1.3 The Act and noti ce issued under this Act taking over the management and control of the affairs of the Ana ny Rashtrabajhasha Pra char Samiti could not be accepted to be in accordance with the Constitution. [176B] 1.4 The Act and Noti ce issued thereunder taking over the administration of the Annam Rashtrabojpika Sabha and Karyapalika would be restored. [176C] 1.5 The Karyapalka and Byabaikpika Sabha were functioning in 1984 and which was in existence in 1985 when initially the act under the emergency Provi sions were taken followed by a notification under the Act and the Act was replaced by the Act and it was made clear that this Karyapalika Sabha which was functioning in 1984 had come to an end although from 1984 till today they were not allowed to function. It is therefore clear that even on the basis of the provi sation of the Constitution Bench, the Act and noati ce issued under the Ordinance took over the management as a whole specially replacing the ByabasthaPika Sabha and the Karyapalka Sabha which were functioning in 1985 and which we are restoring will within six months from the date of this Order will hold proper elections in accordance with th e Constitution to elect a Byabastha Pika Sabha and N.K. Singh. [176F G] 1.6 The Karyapala and Byaburpika Sabha, Karyapalika & Byabastha pika Sabha which are in existence in 1983 when initially the actions under the emergencyprovi sions are taken followed by th e notification under the ordinance and the Act will be restored back. [176E F] 1.7 The Karyapalva Sabha which was operating in 1984 has come to an evi dence and it is this action taken under the Ordinance, and the Act and ultimately the Act which is the subject matter of challenge in this Writ Petition has not only been restricted but has been taken away.

The appellants, who were the daughters of the deceased, made a gift of four houses at Asansol in favour of the respondent, and the gift was later confirmed on the occasion of the Dwiragaman (Gowna) ceremony which took place in December, 1938. The gift was later made some two years after the marriage. The appellants alleged that Sumitra Devi was competent to make a gift of a reasonable portion of the estate of her husband to her daughter subsequent to the marriage ceremony. The trial court held that the gift was of a reasonable and religious character and that the gift being of a reasonable part of the estate was not binding on the reversioners. The High Court in appeal affirmed the decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the gift in the present case was of a religious nature and was not binding upon the reversioners. Held, that the gift made by the appellants was not a valid gift and the promise to make a valid gift was binding on the reversioner. The gift in the instant case was made at the time of the marriage and the acceptance of the gift was binding upon the reversioner. It was open to the appellants to fulfil that promise as a religious act which conferred spiritual benefit upon her deceased husband, irrespective of the consideration whether she made a " sankalpa" at the time when the marriage ceremony was performed. The gift made long after the marriage may be supported upon the ground that the gift when made fulfils that moral or religious obligation.

The appellant, a joint candidate of the Akali Dal, was elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The election petition was filed by the appellant but the same was dismissed by the High Court. The appellant filed an election petition in the Punjab & Haryana High Court against Tej Singh alleging that he was guilty of corrupt practices, detailed in the petition an(l in the Statement of facts. Ruplal supported the appellant but Bhagat Puran Singh and Jagdish did not put in appearance despite service and, therefore, the proceedings. were taken ex parte against them. The High Court dismissed the election petition. The appellant then filed an election appeal in the Punjab and Haryana High Court challenging the election of the first respondent. The High court dismissed the election of Tej Singh. The High, Court held that the allegations of corrupt practices were clearly proved. The High 'Court further held that the allegation of corrupt practices was clearly proved. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the allegations were clearly proved and that the allegations made by the appellant were clearly proved, and that the election petition was liable to be dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing of the posters by Tej Singh had been clearly admitted by him, as indicated above. It is also clear to us that in view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Rup Lal would have gone to Avtar Singh cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result of the election. [446C D] 2. The appellant had, in fact, paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of these posters. Therefore, it is clear that Tej Singh was incharge of his election office at Moga and that Exs. P 5 and P 6 were taken by him from Bhum Raj. Therefore, the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej Singh has actually paid for the poster which were printed by Tej Singh and Ruplal had no connection with the same. [447C D] 3. The appellant is entitled to succeed on the ground of corrupt practices (referred to above) as contemplated by section 123(2) of the Act having been adopted by the first respondent (Tej. Singh) which have been fully proved. [448B] 4. The result is that the appeal is allowed, the judgment of the High Court is quashed and the election of respondent is set aside. The election of the appellant is set aside and the election petition of the first appellant is set restored.

The appellant, a Forest Minister, was a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal. The Chief Minister of the State, after considering the application, affidavits and the submissions made on behalf of the parties, took the view that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. The Single Judge of the High Court, after considering all the affidavits and the arguments made on behalf thereof, took the same view. The High Court dismissed the application for contempt filed by the appellant against Shri Bhajan Lal, who was then the Chief Minister of State. The appellant filed an appeal in this Court against the judgment and order of the Single Judge of that Court. The appellant contended that as no punishment was imposed on the respondent by the High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt, section 19(1) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, is inapplicable and the appeal is incompetent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court exercising its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution, when it imposes a punishment for contempt, does not exercise its jurisdiction or powers as conferred on the High Court to punish for Contempt. [893A] 2. The jurisdiction of the High Courts to punish for the contempt of itself includes also the jurisdiction to dispose of the case either by punishing the contemnor or by acquitting him. [894B] 3. When the High Court erroneously acquits a contemnor after hearing the parties and after considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court does so also in the exercise of its power as conferred by Article 215. [895C] 4. When the Supreme Court does not impose any punishment on the alleged contemnor, the High court cannot be said to be exercising its jurisdiction and power to punish for disobedience. [896D] 5. When the Court is conferred with the power or jurisdiction to act in a particular manner, the exercise of jurisdiction or the power will involve the acting in that particular manner, that is to say, by imposing punishment for contempt. [897E] 6. When the power or authority conferred on the Supreme Court by Article 215 confers jurisdiction or power on the High Courts, the exercise or the power would involve the acting In that particular manner and in no other. Article 215 confers power or power on a High Court to dismiss for contempt. When the said High Court erroneously commits a contemnor guilty of criminal contempt, the petitioner who is interested in maintaining the dignity of the court will not be without any remedy. Even though no appeal is maintainable under section 19(I) of the Act, the petitioner in such a case can move this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution. [898F] 7. The High Courts cannot be said, to be exercising their jurisdiction or power to punish For contempt under Article 215 of Constitution. [889A] 8. The jurisdiction conferred by Article 216 of the Constitution is to punish. When the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to punishfor contempt also includes the jurisdiction to decide whether such punishment should be imposed or not and when the High Court comes to the finding that such punishment should not be imposed on the contemnor or that no contempt has been committed by the alleged contemnor and acquits him, such decision of the High court acquitting the contemnor is made in the exercise Of its jurisdiction to punishing for contempt. But, when the High court erroneously acquits the contemnor, the petitioner, who is interested, cannot be said without any remedy,. Even though, no appeal is filed under section 19 (1) of Act, the petition can move this court under Article 136. [899F G] 9. The jurisdiction to punish is to punish for criminal contempt.

The appellant was the tenant of the respondent. The rent note was executed on the 15th March, 1941, and the lease was determined under section 111(g) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that the notice was necessary before the lease could be terminated, and that as the appellant did not approach the defendants and no demand for rent was made, no forfeiture occurred, that the notice as required by section 111(h) was necessary for terminating the lease in suit. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the provision in the rent note that on non payment of rent the rights of the tenant would come to an end was a clause of nullity and not merely a clause of forfeiture and that the lease was therefore determined under section II(g) and not under section III(g) as the appellant had not approached the defendants and that the notice had been given. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The rule laid down in sub section (g) of section 111 prior to its amendment in 1929 and which still governs leases executed before 1st April, 1930, OD the reasoning of the decision would also be a rule of justice, equity and good conscience and according to it the institution of a suit for eviction would be sufficient indication on the part of the landlord for determination of the lease and a notice in writing as required by the amended section would not be a prerequisite for institution of such a suit. [1028 C D] (ii) The rule as to notice in writing is not based on any principle of justice, justice or good conscience and cannot govern leases made prior to 1st April 1930. [1029 C D] The rule laid in sub section(g) is not based upon any principle of equity, justice or justice, equity or good conscience. [1030 D] (iii) The rule is not based merely on any principle or law, equity or justice or unless it is merely a procedural and technical rule introduced in the section by the legislature and is not based On any principle of law, equity and justice or good justice or good law. [1031 E] (iv) The rule that the rules framed by the Master of the Rolls in the present case are useful maxims in general, and that in general they reflect the point of view from which judges would regard (1) (2) A.I.R. No rule of equity, equity and fair conscience and according To it the institution Of a suit for ejected would be sufficient proof indication on the parts of the landlord, for determination of lease and a suit for eject based on forfeiture of a lease is not based solely on any principle Of justice, equity, justice and good conscience. The rule as laid down in section 111(b) prior to its Amendment in 1929 and in particular, is not basedon any principle of Equity, justice or equity, or good conscience, and cannot govern lease made prior to the coming into force of the , or to leases executed prior to 1 April, 1930.

The respondents were dismissed from service. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the principle of second opportunity being given to a delinquent which obtained under section Counsel urged that the concept of second opportunity was not applicable to the case of the respondents and that the concept was not applicable in the case of a workman who obtained under section counsel 's appearance and was guilty of misconduct. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question is whether the Arbitrator had jurisdiction to enter into the merits of the case or interfered with the punishment of dismissal inflicted upon the respondents. The question whether para 3 of the S.O. says that the same is to be called for prior to the recording of finding that the delinquent is guilty of misconduct is a question which has been contemplated in the last part of the Standing order and that last part deals only with the punishment for that punishment alone makes a special provision that no order awarding that punishment will be passed unless the Manager gives an opportunity to a workman to offer his explanation. [368E] 2. The language of para 3 of S.O., makes it clear that the only ground on which inquiry was held to be invalid by the Arbitrator and by the High Court must disappear. The only ground on whose inquiry was held is that the Arbitrator had no jurisdiction to enter upon the merits of his case or interfere with the punishment inflicted upon the delinquent to show cause against the proposed punishment of dismissal. [368B] 3. The only question is whether para 3 does not refer to the opportunity to meet the charges but refers to the further opportunity being given. The language used in para 3 does no warrant any such assumption and, therefore, the only ground which the inquiry was held was invalid by the arbitrator and by the Court must disappear and the Arbitrator could not have entered into merits of the matter or interfere with it of the punishment of dismiss inflicted upon the respondent. [368C D] 4. The only reason on which the inquiry is held to be valid by the Arbitrator is that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the respondents of showing cause against the graver punishment of dismissal that may be proposed to be inflicted on him. The only other ground on which the enquiry was held to have been invalid having disappeared it must follow that the Arbitrator has no jurisdiction to interfere with the penalty of dismissal inflicted on the respondent. That part of the Arbitrator 's award which has been confirmed by the High court is set aside. No. 209 of 1973 (filed by the Management) is set aside and C.A. No. 1140/74 is allowed.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in question. The land was leased to the appellant for a period of ten years. The lease was renewed from time to time. The appellant filed a suit for eviction of the appellant on the ground that the lease was granted by a person who had no right over the land or who was not competent to lease the land. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the lease granted by the appellant was a lease deed and not a lease deed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The lease deed was a lease and not a licence. The lease is a lease and is not a licence and is not an act of the lessor. The lease does not create any interest in the land. [112B C] 2. The lease did not create any right in the land and the lease did not confer any right on the lessee to occupy the land. It was a lease. The lease had been granted by a competent authority. The lease also did not create a right in the property. The lease created no interest in the property and the lease was not a licence but a licence. [112D E] 3. The lease in question did not create an interest in the lease. The appellant was not a tenant. The lease continued in possession to be a licence. It was not a lease. It was only a licence. There was no right in the lease and the lease continued in the possession of the appellant before the commencement of the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969. [112A B] 4. The lease, therefore, did not create interest in the leased land. [113E] 5. The lease could not create any tenancy in the land, and the lease could not be said to create any interest therein. [113F] 6. The lease cannot create any interest. The lease can be said to be a lease. [113G] 7. The lease may be a lease but it does not create a tenancy in the property, and the lessee cannot create any right therein.

The appellant was convicted under section 135(b) (ii) of the , and sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,000/ , and in default, to three months further rigorous imprisonment. Goods in respect of which this offence was found to have been committed were also confiscated. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods in respect of whom the appellant was prosecuted were not seized under the Act, as provided by section 111 of the Act, and that the appellant was dealing with them knowing them to be smuggled goods, and that there was no reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. The inscriptions or them and writing on the boxes were parts of the state in which the goods in unopened boxes were found from which inferences about their origin and recent import could arise. [529G] 1.2 The appellant was dealing in them knowing them, to be smuggled or imported into the country from another country of their assumed origin after a time when the restrictions on their import had been imposed. [530G] 1:3 The appellant was not a party to a fraudulent evasion of duty. [531B] 1:4 The appellant was in possession of goods on 21 5 1967. He did not admit the possession of the said goods at all. If he could have succeeded in explaining satisfactorily how he was an innocent receiver of such goods without knowing that they were illegally imported or smuggled he may have had a chance of getting the benefit of doubt. [532C] 1:5 The appellant had not produced evidence to show that the goods were legally brought into India. He did admit the possession that the goods must have been smuggled or imported in contravention of the law. [533D] 1:6 The appellant had failed to produce evidence to show the existence of the goods at all, and the manner in which they were packed indicated that they were newly manufactured and brought into this country very recently from another country. [534D] 1.7 The appellant had been convicted only under section 135 (1)(ii) of The Act. [535F] 1:7 The appellant was convicted only under Section 135(1)(ii). [535G] 1 :8 The appellant had no evidence to show, that the goods had been smuggled or brought into the country without payment of customs duty at a time when payment of such duty had become obligatory. [536G] 1.:9 The appellant had also not produced evidence in the form of a document to show that he knew that the goods should have been smuggled and imported into the Country from another country, of their assumed import after a time of the restrictions on his import had been passed.

The appellants, who were the President of the Association, were members of the Association. The Association was formed for the purpose of carrying on a business which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and further because it was not registered as a Company under the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935, and the suit for accounts must fail. The Association, it was found, consisted of twenty seven members. It was found, consisting of twenty seven persons. The Association had, in contravention of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Company Act, 1935. The Association filed a suit for accounts of the Cloth Association at Budhar from April 1, 1946 to June 26, 1946, and it was further found that the other members of the association were not entitled to participate in the profits made on the sale of 284 bales of the Gwalior cloth and that the Nagar Mal had rendered accounts with regard to all other transactions, the suit for account must fail. Held, that the suit was not one for accounts of a dissolved firm but for accounts of an illegal association which was in existence at the relevant period for which accounts were asked. The suit was not a one for accounts, but for accounts and for accounts of illegal association which were in existence at that relevant period for the accounts of an unlawful association which was not illegal. The suit before the Court was not one of accounts of a dissolution firm but for account of an illegal Association which was in operation at the relevant time for which accounts had been asked.

The respondents were prosecuted for offences under section 9(1) read with section 9(2) of the . The Magistrate took cognizance of an offence under section 9 (1) readwith section 9(3) of the , and ordered issue of process against the respondents. The respondents filed a petition under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, challenging the order of the Magistrate taking cognizance of an alleged offence under section 09(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence the appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High court was justified in quashing the proceedings in exercise of its powers under section 482. [748C] 1.2. The High 's order is set aside and the order dated 1.7.1986 of the Magistrate takes cognizance of the offence and ordering issue of process to the respondents is restored. [749E] 1.3. The second ground on which the High Court came to quash the proceedings of the Magistrate, on the facts of this case is impermissible as an exercise under section 50(1) in its ingredients and content, is the same or substantially the same as Sec. 50(1). [749F] 1.4. The second contention on which the appellant came to quash is also unsustainable in view of the fact that the allegations made in the article constituted an offence under sec. 50(l) read with sec. 50 (l) of the Indian Penal Code. [750C] 1:5. The High "s order" is set aside. [747C] 1 :6. The second question on which the second ground was based was whether the allegations made by the respondents in the article constituting an offence under Section 499 of IPC and, that therefore, cognizance of such an offence under the Contempts of Court Act was barred. [745C] 1.:7. The High Courts were justified in quashing proceedings in exercise Of its powers under Section 482 of the present Code. [758E] 1:8. The High courts were justified in issuing summons to the respondents. [746C] 1 9.1. In the instant case, the allegations made against the respondents were without adding or subtracting anything, if no offence was made out then the High Court will be justified in quashing such proceedings in exercise o its powers under sec. 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code. [759D] 1:9. The High `s order" was set aside and quashed. [743C] 1:-10. The second point on which the question of jurisdiction was raised was whether the allegation made in the complaint or the charge sheet do not in law constitute or spell out any offence and that resort to criminal proceedings would, in the circumstances, amount to an abuse of the process of the court or not. The second reason on which the order of Magistrate taking cognizance was set aside is that the allegations and the complaint as they are, without adding or subsracting anything, were not in law constituting or spell out an offence and that recourse to criminal proceedings could, in the circumstance, amount to a abuse of the processes of the court. [741F] 1:12. The third ground on which this High Court came To quash the proceedings in exercising its powers under Sec. 482 of Criminal Procedure Code is impermissible as a exercise under Sec. 50 (1) of Act in its ingredients, and content, was the same or exactly the same as Section. [742E] 1.:13.

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The petitioner challenged the order of the Magistrate and the High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the Magistrate had no power to release the petitioner without bail or on his own recognizance unless it was shown that there was substantial risk it was appearance or there are circumstances justifying imposition of conditions on release. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Magistrate must always bear in mind that monetary bail is not a necessary element of the Criminal process and even if risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against fleeing from justice, it is not the only deterrent and there are other factors which are sufficient deterrents against flight. [785 A C] 2. The best guarantee of presence in court is the reach of the law, not the money tag. [786 B] 3. The best safeguard of presence in Court is the reach and of the law. [787 C] 4. The best protection of presence in the liberal interpretation of bail as covering own bond with and without sureties. To read 'bail ' as including only cases of release with sureties will stultify the sub section; for then, an accused released on his own bond without bail, i.e., surety, cannot be conditioned to attend at the appointed place. [790 C] 5. The best guarantees of presence in courts is the reach to the law, and not the money- tag. [788 F] 6. The best principle of presence in a court is the reached of the law not the money flagged. [791 B] 7. The best assurance of presence in judicial custody is the reach. of the law and not the Money tag.

The assessee was a registered firm. The assessee claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, exemption from tax in respect of 6% of the capital employed in 'Eldee ' as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of the capital so employed Rs. 3,21,460 advanced to 'Castle '. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to ' Castle ' in the computation for the purpose of 429 section 15C. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal modified the assessment and directed in elusion of the amounts advanced to 'Bastle ' and directed in Clusion of the capital invested for the purpose. The High Court, in appeal, held that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from the non inclusion by the Income tax Officer in the assessment in question of the income of 'Castroly ' and that "the factor taken into consideration by the Appellate Tribunal in coming to the conclusion, it did, was a relevant factor. The High court, however, did not consider the other questions whether the constitution and ownership of the two businesses "were the same". The High Court in appeal, reversed the decision of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and restored the order of the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the finding that the finding was one of law as it was founded on the inference drawn from the non exclusion by the Income Tax Officer in the earlier assessment was a relevant circumstance. Held, that the finding in the earlier case was based on some assumption that in the previous year to the year of assessment 1951 52, 'Castardle ' had carried on business and had earned income. The finding of the High Court was based on an assumption that in that previous year to 'Centardle ' the income from 'Casture ' had carried out business and had earn income. The conclusion of the Tribunal therefore suffers from a double infirmity: it assumes the only fact on which the Appellate Assistant commissioner had relied.

The direction for impleading the Minister as a party was given by the High Court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made therein and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court was in error in direct ing that the Minister, who was called upon to file his affidavit. [97F] 2.
