The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of arrears of rent on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rent. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in revision held that arrears of rent due under a lease cannot be recovered under section 259 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the view taken by the High Court that arrears of the rent due under the lease cannot be recoverable under section 259 was incorrect. HELD : (i) The section provides for recovery by suit also and as such it wilI not be possible for the Board to recover rent of land and buildings only if such rent is recoverable by a Board or a Military Estate Officer under the Act or the rules framed thereunder. [347 C] (ii) The words "rent on land and buildings" and "other payments" must equally be governed by the words "claimable by a Board etc." [347 D] (iii) The words 'rent on land" and "or buildings" must equally have been governed by the word "claimable" and that it was not any sum that could be described as rent or fee which could be recovered under summary provisions of that section. [347 E] (iv) The words used in section 259 of Act cannot be used for the purpose of recovery of arrears. [347 G] (v) The words of section 259 of 'the Act ' and the Rules which empower the Board to let out the land or buildings upon the ground that it cannot be said to be claimable or recoverable under any express provision of the Act cannot be employed for realisation of arrears of rents on land and building only provided such rent is claimable by a board under the Act and the Rules. [347 H] (vi) The words in section 259 will apply. [347 A] (vii) The words are not intended to be used for recovery of rent on land and houses only if such rents are recoverable by a board or a Military Estates Officer under the provisions of the Act or rules framed thereunder thereunder. [348 B] (viii) The words must be construed in their widest possible sense and the words must be understood in their widest amplitude. [347 D F] (ix) The words cannot be used in a narrow sense. The words must have a wide meaning. The words are used in the sense of the words used in the Act. The words cannot, therefore, be used in the narrow sense. [347 F] (x) The words can be used in narrow sense. It is not possible for the legislature to use the words in the narrow meaning. The word 'rent ' must be construed as meaning not only as rent or fees but also as rent. [347 B] (xi) The words should be construed in the narrow and technical sense. The word "rent" must be construed according to the context in which it is used. [347C] (xii) The words have a wide connotation. The word is used in the wider sense. The term "rent" is used in a wide sense. The expression "rent" in section 259 is used in wide sense. It must be construed strictly in the sense in which it occurs. [347F] (xiii) The words do not mean "rent" and the word "rent " must be construed accordingly. [347G] (xiv) The words, in section 259, are used in wide terms. The words "claim recoverable by a court" and "rent" are used in a wider sense. [348G] (xv) The words may be used in wide and technical sense and the word 'rent " must, therefore, mean the rent which is recoverable by the Board under the Act.

The appellant was appointed as a Section Salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. The appellant was appointed for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sales of the company 's product in his area. The various correspondence and other evidence produced before the Labour Court showed that the appellant was employed for canvassing and selling the product of the company in his area and that the sales of it were controlled by head office through their territory office situated at Delhi. The Tribunal also found and in fact it has referred to as an admitted case of both the parties that the respondent company sells its product i.e. cigarettes manu factured by it directly through their wholesalers who in turn sell the product to various dealers appointed by the company in the area. Neither the section sales . man nor the local salesmen were employed in the shop of the wholesaler or any retail dealer to sell the products of the company and to collect the amount of sale. The Tribunal further held that the appellant 's services were controlled and controlled by the Head office through its territories office situated in India. The Tribunal held that the appel lant was not a "workman" and that, therefore, the reference was incompetent. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Labour Court had given findings in favour of the appel tant on the question whether the termination itself was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of the Tribunal for coming to the conclusion that the appellant is not a workman employed for manual, skilled, unskilled and/or clerical nature and that the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act were not ap plicable and the reference, therefore, was incompetent. [401C] 2. The Labour Court considered the merits in detail and ultimately held that the termination of the appellant from service was illegal but dismissed the application only on the ground that the was not applica ble. [402D] 3. The Labour Cour ts Court considered the merit in detail and finally held that the respondent was not a workman. In the light of our holding that the is not applicable to him and in view of the fact that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. [403F] 4. The object of this enactment and the employees covered by the enactment also go to show that persons employed for sales promotion normally would not come within the definition of workmen under the Industrial Dis putes Act. The supervising work of the other local salesmen was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the area of his operation. [404C] 5. The supervising works of the other two local salesmen are part of his Work considered by the Tribu nal on the nature of the work considered by it as only incidental incidental to his primary work of canvassing, and promotion in that area. The supervising duties of the other three local salesmen, were part of his duties considered by the tribunal as only incidental, to his main function of canvassing and promote the sale of the product of company in the four districts allotted to him. The supervising function of the other four local salesmen is part of his duty considered by the Tribunals as only incidental and ancillary to his main Work of canvassing and promoting the sale of of the product in the four district allotted to him, and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Tribunal. It is seen from the facts found that the appellant, was employed to do canvassing and promot ing sales for the company.

The appellants, a private limited company, were the owners of the land in question. The Company was in possession of the land. The Company had been holding the land from the State Government after it had been acquired by the Government for a public purpose of the State. The Company failed to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the lease. The Company filed a suit for eviction of the Company from the land in dispute. The Additional Collector dismissed the suit. The Company preferred an appeal against the said order before the Additional Collector. The Additional Commissioner dismissed the appeal. The Company 's appeal was dismissed by the Additional Collector by his Order dated 1.10.1977. The Company challenged the said order by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the Company was not a 'pakka ' tenant ' and did not enjoy the status of a ' Gair Maurusi ' tenant. The High court held that the land admeasuring 495.05 acres was held by the Company in terms of the lease granted by the State and the Company was, therefore, not liable to be proceeded against in terms of section 182. The Company, therefore, was not liable to eviction in terms of Section 182. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Additional Collector was well justified in having recourse to the proceeding prescribed under section 182 of the Code. The finding of the High Court to the contrary was, in our view, totally unjustified and opposed to law. [180B] 1.2 The Additional Collector made his order for eviction of a Company. The finding was in our view wholly unjustified and opposed by law. [181C] 1.3 The Additional Collector had made his order in the earlier proceeding that the land in the question was held by it under lease from the Government after it was acquired by the State Government for a Public purpose of the state. The finding that the Company had not become a 'phakka ' tenant was, in the circumstances, totally unjustified. [181D] 1.4 The High Court had found in the earlier proceedings that the land was held by a Company under lease from Government after it has been acquired by it for a public purposes of the State, and it had never been an ordinary term as defined in the Madhya Bharat Act No. 66 of 1950. Therefore, it was, according to the said Act, an ordinary tenant. [181E] 1.5 The High Court has found in the previous proceeding that the Company failed to make payment of the agreed rents, and thus contravened section 182. [181G] 1.6 The Additional Collector, was well justified. [181F] 1.7 The Additional Collector 's order for eviction was, in accordance with law. [182G] 1:8 The High Court was, therefore right in having recourse under the proceeding prescribed by section 182 of that Code. [182F] 1:9 The High Court, in the earlier order held that the company was not a pakka tenant, as found by the High Court in the earlier judgement, and, therefore, it was not, according to that Act, an 'pakKA ' tenant. [182H] 1:10 The High Court did not find in the earlier case that the land had been held by the company under lease from a Government lessee within the meaning of the Code, and, consequently, it was held that the High Court had, in the previous proceedings held that the Land was held by 'the Company in terms under the old lease or holding, upon termination of that lease, under and in terms of fresh conditions agreed upon between the Company and the Government to enable the Company to remain in possession of that land as a lessee.

The Orissa Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1964, received the assent of the President on October 17, 1960. By section 1(3) of the principal Act it was provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time by notification appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. The Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960, received the President 's assent on October 17. 1960. By a notification dated October 17, 1961, the Government of the United State brought the Travancore Act 14 of 1124 (M.E.) into force, and referred cases of tax payers for investigation to the Commission appointed in that behalf. The Commission appointed in the case of certain tax payers, and the proceedings under the Act were to be taken up for investigation. The Commission submitted its report on October 17 and the Commission submitted its Report on October 17 on the basis of which the Commission appointed the authorised officials and the proceedings were to be completed within a period of two months from the date of the report. The Commission also submitted its report to the Government on October 17 but the Government of Orissa rejected the report on the ground that the provisions of the Travancore Act were inconsistent with or takes away orabridges any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution, and that the plea had found favour with the High Court, that section 47 incorporated by Act 13 of 1965 which provided for compulsory acquisition was inconsistent with or take away orabridge any of the rights conferred by part III of the constitution, and that section 47 was not in force until a notification was issued bringing into operation the provisions of Act 13 of 1966. The High Court held that section 47 of the Travancore Cochin Act was not applicable to the landholders under any law for the time being in force, and that it was not inconsistent with or took away orabairs any of the Fundamental rights conferred by section 45 as amended, there was compulsory acquisition of land which may be laid only if the law providing for payment to the landholder for extinction of his interest, the market value of that part of the surplus land which was within the ceiling limit under the principal Act. The High court also held that section47 incorporated by Act 14 of 1965 which empowered the appointment of a Commission and referring the cases of tax Payers to the Commission, was invalid. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The provisions of the principal act were not inconsistent with the provisions of section 1(2) of the Travancore Travancore Act, and since no notification was issued before Ch. IV of the principal enactment was repealed, there was no ceiling limit applicable to the landholder under any law providing for the acquisition of any land in an estate in the personal cultivation of a person is guaranteed by the second proviso only where the land is within the ceiling limits applicable to him under any law For the time being the law in force. [422 B C] (ii) The provisions in the Travancore Act, which were in force, were not inconsistent or take away any of the basic rights conferred by the Part III of Act 16 of 1960. [423 C] (iii) The provisions contained in the Travancore Cochin Land Reforms Act were not inconsistent and take away or abridge any of the provisions of any law for time being in operation which attracted the application of the second proviso to article 31 A. [424 C] (iv) The provisions made in the Travancore Land Act were not in consistent with article 3 1 A.

The widow 's estate was in the hands of the widow and her self estate was inherited by her husband. The widow 's property was inherited by the widow and the widow 's widow 's husband. The estate was inherited in the hands by the widow. The widow was in possession of the property. The widow filed a suit for possession of the estate. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The widow preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the widow ' 's estate had been completely extinguished by adverse possession exercised by the defendants, and that the widow had no interest left in her, which she could make a surrender of in favour of the reversions. The High court also held that the view expressed by the trial Court was right and that on a surrender by the widow ' her self estate had been extinguished by adverse Possession exercised by the defendant. The High ' Court also held that as the widow herself was in capable of disputing the title of the alienee or of the person who had acquired interest by adverse possession against her, a like disability attaches to the reversioner also who could not have obtained the properties but for the surrender made by the widow, and that on surrender by the heirs, the surrender must take it subject to such prior interest. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The widow ' s estate was in a capable of disputing her title of the reversionary right to challenge the right of a prior alienee from the widow, even though the alienation was not for legal necessity, so long as the widow remained alive; and the same protection could be claimed by one who acquired the limited interest of a widow by adverse possession. [355 D] (2) The widow herself may be incapable of inheriting from her own grant and disputing the alienation which she has herself made; but as has been said already, surrender is not an alienation and as the reversioner does not derive his title from her, there is no principle of law under which the acts of the widow could bind him. [355 E] (3) The widow, her self estate may be incapable or alienable from her own Grant and disputing the alienations which she has himself made; but in the case before us no equitable considerations at all arise. [355 F] (4) The widow her self estate might be incapable of derogating from her own grants and disputing the alienated which she has she made; but the widow 'she gets the inheritance even during the widow 'S lifetime. [355 C] (5) The widow surrender is not a alienation and as such the reversioner 's right to recover possession of the properties during the widow's lifetime on grounds of equity, justice and good conscience in proper cases, it is clear that in the case of alienation by a Hindu widow of her husband 's property without any justifying necessity or in the case o a stranger acquiring title by adverse possession, the reversioners in the sense that she gets the inheritance only during the widow "s lifetime. [356 D] (6) The widow is under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. The widow herself may be incapable, of derogating therefrom from her own granting and disputing the alienee which she has already made; but if the title of such person has been completed already, it could not be defeated by a surrender made by her.

The appellants, who were the Directors of the Polytex Company, were appointed as Directors of the Cotton Mills Company. The appellants, who had been appointed as Directors, were appointed by the Collector of Kanpur in respect of the ten lakhs shares held by the Cotton Mills company. The appellants were, however, appointed by the State Government of Uttar Pradesh as a Director of the Company. The Company was dissolved by the State of Uttar Pradesh on the ground that the appellants had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the Polytechnic Company by reason of the appointment of a Receiver by the Collector. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton Mills Co had ceased to be in the possession of the appellants by reason of appointment of a receiver by the Collector, that the attachment of the shares in question had not deprived the Cotton Mills of its right to vote at the meeting or to issue the notice under section 169 of the Act for appointment of Sitaram Singhania, Rajaram Jaipuria and R.D. and that the order of the Collector being an order in the nature of a charging order the Receiver had obtained an equitable right in the shares in dispute and there being no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, the Cotton Mills had lost its right to the shares. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High Court being an order under the English Law is not the same as an attachment of property or appointment of a liquidator under the Land Revenue Act. [878G] 2. The order passed by the High Court on February 1, 1985 is an order in a charging order. It is also significant that the Directors of a Polytex Company who what that a Receiver had been appointed in respect of these shares had also been pledged in favour of the Government of Uttar Prade. The Cotton Mills Company had in this case rightly treated the registered holder i.e. the Cotton Mills as the holder of the shares pledged in its favour. The costs of all the parties to the appeal and other connected cases shall, however, be borne by the Polytex company. Subject to the above order, the order passed by this Court on February 21, 1985 shall remain in force. [879C D] 3. The order made by this Court in the instant case does not affect the validity of any notice under section 170 of the Act. [888G] 4. The order dated February 21, 1986 passed by the Board of Directors (1) 1 1981]2 S.C.R.533 890 of the Cotton Mill Company that the voting rights in respect of those shares of a company without more cannot, therefore, deprive the holder of his shares whose name is entered in the Register of Members of the Polyital Company in respect of 10 lakhs shares out of the said 10 lakhs shares and also the pledge of 3,50,000 shares out of 10 lakhs share with the Government of U.P. and that orders had been passed under section 18AA (1) (a) of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 taking over six industrial units of the Cotton mills Company did not question the validity of notice. [889D] 5. The order is an order passed in the nature o. a charging order under the Indian Industries (Development & Regulation) Act 1951 taking over four industrial units of Cotton Mills Company held by the cotton Mills Company. It is, therefore, not the same. [881E] 6. The order under the Hindi Law is not an attachment of the property or appointment or of a Receiver under the Land revenue Act.

The petitioners filed a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were the owners in possession of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat, Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala, District Sangrur had no sort of right in the suit land and that the suit land had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Panchayat by the entries made in the revenue records which were not binding on the plaintiffs and for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering with their possession. The trial court decreed the suit. The plaintiffs filed an appeal in the High Court which came to the conclusion that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this petition by special leave. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The civil court had not been taken away by virtue of section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Act which had been inserted by the Haryana Legislature into the Act. [836G] 2. The Gram Panchayat in question had not been impleaded as a defendant. The plaintiff in that case had not claimed that the suit property belonged to him or that it did not belong to the Gram Panchayat. The plaintiff had not claimed any declaration that the land in question belonged to him nor that it belonged to the Gram panchayat. The plaintiff could not by drawing his plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration that the suit lands belonged to him. The plaintiff cannot by drawing his suit cleverly from not claiming a relief that the suit is not shamlat deh vested or deemed to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Act or to question the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner or the Collector or the Panchayat under the provisions of the Act or in respect of any matter which the Commission or the Collector is empowered by or under the Act to determine. [837A] 3. The Gram panchayat in question had specifically claimed that the land belonged to it as shamlat deh. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was shamlat deh or not. [838B] 4. The Gram Panchayats in question had expressly claimed that the Panchayat was entitled to the suit land. The plaintiff was not claiming that the suit had been filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayat had expressly claimed the said claim. The plaintiff, therefore, cannot by drawing their plaint cleverryly by not claim a declaration that he was not shamlat Deh conferring jurisdiction on the civil court when by virtue of Section 13 read with section 13B of Act the jurisdiction of civil court to try such suits had been taken away. [839C] 5. The Gram panchayats in question had clearly claimed that the Gram Panchayats were entitled to the land. The plaintiffs had, therefore, questioned the correctness of the entries in the revenue record which showed that the Panchayat had not been arrayed as a defendant and that the plaintiffs had avoided to seek a 836 declaration that the property in dispute belonged to it. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing the plaint cleverlessly by not claiming the declaration that the lands in question belonged not to the Gram Panchayats. The Gram courts in question had also not been impleaded.

The appellant Board had been conferred statutory power under Section 49(1) of the . The Board had been empowered to determine the conditions on the basis of which supply was to be made. The Board had also been empowered to fix the terms and conditions on which supply was required to be made and the Board had also power to fix the rates of interest. The Board, however, did not agree with the contention of the appellant Board that there was no order of this Court adjudicating the rights of the Board on the consumer in respect of the validity of consumption security deposit being condition precedent for the supply of electricity by the Board as the liability of the Board to pay interest to the consumer in regard to the consumption security deposit. The Board also did not agree to the contention of appellant Board that the Board was keeping the security deposit and depriving the consumer of the use of the money which was alleged to be earning interest with the Board. The Board filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the consumption security deposits. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was a legal obligation to pay interest on a deposit made by the consumer with the Board in terms of Clause 20(a) & (c) of the General Conditions of Supply. The High court held that there was nothing in the Act to show that the Board had been given statutory power under section 49(1). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Board is clearly in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since the money is deposited by the consumer in trust with the Board to secure the Board against default in payment of interest. [278 D] 2. The condition of supply requiring a consumption security deposit has a direct bearing on the operations of the Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. The condition requiring a consumption deposit has a indirect bearing on the operation of the Board. [278 E] 3. The condition is of supply requiring deposit of consumption charges. G., Ramaswami, J. (dissenting) 1. The condition requires a consumption security deposited has a direct nexus with the position that without a law in that form and with that amplitude smuggling might not be possible of being effectively checked, the question arises whether the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by Article 19(1)(f) & (g) as imposing an unreasonable restrain. [278 F] 2. There is no legal obligation to Pay interest to the consumers proceed on the assumption that the Board is keeping the security deposited and depriving the consumers of the use money which is alleged to be earn interest with the board. The condition that requiring a consumption Security deposit has a directly bearing on the activities of the Board, which are to he conducted in such manner as to ensuring a surplus. [278 G] 3. There is nothing in the provisions of the Act to indicate that the Board has been conferred statutory powers under Section 49 (1) of . The condition of the supply requiring a supply of electricity and the conditions on which it is supplied being statutory, the provisions under the conditions of supply that the Board shall not pay interest on the security deposit has no direct bearing on this function. [278 A] 4. The condition in the supply requiring the consumption security deposited had a direct bearing upon the operations of that Board which are required to be conducted, in such a way as to ensure that a surplus. It is not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court. [278 B] 5. The condition regarding supply requiring a production security deposit has an direct bearing on its operations of the board which are to being conducted in such an manner as to ensures a surplus.

The petitioners were working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre of the Posts and Telegraph Department which is directly under the control of the P&T Board of the Ministry of Communications, Government of India. The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belong are not given any Special Pay in these grades and they are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. The direct recruit recruits to which categories the petitioners belong is not entitled to any Special Pay but the transferred officials have to be paid extra amount by way of Special Pay in addition to their scale of pay which is the same as the scale of pay of direct recruits because the transferred officials had to perform in the Telecommuni cation Research Centre duties which are not in their general line. The direct ent recruits to which Category the petitioners belong were not given any special pay in these grades nor they are able to discharge their duties. All the direct recruits are graduate engineers and have been working throughout in the Tele communication Research Centre. It is stated that the total number of officers who are thus getting Special Pay is of the order of 275 while only about 25 officers who are direct recruits working in the Tele Communication Research Centre are not given Special Pay. The direct recruitment to which category of the petitioners belong and the transferred officials has to be paid special pay. The petitioners have raised two grounds, namely, the first relating to the denial of promo tional opportunities to them on account of irregular implementation of the rules of promotion contained in the Recruitment Rules and the second relating to violation of Article 14 and Article 16 of the Constitution by not grant ing them the same special pay which is granted to the trans ferred officers who are working in the telecommuni cations Research Centre in the same posts and discharging the same functions as the petitioners. The direct recruited recruits to which class the petitioners belong, are not entitled to Special Pay but they are given merely the pay at which it is paid to the transferred officers working in that centre with effect from the date on which the transferred officers commenced to draw the Special Pay upto date and to continue to pay it in future also as long as the transferred officers continue to get it. The petitioners are graduate engineers, and have been in working throughout in Telecommunication Research Center. It is contended on behalf of the petitioners that the petitioners are not competent and are not able to discharge the duties. All these direct recruits are graduates engineers and have also been working throughout throughout the Telecommunication Technology Centre. It was also contended that the petitioners were not competent and were not able to perform their duties. The petitioners also contended that they are not able and able to discharge duties. The direct ac cused to which category they belong are not entitled, to Special Pay. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The direct appointees (to which category the peti tioners belong) in the Tele Communications Research Centre are entitled to the Special Pay at the same rates at which it was paid to the transfer officers working in the centre with effectfrom the date on Which the transferred officers have been drawing the Special Pay. [275E F] 2. The petitioners were graduate engineers and had been working throughout the Telecommunications Research Centre. They have been working continuously throughout the Tele communication Technology Centre. They are graduate engineers. They have also been in working continuously in the Tele communications Research Centre. [275G] 3. The direct Recruitment Rules, 1962, framed by the President under the provi so to Article 309 of the Constitution of India, are not applicable to the transferred employees. All the Direct recruits are graduate Engineers and have been serving throughout the Tele communications Technology Centre. [276G] 4.

The appellant was employed mainly in a managerial administrative capacity drawing basic pay (excluding allowances) exceeding five hundred and fifty rupees per month. The appellant was dismissed from service on the ground that he did not make an application under section 42(4) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1947, which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Court and prayed that the order of the Labour Court should be set aside on that ground alone. The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Industrial Court contending inter alia, that the third respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did neither make an application to the Labour Court nor to follow the procedure laid down in section 42(1) of the Act which was a Condition precedent to approaching a Labour Court and requested that the order should be setaside on that ground also. The State Industrial Court held that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedures laid down in the section 42(3) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour court for relief under section 7 8(1) D. The State Government appealed to the High Court contending interalia, that the fourth respondent had failed in complying with the provisions Of law in that the third Respondent had failed to make an application for relief under s.7 8(1)(a) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The High Court held that the third and fourth respondent had not complied with the provisions and that the third respondents had failed to do so. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The scheme of section 7 8 (1) seems to be that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the Labour Tribunal. [782 E] (2) The scheme does not stand on reason that an employer should be able in to side step All this by a direction to the representative of the employees. [785 B] (3) The scheme is that disputes should not be settled as long as possible and ordinarily through conciliation and agreed agreement, it do not stand to reasons that an employee could be able to go to any agreement and an application to that effect had been made to settle the dispute and no agreement had been arrived at. [786 C] (4) The scheme appears to be that dispute should be settled in respect of an order matter or change referred to in the said proviso. Under section 79(1) proceedings before a Labour Court in respect of disputes falling under clause (a) of paragraph A of sub section (1) shall be commenced on an application made by any of the parties to the dispute etc. and under sub section (2) every application under sub section(1) has to be made in the prescribed form and manner. In other words, effort must first be made by the employer intending to effect any change in respect of matters covered by section 42(I) or an employee desiring a change in respect thereof of any order passed by the employer under standing orders which would of necessity include an order of dismissal, to see whether it was possible to come to any agreement or an application to a Labour Court.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that the appellants ' application under section 12 of the Act before the Munsif was not maintain able. The respondents filed an application under section 13 of the Act for evicting the respondents on 16.7.1971 as tenants from month to month. The appellants ' application was allowed and an appeal therefrom filed by the respondents was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner, Ranchi. The respondents then moved the Patna High Court in its revisional jurisdiction, inter alia, contending that the appellants had to make another application under section12(3) of the Act, for evicting the respondent if they did not vacate within the time allowed by court. The respondents thereafter moved the Patna high Court in its revision application, inter alia contending that the application under section 11 of the Act was not maintainable before the Munsif, and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. The respondents also contended that the appellants were entitled to make another applica tion under section 12(3) and the entire proceedings were mis conceived. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question is whether the petition which was filed by the appellants as an application under Section 12 of the U.P. Act, 1950, before the Munsif is maintainable in the facts and circumstances of the present case, in our opinion, the proceeding has to be treated as a suit and the judgment of the learned Munsif as a decree therein. [934G H] 2. The question does not affect the substantive right of the parties as the controversy was concluded by the first appellate court in favour of the appellants. The occasion for filing an applica tion is only where the matter is covered by section 12, and as we have made an assumption in favour of th e respondents that section 12 has no application to the present case. [935G H] 3. The question whether a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term lease is entitled to move the Court by an application under sub section (1) of section 11 or on the groundthat the landlord has any other good and sufficient cause for terminating the lease on the expiry of period limited thereby, he may, within fifty days of the delivery of such notice, appeal to the court in that behalf and the Court after hearing the parties may termi nate the lease or extend the same for such period as it deems proper in the circum stances. [937C] 4. The question of whether a landlord during the period of the fixed term lease can move the Court under section 12 is whether the matter is governed by section 12 of U.P Act. [938D] 5. The question, does not affect, the substantive right or the rights of the parties. [939E] 6. The question also does not affect any substantive right of a party as the controversy is concluded by the second appellate court in favor of the appellants, and the judgment and decree passed by the court would have the effect of a final order under section 47 which would be appealable as a decree and against which no revision would lie.

The appellant Society filed a suit against the respondent for an immovable property through its Secretary, which was numbered as Suit No. 11 of 1973. The appellant Society filed an election petition under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, for setting aside the election of the office bearers of the Society. The trial court after holding that the appellant 's application filed under section 15 I of the Code was not maintainable, proceeded further to consider the question as to who was the duly elected Secretary of the Society, entitled to prosecute or withdraw the suit and accepted the case of Hari Narain Swami. The trial Court after holding that Hari Narain Swami was not the Secretary of the appellant Society, dismissed the appellant ' s application filed under Section 15 1 of Code of Civil Proce dure, but held that the appellant was not entitled to withdraw the suit. The High Court dismissed the appellant appeal. The appellant filed a revision application before the High Court which was also dismissed by the impugned judgment. The appellant society challenged the correctness of the trial court 's finding in favour of the respondent 's case that Hari Narain was not the secretary of the appellant society and was, therefore, not entitled to prosecute the suit. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was, therefore not right in holding that the application of the appellant invoking the inherent jurisdiction of the court was not maintainable. [237B] 2. The High, while confirming the order, said that in the exercise of inherent power under section 151 of the Code, a court can vacate an order obtained by fraud on it. The courts below were, therefore, wrong in dismissing the appellant ' 's application as not maintainable. The High 's revisional power on the assumption that it had no jurisdiction to do so. [237C] 3. The courts were, therefore not justified in holding that it had jurisdiction to cancel the order permitting the withdrawal of the suit under its inherent power, if it is ultimately satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree on a fraudulent repre sentation made to it that the party had actually consented to it. [237D] 4. The High Courts were, therefore wrong in holding that Hari Narayan Swami was not its elected secretary and was, hence, not entitled, to withdraw the plaint. [237E] 5. The High courts were, however, not right in observing that the only remedy of the appellant is to file a fresh suit. [237F] 6. The High Curt was, therefore wrong, in dismissing the appellants ' application as not barred.

The appellant was a citizen of India and was a citizen under the , and was entitled to be governed by the provisions of the , and the Ordinance in question was promulgated in exercise of the emergency powers vested in the Governor General under section 72 of the , of the , as it originally stood. The Ordinance was promulgated in the exercise of the powers vested in him by section 72 of that Act. The Ordinance in question, however, continued in operation even after the declaration of the emergency having come to an end. The Ordinance, however, was promulgated in pursuance of the emergency power vested in the Government of India Act, 1935, and it was promulgated in supersession of the emergency provisions. The Ordinance continued in operation on July 11, 1953, and the Ordinance was promulgated on April 1, 1946, and the Ordinances in question were promulgated in exercise Of the emergency powers de facto. The Ordinance thus promulgated was promulgated in accordance with the provisions of section 72 of which the appellant was a member of the Indian Legislature. The Ordinance had continued in operation for the period of emergency and the Ordinance had been promulgated in exercise, of the emergency Powers vested in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The Ordinance having continued in operation, the Ordinance in the question which had been promulgated, was promulgated on July 11. 1953, and it continued in operation until it was repealed. The Ordinance which was promulgated in January 1946, was promulgated by the Governor General in exercise of his powers vested in it by section 72 Of the , as the case may be, assented to by the GovernorGeneral. The Ordinance therefore continued in operation till it was repealed by the India and Burma (Termination of Emergency) Order, 1946, in spite of the words of limitation " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation " occurring in section 72 of Act, 1935. The Ordinance also continued in operation after the declaration, of the Emergency having come to a end. The appellant was convicted by the High Court and was sentenced to imprisonment for one year. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Held, that the Ordinance was not a law passed by the Indian Legislature without any limitation on its duration but was perpetual in its duration with the result that it continued in force until it was superseded. The Ordinance did not continue in operation after it was repealed, and the Act having continued in force even after the Ordinance had come to an effect, the Ordinance had to be continued in force till it was superseded by the Act. The Act was not a "law passed by the State Legislature without any limitations on its duration" and was not perpetual in its nature. The Ordinance could not be said to be a law passed in the exercise or purported exercise of the power conferred upon it by section 74 of the Act.

The appellants were convicted for murder under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the death sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was in error in confirming the death sentence and that the High court was in error by holding that the death sentence should be awarded. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was justified in confirming the conviction of the appellants. [1077 E] (2) The High court was justified in upholding the death sentence passed under section 368(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [1078 E] (3) The High 'Court was justified in reversing the conviction of appellants. [ 1078 E] In the instant case, the High Court had not given any reasons for confirming the death sentences passed under section 367(a) and (b) of the Criminal Procedure Code. [1079 E] (4) The High Courts were justified in confirming their death sentences. [1080 E] (5) The High "Court was justified by confirming the death convictions passed under section 364(a) read with section 354(3) of the Indian Penal Code. [ 1079 E] In Rajendra Prasad 's case, the Court was justified by holding that on the facts and circumstances of the case the award of death sentence to the two appellants was neither 'erroneous in principle ' nor was 'arbitrary or excessive ', or 'indicative of an improper exercise of discretion '. [1082 E] (6) The High `Court was justified, in confirming the sentence of death to the two accused. [1083 E] (7) The HighCourt was justified to confirm the death sentences. The High ' Court was justified, therefore, in confirming their conviction.

The appellant was charged with having committed a criminal offence under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code. The Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., Lucknow, on a preliminary enquiry held by him, found that the appellant had entered into partnership with others under the name of Gautam Cycle Mart, Meerut, in contravention of the Government Servants ' Conduct Rules. The Commissioner, after considering the evidence of the witnesses, found that there had been an enquiry in 1949 by Shri A. Inspecting Commissioner into some of the matters mentioned in the charges, and about others in 1952 by Shri R. N. Srivastava, another Inspecting Commissioner, and that the appellant was exonerated of the allegations and imputations made against him on each occasion. The Commissioner also found that the inquiry was in progress and that the charges were not proved. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the order passed by the Commissioner of Income Tax was void and inoperative. The suit was dismissed by the Commissioner. The appellant then filed a second appeal in the High Court which was dismissed by a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court. The appellant contended that the order of dismissal was void and ineffective. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant 's appeal was not maintainable as the appellant had been subjected to trial on allegations which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries overlooks that no charge was framed as a result of any previous enquiry. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The order refusing grant of certificate of fitness of the case for appeal to this court must have been before this Court. [58D] (2) The question whether the departmental proceedings were null and void, must be of such nature that it goes to the root of the jurisdiction and the conduct of the department trial and vitiates the result. [58E] (3) The question of the question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. [58F] (4) The question which could effect the result in a civil suit has to be of such character that it goes To the root of jurisdiction and the conducting of the department Trial and vitiates the results. [58G] (5) The question as to whether the departmental proceeding were null and invalid, must be, initially raised in the departmental trial. Unless such a point could be raised, there could be no declaration that the departmental proceedings was null and void. [58H; 59A] (6) The question that could effect the results in a civil case has to be considered of such nature as it goes to root of the Jurisdiction and the conduct and conduct of the departmental proceedings. Unless such an point could be made, there could not be no declaration of that the departmental proceeding was null and invalid. [59B] (7) The question was not enough to merit cancellation of the special leave to appeal which was granted by this Court. The question whether a departmental proceeding was void or invalid, was not a question of law. [58C] (8) The question raised by the appellant which could affect the final decision.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellants were the purchasers of manganese ores within the State.
