The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi 521 Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. He was terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974 with effect from 19th October, 1975 with effect from the date of his termination. The appellant challenged the termination of his service by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the termination of service of the appellant was ab initio void and inoperative and that the termination was held to be invalid. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The termination of service was ab initio invalid and inoperative and a declaration is made that he continues to be in service with all consequential benefits, namely back wages in full and other benefits, if any. [501G] (2) The termination was illegal and inoperative and the declaration was made that he continued to be in continuous service for a period of one year for the purpose of Chapter VA. [502F] (3) The termination is invalid. [503F] (4) The termination does not terminate the service of the workman. [504F] (5) The termination has been held to be void and inoperative. [505F] (6) The termination can be terminated only by a specified date as set out in the order of appointment. [507F] (7) The termination cannot be terminated by a specified period as set out therein. [508G] (8) The termination must be in continuous or continuous service for the purpose for which it is made. [509F] (9) The termination should be in continuous and continuous service for one year. If he has, he would be deemed to be in uninterrupted service for a continuous period of one years for the purpose Of Chapter VA. The termination of his services was ab initio illegal and inoperative. The termination was held not to be invalid and inoperative. a declaration was made in that behalf that he continues in service with full consequential benefits. [510G] (10) The termination did not terminate the services of the appellant. [512G] (11) The termination could not be terminated by the specified date as mentioned in the order. [513G] (12) The termination had been held to have been ab initio void. [514G] (13) The termination by the specified period was invalid and inoperative, and a declaration was issued that he continues and continues to be In service with all consequent benefits, namely, back wages in part and other benefits. [525G] (14) The termination, therefore, was ab initio unlawful and inoperative and was a declaration made that he remained in service for a periods of one year and six months, in any other case.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953 of the Settlement Commissioner of Patiala and East Punjab States Union. The appointment was terminable with one month 's notice. The appellant submitted his explanation to the charge sheet. The appellant was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the Settlement Officer with the view to the Deputy Commissioner agreed. the misdemeanor was proved. The appellant 's explanation to the charges was accepted by the Settlement Officer. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of termination. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of dismissal was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution as no reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order of discharge was at all given. HELD : (i) The order of termination of employment was passed without affording him an opportunity to show that he should be confirmed. The order of dismissal passed by the Settlement officer was therefore not the order pursuant to which employment was terminated. [718 B] (ii) The order passed by the Deputy Commissioner was not the order in the eye of law. [719 C] (iii) The order dated March 17, 1955, was not the final order of the Settlement officer. The order passed in the enquiry will not fall within the principle of Ram Narayan Das 's case. [720 C] (iv) The order was not the one passed by the settlement officer on March 30, 1955. The order was passed by the Divisional Commissioner on March 30. 1955. The appellant had no right to hold the post he was occupying and by the order terminating his employment for unsatisfactory work and conduct. [721 D] (v) The order terminating the employment of the appellant was passed without giving him an opportunity of showing cause in that behalf.

The appellant State Government was promoted to the post of Professor in the colleges. The appellant State Government made a rule for selection of candidates for promotion to the posts of Professors in the colleges, and the appellant State Government had also made a rule in that behalf. The appellant was not consulted either in regard to the principles to be followed in making the promotions in question or on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers. The State Government made an order on November 15, 1968, for selection of the appellant for promotion to posts of Professors. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State Government was consulted in regard to principles to be adopted in making the appointments in question, or on the basis of the recommendations of the Selection Committee, and that the Commission was consulted in accordance with its requirement. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The State Government at first framed rules on November 15. 1968, for selections to be made to posts of Professor in a college, and that for every post of Professor, names of four Lecturers, strictly in order of seniority, were sent to the Commission "at its direction" and they were interviewed and examined by the Selection Committee which was "formed" by the Commission, and a member of the Commission was appointed its Chairman. [875 D] (2) The State government at first framed Rules on November 15 1968, for promotions to the posts in the colleges and the second requirement of clause (b) of sub section (2) of section 133 was also complied with. [876 E] (3) The State of Jammu and Kashmir, hereinafter referred to as the Commission, was consulted on the suitability and suitability of the candidates for promotion as Professors. [878 F] (4) The State Govt. at first framed rule on November 15 was formally submitted to the Commission under the Chairman 's note dated June 2, 1969, and the Commission then took its decision regarding the recommendation to be made. The State Govt., had stated in its reply to the writ petition that for every posts of Professors, names of six Lecturers strictly in order to be consulted, were sent by the Commission to the Commission. The State had stated in the reply to the petition that for each post of Professor names of four lecturers strictly in order, of seniority, strictly in accordance with the rules to be followed, and that it was not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee consisting of only one of its members, so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. [877 G H] (5) The State had in fact placed on record the minutes of the Commission dated July 22, 1969, which make it quite clear that the State Govt referred the selections to the Commission, a Committee was appointed by the Commission for that purpose, the Committee was appointed, and a Member of the Commission, the report of the Committee was formally submitted. [879 A] (6) The State was therefore consulted on the eligibility of the candidates to promotion as Professors, and the second requirements of clause (a) of sub s.(2) of s 133 were also complied with, and the High Court erred in holding that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason.

The petitioner was the Chief Minister of the State of Bihar. He was the Chairman of the Committee. He was elected to the Legislative Assembly. He was declared elected. The petitioner challenged the validity of the election on the ground that the Chief Minister had no power to make the declaration of the petitioner as a member of the Committee and that the Chief Secretary had no power under article 194(1) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner was entitled to succeed. HELD: (i) The privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the freedom conferred on a citizen under article 19(1) (a) of the constitution. [682 F] (ii) The privilege of preventing the publication of its proceedings or portion expunged by the Speaker in respect of the proceedings is only those of the House of Commons of the Parliament of the United Kingdom and of its members and committees, at the commencement of the Constitution, i.e., January 26, 1950. [683 A] (iii) The privilege is preserved despite the provisions of article 194(3) of theConstitution. [684 B] (iv) The privilege granted to the Legislature of the State is subject only to the freedom of speech, etc., in the State Legislature. [685 C] (v) The privilege under article 19 (1) (b) is preserved despite its provisions. [686 D] (vi) The privilege given to the Legislature is subject to article 19(2) of the, Constitution. [690 B] (vii) The privilege, under article 19, is preserved despite all the provisions of the Constitution and, therefore, if the House of the Commons has the power or privilege to prevent the publication of the proceedings, or at any rate of the expunged portions of it, the Legislature of such a State in India, has also a similar privilege or power and it can exercise it, notwithstanding the fact that it infringes the fundamental right of a citizen.

The appellants were working as Readers in different faculties in the said College on the date of the transfer in the scale of pay Rs.510 860/ and Rs.600/ respectively as on the date when they were promoted to the post of Reader. The respondents were appointed as Readers in various faculties in the State. The Government of Orissa took over the management of the College on and from March 9, 1971, and a formal agreement was executed between the managing committee of the College and the Governor of the State. In the meantime, the Government of Orissa issued a circular dated March 23, 1971, which was followed by a formal agreement. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said circular. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in directing the Gov ernment to take into account, as experience, the service of the respondents while they were in the private college since, according to him, the necessary qualification was eight years experience in Class II, Orissa Education Serv ice (O.E.S.). The High Court also erred in directing that the Gov ernsment to take in account, as Experience, the service rendered by the respondents while he was in the private College since, according t o him, the requisite qualification was eight year experience in Class III, Orissa Education Service (O.F.S.). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The condition of draw ing of Rs.600/- or more on the date o take over, which has been laid down in the said circular as a particular qualification for eligibility for appointment as Reader and later for consideration of their suitability by the Public Service Commission for appointment as Readers is arbitrary and discriminatory. [775C] 1.2 The condition of drawing of Rs.100/ or more on a date of take over, is arbitrary and violative of Article 16 in the High Courts. [776F] 1.3 The condition of pay of Rs.200/ or more, on the date, of taking over, which had been laid down, in the said Circular as a particular qualifica tions for eligibility for appoint ment as Reader and subsequent for consideration of his suitability by the public Service Commission for appoint ment, is arbitrary, and discriminatory. The said circular had to stand the test of Article 16. [778G] 1.4 The condition of drawn of Rs.500/ or more is arbitrary and irrational. The only differentia was, therefore, the salary drawn by the Readers on the date Of take over, that action based on the salary aspect under the said circular had also to stand the tests of Article 16 and in the High court, as well, before us. [782A] 1.5 The condition of payment of Rs.300/ or more as on the dates of take over and which has been placed in the said order as a particular qualifications for eligibility for the post is arbitrary and unreasonable. [785B] 1.6 The condition of drew of Rs.400/ or more for consideration of the Public Service Commis sioner whose recommendations will be considered by the Government in the matter of final absorption in the Government College, first time presented before the Public Service commission for consideration of its suitability by the Government for appointment as Professors is a seriously grim issue. Action under the Government circular of March 23,1971 alone, was in controversy in the High courts. The said Circular took recognition of the service in the private colleges in the case of two (1) ; The only differentia, therefore, was the salary drawn on the date on take over. That action based on that salary aspect had to.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1) for plying the passenger vehicles on Khurja Pahasu Chhatari Dabai Rajghat Baba route (route for short) which applications came to be rejected by the State Transport Authority and their appeal to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and writ petition to the High Court was dismissed. The State Transport Authority appealed to the High court and writ petition was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that in respect of the route a scheme has been prepared and published under section 68C of Chapter IV A of . The route in question is an inter regional route and therefore an application for temporary permit for the period intervening between the date of publication of the scheme and the date of publishing the approved or modified scheme has to be made to the State transport Authority under sec. 68 F(I A) of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State transport Authority has power under sub section (1) to grant temporary permits to any person in respect of a area or the route or part thereof specified in the scheme and to grant so to the exclusion of any other applicant. But if the Corporation is willing to operate vehicles to the maximum strength undoubtedly the State Transport authority will have to grant permit to the Corporation under section 68F(1 A) to the exclusion Of any other applicant if the Corporation has applied for all the permits. But if it is unable to provide vehicles for the optimum strength fixed by the State transport authority the remaining permits will have to be granted to any other person willing Jo obtain temporary permit and ply vehicle because in respect of remaining strength there would be no application by the Corporation and section 68 F (1 A) would be squarely attracted. [985 B C] 2. The State Government has power under section 68 to grant temporary permit to any person other than the Corporation to operate vehicles on the route for which the scheme is published till modified or approved scheme is published. But if there are 7 vacancies and the Corporation applied for only 3 temporary permits, once the Corporation made an application for the temporary permit not for the full strength but something short of it there would be a no application by it and section 68F (1 A), would be squarely applicable. [986 C D] 3. The State Road Transport Authority has power to grant temporary temporary permits to persons other than the corporation to operate vehicles for the purpose of the large travelling public. But if a Corporation applies for all the permit, it cannot grant to any one else if the Corporation had applied for all of the permits. [987 D] 4. The State Public Transport Authority has powers under sub section(1) to make temporary permits to all persons other than those Corporation to operate Vehicles on the route. If the Corporation is unable to supply vehicles for the huge strength fixed by it the remaining permits would have to be given to any other persons willing Jo obtain Temporary permit and ply vehicles because in respect thereof the remaining strength there will be no application of the Corporation and Section 68 F(2) would be attracted. But if, the Corporation does not apply for all the temporary permits but only for some, the inevitable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation has made no application for the Temporary permits and section 68 E(1 A), therefore, would be squarely covered.

The appellant, a son of Sarup, filed a suit for partition of his property, which was decreed by the trial court. The appellant 's father, who delivered the judgment of the Board, explained the earlier decision of the Privy Council in Raja Chelikani Venkayyamma Garu 's case (1) and observed that in the village community where a daughter succeeds, either in preference to or in default of, heirs male, to property which, if the descent had been through a son, would be ancestral property. The trial court held that the property inherited by the appellant was not ancestral property but that the property in suit was ancestral property. On appeal, the High Court held that the properties inherited by the respondent 10 were not ancestral property and that the property was governed by the customary law of the Punjab. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the property which was inherited by the father was not ancestral but that the appellant had no right to bring the present suit. HELD: (i) The decision of the first Full Bench in Narotam Chand 's case was wholly unsustainable as a decision on the point of the relevant custom. [707 A B] (ii) The decision in Narotham Chand 's Case (1) was wholly unsustainable. [708 C] (iii) The decision was wholly unsustainable and should present no obstacle in holding that the earlier cases of the Full Bench of the Punjab High Court were not correctly decided. [709 C] (iv) The decision by the first Full bench was wholly unsustainable because a decision on that point of the law was to confer upon the son of the person who inherited the property from his maternal grandfather the right to challenge his alienation of the said property. [710 D] (v) The decision on the question of the relevant customs was wholly unsustainable, as a decision of the earlier Full Bench was wholly unsustainable in law. [711 E] (vi) The decision did not rest upon any evidence relating to custom on the subject but was based on what the majority of the judges considered to be the general principles of the customary law and upon the argument abinconvenienti. [712 E] (vii) The decision that the property of the father is not ancestral property was in applicable and should present none of the obstacle in the holding of that decision.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum, on charges under section 449 and section 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of the 14th November, 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came there and while one of them Abdul Odud pressed his knees and Ekram and Habibullah pressed his chest and hands, Matiullah inflicted an injury on his neck with a dagger. The appellants were convicted under section 449 of the Indian. Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years under section 307/ 34 and to rigorous imprisonment of two years under s. 449 of the Code. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the words "in order to" have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 of Indian Penal Code but in the two succeeding sections 450, 451 and again in section 454 of the Indian penal Code. HELD : (i) The words "in pursuance of the common intention of all, the legal position that results is that each person shall be held to have committed the entire criminal act. [982 G] (ii) The words 'in order to ' have been used in section 449 must in law be considered to have done this act of using the dagger. [983 B] (iii) The words used in section 450 must in law have been used not only in s. 449 but in the three succeeding sections 450 and 451 of the Indian Code. [984 D] (iv) The words in order to 'have committed the whole criminal act must in law mean that each person should be held to be guilty of murder. [985 D] (v) The words must in law take their colour from the words used in the section. The words must be construed in their ordinary sense. The words used must in law receive their colour from each other. The words are used in the sense in which they are used in their ordinary senses. [986 E] (vi) The words are not used in the ordinary sense. They are used in a sense which is not intended to be used in the normal sense. They must be construed as equivalent to the ordinary sense of the term. [987 E] (vii) The words of section 450 must be construed according to their ordinary meaning. The words 'shall ' in law take its colour from the context in which they have been used. They must, therefore, be construed as having been used in the context in Which they have been so used. [994 E F] (viii) The words were used in the general sense. They were used in a particular sense. They could not be construed as synonymous with the words used. They were not intended to take in their ordinary meaning as used in the Act. [996 G H] (ix) The words have been used to take in the ordinary way of committing theft but they were used in different senses. They were intended to take colour from each others. [997 F] (x) The words cannot be construed as referring to the ordinary meaning of the words used by the Legislature. They were meant to take in its ordinary sense.

The appellant, a Sarswat Brahmin, was a Sarsawat Brahmin, resident of Pathankot in the district of Gurdaspur and the last male holder of the properties in suit was non ancestral. The respondent contested the suit mainly on the grounds (i) that the suit for a mere declaration was not maintainable (ii)that the parties were governed by Hindu Law and not by Hindu Law, (iii)that the appellant was not a collateral of Gurdial at all, (iv)that the properties in dispute were not ancestral, and (v) that there was no custom whereby the collaterals of the father who was the last male member excluded the daughter from succession to the selfacquired property of her father. The Trial Court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was a collateral of a Sarsyas Brahmin, and that the properties in the suit were not ancestral and the respondent was not a beneficiary of the custom. HELD: (i) The appellant 's right to succeed to her father 's ancestral propertie 'section The general custom of the Punjab being that a daughter excludes the collaterals from succession to self acquired property of her husband, the initial onus, there fore, must on principle, be on the collaterals to show that the general custom in favour of the daughter has been varied by a special local custom excluding the daughter of the last male person excluded from succession to her selfacquired property. [153 B C] (ii)The appellant 's rights to succeed to his father 's selfacquired property in preference to collaterals even though they were within the fourth degree and it was enough for the Court to say that irrespective of whether the properties in question were ancestral or selfacquired the collaterals in that case could not succeed to her. [153 D] (iii)The appellant was a Sari Brahmin, a Sarira Brahmin, of the Gurdaspur district and indeed a member of this very family of Gurdial Singh, succeeded in preference to his daughter. The appellant ' s right to succeed his father ' s ancestral propertiee 'section The appellant ' 's right was not affected by the custom. [153 E F] (iv)The appellant had not cited a single instance of a daughter having excluded the collaterals therefrom from succession to his selfacquired property, and had, therefore, failed to discharge the onus that was thrown on her as a result of the production by the appellant of the Riwaj i am of 1913 and, consequently, the appellant must succeed.

The respondent was the Managing Director of Messrs Bird and Co. Ltd., and of Messrs Bird & Co., Ltd., which were acting as Managing Agents of several Companies registered under the Indian Companies Act. Das Gupta, J. was of the opinion that the different capacities of the executant were distinct matters for the purposes of section 5, and that the instrument was chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty payable if separate instruments were executed in respect of each of those capacities. Held, that the instrument in question did not comprise distinct matters and therefore the instrument in dispute did not comprise the distinct matters. The instrument in question was a power of attorney, and it was within the very nature of the general power of attorney that all the distinct acts which the donor is capable of performing are comprised in the one instrument which is executed by him, and if that is the position, it is but logical that whatever acts the donor is incapable of performing whether in his individual capacity or in his representative capacity as trustee or as executor or administrator are also comprised within the instrument and are not distinct matters to be dealt with as such so as to attract the operation of section 5. The instrument was executed by one person, if he fills several capacities and the authority conferred is general, there would be distinct delegations in respect of every transaction entered into by him in his personal capacity. The instrument did not comprise any distinct matter and that matter was the execution of a general power of Attorney by the donor in favour of the donees constituting the donees constituted the donees constitute the donees. The instrument, therefore, did not comprise separate matters and that it was not necessary to constitute the instrument one comprising distinct matters and thus requiring to be 855 stamped with the aggregate value of the duties with which separate instruments each comprising or relating to one of such matters would be chargeable under the Act within the meaning of section 5 of the Act within that meaning of section 6. The instrument could not be split up into separate instruments each consisting or relating to a distinct matter in so far as the different capacities were concerned. The instrument had to be construed as distinct matters and the question whether the instrument proposed to be executed by the respondent was one which could be done by the donor himself, whatever be the capacity or capacities which he enjoys and cannot be split up.

The assessee was a Mahalaxmi Mills Ltd., in the other two appeals. The assessee claimed that the depreciation was allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as it had been in force in the past. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that no deduction could have been made on the strength of the words which would have been allowed to him if the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 was in force in that past. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the depreciation availed of by the assessee under the Bhavnagar War Profits Act was a deductible amount in computing the written down value. The Appellate Tribunal, however, took a different view and held that the expression "or which would have be allowed to him" did not permit the Income tax Officer to make any deduction under this bead. The High Court, however, held that the words "any law relating to tax" would also have been omitted and that the words 'any law relating ' to tax on profits of business would also have to be omitted and this part of the paragraph would have read as "all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income tax and super tax or any law relating to taxation on profits of Business which was law of a Part A State would come within the first portion of the clause. The High court, however, did not accept the contention of the assessee that no deduction should have been made under this be that the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 had been in existence in the past as in fact no claim was made or could be made for such allowance, was rejected by the Income tax officer. The assessee appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The words "any tax" would have been omitted, and this part would have read in the context of the words "all depreciation already allowed under any law or rules of any Part B State" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order. [231 B] (2) The words 'any tax" in paragraph 1 of the Removal Order are apt and sufficient to express the intention that if the Income tax Act had in fact been in force, the depreciation that would have been allowable if proper claim had been made should be deducted in ascertaining the written down Value. [231 C] (3) The words used, in our opinion, are apt and enough to express the intent that if the income tax Act, 1961, which was not in force in this State before, had been in operation, the depreciation allowed under any Laws or rules of Part B State before it became included in the Part B State, would come within first portion of clause. [231 D] (4) The words, "any law" in paragraph I of the Removal order, are apt, and sufficient to give effect to this intention. [231 E] (5) The words are apt and adequate to express the intentions that if the words "or any law relating " tax on profits" had been in fact in force, they would have been disallowed if proper claim has been made and substantiated, assuming the Indian Income Income tax Act. 1922, was in force. [231 G] (6) The words in paragraph 1 are apt and reasonable to express the idea that if the Incometax Act, 1922 which was not applicable in the State before it become included in thePart B State, it would be reasonable to think that the words actually used are not sufficient to express and give effect to the intention that the Income tax law would have been allow if proper claim was made should be deduction in ascertaining the Written down value.

The petitioner, a contractor, had submitted tender forms for the construction of a new project. The petitioner, a retired contractor, had also submitted tender forms. The petitioner had also submitted the same. The petitioner was also informed that the tender forms would be supplied at any time. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award of the contract by the Karnataka Power Corporation Ltd. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High Court had erred in holding that it was only para I that stipulates the pre conditions and that all the documents referred to in the other paras can be supplied at the time of the final award of the contracts. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The pre conditions and the pre conditions of eligibility to submit a tender form are only the three conditions set out in para I of the N.I.T. and that all documents referred to therein can be supplied by the intending ten derer. The more harmonious and practical way of construing the N. I.T. is by saying that, before the tender books can be supplied, an intending ten der should satisfy the K.P.C. by supplying such of the documents called for in para V as are material in assessing the fulfilment of the three prequalifying requirements of para I. The more simpler and practical way to construe the N.1.T. of is by saying, that, before a tender is issued, an intending 10 derer should satisfy the M.C.C. that he fulfills the three conditions mentioned in para I. It is for the K. P.C. to assess the value of the certificates furnished in this regard and if the K.p.C. considered them sufficient to warrant the issue of a tender form to the applicant, we do not think it would be able to produce the document by the time stipulated but would have applied had it known that the rule was likely to be relaxed. [237E F] 1.2 The other harmonious and practical manner of construing the two prequalifying conditions of eligibility is by saying "that before the tender Books can be supplied", which sets out the general procedure which the K.A.C. was following in regard to N.I.,T. and the rest of the information were only for information and are such they could be met before consideration of the tenders. The appellant was a displaced person. He was a displaced holder of a evacuee property. He was allotted a evacuee property to the Custodian General of Evacuee Property. The Custodian General of East Punjab, Delhi, issued a notice to the appellant under section 38(1) of the East Punjab Act XIV of 1947, for the cancellation of the allotment of the evacuee property. The appellant filed a revision application before the Custodian General, which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a revision petition before the Custodian of East Punjab. The Custodian of East India, Delhi, set aside the order of confirmation passed against the appellant. The appellant contended that the application for confirmation pending on the date when the Central Act XXXI of 1947 came into force, had to be disposed of in accordance with sections 5 A and 5 B of the East East Punjab Act XV of 1947, as amended in 1948, and that the order of confirmed was not open to appeal or revision and it was specifically declared to be final and conclusive. Held, that the order under appeal was one passed by virtue of the wide powers of revision vested in the Custodian General under section 27 of the Act. The order under appeal did not amount to an order passed by the Custodian or Additional Custodian on an application made long prior to the time when the office of the Custodian General was set up and he was clothed with powers of revision. The order of confirmation was one passed in exercise of the wide power of revision vested under section 27 and was not subject to appeal or revisional. The order was one passed on the application made long after the Central Act XXXIII of 1947 came in force. The order passed under appeal was not one passed by the Administrator or Additional Custodian. The order in appeal was one made by virtue of wide powers of Revision vested in the Central Custodian General under s. 27 of the East India Act XIV of 1948, and the order of the confirmation passed in 1952 would clearly be subject to the revisional power of the CustodianGeneral under section 27 Of the Act.

The High court held that the demand pertaining to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 was not such a matter as had to be adjudicated and it also did not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. The High 'Court also held that the Tribunal had not committed any error in holding that the demand for bonus was not justified. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the Tribunal made short shrift of the workmen 's plea in these words: "In my opinion, the demand pertaining pertaining to the practices or custom prevailing before 1965 is not such a as has to be adjudicated, and it also does not fall under section 32 of Bonus Act, and that the Bonus Act does not provide for those categories of bonus and confines itself to profit based bonus, or does the Bonus Act speak on the topic of bonus of all species and, therefore, stands four square between a claim for bonus and its grant, unless it finds statutory expression in the provisions of that Act ?" Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The subject matter of dispute, as referred by the Government, deals with bonus based on custom or condition of service. The Tribunal, therefore, took the view that so long as that award stood, the same claim under a different guise (the Shops Act) could be subversive of the rule of res judicata. [604 E] 1.2 The main question about the policy of the Parliament that was agitated in that case turned on the availability of the as an independent method of claiming profit bonus de hors the Bonus Act and the Court took the view, that so long that award stood the same claim could be subversive Of the rule of Res judicata. [0604 F] 1.3 The main question regarding the policy of Parliament that was raised in that case was whether the bonus Act was a complete Code and was exhaustive of the subject matter of the dispute, as refered by the Government.

The petitioners in the Writ Petitions were direct recruits appointed to the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab and Haryana and were appointed to the Higher Judicial Service of Haryana and Haryana and the second, between the control over district courts and subordinate courts vested in the High Court by article 235 of the Constitution. The High Court by its judgment dated February 12, 1975, held that the rules governing seniority between direct recruits and promotees appointed to the higher Judicial Service of the Punjab and Haryana were valid and that the seniority of the members of the service, direct recruits or promoted officers, shall be determined by the length of continuous service on a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation. The High court also held that the seniority list of the members, direct recruits and promoted officers, was valid and that it was not open to the High Court to give an arbitrary date of confirmation to the promotees. In the Writ Petitions filed by the direct recruits, the High Court held that the Rules governing seniority between promotees and direct recruits appointed by promotion and by direct recruitment, were valid and the High Court was not justified in applying the rule of rotation at the time of confirmation so that, after every two promotees were confirmed one direct recruit had to be confirmed and until that is done, promotees cannot be confirmed even if vacancies are available within their quota in which they can be confirmed. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the retrospective effect was given to the rules from April 9, 1976 for the mere reason that on August 25, 1976 the High Court had issued a notification fixing seniority of the promotees and direct recruitment of the direct recruits appointed in the service on or after December 31, 1976, and that therefore it was not permissible to the High court to give an erroneous date of confirmation so as to give an undue advantage to the promotees, and that the retrospective operation of the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution was not justified. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The retrospective effect was not given to the Rules from April 9. 1976 for the simple reason that on September 25, 1976, the High court had issued a Notification fixing seniority of direct recruits and direct recruits and appointed to the High Service. The seniority list was drawn by the High Court on the basis of the dates of confirmation allotted to them in compliance with the aforesaid direction (a), and (b). The seniority list will be drawn by the State Government on the basis that the dates of their confirmation were confirmed. [1057C D] 1.2 The High Court was justified in applying that rule of rotation. [1058E] 1.3 The retrospective effect of the proviso was given to rule 8, which was vested in it by Article 235 of the constitution. [1059F] 1.4 The retrospective effect given to the rule from April 9 was given to rules from April 1, 1970 for the mere reasons that on August 24, 1976 the State Government had issued a circular fixing seniority of promotees and direct recruit appointed to the superior Judicial Service of State. The seniority of all officers appointed or promoted to the Superior judicial Service, Punjab before December 31,1976 will be determined by a Court according to the criterion of seniority. [1060G] 1.5 The High Court will re draw the inter se seniority (i) of such of the petitioners and respondents as were promoted or appointed to the inferior Judicial Service prior to December 31, 1977 by the application of the aforesaid principles and in accordance with the Haryana Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1963 1072 as in force on, or as given effect to from April 1. 1970 by the application dated February 12. 3.

The appellant was the auction purchaser in execution of a mortgage decree in respect of a certain property. The appellant filed a suit for a permanent injunction restraining the respondents from interfering with the possession of the appellant. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was the purchaser in execution. The High court held that the appellant had no power to grant the permanent lease in question to the respondents, that the decree which had been passed in the mortgage suit was binding on the appellant and that the Patta being subsequent to the appellant 's mortgage thus came to an end and he was entitled to recover khas possession from the respondents. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant could not grant leases which were not wasteful in their effect the mortgagee 's security. HELD: (i) The appellant could not, in the usual course of management create a ten ancy from year to year in the case of agricultural land or from month to month in the case o property consisting of houses and his dealings with the mortgaged property in the usual way of management, would be operative against the mortgagee. [1106 B] (ii) The appellant was not restricted in the management of the property by making a mortgage and that so long as nothing takes place to impair the value, or impede the operation of the mortgage the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for a term. Mukherjee J. had occasion to consider this very case in Madan Mohan Singh vs Baj Kishore Kumar, ; , and he cited it in support of the proposition that a mortgagor was not restricted by the mortgagee in the management by making a mortgagee and that so far as nothing takes places to impair the valuation of the mortgagee ''s security the mortgagor does not exceed his powers in make a lease for term. [1107 C D] (iii) The appellant had ample opportunity to redeem the mortgage if they so desired but did not choose to exercise their right of redemption, that the execution sale of Gadi Sirampur including the four villages in question was binding on him and that the appellant ' was entitled to khas possession of the four villages of which the defendants were in wrongful possession. [1108 F] (iv) The appellant 's claim and the permanent lease granted by Wazir Narayan to the respondents could not prevail against the appellant. [1109 G] (v) The appellant did not have the power to grant leases which had been granted by Wazir Narain to the respondents. The decree passed by the High Court dismissing the appellant ' suit is set aside and the decree passed by it is restored.

The petitioner, a contractor, was appointed as an arbitrator. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of the contract. A learned Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the petition. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of the Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in the contract to the contrary, cause of arbitration for the purpose of limitation shall be deemed to have accrued to the party in respect of any such matter at the time when it would have accrued but for that term in the agreement. [363E] 1.2 The provisions of section 5 and 12(2) (b) of the Limitation act would apply to arbitration proceedings. [363C] 1.3 The provisions of Section 14 of the Limitation Acts would apply to proceedings in the High Court and the making, after a claim has become statute barred, of a submission of it to arbitration, does not prevent the statute of limitation being pleaded. [363D] 1.4 The provisions of Limitation Act would not apply to arbitrations as it applies to actions in the High Courts and the making after a claim had become statute barred. [363F] 1.5 The provisions of Sections 5 and 12 (2) (a) to (b) would apply to the arbitrations and notwithstanding anything contained in the contract, to the contrary. [363G] 1.6 The provisions of sections 5 and 12 of the Limitation (Amendment) Act, 1976 would apply to Arbitration proceedings. [ 363D] 1:7 The provisions of this Limitation Act would be applicable to arbitrations and unless any term in an arbitration agreement to the contrary is terminated by leave of the Court, or where the Court removed an umpire who has entered on the reference or a sole arbitrator or all the arbitrators, the Court may, on the application of any party to the arbitration agreement, either (b)order that the arbitration agreement shall cease to have effect with respect to the difference referred. [363A] 1.8 The provisions of a Limitation Act would, therefore, apply to arbitrations. [363B] 1:9. The provisions of that Limitation Act would also apply to arbitrations in the High courts and the making of after a claim having become statute barred by a submission of the claim to arbitration, do not prevent the legislature of limitation being urged. [363H] 1:10. The provisions contained in sections 5 and12 (2) of the Act would apply only to arbitrations and not to arbitrations. The provisions would apply to awards and not to arbitration. [363 C] 1:11. The provisions in the Limitation Act will apply to arbitrations, notwithstanding any term or in the contract. [363 D] 1:12. The provisions relating to arbitration proceedings, and like interpretation were given to section 14 of the Act. [363 F] 1:13. The proceedings before the arbitration are like civil proceedings before the court within the meaning of section 14 of Limitation Act, by consent the parties have substituted the arbitrator for a court of law to arbiter their disputes or differences. [363 G] 1:14. The proceedings in the arbitration are both like civil proceedings and civil proceedings before a court within the ambit of section 14. [363 E] 1:15.

The appellants, who were the mortgagees of the lands in question, filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of the amount due to them on the ground that the execution was barred under section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the execution of the mortgage decree was barred under the principles of res judicata and further that the bar of section 4(c) pleaded was not tenable. HELD: (i) The provisions contained in section 16 in regard to the scaling down of the debts due by the proprietors and tenure holders clearly indicate that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under section 3. Therefore, in construing section 4(D), it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions of the Act do not fall within the protection of the Act. [69 G H] (ii) The provisions of section 16 in respect of the scaling down and the recovery of any such money which may be pending on the date of vesting shall be dropped. [69 C] (iii) The provisions in section 16 are not intended to be exhaustive and exhaustive. The object of the Act is to provide for the transference to the State of the interests of proprietors and tenure holder in land and of the mortgagees and lessees of such interests. [69 E F] (iv) The provisions relating to the scaling up of the debts are clearly intended to give some relief to the debtors who have been taken over from them by notifications issued under sections 3 and 4. [69 F] (v) The provisions are intended to give a certain redress to the creditors whose estates have vested in the State and no others. [69 H] (vi) The provisions made in section 16 of the Act in regard to scaling down of debts due by proprietors and tenureholders clearly indicate that a another object which was intended to achieve was also to provide for a transference to State of the interest of the proprietors and tenures holders in land and in the mortgagees and lessee of such interests, and the lessees of such interest.

[58D] 1.2 The Tribunal has not used their expression "may be allowed to sit at the next Civil Service examination subject to the condition that they must be within the per missible age limit and without having to resign from the service to which they have been allocated, nor would they lose their original seniority in the service to whom they are allocated. [58E] 1.3 The Tribunal has used their expression 'may be allowed ' to sit at a next Civil Services Examination subject to t he provisions of Rule 4 of C.S,E. Rules, and that the aforesaid candidate when allocated, to a service subsequently on allocation either on the basis o the previous CSE and that if he fails to join either of the services, his allocation based on one or both the examinations, as the case may be, will stand cancelled. [58F G] 1.4 The Tribunal has wrongly held that the second Proviso to Rule 4 is not applicable to Scheduled Castes and Tribes candi cases. [58G] 1.5 The Tribunal has erred in holding that the second provisos to Rule 4 are not applicable to those cases. [59F] 1.6 The Tribunal has failed to appreciate that the second Explanation appended to Rule4 is not applicable in the case of Schedule Castes and Tribes. The Tribunal had used their expression ''may be allowed" in their expression "shall be allowed to appear in next Civil Service Examinations subject to the conditions that they must have been allocated not to the Central ServicesGroup 'A ' but to the provisions o r Rule 17. [60G H] 1.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by the Central Government under section 3 of the ( COFEPOSA for short). The Advisory boards have, ofcourse, to be fair in permitting assistance to a friend in order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled to representation through a lawyer. The Advisory Committees have to be careful and careful in permitting the assistance of a legal professional or a legal practitioner. Regard must also be had to, the substance and/or not to the forms since, especially, in matters like proceedings of Advisory Board, whosoever assists or advises On facts of law should be deemed to have been in the position as a legal advisor. [796F] 6. The Advisory Advisory Board has, ofcourse to be careful with regard to the matters like the proceeding of Advisory Boards and whosoever assist or advise on facts of Law must be deemed so to be in that position of a statutory adviser. Regard must have the substance and or not to the Form since, especially when, particularly, in matters of proceedings of Advisory boards, whosoever assistor advises on the facts of law, must be deemed, to be in in the position in a legal advisist. The Advisory Panel Board has, in course, to consider the matter, to be prudent in permitting assistance by a legal practitioner, but that the said facility should be denied to the appellant.

The appellants were the owners of certain mills in the State of West Bengal. The mills were requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal under r. 75 A of the Rules. The appellants were the holders of the pucca delivery orders and the mills were estopped from challenging that the property in the goods had passed (see Anglo India Jute Mills Co. vs Omademall (I) and Omademal vs Omadamall (I.L.R. , referred to. Held, that the requisition of the mills was effective service on the mills as owners for the purpose of r. 75A of the Rules and the property in them passed to the Government of india on September 30, 1946, and the property passed to the appellants on September 30. 1946. The appellants had no right to challenge the validity of the requisition. The appellants could not be said to have acquired property on September 30 1946, as the property in their possession was not requisitioned and the appellants could not have acquired the property on September, 30, 1946. The property in the appellants ' possession was not acquired by the Government under r. 76 A (2) of the Rules, and the appellants were not entitled to the declaration. The appellants ' property was requisitioned by the State Government under r, 75 A (2). The appellants could have acquired the land on September 30 and the property was not requisitioned. The appellants did not acquire the property on the date of requisition. The property was requisitioned for the purpose for requisition and the appellants had no authority to acquire the property. The appellants was not entitled to any declaration under r. 74 A (2), and the appellants ' property could not be acquired under r. 77 A (2)(a).

The petitioners in these writ petitions were appointed to temporary posts on the basis of the competitive examinations and those that were recruited by selection, but both by Union Public Service Commission, terming it as arbitrary and not permissible under the equality clause in the Constitution. The petitioners in the writ petitions were direct recruits to the Indian Railway Service of Engineers Class I. The Union Public Service Commissions had taken a decision to the effect that the Officers so absorbed into the Indian Railway service of Engineers would be given weightage in seniority "on the basis of half the total years of continuous service in working posts in Railways prior to their permanent absorption into Class. The Union of India had taken a policy decision to give weightage of half the length of service to Temporary Assistant Engineers (on a later point of time known as temporary Assistant Officers) appointed by the Railway Board pursuant to the authority given by the President of India on the recommendations of the Union Public Service commission. The Union Government had taken a conscious decision to the extent that the Officers appointed to temporary post on the basis that the Officers were appointed to permanent posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the basis the length of continuous service, though they conceded that in any given year, the candidates appointed as Engineers on the basis Of the results of the competitive examination were placed above those appointed on the basis on which the competitive examinations were conducted. The Union Ministry of Railways had taken a final decision to the said effect. The Union, however, took a conscious decision not to give weightage to the petitioners in the matter of seniority. The Union had taken a further decision to the aforesaid effect. The petitioners filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid decision. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the State is prohibited to create separate channels of service and create discrimination by making one as an isolated one, and not providing for promotional avenues reasonably, fell to the ground in view of the bar of re agitation erected by Direct Recruit 's case (supra). Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State is prohibited from creating separate channels of services and create discrimination, by making one As an isolated one and not providing promotional avenues reasonably. [1027C] 1.2 The State is not prohibited to create different channels of service, and create discrimination against making one as a isolated one, or not providing for promotion avenues reasonably, falls to the ground. [1028D] 1.3 The State is restrained to create separate channel of service and created discrimination by making another as an isolated One, and not provide for promotional avenues reasonable, falling to the ground, in view of bar of re strikes erected by Direct Recruitment 's case. [1029F] 1.4 The State is directed to take a conscious decision in the matter. [1030G] 1.5 The State is also directed to take steps to ensure that the officers so absorbed into Class. [1031C] 1:6 The State is further directed to take necessary steps to ensure the implementation of the aforesaid directions. [1032D] 1:7 The State is, however, directed to take appropriate steps to ensure implementation of the directions. [ 1032F] 1:8 The State is to ensure that there is no undue delay in the implementation of these directions. [1002B] 1:9 The State is at liberty to take appropriate action in the matter, if it thinks fit, and if it thinks necessary, it may take appropriate action. [1033C] 1 :10. The State is accordingly directed to take immediate steps to ensure compliance with the directions.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 9 and 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance, and was convicted under section 11 of the Ordinance. The appellant was convicted under sections 9 and 11 and was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for three years. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that sections 9 and 10 of the Saurashtra Act, which empowered the State Government to direct "offences" to be tried by the Special Court constituted under the Act, were ultra vires the equal protection clause of the Constitution and that the notification issued by the State of Saurashtra was ultra vires the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the notification dated September 9, 1948, issued by the Government of Saurashtra under section 5(1) of the Saurashtra ordinance, was not valid and ultra vires the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 14 of t he Constitution. The notification issued by it was, therefore, not invalid. The notification dated September 7, 1948, was not invalid and ultra vires. The notification was, therefore invalid. The appellant 's contention that section 11 of Saurashtra Ordinance, with which we are here concerned, authorises the State Government, to direct " offences" to he tried by the special tribunal constituted under the West Bengal Special Courts Act, was not correct. The notification, issued by it, was, therefore valid. The notification of September 7, 1949, issued by that date, was, however, different from the notification issued under section 5 (1) of that Ordinance. The notification in question was, therefore not invalid.
