The appellant Corporation was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling cement. The appellant Corporation was a statutory corporation. The appellant was appointed as a driver on probation for a period of two years. The services of the appellant Corporation were terminated on the ground of unsuitability. The appellant 's services were terminated on account of unsatisfactory service. The appellant challenged the order of termination before the Labour Court. The Labour Court held that termination of the services of the employees while on probation on ground of unsuitness amounted to retrenchment and for non compliance with the provisions of section 25F of the ( 'Disputes Act ' for short), the termination was bad. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that termination was bad, but set aside the order of discharge. The High Court held that the termination was not bad. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the termination of the service of the employees was not a case of disbanding surplus labour force and, therefore, did not amount to retrenchment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of the employment of a workman on the transfer or closure of an undertaking was treated by Parliament as 'deemed retrenchment '. The excepted or excluded cases are where termination is by way of punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf, and termination of the contract of service of a probationer would also amount to retrenchment, and, therefore did 788 not amount to termination. [793A] 2. The excepted and excluded cases are, where termination is for a reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by means of disciplinary action. voluntary retirement of a workman is treated by Parliament, as 'deemed ' retrenchment '. [794C] 3. The excepted categories of cases are where the termination is by transfer or closure or termination of service of the workman, retirement of the employee on reaching the date of superannuation of the workman. The excepted cases are where retrenchment is by way or termination of the employee, retirement of a probationer, retirement of an employee on reaching a age of superannuation, retirement of such employee on reaching that age of superannuation or termination of his service of a probation period, but does not include (a) voluntary retirement of an workman; or (b) retirement of the worker on reaching the superannuation age of superannuation. [795D] 4. The excepted category of cases are, when termination is by act of employer even if such termination involved was a consequence of transfer or closure, of the undertaking was to be treated as 'retrenchment ' for the purposes of notice, compensation etc. The excepted, or excluded cases, are where termination of service is by way Of punishment inflicted by virtue of transfer or termination of services of a probationer. voluntary retirement is treated by the Parliament as ' deemed retrenchment '. If the contract of appointment between the employer ' and the workman is terminated by act of the employer even if the contract is terminated by the employer even though such termination involved a condition in that behalf. the excepted or excluded categories are where termination involved by transfer or transfer or closure. The excepted classes are where termination involves a stipulation in the contract ofemployment between the employer or the workman concerned containing a stipulation in a behalf, and the termination of service by act of employee on reaching such age of superannuation is to be treated 'retrenchment'. The excepted or exclude cases are where such termination involved is a consequence of Transfer or closure of the undertaking is to be regarded as 'ret retrenchment '. In the instant case, the excepted or exclude categories are where the retrenchment involved was a result of transfer or transfer of the undertaking, and termination is by operation of law. [796C D] 5.

The question referred at the instance of the assessee to the High Court relates to the question whether the assessee Railway in each appeal is a "dealer" within the meaning of the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 194 1 and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. The assessee, a "dealer", was a "dealer". The assessee, in each case, was a " dealer" for the 781 purpose of the Bengal finance (Sales Tax ) Act, 1941. The assessee applied for registration as a dealer under the Bengal Finance Act in respect of unconnected or unclaimed goods, and was accordingly registered. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the assessee 's activities, and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, rejected the revision application on the finding that the disposal was a regular and feature of the assesse s 's activities and that therefore a sale of goods took place. The assessee then proceeded in further revision to the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, West Bengal. The Board of Revenue held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the assessee and that therefore an sale of goods taken place. The High Court held that the activity of so disposing of the goods did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying on business as a dealer liable to assessment. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the assessee was not a "dealer " within the meaning Of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The question referred to the High court at Calcutta is as follows: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Controller of Stores, Eastern Railways is a dealer" for purposes of as sessment under the Bengal finance Finance (Sales tax) Act, 1941." [780C] 2. The High court disposed of the other case on the same basis as found favour with it in the earlier case. [780D] 3. The question whether the activity of a so disposing of goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It seems to South Eastern Railway was a "business" for the 78 purpose of the carriage. It seems that the activity was adjuncictive to the main activity of the Carriage of goods by Railway. It appears to South Eastern railway was a " Dealer" for the 7 purposes of the Bengal Excise (Sales Tax). Act, 1941, and it is engaged in selling scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. In the case of the assessee South Eastern Railway, what were sold were unclaimed goods. The case was covered directly by this decision. [782E F] 4. The case of the asses sion to the High Curt at Calcutta is covered directly in the earlier cases except that the assessee here is the Eastern Railway and it is engage in selling scrap & unserviceable material. The case falls directly by the decisions of this Court. [787F] 5. The question is whether the assessee is a " dealer".

The appellant, a Director of the Indian Bank, was the Managing Director of the Bank of India. He was the Managing director of the Bank. He was a Director of a company. He was also a Director of an Insurance Company. He was appointed as a Director of another company. He had been instructed in September, 1954, that the Bank would be the sole authority to deal with the securities and that the Bank should be the sole agent of the Bank and that the securities should be purchased by the Bank. The appellant was the Managing Agent of the Bank at Bombay. He was authorised to purchase the securities. He was directed to pay the amount of the short fall of securities. The appellant filed a complaint against the Bank for the offences under sections 409 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code. The Magistrate acquitted the appellant. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was not authorised to purchase or sell securities on behalf of a Insurance Company unless he was authorised by the Chairman. Held, that the contract for the purchase of these securities had taken place on September 16, 1955, and that therefore Chokhani did not include those securities in this letter. The appellant had no knowledge of the passing of money from the funds of the Insurance Company to the Union Agencies as he had nothing to do with the diversion of the funds of Insurance Company to its Union Agencies. The appellant could have had nothing to go with the diversion or the diversion of funds of the Bank to the Union Agency, even though he was a Director. The appellant did not know that the amounts which his company viz., Bhagwati Trading Company, was received by the Insurance Company must have purported to be on account of securities sold to the Insurance Company, as that was the business which Bhagwati Trading Company professed to do and, according to him, he knew to be its business, He knew that most of the amounts was passed on to the Union agencies. He knew that some of the cheques issued on behalf of Bhagwati Trading Company in favour of the Union Agencies were deposited in the Bank by Vishnu Prasad himself It was for him how to direct the necessary entries to be made in the advices prepared by Lakhotia on behalf of Bombay Office at Delhi and on the basis of which journal vouchers were to be prepared by Dhawan and entries were to be made.

The appellants were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the erstwhile State of Saurashtra and Kutch. By sub section (1) of section 115 it was provided that conditions of service applicable immediately before the appointed day to the case of any person allotted to another State shall not be varied to his disadvantage except with the previous approval of the Central Government. Under the , the appellants were allotted permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat of the State of Gujarat under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act. By sub s.(7) it was provided, inter alia, that conditions of services applicable immediately before November 1, 1956, shall not be changed except with the prior approval of the State Government. The appellants were allotted temporary posts in the administrative service of the State under section 81. The State Government by its order dated August 19, 1966, directed that the appellants be treated as "illegal, void and of no effect" and to forbear from enforcing its order treating the persons whose names were specified in the annexure to the order as servants of the "Secretariat cadre". The appellants were given temporary posts in connection with their affairs of the State. The State of Gujarat by its order of August 19, 1967, directed that they be treated as permanent employees of the Secretariat and that they be absorbed in equivalent posts in the Secretariat and on terms not exceeding the conditions of service, the State Government should take steps to absorb them in equivalent posts. The appellants challenged the order of the State before the High Court. The High Court held that the transfer of the former Saurashtra and Kutch States Secretariats to the Gujarat Secretariat per se was not open to question. The appellants appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in deciding the case against the appellants. [501 D] (ii) The High court was right in holding that when the ministerial service employees of the former Gujarat and Kutch States Secretariat were absorbed in the districts, they will not be deprived of their statutory right under section 115(7) proviso. [502 E] (iii) The State of Bombay was competent as a matter of provisional arrangement to absorb the former Saurashtra, and Kutch and the posts in the new State of Bombay and later in the State of Bombay were allotted. [503 D] (iv) The State Government was competent as the matter of provisional arrangements to absorb the latter Saurashtra and Kutch and that assignment of duties performable by the ministerial staff in the Secretariat could not be challenged, and that because they were posted between 1956 and 1960 in the Districts they will not, in our judgment, affect the right of the personnel to be absorbed in the equivalent posts in their Secretariat and on Terms not== Nomadica geous to those they were already entitled except with the approval of the Government of Gujarat either to transfer officers from the Districts and to post and assign them duties in the Secretariat or to fix their pay and seniority among the officers in the Secretariat performing ministerial duties. [504 E] (v) The State was competent as an officer of the Secretariat to transfer and did transfer the appellants to perform ministerial duties. The State was not competent to transfer and do transfer the appellants in the Secretariat.

The petitioners, who were dealers in cotton and sell them in the course of inter State trade or commerce, were assessed to sales tax under the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The petitioners challenged the assessment on the ground that the tax was levied on the sale of cotton and sold in the course in inter State trade and commerce, and that the tax levied was in excess of the prescribed limit. The petitioners contended that the tax had been levied on the purchase of cotton and that the petitioners were not liable to pay sales tax under section 5(2)(a)(vi) or a refund under section 12 of the Act. The petitioners also contended that the Act itself did not indicate the stage at which the tax was to be levied and that the Act did not indicate that the stage at where the tax was leviable was not so stated in the Act or the rules thereunder. The petitioners, however, contended that the provisions of section 15(1) of the Central Act were not mandatory and that the provisions were not mandatory. The petitioners relied on the decision of this Court in State of Madras vs M/s. Madras Cotton Mills Ltd. ; and contended that the petitioners had not been able to show that the tax imposed was excessive. The petitioners further contended that the levy of sales tax was in excess and that the State had no power to impose the tax. The petitioners submitted that the tax could not be said to be higher in the case of imported goods. Held, that the tax cannot be said to have been levied on purchase of cotton or sold in the State and similar goods imported in the State are prohibited by that clause. The tax is at the same rate and therefore the tax cannot also be said to ' higher in the cases of imported goods, and the tax cannot therefore be said to been higher in the nature of sales tax.

The respondent mortgaged the mortgaged property to the appellants. The appellants filed a suit for the recovery of the mortgage debt. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment of certain specified amounts by way of redemption. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the view taken by the District Judge was right and should not have been disturbed. The High court was right in allowing the appeal. The view taken by it was right and must not have been interfered with. The subsequent agreement between the parties arrived at in course of the execution proceedings by which the decreeholders agreed to release the interest of defendant No. 2 and that of defendants 3 to 7 separately on payment of some specified amounts by 'them proceeds clearly on the assumption that the mortgage debts and the security have been split up and in our opinion it is not possible for the defendant No. 1 to get the benefit of the scaling down of the decree in favour of defendants 2 to 7. The subsequent agreements arrived at in the course of the Execution proceedings by which, the decreeholders agree to release the interests of defendant No, 2 and that by defendants 2 to7 separately on payment and the specified amounts by "them proceeds clearly On the assumption that a purchaser could get the benefit, of the relief which has been granted to his agriculturist co debtor under the provisions of the Act, the benefit of scaling down the mortgaged property would not be liable to be sold. The subsequent contract between the parties would be of no avail to the defendant No, 1 to get his debt scaled down in favour of the agriculturist mortgagor.

The appellants, who were the appellants in the City Civil Court, were tenants of the premises in question under the first respondent. The first respondent, who was the tenant of the premises, was a tenant of the first respondent and was entitled to protection under the Act and that the second and third plaintiffs were lawful sub tenants of the first appellant and were entitled to possession, use and occupation of the premises as subtenants thereof. The City Civil Court held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but dismissed the suit on the ground that there bad been no lawful subletting by the first respondent of the premises to the second and the third plaintiffs as the provisions of section 10 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bombay Act No. "). The City Civil Judge, however, held that it was not competent to the City Civil Judge to entertain the claim but dismissed the appeal on the ground of non est subletting. The City civil Court, however, dismissed the suit holding that it had no jurisdiction to entertain and try the suit but held that it did not have jurisdiction to entertain it. The City Court, however dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The City Civil Courts Act, 1947, was not applicable to the City civil Court. [734 C] (2) The City civil Courts Act, 1944, was not a law relating to eviction of tenants and those to whom they had sublet the premises was to be determined by the courts specified in section 28 and no other. [735 D] (3) The City Court could not decree the suit of the appellants unless their claim to remain in possession was established under the Act or any of its provisions. [736 E] (4) The City of Bombay Act, 1947 was not applicable in the City civil court. [737 C] (5) The City Act, 1947 did not contemplate the filing of any suit relating to possession of premises to which the provisions of Part 11 of the Act apply and in that suit claims and questions arising out of the Act or the any of its provision had to be dealt with. [738 E] (6) The City Courts Act, 1948, was not an Act relating to eviction and eviction of tenants. [739 E] (7) The City Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, was not attracted in the City of Bombay. [740 E] (8) The City Small Causes Court Act, 1947 had to determine whether the plaintiffs had established their claim to be in possession of the premises within the meaning of the Act and no other, court could have jurisdiction to try such a suit.

The appellant was a managing director of the Company. On July 7, 1955, Dadoba transferred his business to the Company. The appellant contended that the appointment of the appellant was void. The High Court took the view that the word "assignment" in the section included "appointment", and so, such an appointment would also be void under the section. The High court took the view, that the word 'assignment ' in the section includes an appointment of a director by a director of his successor in office, and that since the new Act was a consolidating Act, it must be deemed to have continued the policy of the earlier Act and, therefore, for the purpose of section 312 of the new Act, an "assignment", must include an "appointment". The High Court, however, took the view in the case of Dadoba that an appointment by a director to the office which he previously held but did not hold at the date of the appointment, was not to be included within the word "resignment". The High court, however, did not agree with the view taken by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The proviso to section 86B does not assist the argument that in section 312 of a new Act the word "asignment" would include "appointment". [341 E] (2) The proviso does not indicate that it was intended that the word"assignment" would includes "appointment". It does not indicate, that it was meant that the word was intended that a director by the section would include an appointment. [341 E F] (3) The proviso shows that it was not intended that the words "assignment of his office" in the main part of section would include " appointment". The rule of construction on which the High Court relied in arriving at the view that it did, was put in these words: "It is a well established principle of construction that when one finds a proviso to a section, the presumption is that but for the proviso the enacting part of the section would have included the subject matter of the proviso." [341 E G] (4) The proviso is not intended to relieve the court from exercising its discretion in regard to section 86 B at the most that an appointment of an alternate director by a directors to the office of a director, was not an assignment of his office by him for the old Act contained in section 83B, 340 provisions substantially similar to those contained in section 255 of the new and Act. [341 G] (5) The proviso, therefore, does not assist a construction of section 312, because it does not expressly say that it was used in the main portion of section 86B.

The appellants are the tenants of the premises situated at No. 6 Kasi Chetty Street, G.T. Madras. They carry on business there. The respondent landlord filed an eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart on the ground that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the said shop let out to the said M/s Adeshwar Glass Shop and were liable to be evicted for HAMEEDULLAH sublet under the provision of Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and 419 Rent Control) Act, 1960. The Trial Court held that the appellants were liable to eviction for HAMEEDULLAH subletting under the provision Of Section 10(1)(ii)(i)(a) and (vii) of the said Rent Act. The Appellate Authority dismissed the said appeal. The appellants then preferred a Civil Revision Petition being C.R.P. No. 44 of 1981 in the High Court of Madras against the decision of the Appellate Authority. The High Court dismissed the said revision petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have rightly held that the appel lants had sublet the shop to M/s M/s R. Adeshwar glass Mart and were liable for eviction as sought by the respondent. [420B] 2. The High courts have rightly held the appel late to be the tenant of the premises. [420C] 3. The High court has rightly held that there was no substance in this contention. [420D] 4. The appellants have not challenged the finding of subletting. [420F] 5. The appellants are the partners of the firm. They carry business in the said premises even for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the business there. [420G] 6. The appellants were not the partners of M/S. Adeshwar Steel Mart. The firm was carried on business in that premises even for certain time during which it had ceased to be carrying on the business. The firm had ceased lo carry on the said business. [420E] 7. The appellants had sublet the premises to M/S Adeshwar Glass Plant. The firm, therefore, was carried on by the appellants as respondents.

The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1960 was enacted to provide for the imposition of ceiling on land situate within the urban agglomerations. Section 2(n) of the Act provided that the ceiling area in the case of every individual who was not a member of a family unit, and in the case where any other person was not a family unit at the date of the enactment of the Andhra Pradesh Act, the Andhra Pradesh Land Revenue Act, 1956 would apply to land situate in such area and the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Act, 1957 would apply in relation to land situate within such area. Section 2 (n) of that Act provided that in an area other than that comprised in the urban agglomeration referred to in section 2(n), land held by a person in excess of the ceiling area would be liable to be determined as on 1st January 1975 under the Andhra Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960. Section 2 of the Act defined the expression "family unit" to mean a unit of land which is not a member or a family unit. Section 2 provided that the expression " family unit" shall include a unit of lands which is not an urban agglomeration. Section 3(f) provided that the land held by any person in excess shall be liable to the ceiling area. Section 4 provided that the surplus holding of land in excess of ceiling area shall be determined as if the land was held by a family unit and only land within the ceiling area shall he allowed to remain with him. Section 4(1) provided that in any area other than the urban agglomomerations referred to in Section 2(j), land held in excess of that ceiling area shall, be liable to land revenue. Section 4 empowered the State Government to declare any land as an urban agglomeration. Section 5 provided that the provisions of the Act shall apply to all urban agglomerates. Section 6 provided that the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare any land to be an urban agglomory. Section 7 provided that the excess land shall be deemed to be an agricultural land. Section 8 provided that the total area of the urban aggloms shall be deemed not to be an area of land which was not an urban land. Section 9 provided that the amount of land revenue payable by any person shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of this Act. Section 10 provided that the net area of the land shall be determined by the Collector. Section 11 provided that the Collector shall, on the application of the person interested, determine the ceiling area of the lands in the urban area. Section 12 provided that the determination of the ceiling shall be made in accordance with rules made under the Act. Section 13 provided that the assessment of the ceiling areas shall be made by the Collector in accordance with such rules as may be made by him. Section 14 provided that the rules made under this Act shall be published in the official Gazette. Section 15 provided that the power of the State Government shall be exercised by the Collector on the application made by the person interested. Section 16 provided that the order of the Collector shall be final. Section 17 provided that the orders of the Collector under the Act shall be final and shall not be questioned in any court. Section 18 provided that the powers of the Collector in relation to the ceiling areas in the urban areas shall be exercised in the same manner as the provisions of Chapter III of the Andhra Land Revenue Act. Section 18 provides that the Collector may, on the requisition of the Collector, make an order determining the ceiling area and the ceiling area thereof. Section 19 provided that the said order shall be final, and shall not take effect until the expiry of two months from the date of such order. Section 20 provided that the final order shall be passed in the prescribed manner.

The respondents were workmen of the appellant company. The respondents were directed to be taken back in employment. The workmen were directed to take back the services of the respondents by discharging them with effect from August 24, 1953. The workmen reported for duty on October 2, 1953, and October 2,1953, but failed to produce evidence satisfactory to the Company of their absence as required by the notice dated September 17, 1953. On October 2, 1952, the respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order directing that the employees who had turned up on or before October 2, 1954, must be taken back into employment without condition and of the two men who came later, one was ill of typhoid fever and had sufficient reason for reporting himself for duty on September 17,1953. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Industrial Tribunal had in each case considered the justification for absence without leave and in view of the circumstance that the men were in custody, the Company was not justified in refusing leave. HELD: (i) The Industrial Tribunal had rightly found that the services of Chattoraj were rightly terminated under the Standing Orders of the Company. [696 B] (ii) The Industrial Court had in each of the cases considered the justification of absence without leave, and in view Of the circumstance that Chattoraj indulged in activities prejudicial to the Company and it was now recognised that deliberate 'slow down ' tactics and an incitement to other workmen to adopt such tactics both amount to misconduct. [697 C] (iii) The Industrial Tribunals had in each cases considered the question whether the charges had been proved and the Industrial Tribunal should not have interfered with the decision of the Company unless it found that the decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. [698 C] (iv) The Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1947, was not a law within the meaning of section 2(k) of the Act. [699 C] (v) The Industrial Appellate Tribunal had in every case considered the question of the validity of the Standing Orders and held that the Industrial Tribunals had not interfered with the decisions of the Company, unless it found, that the decision of that Company to terminate the services of such employees was mala fide. [695 D] (vi) The Industrial Courts had in each individual case considered the scope of the Standing orders of the Company and the Industrial Tribunals and found that the decisions of that Company were mala fide or amounting to victimisation. If, on the contrary, the Tribunal proceeded on the footing that the company had decided to terminate the service of Chattorraj on the ground of his prejudicial and subversive activities then on being satisfied that Chattorraj was guilty of such activities the proper order would have been to give the Company permission to dismiss Chattoraj. [694 E F] (vii) The Industrial tribunals had in each one case considered the explanation of Chattorjaj and observed that deliberate ''slow down ' strategy and an incitement ' to other workmen, to adopt such device both amount to ' misconduct. If, however, the Tribunal proceed on the footing, that the company has decided to terminate their services, then on being satisfaction that Chattorj was guilty of misconduct, the proper order will have to give the company permission to dismissChattoraj. If, therefore, the Tribunal proceeds on the footing of that the company was forced to give leave to all of them for a "more or less indefinite period, then on be satisfied that Chattaj was guilty of the said activities the proper orders would have been give the company leave to all them for a 'more or less than indefinite period.

The appellant University of Rajaswas invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under Section 5 of the Urea Kant was mentioned in the reserve list by the Selection Committee. Dr. Urea Kant who was already selected and kept in the reserve pool was appointed as Professor in the Department of Bot any. Dr. Nathawat who was already appointed as Professor on the ground that the Selection Committee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a selected person joins the post, the reserve list exhausted itself. Dr. M.S. Chauhan, who was already selection and kept in reserve list was appointed as professor in the department. Dr. P.K. Chauhan, the appellant, who was earlier selected and kept under the reserve list was selected as Professor in Botany and his name was recommended in the reserve panel by the duly constituted Selection Committee. The Selection Commis sioner recommended the name of the appellant Dr. Section 6 Procedure of Selection Committee for selection of a professor in the Department. The Selection Board approved and recommended the name o f the appellant Dr, Section 6 Procedure for selection of the appellant. The Selection committee approved and recommended his name to the University. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Selection Committee 's order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The very purpose of preparing a reserve list would be defeated if the view taken by the High Court is accepted that once a person selected by the Selection Commisioner has joined that post then selection made by the Committee is exhausted and the reserve list is of no avail and becomes extinct. There was no meaning or purpose of keeping the reserve list alive for a long period of one year, as no person selected for the post can at all be expected not to join for such a long period. [421D] 1.2 The very purpose for preparing a reserve List would be defeated when the view taken of the High Court was accepted that once the person selected by t he Selection Committee has joined that posts then selection madeby the Committee is complete and the reserve s list is of nothing to do with the appointment of a teacher in the university. [422E] 1.3 The very purpose is to prepare a reserve list to the extent of 50% of the vacancies in the post of teachers or officers for which the selection committee was constituted. The suitability of the persons kept in the reserved list is also adjudged by the Selection committee which is constituted for selection of teacher in the University. Thus no fault can be found that the incumbent recommended in the reserved List by the Selection Board was not selected for the concerned post of teacher. [423D] 1:4 The very purpose and purpose of preparing the reserve list would also be defeated if a view taken by t he High Court is accept that once a candidate selected by the selection committee has joined that office then selection made in the last decade from the reserve list, and numerous appointments have been made in the Last decade from the reserved list, and several appointments have been mad in the last year from the reserve lists. In the result, the very purpose of preparation a reserve list will be defeated if it is held that once a man selected by the Committee has joined the post then selection mad by the Committee becomes exhausted and the reserved list becomes extinct, and the reserve List is of no use for the appointment on a vacant post caused during the validity period of the reserve list.

The petitioners, who were owners of certain lands, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was not applicable to them. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Act did not apply to the lands in question and that the Act had no application to the lands. HELD: (1) The Act did not make any provision for the acquisition of any land designated for public purposes under section 7 of the Act at least for 14 years and that the local authority could not protract the acquisition of the land designated for a public purpose under section 7. [285E] (2) The preparation of the draft of a section of the development plan for K, P and R Wards was not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the local authority. If the provisions of the Act were borne in mind and the rules framed thereunder complied with, as appears to have been done in these cases, there was little or no scope for the local authority acting arbitrarily under section 13 of the Act. [285G H] (3) The preparation and the final development plan was not something that was left to be pleasure or discretion or of the local authorities. If the provision of the Act are borne in mind, and the rules made thereunder complied with the provisions of sections 4 to 16 (both inclusive) shall, so far as they can be made, apply in respect of such revision of the development plans. [285B C] (4) The preparation or the final development plans was not something what was left to its pleasure or discretion. If the rules framed under the Act complied with, the question was a simple one as to whether the commencement certificate could be given without doing any violation to the development plan. [285C] (5) The preparation, of the draft development plan or the final Development plan was not nothing which was left left to the discretion or discretion of local authority. [285F] (6) The preparation was not something more than a mere preparation of the final development Plan. If the requirements of the Act had been complied with, there was no reason for the local authorities acting arbitrarily under sections 13 of the . [285E F] (7) The preparation for the final development scheme was not something much which was left in the pleasure or discretionary discretion of the Local authority. If, the provisions of section 4 and 11(3) of the Act complied wit ness, as appears from the rules framed therein, there was hardly any scope for the Local authority acting arbitrarily. [285D] (8) The preparation in the draft of the draft Development Plan or the final publication of the final Development Plan was not something but a mere preparation. [285H] (9) The preparation made of the final plan or the provisional development plan was nothing more than a simple one. [285A] (10) The preparation prepared of the final draft development plan was never something which was to the pleasure of the local author. If the relevant provisions of the statute were borne in view and the rules were not borne in mind the rules framed therefor complied with, it was difficult to envisage what other authority could be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. [285AB] (11) The preparation is not something which is left to the mercy or discretion of a local authority. The preparation of a draft development plan is not something more which was left open to the pleasure and discretion of the State Government.

The territory of the State of Kutch merged with the Dominion of India. The territory of the Union was merged with the State of Saurashtra. The State of Kutch was a part of India and had always been so from the establishment of the two dominions. The territory in this sector was contiguous to and in fact was an extension of the mainland of Sind. The territory was a part and parcel of the erstwhile State of Kutch. The State Government of Saurashtra had no authority to alter the boundary of the State. The State was a part in the territory of the erstwhile Sind and the Union of India had no authority under the Constitution to alter the boundaries of the State in which the territory was merged. The State had no authority in the matter of alteration of the boundaries of Sind and the Rann of Kutch. In the year 1949, the State of Gujarat had been merged with the Union of Pakistan. The State merged with the Central Government. The State continued to be the part of the territory of India. On the question whether the Great Rann of Bhuj was part of the State and was now Indian territory, the High Court held that the Great R Ann of Kutch was part of India. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Great Bann of Kutch was an extension and that the area was in different state at different seasons in the year for part of the year it was water and for the remaining part it was land. HELD: (1) The territory in question was contiguous to the territory of Sind and apart from the survey maps there was no evidence that it was part of Great Rann. The evidence on which reliance was mainly placed in support of the claim was the conflicting alignments in the survey and other maps, the claims made by the Maharao of Kutch aid the Government of India which were not accepted. The boundary between the two States was indefinite and by the award of the Tribunal the true boundary of India and Pakistan was determined. [301 G H] (2) The territory of Sind was contiguous to, and in fact is an extension of, the mainland. The territory which was the subject matter of the dispute was indefinite and the highly discrepant and conflicting claims made from time to time by the British authorities as well as the Kutch State authorities before the State merged with Dominion of India in 1948, and the persistent refusal of the British authorities, though there were several occasions to demarcate the boundary between Sind and the Kutch State authority before the State merger became Indian territory. [301 D] (3) The territory was not a part of the Great Rn of Kutch and was therefore an extension of territory. [304 C] (4) The territory which formed part of the erstwhile States merged with the territory of Pakistan. Even granting that evidence, the claim by Indian citizens to exercise fundamental rights in respect of the territory in that Sector may be entertained only if it be established that the territory was found to be originally governed by the Mahaaji of Kutch. [301 C] (5) The claim by Indian citizen to exercise fundamental right in respect of territory in that sector may be entertained even if it be proved that the territory is found to be initially governed by the then Maharao of Bhuj. [301 E] (6) The claim made by the claimants that in imple menting the award of Map of Kutch an attempt was made to cede any part of the area which formed part part of the territories of Sind and was in de facto occupation and in respect of which sovereign authority was exercised by the Maha Rao of Kutch. It was not evidence of the fact that it was territory over which the Maharao exercised sovereign rights and which by merger of the territory became Indian territory, was determined. The evidence was conflicting alignment in the survey, and other maps.

The mortgagor filed a suit on July 12, 1946, in the Court of the Subordinate Judge at Dhanbad for a decree for enforcement of the two mortgages by sale of the mortgaged properties. In respect of the mortgage dated August 27, 1923, the High Court held that the right to sue where the mortgagee is deprived of the mortgage security or where he is not secured in his possession of the mortgaged property or where possession is not delivered to him as agreed, the plaintiff 's claim to enforce the mortgage was at the date of the, suit not barred by the law of limitation because the mortgage "was partly simple and partly usufructuary" and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon part payment of the principal or interest to extend the period of limitation for the suit, she could still maintain the suit relying upon the dispossession of her mortgagee on April 7. 1937, by virtue of sale under the Money decree passed against her, a cause of action accrued to the mortgagee to enforce the mortgaged property and the plaintiff ' 's suit filed within twelve years from the date of dispossession was within time. The High court also held that Mauza Bahald ih was not given in mortgage to the mortgagees under either of the two mortgageeeds and dispossession of the mortgagees from Mauza Bahaldipur or part payments of principal or interest after the mortgagor had parted with his interest in the mortgage property Mauzas Bansjora and Simitanr could not operate to extend the limitation for the suits. The High ' Court also held in respect of a mortgage dated August 28, 1922, that the claim to enforce that mortgage was within limitation, both on account, of part payment and interest and on the cause of actions furnished by the dispossessed of the mortgagees in respect of 48 annas share in Mauza Baharaldih lands at the Court auction and that the suit to enforce the said mortgage was barred by the Law of limitation. The appellants were employees of the respondent company. They were charged at the rate of Rs. 2 per month for the transport of employees from Chinchvad Village to TELCO factory at Pimpri and back. The appellants were charged at a rate of Rs, 2 per month. The appellants contended that the transport facilities provided to the employees from Pimpri Railway Crossing and onwards to TELC factory were not extended to the other employees and that the appellants were liable to pay the tax as also the penalty. The Commissioner of Pune dismissed the appeals and holding that the challenge to the tax sought to be realised by the Revenue was not tenable and the appellants were not liable to pay tax as also penalty. The appellants filed appeals before the Commissioner of Pune. The Commissioner dismissed the appeals. The appellants then filed appeals before this Court. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The term 'public service vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules but that too does not create any difficulty, because having regard to the Preamble of the Act we are of the opinion that the tax can be levied only on passengers who are carried on a public service vehicle. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. The transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within the ambit of the aforesaid definition. [362E F] 1.2 The transport service provided to the appellants by the appellants could be a public service Vehicle in any sense of the term. [362G] 1.3 The transport service is not a public service vehicles within the meaning of the provisions of the Bombay , the Act. [362B] 1.4 The transport service, in the instant case, which was registered in private service vehicle fell squarely within the purview of the aforesaid definitions. Moreover, in the case of supervisory staff, there was no reason why the same amenities should not be extended to the appellants. [362C] 1.5 The transport service was not a public transport vehicle within the meaning Of the provisions of section 2(7) of the Act. The transport services in the present cases which were registered as private services vehicle fell within the ambit Of the aforesaid definition Moreover, in view of the Preamble of that Act we are not of the opinion, that the tax could be levied only if the passengers were carried on a private service vehicle. [362D] 1.6 The transport service of the appellants was reserved for them only and no other member of the public even if he wanted to pay full charges could be carried on the said vehicle. [363F] 1.7 The transport service used in the present ease which was registered by the appellants was not reserved for them. [362F] 1:8 The transport service which was registered was reserved for the appellants only and no others member of the Public Service Vehicle fell within the purview Of the aforesaid definitions Moreover, in this case, it was not disputed that the transport provided to the employee by the appellants would be a public transport Vehicle in any manner whatsoever. [362A] 1.9 The transport service to the employees of the company was reserved for their only and no member of the community even if he wants to pay full charge could be carried. [362H] 1.10 The transport service for the present case was registered as public service vehicle in any sense Of the term. Moreover, the transport service in this case was registered in the private service vehicle falling squarely within the meaning o the provisions of that Act.

The appellants, who had objected to the grant of a no objection certificate to the third respondent, filed a petition under section 795 of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1960, seeking a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to grant a no objection Certificate for the site on which the cinema house was to be constructed. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the District Magistrate was not influenced by the fact that there was a mosque and a temple in the vicinity of the place where the proposed cinema house was proposed to be constructed but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema licence having been re opened in the locality there was no need for a cinema house with a "temporary" licence and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the State Government, the State Government on being satisfied that there was no impediment to the grant, granted the same and, therefore, it was not a fit case for the interference of the High Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants not being entitled to challenge the grant of the cinema licence to the third respondents, they cannot now be permitted to plead a right to oppose the grant of an "no objection certificate" certificate. [895B] 2. The appellants, not being entitled, to challenge the order granting the no objection certificate, they cannot, now be permitted now to plead a claim to a cinema licence. [896C] 3. The appellants cannot now be allowed to plead a defence right to oppose a grant of a cinema licence, on the same grounds which he took against the "no objection" certificate and had been over ruled, can contest the claim of the applicant to a cinema license. [897F] 4. The appellants ' not being entitled for a cinema licence on the short ground that there was an "no Objection" certificate and having been over ruled the grant of no objection certificate is violative of the principles of natural justice and the order granting no objection certificate was violative of the principle of natural justice. [898F] 5. The appellants were not entitled to challenge that grant of the "no Objection Certificate" to the third Respondent, but they were entitled to be heard.

The plaintiffs instituted a suit (O.S. No. 46 of 1957) against the defendant alleging that by a contract dated August 3, 1957 the defendant had agreed to assign to the plaintiffs his leasehold interest under a mining lease in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekanave Kaval, Hosadurga Taluk, and gave them the right to win and remove the iron ore. The Trial Court decreed the suit. The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there was a contract as alleged in the plaint. HELD : (i) The plaint in O.S. 46 of1957 was not an acceptance of the offer, not was it intended to be an acceptance. It was not usual to communicate an acceptance by serving a copy of the plaint through the medium of the Court. [782 H] (ii) The plaint was not an accepted offer. It was an acceptance and that the service of a copy of plaint along with the writ of summons was a communication of the acceptance. There was no concluded contract between the parties. [785 B] (iii) The plaint did not allege a concluded contract between them. The High court was right in holding that there was no concluded concluded contract between parties. [758 C] (iv) The plaint had been withdrawn. The plaintiffs had not agreed to purchase the mining lease. The offer was not withdrawn. There was nothing to show that the acceptance was communicated to the defendant before withdrawing the offer. There was also no concluded contract.

The appellants were the owners of sugarcane purchased by them from the respondent. The appellants were the purchasers of sugarcane purchased from the respondent on the basis of a purchase order issued by the respondent. On the date of the purchase the sugarcane was purchased by the respondent and the price was fixed at Rs. 1,000 per quintal. The respondent filed a complaint against the appellants under section 3 of the Act on the ground that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of the sugarcane purchased by him within the time prescribed. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and convicted the appellants under sub rule (3) of rule 3 of Sugarcane (Control) Order 1955. The appellants challenged the conviction and sentence before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the investigation which was being carried on against the appellants was in accordance with law and therefore the power conferred on the Government ,under section 3 of Sugarcane Act cannot be challenged as invalid. HELD: (i) The Parliament intended to bring under control the cultivation and ' sale of food crops. The Parliament intended that bring under control of the cultivation and sale of food crops generally or specified food crops generally or specified Food crops and section 3(2)(c) gave the Central Government power to regulate the movement of sugarcane as also the controlling of the price at which any essential commodity may be bought or sold. The power conferred on Parliament under section 3 Of the Act cannot be questioned as invalid. The power of Parliament to legislate in respect of production, supply and distribution of foodstuffs is expressly dealt with by the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937 and therefore the powers conferred on the State Government ,under sections 3 and 3 of the , cannot be challenged. [767 D] (ii) The Parliament had no competence to enact any law relating to the control of sugarcane as that subject is within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State, the same being a part of agriculture. [768 E] (iii) The power conferred by section 3 of Act cannot be assailed as invalid. [766 F] (iv) The power of the Parliament to legislate under Entry 33 of List III is expressly dealt by the Bihar Act. [770 D] (v) The power to legislate in regard to production, supply, distribution and distribution of essential commodities and trade and commerce therein for maintaining or increasing the supply thereof or for securing their equitable distribution and availability at fair prices. [772 E] (vi) The power under section 3(1) of the Act cannot, therefore, be challenged as valid. [775 E] (vii) The power given to the Government , under section 3, of the Act, cannot be challenged in view of article 372 of the Constitution which provides that all laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed or amended by a competent legislature or other competent authority. [776 E] (viii) The power vested in the Government to make laws with respect to the control and regulation of production, distribution and supply of foodstuffs is specifically dealt with by section 3(3) of the Cr. P.C. and therefore the same being part of agriculture, the same is a cognizable offence as defined in section 4(1)(f) of the Code. [778 E] (ix) The power in the State to legislate in relation to production, distribution, distribution and availability of foodstuffs is also expressly dealt with in the Act. [771 F] (x) The power is conferred on the Parliament to make laws in respect of the production, supply or distribution of foodstuffs.

The appellants, a State Government Undertaking, filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th June, 1969 when the order dated 12th January, 1977 was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given to them by the former order as the said grant of concessions constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the basis of which they had acted by starting new industries requiring investment of considerable funds and the Government was not entitled to go back or that promise as it had sought to do by the order dated 30th June 1969. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government of Karnataka that the concessions granted under the said order dated 30.6.1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The doctrine of Prom promissory Estoppel is not applicable in this case because it is found by the State Government that the concessions given by the earlier order had given room for many types of misuse but such a recital by itself cannot establish that the concessions were, in fact, misused. [948C D] 1.2 The doctrine ofpromissory Estoppel is a well recognised principle of law that the doctrine must be regarded as good law in view of the recent decision of this Court in State of Bihar and Anr. vs Usha Martin Industries Ltd., [1987] 65 STC, 430 where a Division Bench comprising three learned Judges of this Court upheld and applied that doctrine must be treated as good law. [949E] 1.3 The doctrine of promissory Estoppel was, therefore, not applicable in a case where the source of power under which it was issued was not stated in an order but can be found on the examination of the relevant Act, the exercise of the power must be attributed to that source. [950C] 1.4 The doctrine ofPromissory Estoppel has no application in the present cases because it was held by this Court in [State of Bihar and Ors. vs Usha martin Industries Ltd. [1987]65 STC, 430 that the doctrine should be regarded as a good law in the view of the latest decision of this court in State of Kerala and Anr. v Usha Martin Industry Ltd., [1986] 65 STC 430, wherein a Division Bench consisting of three learned Judges, upheld and applied the doctrine ofprom promissory Estoppel. [945E] 1:5 The doctrine of Discissory Estoppel, as in the present matter, is by way of refunds of sales tax paid to the extent provided in the Order, and not merely certain words used out of context. Although the benefit regarding sales tax granted to the new industries is by way Of refunds of sales Tax paid to the amount provided in the order, it is clear that, in effect, the benefit granted is in the nature of an exemption from the payment of the sales tax or reduction in the sales tax liability to the extent stated in the order. [946F] 1:6 The doctrine of approissory Estoppel cannot be regarded as bad law in view Of the recent decision in State of Punjab and Anr. etc. vs Usha Devi Martin Industries Limited, [1987] 66 STC, 430, where a Division bench comprising three learned judges of this Court affirmed and applied that principle. [947F] 1.7 The doctrine of Corissory Estoppel does not apply in the present facts and circumstances of the case because it has been found by the High Court that the concessions extended by the said order had been misused and undue benefit was being taken by the newly established industries.

The appellants were tried for the offences under Sections 147, 148, 323, 379 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegations that they caused the death of Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogudem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted A 1 to A 3. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 1 to 3. The appellants preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants being only three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 I.P.,C. if the evidence discloses commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of the persons all. The non applicability of Section i49 I.P,C. is, therefore, no bar in convicting the appellants under 7 Section 302 read with section 34 I.P..C. if evidence discloses commission o f an offence in pursuance of the common object of the unlawful assembly. [815E F] 2. The non application of Section 149 I, P.C. is not a bar in convicting a person under 7 Section302 read with Section 34 I. P.C., if the evidence disclose commission of an offences in furtherance of common intention of them all. PW 1, the wife of the deceased, PW 2, the daughter of the deceased and PW 3, an adjoining land owner, are the three eye witnesses to the occurrence. The non existence of any evidence in support of the prosecution case is not fatal to the prosecution case. [816E F] 3. The non availability of evidence in support o f the prosecution case cannot be sustained. [817G] 4. The non non applicability of section i49 I, P,C. cannot be sustained, if the evidence disclosed commission of an o offence in furtherance o the common intention o the persons all,. The non absence of evidence in respect of the prosecution o f the case cannot be held to be fatal to the appellants under Section 302 read With Section 34 I P.C.. if the evidence reveals commission of an offen tation in furtherance of a common intention of all the accused all.

The assessee, a company, was incorporated in the State of Kerala. The assessee was assessed to income tax on the income of the company for the assessment year 1962 60. The Income tax officer assessed the sum of Rs. 48,500 to tax relying on section 52 sub section (2) of the Act. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of section 52 sub sub section (1) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Tribunal held that the income of Rs. 46,500 was not taxable under the provisions of the Act and that the assessee had not discharged the burden of proving that the transfer was effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of the liability of the assessee to tax on capital gains. The Revenue preferred an appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that in view of the provisions of section 52(2) of Income tax Act the assessee was not entitled to the benefits of section 52 subsection (2) and that the question of law raised by the assessee was decided against the assessee. The Tribunal, however, held that the question whether the assessee was liable to pay tax on capital gain was not a question of law but a mixed question of fact and law. The Tribunal also held that the amount of Rs. 47,500 was taxable under the Income tax law. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The assessee was not liable to pay the tax on capital asset as on the date of the transfer. The real consideration received by the assessee is not declared or disclosed and in most of the cases, if not all, it would not be possible for the Income tax officer to determine precisely what is actual consideration received by him and permit the Revenue to take the fair market value of the capital asset as the full value of the consideration received in respect of the transfer is under stated and since in such cases it is very difficult, if not impossible, to determine and prove the exact quantum of the suppressed consideration, sub section (3) provides the statutory measure for determining the consideration actually received by the assesee and permits the Revenue to taking the fair market valuation of the capital assets as the full amount of the consideration actually receive in respect of transfer. [48F G] 1.2 The true position in law is that a fair market value is a measure of measure of measure for determining a capital asset which is not declared and disclosed by the assessee and the burden of proof of such under statement or concealment is on the Revenue. [48G H] 1.3 The true position is that a capital asset is transferred for a consideration below its market value, the difference between the market value and the full value thereof the consideration actually receiving in respect of that transfer would amount to a gift liable to tax under the Gift Tax Act, 1958, but if the construction of sub section ( 2) is literally construed as applying even to cases where the full value is correctly declared or disclosed by the assessee and there is no understatement of the consideration, it would result in an amount being taxed which has neither accrued to the assessee nor been received by him nor was received by him. It is furthermore necessary that the full value Of the consideration in respect of a transfer is under mentioned or in other words, shown at a lesser figure than that actually received by him, and the burden is on the revenue. If a capital asset was transferred for a purpose below its market Value, the difference would also be liable to tax. [48H; 49A] 1.4 The true position of law is that the fair market price of the capital property transferred by the assessee as on the day of the transfer exceeds the full value value of theconsideration declared by the assessee.

The appellant was charged in the Court of Presidency Magistrate as follows: "That you on 3 12 1968 at 8 a.m. at Bandra in contravention of provisions of section 2(1)(f) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, sold 450 grams of Til seeds to the Food Inspector and that the Til seeds were unfit for human consumption, and thereby committed an offence under section 7(i)(f) of the Act. After the accused had told him that they were not meant for human consumption and thereby committed a offence under section 3(1)(i) and 7 (i) of Prevention of Food adulteration Act, 1954. After the Food Inspector 's denial about such talk, the prosecuting Food Inspector 'S' examined the whole evidence,had concluded that the version of the appellant that there was a tall; about the actual purpose for which the Til seeds at his shop were meant, was more probable because it was supported by what the appellant had written on the cash memo when he sold these Til seeds 'o the Food Inspector. After all, the appellant, who had a grain shop, must have known that the Food Inspector could prosecute him if he kept adulterated foodstuffs for sale for human consumption. The real dispute on facts revolves round the question whether the black Tils were sold to the Food Inspectors specifically for the purpose of Pooja after the accused had informed him that they would write on the cash Memo the purpose for which black Tils are sold. The real controversy on facts revolving round the question as to whether the blackTils were sold or not was more probable. The real question in issue was whether the black tils were sold by the appellant to the Food inspector specifically for the purposes of Pooja after he sold these plants 'o the food Inspector. The real issue was whether there was a lall; about it was part of the prosecution case that the Til plants were meant for human use. The real contest on facts revolve round the question, whether the black Til seeds were sold to Food Inspector specifically for the intended purpose of Pooja. The real point for determination was whether the food inspector 's version or the accused 's explanation was more credible, and whether the Food Inspector had given such information to the Food Analyst. The High Court held that the charge was that the Til bags were unfit for the human consumption. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the whole object of the Act was to prevent adulteration of "food" meant for human Consumption. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The charge was that, the Til seeds with which we are concerned were meant for Human consumption. It was a matter of common knowledge that black Til seeds are not used as food. It is also true that, when the case of the appellant supported by his cash memo, is that the particular black Tils used for pooja for being burnt like incense or thrown into fire in the course of pooja. it cannot be said that this case had been repelled by the mere statement of the Food Inspector that they can be used as food also. [730 C D] 1.2 The evidence of the prosecuting Food inspector, who said that the black Tles were not meant to be sold only as a substance used for pooji and not as human food. The prosecution had to prove that the article which was the subject matter of an offence was ordinarily used for human consumption as food whenever reasonable doubts arise. [731 C D] 2.1 The evidence of prosecution witnesses, who said to have seen the occurrence, was that the appellant told the Food Inspector, that he had only black Tils using for Pooja. It was further stated that the black tles were meant for pooja and not for human consumption but an article kept for a special use.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January, 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August, 1966. The order of dismissal was communicated to the plaintiff on 19th September, 1960. The plaintiff 's suit was one to obtain a declaration that the order of dismissal had been bad and he continued to be in service. The suit was one for recovery of Rs. 1,00,000/ as damages. The suit filed by the plaintiff was one to recover damages for wrongful dismissal from service. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the order was not an order prior to the Constitution and, therefore, the order of the State Government had merged into the order of Central Government and the High Court was right in its view that it had no jurisdiction. The plaintiff preferred an appeal before the Divisional Commissioner which was dismissed on the ground of limitation and the appeal was dismissed. The plaintiff filed a second appeal to the High Court which was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order merged in the order of State Government and the revisional order being after the Constitution came into force, the writ petition would be maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the date of the original adverse order but on the date when the order of higher authority where a statutory remedy is provided 54 entertaining the appeal or representation is made and where no such order is made, on the expiry of six months from the date when cause of action would be taken to have first arisen. [54D] 2. The cause for action shall be computed to arise not on the date of filing of the appeal or making of the representation. [54E] 3. The cause or action shall be deemed to arise not only from the date on which the order of lower authority where a legal remedy is provided but also from the date from which the appeal or appli cation is made and when such order is not made, on or before the date when such appeal was filed or representation was made, the right to sue shall first accrue. [54F] 4. The cause and the cause of action, shall first accrue and where such order is neither made, on that date, cause of action nor representation was made or representation was submitted, the right of sue shall first accrues. [54G] 5. The cause o action shall be determined to arise not by the date of institution of the appeal but on the day when the appeal was filed. [54H] 6. The cause in the present case is the starting point of limitation as prescribed in the relevant statute and if the 49 statute prescribes that it commences from the date the cause of actions shall first accrue, and where such an order is notmade, on the expiration of six months ' period from the date date when the appeal is filed or representation is submitted, the rights to sue shall be first accrue. The Civil Court 's jurisdiction has been taken away by the Act and, therefore as far as Government serv ants are concerned, Article 58 may not be invocable in view of the special limitation. [54A] 7. The cause is of action. The Civil court 's jurisdiction had been taken away and the revisional orders being after the constitution came into force. [54B] 8. The Civil Courts ' jurisdiction has been derived away by the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and, therefore the jurisdiction has been exercised by the State Government and, therefore. as far as government serv ants is concerned, Article ' 58 may not apply.

The respondent filed a suit for a declaration that the decree of the trial court was not a decree of affirmance but variation in the decision of the trial Court. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the decree was not a judgment of affirmance and that the variation in question was minor or minor. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word "decision" does not mean the whole of the decision but the decision of a suit by the trial court and not the grounds stated in support of the said decision. HELD: (i) The decision of the Privy Council in that case construed the relevant provisions of section 110 literally and held that if the appellate decree confirms the decision of that court it is not a decree or of affirmance, that part of the decree should be considered which is proposed to be brought to this Court in appeal. The decision of this Court in that case was not a part of the decision or the grounds stated therein. [419 C D] (ii) The decision in that case did not support the conclusion that the word 'decision ' meant the decision of an appeal by the trial Court and not the ground stated in support thereof. [420 E] (iii) The decision was not a decision of the lower court in the present case. [421 B] (iv) The decision did not support it. The decision in the present appeal was not a final decision of the High Court in the present suit.

The five revision petitions filed by the appellants were dismissed by the High Court. The High Court held that the revisional jurisdiction under section 115, Code of Civil Procedure in respect of an order of the District Court under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, was not maintainable. The High court also held that the High Court had exclusive jurisdiction under section 114, Code of Criminal Procedure in a revision petition filed by the respondents. The High, Court also held that an order of a District Court under Section 25, Provincial, Small Cause Courts (Amendment) Act, 1970 was not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil procedure. The High 'Court also held that a revision petition under section 115 was not maintainable against a revisional order under section 25. The High Courts have also held that in respect of cases decided before 20th September, 1972 and also all cases arising out of original suits of any valuation decided by the District Court, the case would be amenable to the Revisional jurisdiction of the District Judge under section 115. The High courts have also held in favour of the respondents. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Curt had exclusive jurisdiction to entertain a revision petition against an order of District Court under that section. [36E] 2. The High High Court has jurisdiction under section115, Code of civil Procedure over a revisional order made by the District Judge. [36F] 3. The High Civil Court has jurisdiction to entertain revision petition under Section 115, Code, of Civil Procedure. No. 9752 of 1979, the appeal and the associated special leave petitions must be dismissed. No. 2844 of 1979 that in case this Court is of the opinion that a revision Petition under section 115 is not maintainable against an order made by a District Court, it would be competent to exercise the revisional power under section 115 and no question could have arisen of invoking the revisional power of the High court under section 115 in the cases arising out out of original suit of the value of Rs. 20,000/ and above, and exclusive jurisdiction under Section 115 to the District Court in other cases. [36G H] 4. The High curt has rightly rejected revision petitions filed under section 115 on the ground that the revision petition under s. 115 is not tenable against a revisional application under section 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Court Act. [36H; 36A] 5. The High. Court has rightly rejected the revision petitions filed against the revisional orders of the District Curt. under section 25 and no question can arise of invoking the revision power of the District court under section115 of the Code. [36A] 6. The HighCourt has rightly rejected Revision petitions filed under s.115 of the Civil Procedure Code.

The respondents, who were the owners of certain lands, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the notification issued under section 52 (1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, by a petition under Article 226 of the constitution for quashing the notification issued by the State Government of Rajasthan under section 52(1) of that Act for the acquisi tion of certain lands belonging to them required by the Urban Improvement Trust , Jaipur for a public purpose, namely, for implementation of a development scheme viz. for implementation of the development scheme viz., for implementation of an development scheme viz, for implementation a development scheme, viz. for the implementation of a Development scheme viz. the Civil Lines Extension Scheme, the Civil Lines extension Scheme, the Land Acquisition Officer, Jaipur, and the Land Acquisition officer, Jaipur, respectively, for the acquisition of the said land. The State Government issued a notification under section 52 of the Act for the acquisition and the notified land vested in the State Government free from all encumbrances. The respondents challenged the validity of a notification issued by a Special Officer, Town Planning Department, Jaipur, under section 52A of the Act on the ground that the land was actually needed by them bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition on one ground or the other. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petition filed by the respondents purporting to be under article 226 was not maintainable. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the petition under article 227 of the Constitution was not maintainable as the petition filed under article 226 had been filed by the appellants purporting to be in the Calcutta High Court and the rule nisi thereon and the ad interim exparte prohibitory order obtained by them on the basis of such petition from the learned Single Judge on March 13, 1984 when there was total lack of inherent jurisdiction on the part of the (1) ; , 602 the Calcutta High court to entertain such petition, constitutes a flagrant abuse of the process of the Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The petition filed by respondent purporting to be Under article 226 of a Constitution in the Calcutta Court and the ad ad interim exparte injunction made by him on the basis that the land is really not needed by them mala fide and their true object was just, to get the property released from acquisition. [605F] 2. The petition under article 32 of the Constitution filed by the respondent purporting to have been under article 226, was not maintainable in the High Court at Jaipur Bench, where the cause of action wholly or in part arose.
