[606F] 3. The petition was not maintainable because the petition filed in the Calcutta Bench was not maintainable, because the cause of the action wholly or partly arose. [ 602A] 4. The petition in the Calcutta City High Court and in the High Courts were quashed.

The appellant landlord purchased the building in 1968 and that it was covered by the new Rent Act. The first ground was based upon sub s.(2) of s.2 which provides that nothing in this Act shall apply to a building during the period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. The first grounds were based upon sub section (2) of section 2 which provides that anything in this Act will apply to a house during the period from the date of its construction. The High Court accepted the finding of the Additional District Judge that the building in question was constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to s.2(2) of the new Rent Acts. The High court also did not endorse the finding of Additional District Judge on that ground. The only point argued before this Court was whether the building in suit was constructed substantially by the co operative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the new Rent law had no application to the building in dispute. Allowing the appeal, HELD: The building in question had not become ten years old on the date of the suit and was exempted from the operation of the new Act. The Additional District Judge had found that the building had not become more than ten years old. The Additional Judge had found in that case that the building was subject to assessment therefore it will be deemed to have been completed on the date on the date when the revision came to be decided by the High Court. [343 D E] The question in the present case is whether by seeking the benefit of s.39 of the new rent Act, there is a change in the cause of action. The question in this case is whether the building had become more than 10 years old on 1st October, 1971. The Additional Civil Judge had found the building to be deemed to be completed on the dates of assessment which was 1st October. 1971. The High, however, did not endorse that finding of the Addl. District Judge that it was the date of assessment of the house tax and water tax held that the building would be deemed to had been completed on 1st November, 1971.

The appellant entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings, stores and other works at Ranchi, the first of them being contract No. 21 of 1942 dated November 5, 1942, and the other two being contracts Nos. 21 of 1943 dated November 5. 1942, and November 5, 1943, and the contract Nos. 21 and 1943 respectively. On the first question, the appellant contended that the agreement for reference to arbitration did not comply with the requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the constitutional provision in force at the relevant date, and it was therefore void that the award passed in proceedings founded thereon was a nullity and that no decree should be passed in terms thereof. Held, that the copy of an instrument cannot be validated: That was held in The Rajah of Bobbili vs Inuganti China Sitaramasani Garu (I.L.R. , referred to. The document in court which was a copy of the instrument cannot be said to be an instrument relating to the execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of the bills, and that the law did not provide for the levy of any penalty on lost documents, and that it was sufficient for the purpose of section 175 (3). Held, further, that the document in court was not one relating to execution of works, as that had not been completed and, therefore, secondary evidence of its contents cannot be given. Payment of penalty will not render secondary evidence admissible, for under the stamp law penalty is leviable only on an unstamped or insufficiently stamped document actually produced in Court and that law does not provide for levy of any penalties on lost documents.

The respondent was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. He was prosecuted and punished for the offence of criminal misconduct under section 409 IPC. The trial court acquitted the respondent. The High Court quashed the prosecution and convicted the respondent. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that keeping in view the scope of Article 309 as also the purpose of Rule 2.2, the said rule cannot be interpreted to be a rule placing an embargo on prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of a period of four years from the date of cause of action or event mentioned therein. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The third proviso to clause (b) of Rule 2, which provides for the benefit of a government employee and virtually incorporates the principle underlying Article 21 of the Constitution by fixing four years as the limit for initiating prosecution. That apart, even if a government servant is prosecuted and punished in judicial proceedings instituted in respect of cause of actions which arose or an event which took place more than four years before such institution, as has been held by the High Court can be treated to be a Rule regulating the condition of service of such a person. [920C D] 1.2. The third Proviso to clause (a) of Rule2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules has not been framed for that purpose but has been framed for a different purpose namely to provide an exception to the power of the government in the matter of withholding or withdrawing etc. of pension of a retired government servant contained in clause (b). The embargo on prosecution spelt out by the High court is not to be found in the main rule 2.2. There is no doubt with regard to the interpretation of the said rule. [921D] 1.3. The third provisos to clause (c) of Rule 3.2 of Punjab Civil Service (Pension) Rules, 1972 have not been framed in the case of Des Raj singhal and did not consider other grounds, if any, that may have been raised by him for quashing of the prosecution. [922D] 1:4. The third exception to clause (d) of Rule 4.2 of 1972 Rules has not not been framed. [923D] 1 :5. The third limb of clause (b), which provides for an exception to a power of the Government in the matter, of withholding or withdraw etc. of a pension of a government servants contained in clause(b) of rule 2. 2. The third part of clause (a), which provides that even if a Government servant is prosecuted or punished in judicial proceeding instituted in respect for cause of action which arose or a event which tookplace more than four year before such institution the government will not be entitled to exercise the right conferred on it by the substantive provision contained in clause 2.2 of Rule 2 of 1972 Rules. [924E F] 1:6. The third clause of clause (c), which provides the benefit of the said Rule, has not been made for that purpose. [925E] 1:7. The third portion of clause (d), which provides a benefit of the Rule, has been omitted by the Punjab Civil Services (Pension) Rule, 1972. [926G] 1:8. The third sub clause of clause(b), which deals with the benefit of pension of such a government servant, has not not yet been framed for the same purpose namely to providing an exception to his power of withholding or withdrawal etc. of the pension of a retiring government servant contained In clause (b); and the third proviso to Rule 2.3.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares of Rs. The preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to a fixed dividend of 71 per cent on the face value of the shares, with no right in the balance of the profits. The respondent company was a public limited Company under the Indian companies Act 1913, and the shares were allotted uncoiiditionally to the public. The authorised capital was 7,500 ordinary shares and 4,000 preference share of Rs. 1,375, but the preference shareholders were entitled to a specified dividend of 71% on the facevalue of the shares. The respondent was a public company under the , Indian Companies Act, 1913, to which the provisions of section 23A were correctly applied for the three relevant years. The authorised Capital of the company, was 7,250 ordinary shares and 2,000 preference shareholders were also under the Articles Of Association entitled to fixed dividend of 70 per cent on their face value of shares. The preference shareholder was under the Articles entitled to a fix y of dividend. The respondent, company was floated in the trade name of "Amritanjan". The respondent company, was floated as an "public limited company" under the Indian Company Act 1913, for the purpose of acquiring and carrying on the business in the trade of manufacture and sales of "Amratanjan". The shares were allotted to the public limited company. The authorised share shareholders were under a special control of the company. The respondent 's share was 7,200 ordinary shares and 5,000 preference equity shares of Rs, 1,375 and 3 preference shares of the respondent company were under the articles of Association entitled for a fixed dividend. The preference shares were allotted unconditionally to, or acquired unconditionally by or is beneficially held by the public. In September 1936 the respondent company was issued a notice under section 23A of the Income tax Act, 1922, to acquire, carry on the trade name and carry on its business of manufacture, and sale of the "Amrutnamanjan". The appellant company challenged the validity of the notice on the ground that the respondent company had no jurisdiction to pass the order under section 23, A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that the respondent was one in which the public were substantially interested, and there fore the Income tax Officer had no jurisdiction, to pass the impugned order under section23, A of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23 A was in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which the Public are substantially interested, is. (2) Where not less than twenty five per cent of the voting power is allotted unconditionally to or is acquired unconditionally by, or is beneficialously held by the company, it shall be presumed that the company is one in which, the public are substantially interested. But the Legislature by the Explanation has raised a conclusive presumption in those cases where shares of the company carrying not less than fifty five per cent or more are held by persons other than the controlling group, the shares yielding a fixed rate of dividend have to be excluded. But the legislature by the Explanation had raised a conclusive presumptions in those cases, where shares of a company carrying not more than twenty five percent of the voting right are held by the persons other than, the controlling group.

The appellant was a del credere agent of the first appellant. He was authorised to take delivery of the goods on behalf of the first respondent. The goods were delivered to the appellant on 17th February, 1947, and sent them to Dharsi Moolji. The goods remained in the Dady Seth godown under the control of Dwarkadas Khetan & Company. The appellant was authorised to deliver them to the respondent on the ground that the goods were not physically delivered to Messrs. Dwarkadaswani & Company. On the same day, however, the first appellant credited Dwarkadas]' with the money he had received from Dharsi Mooljibhai on account of the 13 bales less Dwarkadas ' commission. The appellant then sent them to the Mills on 17th March, 1947, but the Mills did not deliver them to them. The Mills sent them to their godown on 17th April, 1947, which was later on transferred to Dharsi Morji. The Mills did not take delivery of them. The appellant thereupon filed a complaint against the respondent on 28th February, 1950, alleging that the goods remained in their possession at all material times and were not physically deliver to Messrs. Shree Kishan & Company. After the complaint was filed, the Magistrate issued a notice to the appellant to show cause why the goods should not be delivered to them. On the failure of the appellant to comply with the notice, the Magistrate passed an order directing the appellant to deliver them. The respondent thereupon filed a petition in the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the Magistrate. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant was not entitled to the relief claimed by him. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that in the present case, the appellant was entitled to the reliefs claimed by him in the petition. [833 A] (ii) The High court was in error. [834 B] (iii) The appellant was entitled under article 226 to the limited extent of the relief claimed. [835 C] (iv) The High ' Court was in wrong in holding that a person to whom physical delivery of the property had been made, who may be. in possession of the goods, has to be within his rights (a) to refuse delivery to anybody till he was paid and (b) to deliver them, despite anything the first appellant might say once he received his money; also because Dwarkadasmati had control over the godown, the control was exercised on behalf of and as the agent of the Mills. So, even if Dwarkadas discontinued had control over his godown, the controlled control was exercised by and as the agents of the Mills, and so, the appellant could not be said to have been within his rights. [836 D] (v) The appellant had been entered as the agent for Dwarkadas Hassan for the goods and the Mills sent the bales to Dharsi Gokulji for delivery in the same truck as the 13 bales. [837 A] (vi) The goods left the Mills ' premises, the property in them had passed and when Dharsi Moolaji refused to receive them they were handed over to Dwarkadas KS and not taken back to the Mills. But the learned Magistrate imposed. the penalty of Rs. 1,000 on the appellant.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of the Ninth clause of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code. He was prosecuted for offences under section 5(1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, read with section 5(2) (d), of the Prevention and Corruption Act, 1988, and section 5(3) (d). The trial court acquitted the appellant. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the ninth clause of section21 of the Indian Act was wider when it came to the case of an officer who was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of any public duty and it was not necessary that the remuneration by any of fee or commission should be paid by the Government as is now necessary under subclause (a) of the Explanation to section 21 of Indian Penal Code, keeping in view the capacity in which and the nature of the duties which he was Performing as an Examiner of University which, it had been found, had no connection with his being a Government servant. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD : (1) The word "obtains" on which much stress was laid does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of the receivers One may accept money, that if offered, or solicit payment of a bribe, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion; in each case, lie obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position as a public servant. [775 D] (2) The use of the word "obtaining" on which considerable stress was laid did not eliminate the possibility of acceptance of whatever is given or offer to be given. [776 D] (3) The abuse of the position would be the necessary ingredient of the offence; the abuse being either by corrupt or illegal means or by other means of the nature mentioned in Narayanan Nambiar 's(1) case. [778 E] (4) The abuse being either through corrupt or illegal methods or by other modes of the nature referred to in Narayanan Nambiar "s(1), case. lie obtains a monetary advantage by abusing the position as a Public servant. [779 G] (5) The abuse was either by corrupt and illegal means or otherwise abusing his position in a manner which could well be regarded as public servant. The abuse being neither by corrupt or unlawful means or by any other means. [782 E] (6) The abuse in the position would not be the necessary ingredients of the offence. [785 F] (7) The abuse would be the essential ingredient of the offences; the abuse was either either by corrupt, illegal means or through other means of a nature mentioned in the sub section. [786 G] (8) The abuse is either by corrupt means or by some other means of his nature mentioned in gran tions of sub section. The abuse of position as apublic servant is clearly implied. It would, therefore, be reasonable to put on clause (d) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section,. The abuse was neither by corrupt nor illegal means or any other means of that nature mentioned inharan Nambiar 's (1) case, and it was wholly immaterial in what capacity he has committed the offence under sub clause (d). [786 E] (9) The abuse by corrupt or wrongful means or by others, by other means, of the nature stated in Narayanan Nambiar vs. State of Kerala, ; , referred to.

The petitioners in each of these applications were engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the Construction Department of the Signal Unit in the Northern Railway. All the writ petitions having disposed of by a common judgment as questions of law and fact involved therein were similar. The petitioners alleged that notwithstanding the fact that each of them had put in continuous service for quite a long period, the Railway Administration, respondent herein, has not treated them as temporary servants and has applied discriminatory rates of wages. They have asked for a direction to treat the petitioners at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in the regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondents. The petitioners have asked for the direction to treat them at par with regular employees and to declare the petitioners at the par with maintenance worker and to declare them to be entitled to equal work and has asked for their absorbed in the regular Cadre in the permanent cadre in the Permanent category as per circulars issued by Railway Board. The petitioners also asked for a declaration that they are not entitled to all the privileges as applicable to open line temporary railway servants after attaining temporary status. The respondents have denied the claim of the petitioners. The petitioners contended that the Railway Administration was anxious to take appropriate steps to remove the difficulties faced by the casual labour but there was no break in such continuity the previous service is also taken into account. The respondents contended that the Administration was anxious and anxious to take necessary steps to screen such of the petitioners who have not yet been tested for the purpose of regularising their service. The respondents further contended that the petitioners should be entitled to the same pay as is 1) admissible to others either in the project or in the open line. The respondents also contended that the employees in the open Line acquire temporary status on completion of 120 days of service as against 180 days which was the previous requirement. The respondents denied the claim. The petitioners further contended that though prior to the issue of the Railway Board 's directions on January 1, 1984, project casual labourers were not entitled to the privileges as admissible to open line Temporary railway servants after completing 180 days of continuous employment previously. The respondents, however, denied the claim and contended that the benefits of Discipline and Appeal Rules are also applicable to casual labour with temporary status. They have also denied the claim that the petitioners are project employees and do not belong to the open line acquire temporary status. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The Railway Administration to take prompt steps to screen the casual labour and to make suitable arrangements to remove such difficulties faced by casual labour but the same was not done. [144G H] 2. The Railway Board 'S order of 1st of June, 1984 had not been given but with those directions now holding the field, the ambit of grievances has been very much reduced. [144A] 3. The Railway administration to take prompt action to remove such of the Petitioners who have not been yet tested for the purposes of regularising the service. [144B] 4. The Railway Establishment, to take prompt step to screen such casual labourers, who acquire temporary status for the conferment of attendant benefits like regular scales of pay, increments etc. [144C] 5. The Railway, Board 's order of 1 st June, 1984, had not been issued but with those instructions now holding the same field, the scope of grievances has not been very much increased.

The Forward Markets Commission, constituted under the , framed bye laws of the Association for the purpose of carrying on the business of the Association. The bye laws were framed by the Association under section 11 of the , and the bye laws were published in the Gazette. The bye law was amended by the Central Government by a notification dated January 21, 1956. The byelaw was amended by a notification on January 21, 1957. The byelaws were amended by a subsequent notification dated January 24, 1956. By a notification dated February 21, 1956, the Central Government made a bye law relating to the framing of bye laws of certain associations for the purpose. The bye bye laws were amended by the notification dated January 22, 1956. In the meantime, the Forward Markets Commission issued a notification under section 12 of the Act, declaring that the Forward Markets Act, 1951, was ultra vires the powers conferred on it by the amended bye law 52AA. The appellants contended that the notification was ultra vires section 12(1) of the Act and that the power of the Central Government under section 12 was not competent to confer any power on the Commission. Held, that the power to make bye laws under section 12 is a co extensive with the power of Association to frame bye laws. The power of the State Government to make bye law is undoubtedly co extensive with that power of the Association to frame byelaws, but it is not necessary to refer to the terms of the bye laws of a recognised association. The power to make a bye law is, therefore, co extensive with its power of the association to frame bye law assigning any function to the Commission. The power is, therefore co extensive with, the power of making bye law assigning a function to the commission. The power conferred on the Central Government to make a byelaws is undoubtedly coextensive with the power conferred on it under a bye law made by the Government under section 11 or as may be prescribed by the rules made under the Act. The power under section 12(i) is, therefore not co extensive with it. The power given to the Central Government is, therefore clearly co extensive with and the power of framing bye laws is, therefore. co extensive with power of the Associations to frame bye bye laws made by the Central government under section 12. The power, therefore, is not co extensive. The power can perform the functions assigned to it by or under the Act, or as may, be prescribed by rules made under section 11. The power cannot, therefore, be said to be co extensive with those of the Association which is a recognised association, or as the case may be, of the Association, be, of its own force.

The assessee, a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd., was a shareholder of the Ukhaira Estates Zamindary Ltd. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ for the year 1358 B.S. Rs. 37,125/ for the years 1358 B, and Rs. 21,822/ for the assessment year 1358 C.S. were taxable as dividend, and the remaining amounts were not taxable, since they were declared out of capital gains of the Company which comprised salami or premia received by it as consideration for grant of long term mining and other leases and as compensation for compulsory acquisition of lands for public purposes. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire amount for each year was income in the hands of the assessee, but only a part of it being dividend, within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act 1922, was liable to be grossedup. In second appeal, the Tribunal held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the assessee for the grant of longterm leases after the 31st March, 1948, was not taxable as dividend but as income of the assessee from "other sources". The High Court held that the whole amount for each of these three years was income in its hands, receipt of dividend within the meaning Of section 2(5A) of Income tax Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the distribution to the assessee of the amount attributable to salamis realized by the Ukhaura Estate Zamindaries (P) Ltd., after the 31 st March, 1948 was in the hands and of the assessee receipt of dividend, within that meaning of section 12 as dividend income liable to tax, and that the entire amounts for each year were income in the hand of the assessee and taxable as the income of the assesee from other sources. Dismissing the appeals, HELD : (1) The distribution to the assesee of the amount relatable to salami or premium received by it from the assessee for grant of short term leases after the31st March, 1949, was in the nature of a capital nature: Senairam Doongarmall vs Commissioner of Income tax, Assam, ; , referred to. (2) The distribution of dividend out of capital assets of a company is of a capital character: Senai Ram Doongar small vs Commissioner of income tax, Assam and others, , distinguished. (3) The distribution made to the assessee by the U.K. State Government for grant of lease of long term leases after 31st March. 1948, was in accordance with the terms of the lease. The assessee had to record their answers and their reasons in support of the answers. Those answers were, insofar as the High Court was concerned, final. [775 B C] (4) The distribution was made to the assesees of the amount relating to salami and premium received by them as consideration for granting long term leases. The distribution to them of the amount related to salami, premium and compensation for compulsory acquisitions of lands for private purposes. The distribution was in the interest of the assessee. The distribution made was in the interests of the assessee as a result of the grant of lease. [776 C D] (5) The distribution in the assessee 's favour was in the public interest. The distribution of the amount was in the best interest of the assesees.

The Karnataka Forest Act, 1963 incorporated in its definition of forest produce Sandalwood oil and agar wood oil, apart from oleo resin and wood oil derived from exudation from living trees in the forest area. The wood oil is a natural produce of the forest directly derived as an exudationfrom living trees in forest belonging to the family of the Dipterocarpucoae trees while sandal wood oil is one of the enumerate items as well as roots of sandalwood and rosewood. The wood Oil is a natural product of the forest indirectly derived as an ad hoc measure from living trees. The wood oils are a natural produce and are used in the manufacture of sandalwood andro rosewood and are used for the manufacture of the sandalwood. The wood on which the wood oil is used and the purpose the Act seeks to serve and the family to which sandal wool oil belongs being an essential oil would include wood oil. The wood is a natural substance of the forest. The wood which is a natural article of the forest is directly derived as a forest produce. The wood has to be understood in its technical sense and the purpose of the Act seeks To serve and the families to which sandalwood oil belongs being An essential oil would included wood oil. It must be noted in this context that there are several types of essential oils in India, the important being Sandalwood Oil, agar wood Oil, agari wood oil, deodar oil and pine oil apart from oleso resin andwood oil derived from the exudation of living trees in thorum Album. The wood, oil is a well known product of the forests directly derived as forest produce. An interpretation clause of the inclusive definition is not meant to prevent the word receiving its ordinary popular, popular and natural sense whenever that word would be properly applicable, but to enable the word as used in the Act, when there is nothing in the context or the subject matter to the contrary, to be applied to some things to which it would not ordinarily be applicable. . The restricted meaning canvassed by the counsel would defeat the purpose of section 2 (f) (i) of the Act and the literal interpretation giving narrow meaning to the word wood oil ' should be excluded. The restricted meaning contended by the counsel will defeat the purpose and the literal construction giving narrow meaning, to the word `wood oil ' should have been excluded. The High Court had rightly construed the meaning of the word `forest produce '. The Division Bench had rightly construed Sandalwood Petroleum and agarwood oil as defined in section 2 (k) (i). The Division Bench was correct in holding that sandal wood oil being the bye product derived commercially manufacturing process is not wood oil.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. The Sessions Judge acquitted the appellant. The High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted the appellant under section 302. The High court, on appeal, reversed the acquittal. The High Courts, however, held that the evidence of the doctor was comparatively young and that his statement was not in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon. The High, Court, however, set aside the acquittal and acquitted the appellant under s.302 read with section34 and sentenced him to transportation for the life. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The High Court should not set aside an acquittal unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons for doing so. The High ' Court should not interfere with the findings of the trial Court because its conclusions on the evidence as to the guilt or innocence of the accused differ from that of the High Court. [858 B] (ii) The High Courts should not setaside an acquittal unless it is satisfied that there are "substantial and compelling reasons" for doing so, but where the evidence is such that no Tribunal could legitimately infer from it that the accused is guilty this court would set aside the conviction. [859 C] (iii) The High 'Court should not set out any reasons justifying interference with the findings. [860 C] (iv) The High court should not set down any reasons justifying interfering with the findings, because its conclusions are such that no tribunal could legitimately infer therefrom from it that no accused is guilty.

The appellant company was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. The factory at Jamshedpur was an establishment within the meaning of the Bihar Shops & Establishments Act. Certain disputes having arisen between the appellant company and its workmen employed in the factory at Jamshedpur, the commis sion of the I.N.T.U.C. was amended as from January 6, 1963. The dispute having arisen between a_appellant company and its employees employed in the appellant company 's factory at Jamshedpur and their workmen represented by their union, the Indoxco Labour Union, Jamshedpur made a joint application dated September 7, 1963 to the Government of Bihar for a reference under section 10(2) of the . The dispute was referred to the Tribunal by the said notification. The Tribunal found that the dispute raised by the union was in respect of the employees of the appellant company wherever they may be stationed, and that consequently it made no difference that the name of Indoxco labour Union as representing the workmen concerned was mentioned in the said agreement and the said statement and not that of the Indian Oxygen Workers Union was erroneous and cannot be sustained. The Tribunal further found that the union 's constitution was duly amended on either January 6,1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the said purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company and IndoxcoLabour Union does not materially affect the position that the dispute raising by the union is in respect of employees of the company wherever they might be stationed. The Tribunal also found that the Union 's constitution had been duly amended on January 6, 1964 and that as there was no dispute between the management and the workmen of the appellant 's factory, the reference extended to them also and the Tribunal 's award would cover them also. The appellant company filed an appeal before the High Court against the award. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal was not justified in obliging the appellant company to grant special leave demanded by the union. HELD: (1) The Tribunal was not right in obliging it to grant special Leave demanded by the Union. The Tribunal was, therefore, not justified in directing the appellant company not to grant special permission demanded by the company. [501 B] (2) The Tribunal 's order was operative in respect of all the workmen of a company. The Tribunal 'on the considerations aforesaid, was not justified. [502 C] (3) The Tribunal, on the considerations aforesaid was not justified, in obliging, the appellant company, to grant special special leave demanded from the union. [503 D] (4) The Tribunal on the considerations, was not unjustified in obliging its appellant company to granting special leave demanded in the Union.

The assessee was carrying on business in timber at Abdullapur. The timber business of the firm was taken over by two partners of the firm Gajjan Mal and Jodha Mal. The firm was taken on April 1, 1939, and the business was taken over on April 1. 1939. The assessee was dissolved and on that account the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the firm was dissolved on March 31, 1939, before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 came into force and that the firm alone was entitled to the relief under section 28(4) and to the second succession which took place on April 1 1939, after Act 7 of 1940 was brought into force relief under section25(4) was not admissible. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the assessee was carrying business at the commencement of the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Ordinance 7 of 1939, and that it succeeded to the business on April 1., 1939, after the Act 7 of 1938 was brought into operation. The High Court held that the business of the assessee was at the commencement when the assessee was dissolved, and that the business at Abdullpur Depot, Simla was taken over, and that there was no other evidence in that behalf. The assessee appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The assessee was constituted to carry on the timber business allotted to it at the time of dissolution from April 1, 1938, and immediately thereafter the business of that assessee commenced. The assessee started doing business immediately after the dissolution of the firm Messrs Hakam Mal Tani Mal became effective. The partnership therefore came into being at the material time at which the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Bill 7 of 1939 was brought into existence. [696 B] (ii) The assessee started carrying on business immediately after its dissolution from April I, 1939. The partnership was therefore at the material point of time at which it was constituted. [697 C] (iii) The assessee commenced doing business immediately before the dissolution of that firm Messrs Hakham Mal Tanimal became effective. [698 C] (iv) The assessee did not carry on business at the date of dissolution from the date of the firm 's dissolution. The partnership thus came into being on April 1 9 1939. [699 D] (v) The assessee had commenced doing business at the time when the Indian Incometax (Amendment) (Amendment) Acts 7 of 1939 were brought into force and it could not be said that the assessee had commenced business immediately after March 31, 1938, or immediately thereafter the Business of the assessee commenced. [695 E] (vi) The assessee could not be held to be carrying on business at any time after the dissolution from April l 9 1939. No date of the oral agreement constituting a separate partnership of the assessee is set out in the instrument.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1945 for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimoga, by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. Some of the respondents preferred appeals against the said order to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and obtained stay of the order of the State Transport appellate Tribunal. The appeals of the respondents were allowed by the State Transport Tribunal by majority on January 29, 1969. The State Transport Appellate Tribunals had been challenged by the appellant before the High Court. The High Court was of the view that there was no period of limitation under rule 151 of the MysoreMotor Vehicles Rules, 1963, which was applicable to his case, for the issue of a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional Transport authority granting the permit. The High court was of the opinion that there was a clear error of jurisdiction on the part of both the Tribunals in interfering with the grant of the permit to the appellant. The High 'Court was of the further view that there had been a clear error in jurisdiction on the face of the record. The High Courts were, therefore, not right in dismissing the writ application of the appellant which ought to have been allowed. The appeal of the appellant to the Revenue Appellate Tribunal against the order of State Transport Appellate tribunal was dismissed. The appellant filed a special leave petition against the order granting the permit to him. The appellant contended that the issue of the permit was made beyond the prescribed period of limitation prescribed under rule 119 of the Mysore motor Vehicles Rules, 1961, after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of permit. The appeal was allowed by the High Court by majority on February 27, 1967. The State Government appealed to this Court against the order. Allowing the appeal, HELD : The appeal is allowed. The order of the High Court is set aside and necessarily the order of that Tribunal of January 29, 1968 and the order of Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal of May 8, 1970, also fall.

The appellant contested the election on the ticket of the Republican Party. He was then a sitting member of Parliament. The appellant alleged that at the Hapur meeting respondent Prakash Vir Shastri and his supporters delivered inflammatory speeches against the appellant and thereafter the said respondent Shastri 's supporters entered the office of the Republica Party. The appellant 's election was challenged by the respondent. The appellant contended that the meeting was held at Hapur and the appellant was denied the opportunity of meeting that case. The High Court rejected the appellant 's contention and dismissed the election petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, because the appellant ' s election was challenged on the ground that the appellant ' was not entitled under section 123(1) of the Act. HELD: (i) The appellant ' s case was that on 18 February, 1967 an election meeting was organised in support of the candidature of the appellant 'and the supporters of respondent Prakash Virry created disturbance with the result that the meeting could not be continued and the supporters of the appellant were alleged to have chased the appellant. The appellant failed to prove that respondent Prakash Vir was guilty of corrupt practice in relation to the personal character and conduct of the appellant. [895 A B] (ii) The allegations are that on 2 February, 1967, an election meeting at the Town Hall Maidan at Hapur was organised in respect of the attack on the office of Republican Party on 7 February, 1967 at the Town Hail Maidan, Hapur. The appellant did not prove that respondent No. 2 was guilty of any corrupt practice in connection with the personal character or conduct of the respondent.

The appellant, who was the auction purchaser, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure for delivery of possession of the property auctioned purchased by him. The application was rejected by the District Judge, Jaipur City, on the ground that the application was within the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 136 of the . The appellant 's appeal to the Division Bench was dismissed by the High Court. The appellant ' s appeal to this Court was dismissed by this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The application for setting aside the sale on the ground of fraud was made after the sale was confirmed. The Full Bench took the view that after the insertion of Explanation II to Section 47 of the Code, an application for settingaside the sale on grounds other than those mentioned in the said Rules cannot be equated with an application for the execution of a decree for possession so as to apply 12 years ' period of limitation. [712G H] 2. The application of the judgment debtor 's claim for setting aside sale on the grounds of fraud was not maintainable and the period of Limitation as prescribed by article 136 of the Limitation Act cannot be computed from the date of the first confirmation. [713C] 3. The application under Order 21 Rule 95 of Civil Procedure by the auction purchaser for setting aside a sale on the basis of fraud was within one year of the dismissal of the second application for setting setting aside the auction sale. [714D] 4. The application filed by the auction purchasers for setting aside auction sale on the plea of fraud was therefore within the period prescribed by Article 134 of the Limitation Limitation Act. [715E] 5. The application made by the auctionpurchaser for setting aside of the sale on ground of fraud is not maintainable and that apart from the provisions of Rules 89, 90 and 91 of Order XXI of the Code an application for set aside sale can also be made within a period of 12 years from the date o the first confirmation, even though the application is not one as contemplated by Rules 89,90 or 91 of Order 21 of the Code.

The appellant was the election agent of the first respondent. The first respondent was the election Agent of the first Respondent. The appellant was the first respondent and the first respondent was his election agent. The first Respondent was the election agents of the first and second respondents. The first and second respondent were the election agents. The first appellant and the second respondent were elected as the first respondent, and the first and third respondents were the election agent. In the election petition, the first respondent challenged the election of the appellant to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattancherry Constituency No. P 14 and P 15, the High Court had recorded a finding that the wall poster was pasted on a wall at the instance and with the consent of the appellant 's election agent. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the wall posters were pasted on a walls at the instance of the appellant and that the appellant ' s election agent was not aware of the fact that the incident had taken place the previous day but he himself was of the view that the publication was meant to create such impression and did create an impression that the incident of murders had taken place a day previous to the election. The High Court, however, recorded a finding on the basis of the evidence of the witnesses that the wall was pasted on the wall at the behest and with the permission of the appellant. The High court, however, held that the wall painting was pasted on wall at the instigation of the appellant, and that the wall corrigendum was pasted on it at the instance, and with the knowledge of the appellant the publication was intended to create an impression and did creating an impression that it did so. The High ' Court, however held that the evidence of PW 1 was not reliable and that the evidence was not reliable. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on the appellant that (1) the appellant had not pleaded and proved that he had not taken the photographs even on 25th and 26th March, 1987, but at a much later date and just prior to the filing of the present election petition, he had stated that he had taken the photographs in question on 25th, and 26th and that he had "seen them earlier" and that he did not know who pasted exhibit P 1 near exhibit P 1, and he did not see the actual pasting of exhibit P 1. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contents of this wall poster directly named the first respondent as the murderer of the four victims, and if it is proved that the said poster was affixed prior to the election by the workers of the appellant with his knowledge and consent as alleged in the petition, nothing more has to be established to hold the appellant guilty of the corrupt practice within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Act. [776F] 2. The contents in this wall poster indirectly named the first appellant as the murderer. The appellant 's cross examination of this witness was directed to prove that he had no knowledge of the fact of pasting of the poster on the said days, that will not support the first respondent 's case that the said posters were there prior to the elections. [778G] 3. The contents, of this wall posters directly named the appellant as the candidate of the election with his knowledge, consent as alleged by the appellant. [782A] 4. The contents were not defamatory or that it was then true of the appellant who had taken the photograph in question on the said dates, that will also not support the appellant ' 's case. [786B] 5.

The respondent No. 5 submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay for the construction of a five star hotel. The Commissioner of the Municipal Corporation rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said land under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the said rejection of the plan, the respondent No. 2 filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondent No, 2 had no authority to sanction the plan submitted by the respondent No 5 for the construction on the said land. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent No. 1 is not concerned with the question as to the legality or otherwise of the exemption granted by the Government to the respondent No., 5. The respondent No, 5 is not concerned about the legality or validity of the resolution. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 are not, in our opinion, concerned with the legality or/ otherwise of the exemptions granted by the State Government to the Respondent No. 5. The Municipal Corporation has, subsequent to the judgment of the High Court, prepared and published on April 30, 1984 a draft revised development plan. The plan, as sanctioned by the respondent Nos.1 and 2, has since been published and the plan submittedby the respondent No 4 and conditioned by the respondent NO. 5 and conditioned by respondent No. 4. It is, therefore, apparent that in granting sanction to the plan, it the respondent No 1 has, subsequent, to the judgment, prepared and publication on April 30. 1984 a draft draft revised development Plan. The plan as sanctioned by respondent Nos. I and 2, had since been published. The plan submitted by respondent Nos 1 and 2 and conditioned by Respondent No. 4 and conditioned on the respondent No 2 and conditioned on respondent No. 3. It is not, in any way, concerned with any question as to whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved for park and recreation ground. [922D E] 1.2 The respondent No., 2 directed sanction of the plan out of 44,820.49 sq. yds. belonging to the respondent Nos 1 & 2 and conditioned upon by the respondent no. 4. The plan was prepared in accordance with the direction of the respondent No 3. The plan had since been notified and the plan prepared by the respondent authorities. The plan and the plan were submitted by the Respondent No 4. The respondent authorities were, therefore, not justified in rejecting the plan on that ground. [822D E; 823A B] 1.3 The respondent No 2 directed sanction for the development plan out of 43,820.50 sq. yds., belonging to the Respondent Nos. 1 & 2. It is also apparent that in the sanctioned plan, the Municipal Corporation has also, subsequent to that judgment, prepared the draft revised development plans. The plan has since been printed and the plan has been submitted by the Municipal Corporation. The plan is, therefore apparent that in grant sanction to the Plan, the respondent Nos, 1 and 2 directed sanction to the building out of 44.820.49 Sq. yds. belongs to the respondent NO 5. It is therefore, apparent, that in granting the exemption to the respondent, the respondent no 1 and 2 have all been considered and taken into account by the High Court.[823D E] 2.4 The question whether or not adequate quantity of land had been kept reserved, for park and recreational ground has been adequately considered and taken by the High court.

The appellant union was a registered trade union. The workmen were re employed. The appellant union was not re employed. On the other hand, the appellant union was re employed. In order to be assured that the undertaking is carried out in letter and spirit, the workmen will be re inducted in service. But there is a statement of law made by the Industrial Court while rejecting the complaints filed by the appellant union which does not command to us and to avoid any such error being repeated in future, the Industrial Court before which the action of the employer is questioned must keep in view all the relevant circumstances at the time of closure decide and determine whether the closure was a device or a pretence to determine the services of the workmen. The parties were at variance whether the employers have imposed a lockout or have closed the establishment it is necessary to find out what was the intention of the employer at the time when it resorts to lock out or claims to have closed down the industrial activity. The parties are at variance whether they have imposed a closure or have closed down their establishment it is essential to find out how the closure was bona fide one or was a device to determine the intention and bonafides of the employer. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intent and bonafides and of the employer in order to determine whether the employer is guilty of unfair labour practice. To accept the view taken by the Industrial court would lead to a startling result in that an employer who has resorted to closure bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activity he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a device or pretence. The duration and duration of the closing may be a relevant fact to determine whether a closure was a consequence of imposing lock out or the owner employer had decided to close down the industrial activities. To accept this view, the correct approach ought to be that when it is claimed that the employer is not guilty of imposing a lockout but has closed the industrial activity, the industrial court before which the actions of the employer are questioned must keep In view all the facts at the time the closure was made and the Industrial Court after considering all the relevant facts at the stage of closure of the industrial activity and after giving an opportunity to the parties to adduce evidence, framed an issue whether the employer had imposed a lock out or had closed down the business. The Industrial Court held that the closure had to be irrevocable, final and permanent and that lockout was necessarily temporary or for a period. The Industrial Tribunal also held that the new workmen were not being re employed and new hands arc being recruited. The Industrial Appellate Tribunal also held against the appellant union. The appellant Union filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant union that the industrial undertakings of the employers had never been closed or at any rate had resumed working in full and that the old workmen are not being re employcd and new hands are being recruited. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The true test is that when it was claimed that the employee is not guilty o imposing a lock out but has closed his industrial activity, he can not doing so on the ground that the closure was not a device or device to determine determine the intention of employer at the place of business, or the suspension of work or the refusal by an employer to continue to employ any number of persons employed by him.

The appellant was appointed to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. In 1949 he was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On June 19, 1951, he was appointed as Subordinate Judge. On June 20, 1951, the appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954, on the grounds, firstly that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953, with effect from October 1, 1953, the enquiry into the conduct of the Government servants on a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above could be held only by a Tribunal to which the Government might refer the same, and that, therefore, the proceedings of the High Court after October 1, 1954, culminating in the order of Suspension dated January 28. 1954, were without jurisdiction, and secondly, that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the enquiry was not properly held by the High Court. The order passed by the High court on January 28, 1955, was merely one of suspension pending enquiry into grave charges under rule 17(e) against the Members of the State Judicial Service. The order was merely one one of suspension Pending final orders by the Government, and such an order was neither one of dismissal nor removal from service within article 311 of The Constitution. The order of suspension made by the High Courts on January 28.1954, was merely an one of suspension and pending enquiry into serious charges under rule17(e) of the Madras Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1951, and such a order was neither of dismissal nor of removal from service.

The appellant, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company, died on May 13, 1945, having made and published a will disposing of his extensive estate in the United Kingdom and in British India. The Income tax Officer, by his order dated May 13, 1946, assessed the appellant as the holder of 2673 shares of Gannon Kapur & Company. The appellant contended that the income received by the appellant before his death and received by his heirs and legal representatives after his death in that previous year became assessable to income tax in the relevant assessment year, but not receipts by the legal representatives after the expiry of the account year in which the income was to be deemed to have been received by him or his legal representatives after their death in that year. The Income Tax Officer rejected the appellant 's contention and held that the income was not liable to be taxed in the hands of the legal representatives of the deceased, and that the appellant was not liable for the income tax in respect of those years. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that the appellant had not made any provision in the Act for collecting tax from the estate of a deceased person in the years of assessment succeeding the year of account in which such notional income must be deemed to be distributed as income of the deceased. The High Court held that the provisions of section 24B were not applicable to the appellant ' s case and that the income of the appellant was liable to be assessed in the hands Of the legal representatives. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Legislature not having made any provision generally for assessment of income receivable by the estate of the deceased person, the expression "assessee" in section 2(2) as substituted by the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act 25 of 1953 with effect from April 1, 1952, means a person by whom income tax or any other similar 601 every person in respect of whom any proceeding and this Act has been taken for the assessment of his income or of the loss sustained by him or of the amount of refund due to him. The Legislature has not provided that the income so received by a legal representative which would, but for the death of the deceased have been received, by such deceased person, is to be regarded as extended to the end of the year in which such person died. [357 F G] (2) The expression "assessee ' in section 2 (2) as amended by the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Ordinance 25 of 1953, means a persons by whom income Tax or any other allied 601 every person In respect of whom no proceeding and this is the personal income of the legal representative to tax, that the expression "any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" cannot be deemed to include the income of a deceased, and on the latter part of the opinion sought to raise two arguments (1) that even if after the expiry Of the year of accounts receipts which if the person earning had not died would have been treated as his income, ceased to be liable to assessment as income of that deceased, they could still be taxed as his income in the hands, of the legal heirs and legal representative who cannot be deemed as assessees for the purpose of assessment in regard to those years, and on that latter part of that opinion sought to raised two arguments (2) that even though after the expiry period of the year of assessment receipts which if he had died would have come to an end for the purpose for assessment as the personal income, ceased not to be liable for assessment as income. [358 C] (3) The expression 'assessee ' in s. 2(2), as substituted by Act 25 of1953 with effect from March 1, 1952.

The appellant was a Ruler of the State of Baster. He was a Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. He was the Ruler of the said State. He was also a maufidar. The appellant was the Ruler and absolute holder of the villages mentioned in Schedules A, B and C of his petition. The High Court held that if the appellant was a mauffidar, there was nothing to show that with reference to any village held by him it was entered in the wajib ul arz with respect to any of his maufi villages that he had a right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such village. The High court also rejected the contention on behalf of the appellant that as he was a "Ruler" within the meaning of that expression in article 366(22) of the Constitution he did not come within the expression "ex Ruler" as contained in the definition of the word "proprietor" in the Act. The High ' Court also rejected the contentions on behalf of appellant that as the appellant was the "Rulers" within the definition of that expression, he did not fall within the definition in the Act, and that article 366(24) of the constitution did not apply to a Ruler or to the private property of a Ruler which was not assessed to land revenue. The High, Court also rejected this contention on behalf the appellant that the appellant was not a "Rurer" as contained under the definition of "proprietor" as contained In the Act. Held, that the High Court rightly held that the appellant had given no evidence to establish that the appellant as a mauzidar had no right to recover rents or revenue from the persons holding land.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India, (Ministry of Environment and Forests, Government of India). The respondent submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. tie complained that some other officials who have been serving at Shillong for a longer period, have been allowed to continue at Shillong. The respondent submitted his representation to the Director, SE, Bot Panical Survey of Indian India, (Mines) and requested him to transfer him at Shillong. He submitted that the guideline contained in Government O.M., dated 3.5.1986 have been kept in view while ordering his transfers. tie complained of that some other officers who have been served at Shillong for longer period, had been allowed to remain at Shillong. In the meantime, the respondent was transferred to Shillong and he was transferred to Pauri. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of transfer. The High Court quashed the order of the transfer on the following reasoning: the decisions of the Courts establish that the power of transfer is not an unfettered one but is circumscribed by various circulars/guidelines contained in the administrative instructions issued by the Government. The guidelines say that as far as possible, husband and wife must be posted at one pi" as far as practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. The High court quashed the order on the following grounds: (1) The guidelines contained in the Government of India Office Memorandum dated 3.3.1986 have no been kept in the mind while ordering the transfer; (2) The guidelines say, that as far possible, husband & wife must be transferred where, is a matter for the appropriate authority to decide; (3) The Court or the Tribunal can quash the order of transfers if any of the administrative instructions/guideline are not followed, much less can it be charactrised as malafide for that reason. To reiterate, the order of transferring can be questioned in a court or Tribunal only where it is passed malafide or where it is made in violation of any statutory provisions, the Court cannot interfere with it. While ordering the transfer, there is no doubt, the authority must keep in mind the guidelines issued by the Central Government on the subject. Similarly if a person makes any representation with respect to his transfer, the appropriate authority must consider the same having regard to the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees. After giving preference to the career prospects by accepting such a promotion or any appointment in an all India service with the incident of transfer to any place in India, subordinating the need of the couple living together at one Station, 'they cannot as of right claim to be relieved of the ordinary incidents of all India service and avoid transfer to a different place on the ground that the spouses thereby would be posted at different places.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34, IP.C. and were sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The third charge related to rioting wherein A1, A2, A4, A6 and A3 armed with sticks, A3 armedwith aruval (bill hook) and A6 armed with aruval, attacked Jawahar at about 8.30 A.M. on January 2, 1977 and caused him multiple injuries as a result of which he died on the same day. All the acused persons were acquitted by the learned Trial Judge. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1 to A3. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar has been proved beyond doubt. [319D] 1.2 The participation of A1 in the occurrence resulting in the death o r the deceased and the facts and circumstances of this case the 3 offence committed by them came within the mischief of Section 325 read with Section34, I.P.C., and as such the offence committed by the appellants came within the purview of Section 325, I. P.C. read with Section 149, I. PP.C. [321B] 1.3 The participation of all the appellants in t he occurrence which resulted into the death of the Jawahar has been established beyond doubt. The High Court while consid ering the nature of offence observed as under: "These accused and their associates who be set themselves on Jawahar could never have intended to cause the death of Manohar for, if such was their intention, they could have certainly killed him especially after carrying him into the cholam field and left him dead there instead of merely causing grievous and grievous injuries to him. Even according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit P 6) all that first accused had remarked was that the attack on him was in retaliation for the injuries Jawahar had caused on the first accused a few weeks earlier. " Agreeing with the above observations of the High Court, the appellants shall undergo rigorous imprisonment of five years. [322C D] 1.4 The appellants shall deposit Rs. 7,000 each before the Trial Court within four months from today. In the event of non payment of fine the appellants shall be undergo rigorous imprisonment imprisonment for five ye years. The amount of Rs. 21,000 rea lised as fine from the appellants be paid to Indra sister of deceased Jawahar. [323D] 1:5 The amount of fine shall be paid to the father/mother of deceased Jawahar." [323F] 1.6 The appellants shall undergo imprisonment for five year. The amount shall be paid by Indra sister of the deceased Jawahar. In the case of none of them surviving the amount shall be pay to Indra sister.

The appellant Bank was constituted under the Banking Companies Act, 1949. The Banking Companies Act was passed by the British Parliament. The Banking companies Act was passed in 1969. The Banking Company Act was passed on the day the Act was passed. The Banking Corporations Act was passed, the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 was passed. Section 4(e) of the Act was amended by the Banking Companies Amendment Act, 1969. The appellant Bank filed a suit for recovery of the amount due from it. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that the words `special Indian law ' in section 4(e)(a) of the Banking Companies ' Act, 1949, refer or relate to a special law enacted by the British Legislature for India, and that the Banking Companies Acts are not applicable to the appellant Bank and, therefore, the provisions of section 4(d) of the said Act will not apply inasmuch as the appellant Bank was not formed in pursuance of any `special Indian Law ', and that as the words `formed in pursuance of ' in section 3(27)(a) were placed after the words `an Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom ' and before the words `Royal Charter or Letters Patent ', it must be held in view of the setting that the expression `formed in pursuant of ' in Section 4(d)(a) means a law enacted by a Legislature of British Parliament for India. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words `any special Indian law ' refer and relates to a law made by the Indian Legislature and not by the law itself. [969G] 2. The words 'any special Indian Law ' refer and relate to a law enacted under the law and not by a law itself. The words "any special Indian laws" refer and relate only to a law which is the creature of a special Indian law. [968G] 3. The words are `formed in furtherance of the ' in section4(e) and not by ' the law itself, and that 'the phrase `formed in compliance with ' in section ' 4(e), signifies a process of formation of a corporation under the law ' and not by any law itself. Therefore, the words `any Special Indian law ' refers and relates to the law made by Parliament or Legislature of the United Republic. Therefore, by using the expression `in pursuance of ' ' in section 2(e) the Legislature has not meant that the corporation in question should be formed by a third party in pursuance of the law and, not by the Law itself in order to come within the purview of section 4 (e) of The Act. [966G] 4. The words ''any special Indian ' refers and relate to the law ' made by the British Government. The words, `any special law ' refer to a law ' made under the law. [969A] 5. The words of `any special ' Indian law ' referred and relates to 'a law made by a Legislature or Legislature of a State. [969B] 6. The words "'any special Indian" refer and relates only to a special Indian Law. [969C] 7. The words have not meant that 'the corporation in question must be formed by an third party in pursuant of the law. Therefore, there is no justification for laying down that the expression 'any special 'Indian law ' refers or relates to a special ' Indian Law. Therefore, it is not possible to say that the corporation has been formed by or under a special Indian statute. [969D] 8.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of sugar in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar, raised the following points in support of their contention that the impugned notification is illegal and invalid (1) The impugned notification is beyond the ambit of authority conferred on the Central Government under section 3 of the Act and clause 5 of the Order, and (2) the impugned notification merely fixes ex factory prices and is bad, firstly on the ground that the Act and the Order do not authorise the Central Government to fix ex factory prices. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) There is no discrimination after the control of sugar 136 prices in these three regions and the contention that the factories in the other areas are left uncontrolled with the result that there is discrimination is purely theoretical, in view of the economic factors which control the price of sugar in this country. [134 E] (2) The impugned Notification merely fixes ex factories prices and is not bad, firstly, on the ground of the economic factor which control the prices of sugar in these three areas and that there is no reasonable basis for such clasification ; factories in other parts of India are left uncontrolled without the result that the industry in the other regions which are said to be mainly deficit, are concerned. [134 F] (3) The impugned notifications merely fixes exfactory prices and is, therefore, bad. [134 C] (4) The impugned order merely fixes ex-factory prices and does not warrant any inference that the factories are left uncontrolled by the result that they would fix prices separately so far as factories in other States which are said not mainly deficit, were concerned. [135 D] (5) The impugned Act merely fixes ex manufacturing prices and is therefore bad.

The workmen of the appellant company, were employed in the manufacture of pharmaceutical products. The workmen of the company were employed in a factory at Calcutta. The workmen were employed in Calcutta. The company was a registered company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The workmen employed in Calcutta were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 350 per month. The workmen claimed that the workmen were entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 19(6) of the Act. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the working class cost of living index in the year 1951 was taken as the basis, and that the workmen had been paid wages at a rate of Rs 350 per month, and that in view of the provisions contained in section 19(1) of the Amending Act, the reference was bad in law. The High Court dismissed the reference. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal wrongly relied upon Exhibit 3, corrected on the basis of the information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal for ascertaining the working class Cost of living index since August 1954 up to March 1957. HELD: (i) The Tribunal wrongly relied on Exhibit 3, prepared by the State Government for ascertaining the work class cost of working class cost, of living index, since August 1954. The Tribunal wrongly relying upon Exhibit 3. The Tribunal rightly relied upon Exhibit 2, corrected on that basis. The Tribunal was wrong in relying upon Exhibit 2. The Tribunal erred in relying upon the information given in the State Statistical Commission 's report, for ascertaining the Working class cost of the living index since September 1954 up to February 1957. [148 E F] (ii) The Tribunal rightly held that the work class of living index was at 344.1 in August 1954 and it rose to 4006 in May 1957. [149 C] (iii) The Tribunal erred on the basis that the working classes cost of living Index in the year 1957 were taken as the base, and that it rose only to 4006. in May 1957, with the result that there was a rise of 56 points, a substantial rise in the cost of living cost by dearness allowance could not be permitted and therefore allowed them only 75 per cent. of the increase in the dearness allowance to which they would have otherwise been entitled on the basis Of the rise in the Cost of living Index. [149 D E] (iv) The Tribunal was right in holding that the working Class cost of living class cost of live index stood at 344. 1 (v) The Tribunal had wrongly relied upon the evidence of the State Statistical Institute, West Bengal, for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working class costs of living index by dearness allowance.

The appellant, a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism, was a religious institution, dedicated to the religious and charitable purposes of the Veerasava Rajendraswami of the Veerada Saiva cult. The said management continued as before and the fact that an Executive Officer had been appointed under the scheme made no difference to the actual administration of the Mutt. The appellant 's writ petition was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The scheme was framed and the Executive Officer was appointed as early as 1939. If the Executive Officer could not take over the actual administration, it was partly because the appellant had continuously challenged the implementation of the scheme by legal proceedings and partly because he had otherwise obstructed the said implementation. But it was clear that when the scheme was framed, the appellant had been deprived of his fundamental right under article 19(1)(f). [267 D E] (2) The scheme had not been completely imple mented till 1952, and it was in respect of such invalid orders that the Court held that the appellant was entitled to seek the protection of article 19(l)(f). The deprivation of the appellant 's property rights was brought about by invalid orders and it was not open to the appellant to challenge the validity of the scheme oil the ground that it deprives him of his fundamental rights under article 19. [267 E F] (3) The scheme did not contravene the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution. [267 D] (4) The scheme could not be challenged on the ground that some of its provisions contravened the fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens of this country under article 19 (1)(f) and as such, invalid. [267 F] (5) The scheme, therefore, was framed and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed in courts of law. [267 G] (6) The scheme having been framed and a reference made to the relevant provisions of the latter Act, it was open to the petitioner to challenge the legality of the scheme on the ground, that it deprives the appellant of his fundamental fundamental right under Article 19(1) (f). [268 E] (7) The scheme must now be deemed to be a scheme which 51 S.C.R. 276, referred to the relevant sections of the Constitution in respect of fundamental rights retrospective in operation. [268 G] (8) The scheme to which section 103(d) applies, has to be deemed to have been settled or modified under the provisions of the former Act without examining whether all the provisions of that Act are necessarily justified by or consistent with. the provisions of this latter Act. [268 D] (9) The scheme is framed and the executive Officer was appointed in the present case. If the executive Officer could not, take over the management and its properties, it was wholly because the appellant has continuously challenged the scheme by Legal proceedings and partly Because he has otherwise obstructed the implementation of that implementation.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986. The appellant continued to serve as Hindi Teacher with repeated spells. The managing committee even passed a resolution on July 6,1987 requesting the educational authorities of the State of Orissa to approve the continuous appointment of the appellant as Hindi Teacher.
