The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi Teacher and also for a direction to regularise his service in a substantive vacancy because of the Validation Act. The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation and held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Validation Acts on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. The appellant preferred an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court erred in denying the benefit of Validation Act to the appellant on the ground of his initial appointment to 89 days. [912D] 1.2 The High Court committed an error in denying the benefits of the Validation act to the appellant. [913E] 1.3 The High Court was wrong in denying the relief to the appellant in the absence of the approval by the educational authorities for the period subsequent to 1986. [914G] 1.4 The appellant was appointed on July 12,1982 and has been working with the approval of the authorities for almost 4 years with short breaks. The case of the appellant is, thus fully covered by Section 3 of the Validation Ordinance. [915E] 1:5 The High Court rightly held that the initial appointment for 91 days was conditioned on the stipulation that the appellant would continue until replacement by a candidate of the select list, and that the case of the Appellant is, thus, fully covered by section 3 of the validation Act. [916F] 1:6 The High Court has erred in denying to the appellant the benefit of his Validation Act to his appellant on the grounds that his initial appointments for 89 days were conditioned by the condition that he would be continued until replaced by another candidate from the Select list. The High court erred in denying that the initial appointments for 91 days were conditioned on the condition that the appellant will continue until replaced By a candidate from select list. [917G] 1:7 The appellant was working with the approved approval of the authority for almost 4 year with short breaks and in the process denying them their rightful dues and other service benefits. The case is, thus clearly covered by Section 2 of the Validation ordinance. [918G] 1 :8 The High Court failed in denying the appellant the benefits of Validation Act.

The Chairman and Members shall not be entitled to any mileage allowance. (2) A Chairman or Member may, at his option draw one daily allowance in lieu of mileage allowance plus half daily allowance for the day of departure and half daily allowance in respect of a journey performed for any of the purposes specified in rule 5: Provided that the Vice Chairman and Members may at his option pay one daily allowance for a day of departure or half daily allowance plus half monthly allowance for the days of departure in connection with a journey performed within the district. (7) A Chairman who is treated as a State guest while attending the meeting or while on duty within or outside the district his daily allowance in addition to the travelling allowance, daily allowance or any other allowances to which he might have been entitled in order to compensate him for expenses incurred in connection with the discharge of his official duties, shall be limited only to one fourth. (8) A Chairman is entitled to Rs. 100/ as a consolidated amount in lieu of the travelling allowance and daily allowance under r. 3 to 7 made the office of Chairman of a Zila Parishad at Rs. 3 of the Rules, provision was made for this monthly allowance of Rs. 100/- as a consolidated sum in lieu of travelling allowance, Daily allowance or anyother allowances to which the Chairman might have been paid in order to entitle him in order to compensation for expenses incurred by him in connection with his discharge of his duties. (9) A Chairman cannot be allowed to draw any mileage allowances. (10) A Chairman must be making gain out of the payment to him of daily allowance. (11) A Chairman/Member travelling in a car belonging to any one Member, ViceChairman or Chairman shall be entitled to Rs, 100/ as consolidated amount in addition to his travelling allowance, and daily allowance for day of departure preceding and following the day(s) of halt. (12) A Chairman 's Vice Chairman or Members shall not, except with the permission of the Panchayat Samiti, be entitled, to any mile mileage allowance, and Daily allowance allowance. (13) A Chairman in the case of a Chairman, ViceChairman, or Member who is treated by a Panchayat Samiti under r. 5 shall not be disentitled to any mile Allowance.

The appellant was tenant of a residential building. The tenanted premises was let out to the appellant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The trial Court held that the partition wall in the hall did not constitute material alteration, it further held that the tin shed marked by letters ABHG had been constructed by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin shed marking with letters CDGH had been constructed without respondents ' consent which materially altered the accommodation and on that findings the trial court decreed the suit. The High Court also held that the appellant had been tenant of the tin shed in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The High court also held that since two sides of the tin sheds were resting on the pucca wall it constituted a material alteration in the accommodation and that the tin sheds marked with letters C DGH had been built by the appellant subse quently without respondents ' Consent which materially altered it and on that finding the trial court decree decreed the suit, and decreed the suit for eviction. The appellant has appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts committed error in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the lower courts on the question whether tin shed and the partition wail constituted material alterations in the accommodation. [975F] 2. The High ' Court committed error in interfere with the findings recorded by the first appellate court on the question Whether tin shed and partition wail formed material alterations. The High, Court committed error of interfering with the finding of fact recorded in the first appeal. [976F] 3. The High. Court committed error by interfering with the concurrent findings of fact. [978F] 4. The High' Court committed error. The High "Court committed error in interference with the findings.

The appellant company filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent firm on 22 4 1975 against the appellant. The Trial Court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975 about the passing of the ex parte decree. The High Court allowed the revision set aside the judgment of the Trial Court and upheld the passing of ex parte decree, and the passing of a decree. The appellant company filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. The meaning of clause (b) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the Code in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summons on natural persons. [1032C D] 2. The meaning clause (b), has got tobe understood in the context of the provisions in Order 5, which is meant to issue and service summons on natural person. [1033E] 3. The meaning is of the word "Principal Officer". In Rule 17 of Order 5 it has been provided: "Where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or where the serving officer, after using all due and reasonable diligence, cannot find the defendant, and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving officer shall affix a copy of the summons upon the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain, 1032 and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued, with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the copy, the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed. " [1034G H] 4. The meaning given to the word "principal Officer" in Rule 2 of Order 29 of the Code is that managing agents and the it can, by virtue of Rule 17 of order 5, be on juristic person. [ 1034A] 5. The meaning in clause (b)(i) has got significance in the context in Order 5. [1035B] 6. The meaning "principal Officer", in Rule 2, has got to he understood in the light of the provisions contained in the Code in order 5 which is intended for issue and Service of summons on Natural persons.

The appellant was the owner of the land in dispute. The land was acquired by the State Government under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Magistrate. The High Court allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate. In the meantime, the Magistrate passed the final order in favour of the appellant. The High court allowed the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the final order of the magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that there was an apprehension of breach of the peace existed at the time the order was passed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The High Courts in Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal & Ors. ; , followed. 1.2. The High 'Court was right in holding that the final decision of the Magistrate was vitiated in view of the finding that there existed a breach of the law. [951G] 1.3. The HighCourt was right, in holding that there was no question of the dispute having ended so as to lead to cancellation of the order under sub section (5) of section 145. [952B] 1.4. The High, Court was right in observing that the final orders of the Magistrate were vitiated in absenceof a finding that breach of the wall existed at the relevant time. [953C] 1.5. The High "Court was right to hold that the final judgment of the Magistrate is vitiated in absence Of a finding that a breach of peace existed. [954D] 1.6. The High `Court was right. [955E] 1.7.

The appellant was a resident of the State of Madras. The income tax authorities assessed the appellant under the provisions of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the basis of the agreement between the appellant and the respondent. The appellant contended that the transactions were benami transactions and that the profits could be taxed only if they were remitted to British India. Held, that the finding of the Commissioner was correct. The finding of the Tribunal on the facts found was a pure question of fact and was not open to challenge in a reference under section 66(1). The decision of the High Court was correct. It was not open for the appellant to raise the contention that the decision of the Tribunal was final even though the court might not, on the materials, have come to the same conclusion if it had the power to substitute its own judgment. The decision of this Court in Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co. (1) and Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay vs Ahmadbhai Umarbhai & Co. (2) was not applicable to the facts of the present case. The decision in Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay vs Bombay Ahmedbhai Umarabhai and Co. ([1951] S.C.R. 869), relied on. Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay vs Sardar Ahmedbhai Umarubhai and Co. ; , referred to. The decision was not open under section 66 (1) (c) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The decision did not lay down any principle of law that a finding on a question of fact is open to review by the court only on the ground that it is not supported by any evidence or perverse but also on the ground of some other facts. The decision, therefore, did not lay any foundation for the view that the decision was a pure one of mixed law and fact.

The assessee was appointed as a General Manager of the respondent company. The company was a private limited company. The assessee was appointed in the year 1948 49. The company made a claim for deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to the General Manager. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee was in no way related to the proprietors of the firm and the commission on profits clause was inserted to create the interest of the General Manager for accomplishment of the task entrusted to him. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount of Rs. 37,733 paid to the assessee was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee and was wrongly disallowed by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal held that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct after the death of Shri Vaish, the General Manager and the assessee was entitled to consider the extent of his business, the nature of the duties to be performed and the special aptitude of the employee, future prospects of extension by the business and a host of other related circumstances. The High Court, on reference, held that the assessee had taken over the mill at a time when it was old and dilapidated and in the first 14 months the mill made no profit and the assessee had not taken any profit. The High court, on reference held that the income tax Officer was wrong in taking this circumstance into consideration. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the amount laid out in the statement of case under section 66(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 on the following question of law : "Whether in the circumstances of the case, the sum of Rs.37,733 was an amount laying out or expended entirely or exclusively for for the purpoSe of business, profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act ?" HELD : (i) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in the circumstances established by the assessee the entire amount of Rs, 75,465 paid to the general manager was an amount lay out or expended exclusively for the purpSe of business. [475 D] (ii) The principle that the principle of this Court applies to the facts and in the light of the circumstances of each particular case. is that in the light Of the circumstances of a particular case, the entire amount must be paid to an employee of the assessee. It is open to the Appellate Tribunal to come to a conclusion either that the alleged payment is not real or that it is not laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business. [575 E] (iii) The principle applies to the case and it cannot be said that in the present case the entire amount was laid out or incurred wholly and exclusively exclusively for the business of assessee and to disallow it. [576 D] (iv) The principle is that in a case where an employer in fixing the remuneration of his employees is entitled to consider, the extent of its business, the character of the duties, to be performed, and the special Aptitude of the employees, future prospects, of extension by, the business and the a host of others related circumstances.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. He was a member of a trade union. He was actually represented in the proceedings before the Tribunal by an officer of that Union. The appellant filed his application to the Patna High Court on March 13, 1957, praying for an issue of an appropriate writ or direction quashing the Tribunal 's order of February 26, 1957, by which the Tribunal had rejected his prayer for representation by a person of his own choice in place of Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union and that he had not authorised Fateh Singh to enter into any agreement in his case and praying that the agreement filed in respect of his case should not be accepted and that he and his agents should be heard before the disposal of the case. The High Court dismissed the application. Held, that the Tribunal committed a serious error in rejecting the appellant 's prayer for representation through representatives of his own choosing in preference to Fateh Singh, and the Secretary of Union. The necessary corollary to this is that the individual workman is at no stage a party to the industrial dispute independently of the Union which has espoused his cause. It has been suggested that the Union 's Secretary Fateh Singh himself had made the complaint against the appellant which resulted in the order of dismissal. It has to be observed however that in spite of everything, the Union did take up this appellant 's case against his dismissal as its own. In view of all the circumstances, it cannot be said that the Tribunal was committed any error in refusing the appellant ' 's prayer to representation through representatives.

The appellants were the tenants of the premises in question. The suit was decreed against both the defendants and for arrears of rent against defendant No. 1. The appellants filed an appeal against the decree in the High Court. The High Court reversed the decree and restored the decree in favour of all the original plaintiffs and defendant No. 2. The appellants then filed a second appeal in the High court which was dismissed. The appellants thereafter filed a second revision petition in the High, Court. The appellants contended that the surviving appellants were competent to continue the appeal in view of O.XXII, r. 3 of O.XXXII, r, XXII and not of r. 3. Held, that the High Court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving appellants when the appeal by the kedar Nath had (1) 53 I.A 84 560 abated as all the appellants had a common right and interest in getting a decree of ejectment against defendant No, 2 and such decree could have been on a ground common to all of them. The appeal by the surviving appellants was not competent in the circumstances of the case and, therefore, the provisions of 0. XLI, r. 4 when the decree proceeds on a ground different to all the plaintiffs or defendants, if all the plaintiffs and the defendants appeal from the decree and any of them dies and the appeal abates so far as he is concerned under O.XXI, r. 33 is of no greater help to the contention of the appellants. The appeal filed by the surviving appellant was not competent under the circumstances of this case and, consequently, the provisions Of 0. XLI of r. 4 were not intended to apply to an appeal which was not a competent appeal against a party under the Code or under the Letters Patent.

The landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) of the TP Act, as amended by the Amending Act of 1929, under section 111 (g) of which no notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 was needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111(h) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the provisions of the TP act would regulate the matter as could be held to be consistent with the rules of equity, justice and good conscience and the question was clearly answered in the negative. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the lease having expired by efflux Of time limited thereby, under section111(g) and no notice terminating tenancy under section 107 was needed and that the forfeiture was not in terms of section 111(a) and no notices terminating the tenancy were needed and further, that the forfeiture could be availed by the landlord only in the absence absence of a written notice as contemplated under section 111 of the TPAct, and that the principles of justice, equity and good conscience, which alone applied, did not desiderate the technical requirement of a notice in writing of an intention to determine the lease on forfeiture, and that no notice terminating a tenancy under section106 was needed and, further, that in the absence, no notice terminating any tenancy under section 116(g) was needed and hence, the forfeiture of tenancy caused by the sub letting in contrary to the principles embodied in section 111(b) of the said Act could be availed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The question whether the provisions of section 111 (h) of TP Act, which regulate the matter in regard to notice were inconsistent with the rules and of justice, justice and fair conscience, which itself applied, did neither do nor did it affect the bases made prior to the coming into force of the TP Acts. The crucial principles, not the technical rules, of the TP Rules form part of justice, Equity and good conscience. The conclusion emerges that the landlord 's termination of the tenancy in this case was good even without a written notice. The statutory law as it now stands, however, is that the happening of any of the events specified in section 111 (a) does not, ipso facto, extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right, if he so chooses, to determine the leased, by giving notice in that behalf. The essential principles, not technical rules, or of the TP statute form part of equity, equity and justice. The conclusion emerged that the landlord's termination of the lease in this case is good even without any written notice.

The respondent was dismissed from service on the ground of conduct which led to his conviction on a criminal charge. The respondent challenged the order of dismissal before the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to be reinstated in service. The High court held that the order of termination was illegal and that the order was illegal. The respondent appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The Governor had to arrive at was that it was not expedient to give the respondent an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The satisfaction under the unamended provision, therefore, that the Governor had to arrived at was that he was not expedient in giving the respondent an adequate opportunity of showing his cause against the proposed action. [489 E F] (ii) The satisfaction under section 3(2) of the Act that the Governor has to arrive at is that it was expedient to hold the inquiry under the principal clause, that clause shall not apply. [489 G] (iii) The satisfaction of the Governor under the unamended clause (2) of article 311 of the Constitution, therefore, was that it had to arrive in was that it is not expedient to hold such inquiry. [489 C] (iv) The satisfaction required under the unamended sub clause (c) of the proviso to clause (2), therefore, that he had to arrive before the satisfaction required was that in the interest of the security of the State it was not desirable to hold such an inquiry. [490 D] (v) The satisfaction contemplated under the unamended section, therefore, did not require that the Governor should arrive at was the satisfaction required. [490 E] (vi) The satisfaction was that it should be reasonably practicable to hold such enquiry. The satisfaction contemplated by the amended clause (2)(b) of article 310 of the Constitution was that it would not be expedient to hold that in the interests of the security it was not practicable to hold the enquiry under the principal clauses. [490 G] (vii) The satisfaction must be based on the evidence adduced during such inquiry. The satisfaction must have been based on the material before the authority. The satisfaction of such authority must be based upon the material before it. [490 F] (viii) The satisfaction is based on the materials before it and the satisfaction must be founded on the material on which it is based. [490 C] (ix) The satisfaction, under the unamended provisions, therefore, must be based not on the material which is based but on the evidence led during such inquiry, and must be based solely on the evidence. [490 A] (x) The satisfaction that the Governor was satisfied that in the public interest it was not necessary to hold such a inquiry was not necessary.

The petitioners, who were the Shia Wakfs, filed a suit for the enforcement of which the instant Writ Petition had been filed. The petitioners contended that the Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi, had been registered as Shia Wakfs for purposes of performing their religious ceremonies and functions over the plots and structures thereon under the Notification dated 26th February, 1944, and published in the U. 5(2) of the Act, and published the Notification dated 1st December, 1956, and published therein in the U U. 5 (2) of U. 5 of the Act. The petitioners also contended that the Notification dated 25th February, 1945 issued under section 5(1) of the U.P. Act, 1936, by the Sunni Board was of no avail to the Sunnis for the purpose of defeating the customary rights of the Shias to perform their religious ceremonies, functions and duties over the plots, structures thereon and structures thereon. The petitioners further contended that the notification dated 25th March, 1945, issued under section 6 of the Act was of no assistance to the Sunkar for the purpose for which the Shia Waqfs were registered as Shias Wakfs for purposes Of performing their religious rites and functions on the other plots and structures thereto under the Notification of 26th February 1944, particularly when it was later found that the Shias had not raised any dispute of title and the Shia communities of Mohalla Dosa Wakfs had not raised the disputed questions of title and, therefore, the Notification dated 27th February, 1946, issued under Rule 5411(vii) was not of any avail to the petitioners and through them the Shia Muslims of Mohalla Darshipura, which had been listed as Shia Waqf for purposes of discharging their religious ceremonies. The petitioners, however, contended that the impugned Notification dated 25rd March, 1945 issued by the Sunni Central Board of Waqf was of no help to the Sunnnis for the purposes of defeating the religious ceremonies of Shias to performing their religious duties and functions on their other plots and structure thereon. The respondents, however, disputed the maintainability of the suit on the ground that the Shian community of Mohalla Darhipura, Lucknow, had been established and was the subject matter of a judicial pronouncement and decree of Civil Court of competent jurisdiction as also by reason of these properties having been registered as Sunni for purposes of perform their religious rites, practices and functions and their complaint had been that the power under section 144 was being exercised in utter disregard of the lawful exercise of their legal rights and every time instead of exercising the power in aid of their rights it was being exercised, in suppressing their rights under the pretext of imminent danger to peace and tranquillity of the locality. The respondents contended that the petitioners and their Shia community had established their customary rights to perform their respective religious ceremonies and function over the plots in question and structures thereon and their complaint has been that the powers under section 144 were being exercised in suppressing their right under the pretext for imminent danger to life, peace and tranquillity and their complaint having been that the jurisdiction under section 144 Cr. P.C. was being exercised by suppressing their rights, it was being exercise in suppressing their lawful rights under the guise of imminent danger, to peace and tranquility of the locality and that these earlier litigations which were fought right up to this Court cannot be regarded as between the same parties who are before us; further, where it was felt by this Court that proper adjudication would not be possible without impleading the two Boards (Shia Central Wakf Board and Sunni Central Wakf Board) notices were issued to them and they were also im 1135 pleaded as parties to the petition who have filed their affidavits in the matter and have been heard through respective counsel.

The assessee, a company, filed its return showing the loss of its business during the previous year ending on 31.12.1957. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that when in the assessment year 1957 58 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of the assessee 's appeal had stated that it was a notional capital loss. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal by holding that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional in nature and that the claim for setting off to be admissible had to be notified by the Income tax Officer under Section 24(3) of the 1922 Act to the assessee by an order in writing. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner and the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal. The Revenue preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that there had been no genuine loss and it was essentially notionally notional in nature. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The benefit conferred under Section 24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of Section 80 of the latter Act, the High Court was Fight in holding that the claim of set off was admissible in our view. on a bare reading of these provisions, and without reference to anything more, this appeal can be disposed of. [1166C D] 1.2 The benefit conferred by Section 24 of the 1922 act continued to be granted effect to under Section 24 (3) of 1922 Act. [1167E] 1.3 The benefit conferred thereunder continued to be effective under the 1961 act and notwithstanding the words of Section 80, the High court was Fight In holding that the benefit conferred under section 24 of 1922 act continued in force. [1168C D] 2.1 The High Court was clearly Fight in observing that the benefit granted under Section 24 was given effect to. under the 1961 Acts and notwithstanding the expressionings of Section80 of the latter, the High Curt was Fight. [1169E] 2.2 The High Court had rightly held that the claim was admissible in its view. [1170F] 2.3 The High Court has rightly held that there was a genuine loss and the claim of the set off was allowable in its view.[1170F G] 2.4 The High Court rightly held that in the instant case the claim of setting off was admissible. [1171G] 2.5 The High Court erred in holding that there is no genuine loss. [1172G] 2:6 The benefit conferred was given effect t o under the 1961 Income tax Act.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P). The Defence Science Service had three units under it, namely, 1) Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), 2) Director ate General of Inspection (DGI) and 3) Directorate of Tech nical Development and Production, (Air) and 3 Directorate of Technical Development and production (Air) & Production (Air), (DTD& P). The recruitment was made always to the Defence Science Services, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the said three units. All, the service conditions of the persons working in the three units including scales of pay, superannuation age, etc. were the same and were regulated by the same set of Rules, viz. Defence Science Service Rules. When the trifurcation was made, the Service Rules governing the three units had a common Rule which was Rule 12 in DAQAS and DQAS, and Rule 13 in DRDS which reads as follows: "Other conditions of service: (1) The conditions of service of the members of the service in respect of matters not expressly provided for in these Rules, shall mutatis mutandis and subject to any special orders issued by the Government in respect of the service. (2) The conditions relating to service of the member of the service shall mutatis mutandis be subject to any general orders issued by Government in respect o f the service, be the same as those applicable to officers (Civil ians) of corresponding status in similar scientific institu tions/organisations under the Government of India. (3) The conditions regarding service of the employees belonging to the different units, and merely because the superannuation age of the members was increased, it could not be held that the respondent who belonged to another unit, viz. DAQAS, was entitled to the said benefit. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the re spondent was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years his superannuation age being deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of the OM dated 24.12.85 read with OM dated 10.2.86 referred to above. The Tribunal also held that the decision of the Tribunal was both proper and valid and there was no substance in the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The denial of the benefit of enhanced superannuation age to the members of one 24 unit while the same is granted to the members o f the other unit amounts to discrimination, violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [785C] 1.2 The denial of benefit of enhanced retirement age to the member of one 24 units while the same was granted to the member o f another unit amounts to discriminatory violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.[785D] 1.3 The denial of benefits of enhanced superannuation superannuation age to members of one24 unit while the Same is granted to members of other unit amounts, to discrimination, violation of Article 16. [786F] 1.4 The denial of this benefit to the members Of one 24 unit amounts to denial of the enhanced superannuation age of 60 years in spite of the decision of Tribunal and even pending this appeal when no stay was granted, the Appellant Union of India retired the respondent at the age Of 58 years.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The election of the appellant was held under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965. The appellant was declared elected. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the election of the respondent was void on the ground of corrupt practice. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the first publication having taken place on the 8th June, 1967 the High Court was not right in refusing to quash the order. HELD: (i) The first publication having been taken place on 8th June 1967 the date of the election was beyond time and should not have been entertained. [975 E] (ii) The allegation of corrupt practice was of a serious nature and if the appellant was found guilty of the commission thereof, the period of five years ' disqualification would certainly not be inappropriate. [976 D] (iii) The allegations of corrupt practice were of a serious character and if the High Court had set right the order of the Judge based on the evidence of these witnesses, the High Court could not have interfered with the order of acquittal. [978 E] (iv) The allegations regarding corrupt practice were not of a serious kind and if the trial Judge accepted the evidence with regard to the distribution of the pamphlet by the appellant the High Court would not have set right by quasbing the order of dismissal. [982 G] (v) The allegations about corrupt practice were only of a serious type and if the charge had been proved, the period for limitation would certainly not have been inappropriate.

The petitioner company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State of Uttar Pradesh imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The petitioner company challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was ultra vires entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The High Court held that there was no power in the State to issue the impugned notification under section 3 A on March 31, 1957, as that section was itself to come into force only on April 1, 1956, vide Adarsh Bhandar vs Sales Tax Officer (1). The petitioner company appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The Validation Act is not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54 of the List II or List III of the Seventh schedule to the Constitution, under which the legislation could be justified, it must be held to be ultra vires. [934 C] (ii) The Validation Acts are not ultra vires. The Validation Act was not ultra vires, and the Validation Act is therefore not a law in respect of tax on the supply of materials in a contract for the construction of works simpliciter on the footing of a sale was held to be outside the entry, and the validation Act is therefore ultra vires. (iii) The Validation Ordinance is not ultra. [935 D] (iv) The Validation act is not ultra within the saving of the Validation Act. The Validation Acts were not ultra vires and the Validation Acts are therefore not ultra vires Entry 54 of List I or List III. [937 E] (v) The Validation acts are not ultra. The Validation acts were not ultra within Entry 54 of the Seventh List. [938 B] (vi) The Validation of the Validation Acts is not ultra, and the impugned notification is therefore not ultra. (vii) The Validation and Validation Act is also not ultra vires entry 52 of List I. [939 E] (viii) The Validation is not ultra because it operates retrospectively. [940 D] (ix) The Validation, Act is not intra vires the powers under entry 54, for the reason that it operates retrospectively, and the Validating Act is therefore, not a law within the saving Of the Validation Act, and as there is no other entry in List II or Lists III of the Constitution, the Validation Act cannot be held to have been ultra vires.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court affirmed the conviction. The appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant is not a 'habitual ' and has no vicious antecedents except this fugitive,INSTy molestation which is bad enough in a society where women are socially weak and sexually victimised. The appellant has a reasonable prospect of shaping into a balanced person, given propitious social environs, curative and congenial work and techniques of internal stress release or of reformatory self expression. The present effort of Governments, Central and State, to reform jail regimen, and we hope, will give a better deal to the caged community. For these reasons, in this case, we deem it desirable to superadd to the sentence of imprisonment a few directives to ensure that the carceral period reforms the convict. The current efforts of Governments, central and State, will give an better deal to each caged community, and, in this perspective, we blend deterrence with correction and reduce the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for two years. [682G H; 603A B] 2. The appellant was not a ' habitual ' and has not no vicious antecedent except this fuagitive,INSTary molestation which was bad enough in the a society where woman are often socially weak and mormised. The crime is a serious one. It is a serious offence. It is not a case of rape. The offender is in his early twenties and signs of repentance are seen. The victim and her parents have forgiven the criminal. They have forgiven them the molester who is a first cousin, say counsel. An affidavit from the father in law of the woman has been filed and, if needed, counsel is ready to produce the victim 's statement that she has forgiven the Criminal. The appellant and her parents had forgiven the molesters who are a first cousin. An affidavit by the father in Law of the woman had been filed and the, if needed. counsel is ready for producing the victim ' sortie. The appellant, therefore, deserves judicial cognizance. [690B C] 3. The appellant 's conviction is set aside. The appellant be released forthwith.

The assessee was a limited company dealing in land. It maintains its accounts on the mercantile system. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the assessee. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Arbitrator, 24 Parganas, Calcutta. This represented the difference between the sum of Rs 7,37,190 payable to the assesseee and a sum of RS.12,276 out of that amount which had already been assessed to tax. The Income tax Officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assessee on the date of the award. The Income Tax Officer treated the amount as liable to tax. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal rejected the first contention and held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the assessee, but was, therefore a trading receipt. The High Court rejected the first argument and held that it was on the final determination of the amount of compensation that the right to receive payment was in dispute and it was not a receipt of a revenue nature. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The legal position was explained in further detail by the Gujarat High Court in Topandas Kundanmal vs Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat, The High Court was called upon to decide without the right to receiving the enhanced compensation under the Land Acquisition Act accrued or arose to the assessee when he sought 396 a reference under section 18 of the Act or when the award was made by the Civil Judge though an appeal was pending against that award. [396B] The legal position is explained in further details by the Gujarat and the Gujarat High Courts in TopASHandas Kundanmal etc. vs Commissioner of income tax, Gujarat [1962] 1 SCR 676 and State of Gujarat vs Topandas Karmal & Ors., [1962] Supp. 1 SCR 676, referred to. The legal position, was explained in detail by the Madhya Pradesh High Court in State of Gujarat & Anr., [1962) Supp. 1 S.C.R. 676, followed. The legal status of an award made by the Collector was an inchoate right until the compensation had been actually determined and had become payable. It must not be forgotten that, even if a court was awarded enhanced compensation, there is a right of appeal by the Government to the High Court, and the High Court may either disallow that claim or reduce the compensation. [396C D] The legal status was explained in the further detail by this Court in T.K. Krishnan & Ors. vs State of Tamil Nadu & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellants landlord filed a suit against the appellants in the Court of Second Civil Judge, Class II, Gwalior for a decree for eviction from the suit premises and for certain other reliefs. The appellants landlord filed an application to that effect in the Trial Court which passed a decree for possession unconditionally. The appellants contended that the compromise was legal and was in accordance with the terms of the compromise. The Trial Court decreed the suit. The appellants filed an appeal to the High Court which dismissed the appeal. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the decree. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the compromise decree was legal and valid and that the suit was not maintainable. HELD: (1) The compromise was legal, that is to say, lawful and was in conformity with the plaint. [881 A] (2) The decree was clearly valid and executable and the suit was decreed. [882 B] (3) The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree for ejectment because the landlord, in the circumstances is entitled to have such a decree under the law. [886 C] (4) The Court passes a decree for the eviction only if it is satisfied on evidence that a ground for passing such a decree in accordance with law has been established. The Court passes the decree on the basis of the compromise, and if necessary, by considering them in the context of the pleadings and other materials in that case that the agreement is lawful, as in any other suit, so in an eviction suit the Court is bound to record the compromise and pass a decree in conformity therewith. [887 D] (5) The Court can pass a decree on the ground of the compromise if it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise. The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 23, Rule 3 when it says "Where it is proved that a ground has been established". The protection is inherent in a language of Order 21, Rule 3. [890 A] (6) The protection of a tenant is inherent to the language of order 23, Rule 2 when it says that "Where it was proved to the satisfy of the Court, that a suit had been adjusted by a lawful agreement or settlement. the Court is entitled to pass a decree for evict only if it was satisfied on evidence, that a ground of passing such a order in accordance with " the requirement of the Statute has been established". [890 B] (7) The Court cannot pass a decree merely because it is satisfied that a ground is for passing such decree in accordance therewith.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of tea. The assessee company was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1962 60. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee company on the ground that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the loss was a capital asset and that the loss of Rs. 12,00,000/ was due to the loss of depreciation in the value of the shares of the company in Elphinstone Mill Ltd. of Bombay. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee company had suffered a capital loss of Rs, 12,00.000/ and that the amount of any other tax levied under any law for the time being in force on the company by the Government or by a local authority in excess of the amount, if any, referred to in clause (a) or clause (c) and the dividends actually distributed, if any. The High Court in appeal held that the amount was a capital gain and that the assessee had suffered a loss of Rs 12,00 and that the High Court was in error in holding that in view of the capital loss of the shares held by the company on account of depreciation in its value of 83 shares held by it in Elphinsstone Mill Ltd., the loss of the value of Rs.12,00, 000/ suffered by the assessee on account of the depreciation in the valuation of the shares was a capital expenditure. The High court in appeal held on the question of the law laid down by this Court in Commissioner of Income tax vs Elphin stone Mills Ltd. ; , that the word "having regard only" to losses previously incurred by the assessee company was never lost sight of. The question was whether the value of shares may not go up in future but whether the Directors were justified in not declaring dividends in view of section 23A(1) of the Act. HELD : (i) The word "having respect only" is not lost sight of require all matters relevant to the question of unreasonableness to be considered capital loss, if established is one of them. [864 D] (ii) The statute by the words used while making sure that "losses and smallness of profit" are never lost sight. Their Lordships are of the opinion that the statute by the word used while making57 sure that " losses and smallity of profit" were never lost sight Of require all matters necessary to the question. [865 E] (iii) The statute does not say "having regard both to losses previously incurring by the company and to the smallness of the profits made. Their Lordships were of the opinion, that the statute was not applicable to the facts of the case. [866 F] (iv) The statute in question does not say 'having regard only to losses previously incur by the company. It does not say"having regard only ' to losses previously incurs by the company, and to the largeness of the profit made. Their Lordship were of the view that the statute did not say " having regard only to loss previously incurred by it and to the Smallness of the losses made. Their lordships were of the Opinion that the statute had not stated "having regard to losses previously suffered by the company" and to the smallerness of the income made. Their Judges were of the unanimous opinion that the Statute by the words "having regard also to losses previously sustained by the company would have done just what the Directors of the company did. The question is not whether the value or the shares may not gone up in future. [867 G H] (v) The statute is not a matter primarily for the Directors of a company.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of the superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the Corporation without making any rules or regulation in that behalf. The Corporation passed a resolution for the first time making 75 per cent of the posts of superintending Engineer available to the executive Engineers holding degrees and 25 per cent to the Executive Engineers who were diploma holders. This resolution was also admittedly not a regulation made under the said section 64. However, since respondent No.2 was a degree holder, he got the said resolution and was promoted to the said post on that date. The petitioner challenged the validity of the resolution on the ground that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the post of superintending engineer, since they belong to the same cadre of Executive Engineers and do the same work. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The rule providing that graduates shall be eligible for such promotion to the exclusion of diploma holders does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [775B] 1.2 The rule providing for the service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. The principle that in the absence of rule or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by Executive instructions and this was what was done until the year 1988, and is also seeking to be done Since 1988 by the resolution, the authority can prescription service conditions by administrative instructions and this cannot be done except by carving out two classes in the same category of junior Engineers. Hence, the observation are per incuriam as regards the next contention, admittedly neither the practice followed till 1988, nor the resolution passed by the respondent Corporation in 1988 nor the resolution made in accordance with section 64 of the Act. [776C D] 1.3 The contention that in the instant case, the petitioner was diploma holders in Engineering and hold the post of Assistant Engineer was rightly rejected. [778E] 1.4 The contention that the petitioner was a degree holders, was rightly rejected by the High Court. [782F] 1.5 The contention that if direct recruits and promotees are integrated into one cadre, they could, for purposes of promotion to that cadre of Executive Engineer, be classified on the basis that they were drawn from different sources. [785F] 1:6 The rule providing reservation for promotion to the cadre of Executive Engi cutioners is well known and permissible. The rule providing such reservation is what was taken till the year 1989 and is also seek to be done till the years 1988 and is again sought to be taken since 1988 by resolution. The proposition that in the event of direct recruits and promotee integrated into one class, they cannot be classified for purposed of promotion on a basis other than that in the case before the them the classified for purpose of promotion on the basis merely of their qualification which is not permissible in law though the creation of selection grade in the same class on the basis basis of merit and on seniority is well known. [786F] 1 :7 The rule providing reservations for promotion to posts of Assistant Engineer does not violate Article 14 and 16. [787G] 1.8 The rule providing 15 per cent reservation for promotion is well known, and permissible. [790A] 1.9 The rule providing 30 per cent reservation is also permissible.

The petitioners who were working as Judges of the Supreme Court were appointed as Judges of a High Court. The petitioners were appointed as judges of the Supreme court. The petitioners challenged the appointment of the petitioners on the ground that the appointment of Judges of the High Court was illegal. The petitioners contended that the appointment was illegal as it was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners also contended that the appointments were illegal as the appointments were made without the approval of the Chief Justice of the High Courts. The petitioners further contended that the Chief Justice had no jurisdiction to make appointments to the Supreme Court and the failure, if any, was a matter of public interest and the writ petitions requiring a direction to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies were maintainable. The petitioners, however, contended that the selection of a person as a Judge has nothing personal either to the Chief Justice or the Chief Minister of the State concerned. The petitioners submitted that the Chief Justices of the High courts and the Supreme Court as the highest judicial authority in the country, had no jurisdiction in the matter of appointments to the High Court and the default, if any was a matter in public interest and that the writ petitions require a direction to fill up all the vacancies. The petitioners relied on the decision of this Court in S.P. Gupta vs Union of India, ; and contended that the decision in S. P. Gupta 's case relating to the status and importance of the Chief Justices was not justiciable. The petitioners therefore contended that the determination of the strength of the Chief Judges of the Judges of the Court was not justiciable and that the failure, of the ChiefJustice of the High court to consider the matter was a matter which was of public interest. The petitioners urged that the appointment made by the Chief Justice was illegal as the appointment was made without the sanction of the Chief Judge and that the delay, if any in the appointment was a matter for public interest and, the writ petitions were maintainable. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Constitution of India provides that "there shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law pre scribes a larger number, of not more than seven other Judges". The matter is not, therefore, to be considered that the final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government. The correctness of the opinion of the majority in S.S. Gupta ' 's case relates to the status of the Chief Chief Justice of a High court and the view that the fixation of Judge strength is not justiciable should be re considered by a larger bench. [460G H; 460A] 1.2 The correctness of this opinion of the minority in S.K. Gupta ' s case relating to this status and importance is not justiciable. [460C] 1.3 The correctness of that opinion of the dissenting Judges in S.R. Gupta 'S case relating to a status and importance, the primacy of the position of the Chief Minister and the view view that the fixing of Judge strength was not justiciable should not be re considered. [460F] 1.4 The correctness of opinion of the learned majority in S P. Gupta vs State of U.P., ; ; and primacy of the status of Chief Justice of Indian and the view of the minority that the fixation is not justiciable must be re considered in the view of this Court. [460D] 1.5 The correctness of a opinion of the Supreme Judge in S.C. Gupta ''s case relating to appointment to the Supreme court and the views that the fixation Of Judge strength is neither justiciable nor should be re re considered by larger bench. The correctness, correctness of the view of majority in S S.P Gupta 's Case relating to the Status and importance of fixation of Judge s.

The respondent was appointed as an Enquiry Officer under the Chief Executive Officer 's Order dated January 9, 1979, which reads as under: "Pursuant to the powers vested in the Executive Director by the Chairman and Managing Director of the Bank, as per his office order dated 20th December, 1978, authorising him to appoint Enquiry Officers and Appellate Authorities under the provisions of Chapter 19 of the Bi parTrade Settlement dated 19th October, 1966, the undersigned is pleased to appoint Shri U.B. Menon, Special Officer, under the provisions o. Chapter 19 of Bi parTrade settlement dated 19th Oct. 1966, the Secretary, State Bank of Mysore, as per the powers vested under the Executive Director, by the Chairman & Managing Director of State Bank of India, as per their office order dated 21st Oct. 1966. The respondent did not raise any objection against the continuance of the enquiry by the said Enquiry Officer and therefore the High Court ought to have remitted the matter to the competent Disciplinary Authority to take a fresh decision based on the report of the Enquiry Officer. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of punishment and the High Court quashed the order of dismissal and directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. The respondent preferred an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was in error in directing payment of all consequential benefits flowing from the declaration that the impugned order was bad in law. [635C] 1.2 The respondent succeeded in getting the order of penalty quashed on a mere technicality and that too on the conten tion belatedly raised before the High Court for the first time and, therefore, the High Court was right in quashing the impugned order of punishment. [636D] 1.3 The respondent succeeded by getting the order quashed on a technicality and, therefore the High court was in error. [637C] 1:4. The respondent succeeded on getting the order o f punishment quashed on a simple technicality and the same too on the basis of the report of Enquiry Officer. [638D] 1:5. The respondent had admittedly retired from service in 1986 and if the order imposing punishment is quashed he would ordinarily have to be paid his wages etc., upto the date of his retirement. [639E] 1:6. The respondent was not entitled to any consequential benefits flowing out of the declaration that he was duped or not would be a different matter. [640E] 1.7. The respondent, therefore, succeeded in getting his order of punishment quashed on the mere technicality, and that too at the stage pre ceding the issuance of a second ,how cause notice could be saved because both sides to the proceedings had not raised any objection to the continuance of enquiry by the respondent. [642D] 1 :7. The High Court, therefore, was in error by directing payment of 'all consequential benefits flowing therefrom the declaration that 'the impugned order was unsustainable in law. The ends of justice would be met if instead of directing 'all consequen tial benefits ' the appellant is ordered to pay '50% of the consequential benefits ' flowing from the declarations that the impugned orders were bad in law.[642D E] 1:8. The ends Of justice would be meet if instead of ordering 'all consequens tion ' flowing from ' the declaration that "the impugned order is bad in law" the appellant is directed to pay 'all consequential bene fits ' flowing from his declaration that the order was bad. For the above reasons, the appeal will stand allowed to the above extent but, in the facts and circumstances of this case, the parties should be directed to bear their own costs.

The appellant, a Municipal Corporation of Delhi, was granted a building permit on the basis of a Master Plan prepared under the Delhi Development Act, 1957. The building operations were allowed to be carried on, there will be a violation of the Master Plan, and in consequence of the provisions of section 14 of the Development Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Commissioner refusing sanction. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Commissioner had no power to sanction the plans submitted by the respondents, and that the Commissioner was not competent to grant sanction. HELD: (1) The Commissioner has to give sanction for the erection of a building or the execution of a work unless such a building or work would contravene any of the provisions, of sub section (2) of section 336 or the provisions of sub section(2) of Section 340 or the provisions thereof. [739 E] (2) The Commissioner is not competent to sanction the plan submitted by the appellant. The Master Plan is prepared for the area, before it comes into operation in the Zone, the procedure indicated in section 10 will have to be followed and parties will have to have to be given an opportunity of placing any objections or making any representations or offering any suggestions. [740 E] (3) The Master Plan has been prepared under section 7 of the Delhi Development Corporation Act, 1957, and it has come into operation, under section 11, in the area concerned. Therefore, in order to sustain the validity of the order of rejection passed by the Commissioner the appellant has to establish, as it seeks to, that the proposed building or the use of the site for the building, by the respondents would contravene the provisions of 'any other law '. [741 E] (4) The Master plan has been prepared for the Area, before it came into operation in Delhi, the procedure specified in section 10 would have to be adopted and parties will be given an opportunities of placing any objection or making any representation or offering any suggestion. So far as the respondents ' lands are not in any manner indicated as being taken up by any part of the proposed road, mentioned in the Master Plan and, if that is so, there is no violation of section 14. [742 E] (5) The Master Plans have been prepared under the Development Act, and it is, therefore, not possible to accept the contention of the appellant. [743 B] (6) The Master plans have been prepared for a particular use of any land or building in the area or Zone, section 14 will quite naturally stand attracted, because any user of a land or building otherwise than in conformity with the Zonal Development Plan will be hit by that section.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No. 2. The appellant No. I was the Minister. The appellant was asked to see the appellant No, 1. The appellant 's statement was made by the appellant No., 1 and the appellant 's brother. The appellant asked the appellant No to see the respondent No. 1. The respondent No. I replied the appellant No 's statement. The appellant objected to the statement made by the respondent No, 1 and asked the appellant to see the accused. The appellant replied that the appellant No was not in a position to give the statement. The respondent replied that the statement was not recorded under the provisions of section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The appellant denied the suggestion that the statement made was not recorded by him in accordance with the provisions of the section 164 of Criminal Procedure Code and he was therefore tried for the offence of the taking of the bribe or illegal gratification by the appellant. The trial court acquitted the appellant. In appeal to the High Court, the appellant contended that the statement of the appellant No,. 1 to the police authorities was inadmissible in evidence and could not be proved orally by him. Held, that the statement given by the appellant to the police officers and the handing over of the currency notes to Nagindas when the raid was organised and which numbers were also specified in the memo prepared at that time was enough to establish the falsity of the allegation made by the appellants No. 1 and were certainly brought there by Nagindas and handed over by him to the appellant No 1 or at, the instance of the appellant as alleged by the prosecution the appellant No.' 1 or at the instance of appellant No.1 as alleged by ' the prosecution the appellants were certainly brought There was no reason why the statement should not be discarded. The statements made by the accused in regard to the statement were admissible in evidence and they could not be established orally by them. The statements were admissible in the evidence and they were admissible in proof of the truth of the allegations made by the prosecution. The statements of the witnesses in regard to their statement made by them were admissible in law. The statements could not be used to corroborate the evidence of the witnesses. The statements in regard to these statements could not, therefore, be used to contradict the evidence of these two witnesses. The statement made by a person who is a member of the judiciary be used to support the evidence of a witness who is a party to the proceedings. The statements given by a person in the course of the proceedings of the court of the Magistrate are admissible in evidence. The statements are admissible in law and they are admissible in the trial of the case. The statements can be used to corroboration the evidence of witnesses. The evidence of the two witnesses in regard thereto could not be relied upon in the trial. The statements cannot be used to lend assurance to the evidence of an accused person. The statements may be used to aid the prosecution in support of the prosecution case but the statements cannot be relied upon for corroboration. The statements must be admissible in evidence in the absence of corroboration. The statement of the accused must be admissible under section 32 of the Evidence Act. The statements should be admissible in the absence Of corroboration. The evidence must be such as to inspire the confidence of the Court. The statements which are admissible in Evidence cannot be used for corroboration. In the present case, the statements of the two accused were admissible in Evidence and they could be proved in evidence. They were admissible in terms of section 32 of Evidence Act.
