The appellant was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. The Income tax officer held that the transactions were not speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal held that the transaction was not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court. The Tribunal held that the sales in question were speculative and consequently the losses suffered by the appellant in these transactions could not be set off against the profits made by the appellant 's non speculative business. The Tribunal also held that the loss should have been treated as business losses relying on two judgments of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh (1) and D. V. R. Mukherjee vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, (2) and D 's case, (3) and held that the losses suffered were business loss relying upon two decisions of the High Court: Bata Bhimayya and Duni Chand Rataria vs Bhuwalke Brothers Ltd. (4) and Dunichand Rataria vs Commissioner of income tax, Calcutta (5) and held in favour of the revenue. The High Court on reference held that the sale in question was not speculative but was speculative and consequently, the losses suffered in these transactions should not be set aside against the profits earned by the appellant. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (1) The question referred to the High Court in the present case has been correctly answered by this Court in Raghunath Prasad Poddar vs Commissioner of Incometax, Calcutta, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 869. (2) The question whether the transactions described above entered into by the appellant were mere sales of delivery orders or sales of goods so as to bring them to charge under section 24( 1) of the Act does not arise for decision in the present appeal. [184 D] (3) The question that arose for decision was whether the transactions entered into by D. V., R. K. Mukherjee, R. K., Mukherjee, R K. Mukherjee and R. K, Mukherjee, R, K. Mukherjee were mere sales or of goods so that they could be set off only against a profit in a transaction of the same nature. The answer to the question referred to was in the negative. [184 E] (4) The question was whether the transaction described above entered by the appellant was mere sales of deliver orders or sales or of any goods so as not to bring them into charge under section24(1) Of the Act. [184 F] (5) The question as to whether the transactions were mere sales was not to invalidate the transaction which were not completed by actual delivery of the goods to the transferee. What has to be seen in such cases is whether the ultimate purchaser of the P.D.Os. is not followed up by actual delivery or of the goods sold. It is not necessary that the transfer in question should be followed up by physical delivery of the commodity or the scrips. [184 G] (6) The object of the explanation is not to invalidate any transaction of sale wherein the goods are not physically delivered by the seller to the buyer but only to brand them as speculative transactions so as to put them in a special category for income tax purposes. [184 B] (7) The object and the explanation is to ensure that the ultimate purchaser is not allowed to be set off in a transaction which is otherwise speculative in nature. The object of explanation is not merely to invalidate the transactions which are not completed by physical delivery or of goods.

The appellant was a candidate for the election to the Pun jab Legislative Assembly. The respondent was a candidate of the Pun jib Legislative Assembly. He was declared elected. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the nomination paper was invalid on the ground of non compliance with the provisions of section 33(1) of the Act. The Election Tribunal held that the nomination was invalid on account of non compliance of the provisions of sections 33(1), 33(1)(a) and 33(1). The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to the declaration of the result of the election. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the nomination papers were not signed by the proposers and seconders in the usual way by writing their names, and that the nomination were invalid on the grounds of non compliance. HELD: (i) The word "subscribe" in the context of a will or a mortgage and is on the same footing as the word "subscribing" in the special way prescribed by the Act but in the ordinary way. [488 E] (ii) The word 'subscribe" is not defined but it is equally clear when the Act is read as " a whole along with the form in the second schedule, that "subscribe", can only be used in the sense of making a signature and as the Act tells us quite clearly how the different types of " signature" are to be made, we are bound to give effect to the general policy of the Act by drawing the same distinction between signing and the making of a mark as the Act itself does in the definition of "sign". [488 F H] (iii) The word sign 'subscribe ' is not defined and it is equally possible to import the special definition of " sign " in the General Clauses Act because that also defines only "sign" and not "subscribe". [488 E F] (iv) The word is not defined. It is equally clear, when the Act was read as " whole along with" the form in which the word "sign" can only be use in the sense that it includes the making of the mark as the act itself does in its ordinary sense, it includes the giving of assent to or to attest " or written upon "(3) "subscribe "" in the general sense means to give assent to or attest " or "written upon "(3). The word " Subscribe" is used in its ordinary meaning. It is also clear that when the Act has been read as "a whole along with " the form in" the second schedule it is clear that they have not been " subscribed" because " subscribing" can only mean both signing, so called, and the placing of a mark is to be rejected and their absence could not be dismissed as technical and unsubs tantial. [488 F G] (v) The word `subscribe" does not define the word " Subscribing any more than the Representation of the People Act because it is equally obvious that it includes both signing, and the making and of a mark. [488 G H] (vi) The word, "subscribe ' in the special sense means to include the making of an mark as the statute itself does in ordinary sense include the making or signing of a mark, as the Act does in the definitions of "signatures".

The appellants were workmen of the respondent company. The Company had been dismissed by the Company on the presumption that they were no longer interested to continue in service of the Company and had totally abandoned the Company 's service. The Company filed a complaint against the appellants and 10 others alleging that they had voluntarily abandoned the service of the company and had totally lost the Company ' 's service and had totally discontinued the Company '. The Company also alleged that the appellants had abandoned the service and had thereby abandoned the Company service. The appellants contended that the action of the Company in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls was illegal and arbitrary and that the appellants were not entitled to any relief. The Company, however, raised a preliminary objection that the action was by way of victimization for their participation in the strike. The Company contended that the appellants having voluntarily abandoned the services of the Company, their names had been struck off from the rolls of the Company from that date. The Company 's stand was that the letters of the Company dated September 7, 1972 and September 26, 1972 were received by them on September 20, 1972 and not earlier was never denied or refuted by the Company in the correspondence that passed between the parties. The Company further contended that the Company ' had not abandoned the service. The Tribunal held that the action in removing the name of the appellants was illegal and invalid. The Company appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellants had along with 229 other workmen gone on indefinite and peaceful strike which ended on October 22, 1972 in response to the strike notice given by the union to the Company to press its demand for re instatement of its three dismissed leaders and had not only by their letters dated September 21, 1972 and October 26, 1972 unequivocally intimated to the Company that they did not intend to abandon the service but had also returned the cheques sent to them by the Company. The appellants had also along with 229 others gone on indefinite strike which ended in October 22,1972 in response to their strike notice given to the Company by the union. Thus, their being no provision in the certified standing orders by virtue of which the Company would have terminated the services of their appellants in the aforesaid circumstance, the impugned action on the part of the Company clearly amounted to a change in the condition of service of the appellants during the admitted pendency of the industrial dispute before the Labour Court which adversely affected them and could not be countenanced. [655G H] 1.2 The appellants had throughout gone on indefinite, peaceful strike which resulted in the termination of their services. They had also along along with 229other workmen gone on strike which ended at on October 22. 1972 in response thereto the strike notice issued by the Company to the Company. Thus, there was nothing in the surrounding circumstances or the conduct of the appellants indicating or suggesting an intention on their part to abandon service which in view of the ratio of Gopal Chandra Misra 's case, can be legitimately said to mean to detach, unfasten, undo or untie the binding knot or link which hold one to the office and the obligations and privileges that go with it Their absence from duty was purely temporary and could by no stretch of imagination be construed as voluntary abandonment by them of the Company ''s service. [656C D] 1.3 The appellants had in their letter dated September 7. 1972, addressed to the Company returning the cheques sent by the Company and stating that they did neither intend to abandon service nor had returned the cheques. The appellants were not aware of the fact that they had not abandoned service. They had only by their letter dated October 26,1972 and September 26.

The respondents were trustees of a public trust, styled "Shri Tricumraiji". In March 1950 the trustees mortgaged a house belonging to the trust to one Saheba to secure repayment of Rs. 5,000. The trustees did not pay the instalments due under the decree. The trustees filed an application for execution of the mortgage. The trial court held that sale of the mortgaged property which belonged to a public trust was invalid and on that account a sale in execution of a decree held without the previous sanction of the Charity Commissioner must be deemed invalid. The High Court in revision held that sale in execution was invalid and that the sale was invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the expression 'sale ' in section 36(a) includes a sale of the property of a public Trust in execution of the decree and on that view remanded the case to the District Court for decision on all the points correctly arising out of the matter. HELD: (i) The expression 'sale in section 36 (a) includes an execution of a decrees for sale of mortgaged property, enables any person either owning such property or holding an interest therein by virtue of a title to apply to have the sale set aside on his depositing in Court, the amount specified in the proclamation of sale as that for the recovery of which the sale was ordered, less any amount which may, since the date of such proclamation of sale, have been received by the decree holder. [782 E] (ii) The expression "sale in section 37(a) means a sale of immovable property in execution of decrees for recovery of a debt due by the trust, and on that basis a sale in Execution of a decree is not invalid. [785 B] (iii) The expression sale in section 36 is not confined to a sale of property in execution. The expression 'Sale ' in section 37 is not confined only to a sale in enforcement of a decree for sale of immovable properties. The expression "Sale ' in the section is not confined merely to a sale which is in execution of an decree for sale. The expression sale is confined to a purchase in execution of decree for sale in execution. It is confined to the sale in execution in execution of which the decree is passed. The expression is confined to an sale in execution for which the sale is ordered. The expression includes execution of a contract for sale of movable property. The expression in section 36 does not mean that the source of the authority is in the order of reference. [786 E F] (iv) The expression is not confined in its scope to a sale for which the property is sold. The expression means a sale in the execution of a suit for sale of immoveable property. The word 'sale ' is confined to sale in execution and is confined to any sale in execution thereof. The expression does not mean a sale in respect of which the property has been sold. The word "sale ' in the context in which it occurs, is not confined confined to a transaction in execution of any decree for sale for which a sale is ordered; it includes a sale in which the property in question is sold.

The respondent was a Government serv ant in the Indian Railways. He was compulsorily retired by the Government on June 4, 1935. The respondent challenged the order of retirement before the Central Administrative Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the respondent was not entitled to premature retirement. The Tribunal also held that the order of compulsory retirement was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The High Court held that the Government of India had issued instructions dated July 11, 1955 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retirement under Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. The High court also held that Rule 2(1) of the Liberalised Pension Rules was ultra vires Article 14 and 16. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The Railway Pension Manual is different from that of clause (h) and (k) of Rule 2946 of the Rules. Rule 2(3) of Pension Rules is also similar to Rule 2(4) of Pension Rule. The memorandum is in the nature of executive instructions issued in the name of President of India as required under Article 77(1) and as such cannot be statutory. The memorandum has not been issued under Article 309 of the Constitution. The memorandum of the memorandum is in nature of executive instruction but is in the form of executive instructions. The memorandum does not contain any guide line provided in the Rule to this effect. The memorandum, therefore, cannot be statutory and is not statutory. [799B C] The memorandum is not in the nature as required under Rule 2 (2) of Pension Scheme. The memorandum was in the nature o executive instructions but is a compendious rule, the railway employees are only gover 802 ned by the said rule and para 620 was void and inoperative. The memorandum also does not contain anything inconsistent with it. The memorandum in the nature is in the character of executive instructions but it is equally worded as Rule 2(5) of Pension scheme. The memorandum cannot be statutory because the memorandum is not issued under Article 161 of the Constitution and as such can be statutory. [700C D] The memorandum, in the nature, of executive instructions, but is similarly worded as Rule 2046 of the Pension Scheme, is statutory and has the effect of amending Rule 2( 2) of Pension Regulations. [700D] The memorandum does contain no guide line provided for in the Rule. The Memorandum is in the type of executive instructions and is in the shape of executive instructions which is inconsistent with it, and para 620 of the Manual being executive instructions. [700E F] The memorandum has no parity with Rule 2(7) of Pension Schedule. The memorandum contains no guide line and gives absolute discretion to the Government to retire a Government servant at any time after he has attained the age of 55 years. The memorandum and the memorandum are in the nature Of executive instructions. Rule 2 (3) of pension Scheme is a statutory rule. The memorandum must be in the nature and effect of amending the statutory Rule. The rules are in the form and substance of executive instructions as provided under Article 77 (1) of Pension Regulation. [700G H] The memorandum and memorandum are in conformity with the statutory Rule 2046. The memorandum are in terms of executive instructions of the Government of india. The memorandum clearly shows that the power under Rule 2 of Pension Rules can only be exercised to weed out unsuitable employees. The memorandum itself does not contain the guide line provided under Rule 2. The memorandum merely states that the power to retire under Rule 2 was in addition to the power already contained in the Pension Rules. The memorandum further does not contain a guide line provided by the said Rule to this. The memorandum dated November 30, 1962 and February 8.

The assessee firm was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period was 1 4 1943 to 31st March, 1941. The chargeable account ing period was 1st April, 1943 to 31.3. 1941. The assessee was an unregistered Firm carrying on business in manufacture and sale Of katechku. The chargeable accounts period was 1 1st April 1943 to 31 st March, 1943. The chargeable year was 1 4 1944 to 31st march, 1943. There were two partners of the assessee firm, namely, L. The Excess Profits Tax Officer did not set off the said deficiency of profits that accrued in respect of the chargeable accounting period from 1st April 1941 to 31st December, 1941. He, therefore, confirmed that there were no profits and losses during the chargeable accounting periods ending 31st March 1943 and 23rd November, 1942 to 31st January, 1943. In appeal, the assessee had urged that the deficiency in profits pertaining to the chargeable accounting years from October 1940 to 31st July, 1942 should be allowed a set off in computing the excess profits for the chargeable accounting year under consideration. The High Court, however, did not accept the opinion of the Tribunal that because the chargeable accounting Period ending 31st December 1941 and 31st March 1942 were occupied with manufacturing activity alone and there were no sales, therefore, no part of the profits realised upon the sales could be apportioned to those chargeable accounting periods and consequently that it could not be said that there was any deficiency of profits during those periods. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The chargeable accounting periods were the period from 1 st September 1939 to 31st Mar, 1944. [639 F] (2) The chargeable accounts periods ending 31 st March 1944 and 31st march 1942 were occupied by manufacturing activity alone. The question was whether the activity which the assessee carried on at Raichur was part of their business within the meaning of the third proviso to section 5 of the Act. [640 G] (3) The chargeable years were 1st April 1944 to 31 March, 1946. The assessee had urged before the High Court that the deficiency of profits for the relevant chargeable accounting periods ended 31st March 1944 and the deficiency of profit worked out on that basis in respect of that chargeable accounting period ending 31st march 1944 and the deficient of profits worked out on the basis in respect thereof in respect of chargeable accounting period ended 31st march 1945 and the deficiency in profit worked out at that basis in regard to the chargeable business period ending 31 st march, 1944 and the deficiencies of profits workedout on that basis were set off in calculating the excess profits. [642 C] (4) The assessee had contended that the deficiency was of profits pertaining to sales effected during the chargeable year ending 31st August, 1941 to 31 st march 1945 and that therefore it could not he said that there had been any deficiency of profit during those periods and consequently the deficiency of income worked out on this basis in respect Of the chargeable accountingperiod ending 31st Mar. 1944 and the shortfall of profits worked up on that basis. [643 D] (5) The assessee was entitled to a set off of the deficiency only for the chargeable business periods ending 31th March, 1944 and 31 st March 1945. [644 E] (6) The assessee could not be held to have suffered any deficiency of income during those periods, because the chargeable accounts periods ended 31 st March 1941 and 31 st march 1942.

The petitioner, who had qualified in Civil Engineering, was one of the Special Leave Petitions before the Kerala High Court. He challenged the judgment of the Kerala High court in a number of writ petitions. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and directed the Government of Kerala and the Public Service Commission to prepare "two separate lists, namely, one for the Civil Bench and the other for the Mechanical Branch. The Kerala Government and the KPSC accepted the directions given by the Single Judge and proceeded to take steps for the implementation thereof. However, some of the aggrieved respondents in the Writ Petitions filed appeals before the Division Bench of the Kerala and the K PSC faced difficulties in giving effect to the directions given in his judgment in effect upheld by the Division Bench. The Kerala Public Service Commission filed appeals before this Court for clarifications. The Kerala State Government and the Kerala Public Service Commissions filed appeals before a Division Bench of that Court. The appeals were ultimately dismissed in view of the fact that the KP SC faced difficulties in providing better quality education to the students. The Kerala High Court held that the petitioner will be entitled to exercise his option and then take his turn according to his rank in the common list prepared by the Public Service Commissions. The Kerala Legislature and the K.PSC were directed to prepare two separate lists, one for Civil and Mechanical Engineering graduates and the other, for the Mechanical branch. The Kerala Legislative Assembly and the K Public Service Commission were directed to make separate lists, viz., one for Civil Judges and the other in the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted. The Kerala Service Commission and the KPCSC were directed by the Single judge to prepare two combined rank lists, one in the Civil and Mechanical Branch on their basis of examination, already conducted. On receiving information from the Government on the above lines, the Public Service commission is directed to prepare the two separate rank lists, namely one for Civil Judge and other for the Civil Judges. The Kerala Administrative Tribunal and the KPPSC accepted the direction given by the High Court and proceeded to prepare separate lists. However, certain aggrieved respondents in these Writ Petitions filed petitions before the Division bench of the KeralaHigh Court. The Kerala and the Kerala State Public Service Commission contended that the petitioner had come high in the Common list prepared by Public Service Commission. It was contended that the petitioners who had qualified for Civil Engineering question paper and answered the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had qualified In Mechanical Engineering and answered questions indicated in Category II in the question paper could not rationally be included in a common rank list after the interview. The Kerala Civil Service Commission and KPSC were not directed to prepare a common list. The Kerala Subordinate Service (General Branch) Rules, 1979 were challenged. The High court allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Public Service Tribunal to prepare "one separate list, one for Electrical and Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the Kerala Engineering Subordinate Service ( General Branch). The Kerala Public Services Commission and the Kerala Subordinate Service Commission were also directed to prepare "three separate rank lists" on the basis that already no common list was directed to be prepared or was prepared by the KPPCSC. The Kerala Legal Services Authorities were directed to take steps to implement the directions given to the Kerala Public Services Authorities. The Kerala Revenue Tribunal and the Kerala High Courts were directed to implement the same. However, the Kerala Public Public Service Commission and Kerala Public Service Authorities were directed by this Court to prepare "four separate rank lists", one for Civil Engineering graduates and other for Mechanical Engineering graduates. The Kerala Private Service Commission and other Authorities were directed not to prepare a separate list. The KPSC faced difficulties for giving effect to these directions. The Kerala Land Revenue and Land Revenue Department filed appeals before various High Courts.

The respondent No. 1, a partner of a partnership business along with his brothers defendant Nos. 1 and 2, and the plaintiff, a partner in a partnership business, filed a suit for dissolution of the partnership firm. The plaintiff respondent No.1, claimed that he was a partner of the partnership business alongwith his brothers defendant No. 2 and that he had effectively taken charge of the business and excluded the plaintiff. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, in appeal, held that the valuation of the suit was beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the valuation put by the plaintiff was arbitrary and unreasonable and that the court was bound to accept that valuation made on behalf of defendant No. 1 was arbitrary and unacceptable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The interpretation put by the learned counsel on the decisions of this Court is not correct and cannot be accepted. It is true that in a suit for accounts the correct amount payable by one party to the other can be ascertained only when the accounts are examined and it is not possible to give an exact valuation of the claim at the inception of the suit. In such a case it is not only open to the Court but its duty to reject such a valuation. The cases of some of the High Courts which have taken a different view must be held to be wrongly decided. [630G H] 1.2 In a suit for accounting the correct amount of money payable by one of the parties to the suit can be ascertained even when the accounts and he may, therefore, put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, ILR (1947) Nagpur 933, the plaintiff non applicant before the High Court filed a suit to set aside the valuation put on by the plaintiff on the relief claimed in the suit. [631C D] 1.3 In a suit of accounts the correct value of the claim payable by one parties to the other could be ascertained only if the accounts are scrutinised and it is found that the final valuation of the case would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction.

[611D] 1.4 The notification does refer to the exemption and the procedure to be followed in the grant of incentive for setting up newIndustri ties. [612E] 1:5 The notification does mention the conditions on the which, and procedure in accordance wi th the Director of Industry is to issue the Eligibility Certificate. The Director of Industries has to certify that the applicant is entitled to the exemption on the terms and condition set out in the notification and not on the basis of any further requirements not so set out. No. With a view to enabling those new industrial units who opt for the alternative concession of deferment of payment of Tax, a special provision in the shape of section 22 D has been inserted in the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958 with effect from 1st April, 1981, according to which the facility of deferment of tax is only in the nature of an alterna tive to the provision for exemption and the former is not available to traditional industries because of rule 14 above, the same should be the position in regard to the exemption provision also. [613C D] 2.1 The Notification does not set down the conditions on what and the procedure procedure should be followed. The Director, of Industries has, therefore, to certify that he is entitled to exemption on the conditions set out in that notification and not On the basis of no further requirements not set out.

The petitioners in WP No. 5669 of 1980 were appointed to temporary posts in the Delhi Judicial Service in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service in accordance with the Rules of the Delhi Higher judicial Service. The petitioners in the writ petition were appointed to permanent posts in the service in accordance with rules of continuous officiation in the cadre post. The petitioners were appointed to the permanent posts in accordance with Rules of continuous officiation. The petitioners, who were appointed in substantive capacity to temporary posts, were appointed in a temporary capacity to substantive vacancies in the service. The petitioners who were appointed to substantive vacancies, were appointed to posts in the Service in accordance With the Rules of continuous officiating appointment. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the seniority of direct recruits vis a vis the promotees shall be determined in the order of rotation of vacancies between the direct recruits and promotees based on the quota of vacancies reserved for both the categories by Rule 7, provided that the first available vacancy will be filled by a direct recruit, the next two vacancies by promotees and so on. It was further contended that the seniority in the cadre of Additional District and Sessions Judges should be determined according to the dates on which direct recruits were appointed to their respective posts and the dates from which the promotees had been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the Service or in substantive vacancies to which were appointed in the substantive vacancies to Which were appointed in an officiating capacity. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The seniority of direct recruit vis a vis promotees shall be governed by the rules of continuous officiating officiation in the Cadre post i.e. a direct recruit who is appointed after a member of the Delhi Judicial service thus promoted, he will rank lower in seniority than the latter in the list of seniority. If temporary posts in a substantive capacity are created as has been done in this case by the Administrator as envisaged by Rule 16(1) and if such posts have been filled in as it appears to have been done here in consultation with the High Court from amongst members of the Delhi judicial Service as required under Rule 16(2) of the Rules, quota rule assuming that there is any, cannot apply to such appointments. [739C D] 1.2 The seniority of promotees vis a vis promotee shall be governed in accordance with Rule of continuous officiation, in the cadre posts i.e., a direct recruit appointed after a person has completed not less than ten years of service in the Delhi judicial service as required by Rule 7(a) and if he was appointed on the basis of selection from amongst the members of the said Delhi Judicial Service thus promoted, him would rank lower in the seniority than the former. [740E] 1.3 The seniority of promotee vis a vis a vis vis the promotees would be governed by Rule 16 of the Rules of uninterrupted officiation in the service post i. e. a direct promotee who is appointed before a member of Delhi Judicial Service is appointed in a substantive vacancy of Additional District & Sessions Judge, cannot and should not rank higher than the latter, in the list Of seniority. If a direct recruit is appointed after an member of the said service thus promoted he will rank senior in seniority than that of the latter. Janardhana vs Union of India and ors.

The assessee, a member of a Hindu Undivided Family, was assessed to income tax under the Income tax Act, 1922, on the finding that the business was carried on by an association of persons and the income from the business was liable to be brought to tax on that footing. The Income tax Officer assessed the assessee in the status of "an association of persons". The Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the direction for assessing the income in the hands of the assessee be deleted. In appeals by the Commissioner, the Tribunal confirmed the orders of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and directed that "the direction for assessing and directing the Income tax Officer to assess the members individually be deleted. " The Commissioner of Income tax, U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, ; , held that the income belonged to the Hindu Undivided Family of which he was a member. The High Court, however, set aside the direction to assess the income in ' the status of association of persons, and directed that" the direction for assessment be deleted. The Commissioner of Incometax, U. P. vs Kanpur Sugar Mills, ; , applied. The High court set aside the directions of the Appellate Tribunal and directed that a direction be made to assess the Income tax officer to assess the member individually. The Commissioner, however, directed that the order for assessing the members individually. be deleted. Held, that the Appellate Assistant Tribunal was not competent to make the direction. The Appellate Assistant Tribunal had directed that the income in question be assessed in the hands Of the family of Debi Parshad. The High, Court was, therefore, in error in holding that the income of the Ambala Flour Mills could not be assessed in view of the order of the Appellate. Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal was, therefore. competent to set aside the assessment and to direct the Income tax Officers to assess the Members individually.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share in the suit property on the ground that the value of his share was less than Rs. 15,00,000 and that the proper court fee to be paid on the memorandum of appeal had to be determined under section 7(iv)(b) of the Act. The appellant contended that the proper Court fee to be payable on the memorandum was determined by article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act and that the valuation was not made by article 17B of Schedule II. Held, that the memorandum of appeals should be taxed for the purposes of court fees under section 7 (iv)(b), and it cannot be reopened at this stage. The court fee has to be paid either under section 7 or under section 7 of the Act, and it provides for the determination of the value for jurisdiction on the basis of such claim. The court fees has to be determined by article 173 B of Schedule I of the Act in respect of suits falling under sub section (iv) of section 7 of that Act. The court Fees has to be fixed under article 173 B. The court has to determine the value of the claim for the purpose of jurisdiction on the facts and circumstances of each case. The court is not bound to accept the valuation made by the plaintiff for the purposes for which relief is sought for. The court, therefore, has to determine whether the case falls under section 7. The court must determine the value for the purpose for which relief has been sought for. If the court comes to the conclusion that the case falls within section 7(v)(b) or section 7(iii)(c) ordinarily liberty should be given to the plaintiff to amend his plaint and set out specifically the amount at which he seeks to value his claim for the payment of court fees.

The Respondent No. 1, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, sought to impugn the decision of the NDMC dated 18.2.1988 of the NDMC in Civil Writ Petition 3090 of 1987. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that Bye law 16.4.8 as to the disposition and location of the "Refuge Areas" is violative of the Bye law 16 of the Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) Act, 1957. The High court also held that the structural nature and basis of its calculation of the extent of these "Refuge areas" are dealt with by Bye law 16 and the Chief Fire Officer preferred to accept them. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the structural character and basis of the calculation of the area of these " Refuge Areas" are dealt by Bye law 2.27 to say that a wall abutting an inner vacant space is also an "external wall" and the acceptance of the cor rectness of this position was implicit in the clearance given by the Chief Fire officer. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The structural nature and the basis of its calculations of the extent thereof are dealt with in Bye law 16,4.8.1. which provides for refuge areas in the ratio of one sq. metre per person on each floor at the rate of 1 sq. m. per person. [601C] 1.2 The zonal developmental requirements in this behalf and the difficulties and prob lems inherent in the insistence upon construction of such pedestrian walk way in an isolated case, could be reconciled is to direct the NDMC, in the event of its ap proving the plans otherwise, to keep the requirement of the pedestrian walkway and Podium in abeyance for the present, subject to a written undertaking to be lodged with it by the respondent 1 and 2 to the effect that whenever the policy to implement the Zonal Developmental requirements in this respect is finally decided upon, the respondent 1 would undertake to put up such a pedestrian walkways and Podium. [602D] 1.3 The zonal developmental pro vided further, that they are located on external walls "by cantilever projection or in any other manner" abutting a vacant space from which rescue operations are rendered possible. [603E] 1.4 The only way in which, perhaps, the zonal developmental requirements are considered to provide for the safety in a measure better than those envisaged by the Bye laws and the Chief fire Officer preferred to accepting them. As to the requirement of bye law 16.1.8, the wall abutting such inner vacant space would not be an "ex Internal" wall for purposes of the said bye law. The only way that in appropriate cases, where the plans and designs incorporate fire safety measures which, in judgment of the NDMC, are considered to be provide for the protection in a measure less than those envisaged in Bye laws 16.4,8.1, the wall around such inner vacant spaces would not be a "external" wall for purpose of the said Bye law. [604E F] 1.5 The only way, in which, probably, the zonal developmental requirements in the context of specific objectives of bye laws 16. 4.8.2.8.3 and 16.48.1 are considered to providing for refuge areas, in accordance with its bye laws or in a better measure.

The appellant, who was the owner of a liquor shop, filed a suit for partition of the business of the appellant, and for a declaration that the compromise was made in a hurry, that the compromise in the previous suit was not due to a mistake or misunderstanding. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the cause of action for the present suit was different from the cause of the action in the previous case and that the suit was barred by res judicata. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The cause of action in the two suits being the same, the suit is barred under Order II, rule 2(3), of the Civil Procedure Code. [104 E] (ii) The cause for action in the first suit was the desire of the appellant to separate from his brothers and to divide the joint family property. That suit embraced the entire property without any reservation and was compromised, the plaintiff having abandoned his claim to account in respect of 108 the motor business subsequent to March 31, 1946. [104 G] (iii) The cause Of action in the subsequent suit was the intention of the appellant and was present to the minds of the parties; but if he wanted that accounts of the other businesses should be taken up to the date of the final decree, there was no point in mentioning the 31st March, 1946. The cause of the second suit was the apprehension of the appellant that the accounts of the various businesses should be up to March 31. 1946, and the plaintiff was bound by the terms of the compromise and the consent decree following upon it. [104 C] (iv) The cause in the subsequent suits was the desire and intention of the plaintiff to separate from the brothers and to split the joint family properties. That suit did not fall within the scope of Order II, Rule 2(3) of the Civil procedure Code. [105 E] (v) The cause and cause of action were identical. The cause Of the action in both the suits being the desire of a plaintiff to separate, from his brothers, after the 31st march, 1946, and, therefore, implicitly of not explicitly relinquished his claim to the account for the subsequent period.

The appellant was employed as a Manager in the Salt Works. He was prosecuted for the offence of manufacturing and selling salt. The trial court acquitted the appellant. The High Court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 92 of the , and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the process of converting sea water into salt does not amount to "manufacture" as defined in the Act. Held, that the process carried out in the Salt works and described above, come within the definition of " manufacturing process " in el. (k) of section 2 of the Act. The word " premises " is again a general word which is applicable to both open land and to buildings and its use in this section indicates that the Act can be applied to works carried on in a building. It is not clear from these observations alone why the slate quarries where work was carried on in the open air and not in building, was not held to be "a factory" on that account. The process carried out by the appellant in the Salt work and described above comes within the definition Of " manufacturing process" in el. 2 of the definition of the word "factory " and would be a factory if the work carried on there comes within the meaning of the expression " manufacturing process". The process carried on in Salt Works and described above come within the meaning Of the expression " premises " in the definition of manufacturing process " inasmuch as salt can be said to have been manufactured from sea water by the process of treatment and adaptation of sea water into Salt Works.

The respondent was sent on deputation to serve in the Polytechnic at Devangere as Instructor in the Department of Public Instructions. In 1949, three occupational Institutes (Polytechnics) at Hassan, Devangere and Chintamani were started in the State. The respondent was sent to serve in that Polytechnic at Palghat as Instructor in Tailoring and he joined the new post on November 28, 1949. The respondent continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were taken on deputation from other Departments, he should also be absorbed in the Department. The Public Service Commission referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission who examined it and by a communication, dated February 2, 1960, made these recommendations in favour of the respondent. The respondent 's claim was rejected by the State Government. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court which allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption of the respondent in the Department was to take effect from November 28,1949, when he initially resumed duty on deputation. The High Court allowed the writ Petition and issued a mandamus directing the absorption of respondent in the department of Technical Education with effect from November 1, 1949, when he was initially repatriated to service. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed in that service of the Department of Technical Education from a particular anterior date, or to be given the revised pay scales applicable to those borne permanently in the service of that Department. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The respondent ' s work in the Department, of Technical Education was found unsatisfactory or that he was not otherwise suitable or qualified to hold the post of Tailoring Instructor in that Department. That he was suitable to be absorbed as Tailoring Instructor from the date of his appointment as such as has been ordered in the case of Sri K. Narayanaswamy Chetty, whose case was identical in all respects, and six other officers who were similarly situated, were absorbed permanently in the Department in 1955 56. [261E F] 1.2 The respondent 'S work in the department was found unsatisfactory and was implicit in the impugned order, itself. [261F] 1.3 The respondent was suitable to hold the posts of Tailoring Instructors in that Department, and was implicit In the impugned order itself. [262F] 1:4 The respondent was, in all material respects, in the same situation as K. This was not the case of the appellant. [262G] 1:5 The respondent was in all material respect, in the very same situation as Sri K. Rangaswamy Chetty, who was admittedly junior to him in the parent Department. That was the reason why the absorption in the Department could not be treated as a break in his service, this period having been treated as leave. [262B] 1:6 The respondent was not similarly situated because there was a break in the respondent 'S job with the Department of technical Education. That he had been in all material particulars in the same position as K. Rangaswami Chetty, who had come on deputation from another department to the Polytechnics and all of them, excepting the respondent, were absorbed temporarily in the Department and were absorbed permanently. [262E] 1:7 The respondent was a suitable and qualified to be absorbed permanently in that post, is manifest from the recommendation of the Public Service commission and is implicit in the order itself. For the reasons aforesaid, the High Court was fully justified in granting the relief, it did, to the respondent, to the extent that it did, in the special circumstances of this case, to the effect of the absorption in that Department and was implicit, in the impugned orders, itself.

The appellant, a foreign parent, was appointed guardian of a child in the courts in Bombay, Delhi and Gujarat, and for Enfants de L 's village of India. The appellant, a Foreign parent, was a minor, and was a minor. The appellant was a minor and was a student of the school. The appellant filed an application for appointment of a foreigner as guardian of a minor. A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the application holding that the appellant was not a foreigner. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Division Bench. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Indian Council of Social Welfare of the Indian Council of Child Welfare to which notice is issued by the court would have to scrutinise the application for guardianship made on behalf of the foreigner wishing to take the child in adoption and after examining the home study report, the child study report as also documents and certificates forwarded by the sponsoring social or child welfare agency and making necessary enquiries, it must make its representation to the court so that the court may be able to satisfy itself whether the principles and norms as also the procedure laid down by the Supreme Court in this judgment have been observed and followed, whether the foreigner will be a suitable adoptive parent for the child and the child will be able to reaches to the child. [847C D] 1.2 The Indian Council is of Social Welfare and the Indian Council should, with the assistance of the Government prepare a list of recognised social or child Welfare agencies with their names, addresses and other particulars and send such list to the appropriate department of the Government of each foreign country where Indian children are ordinarily taken in adoption so that the social or child health agency in India they should approach for processing an application of its national for taking an Indian child in adoption. [848C D] 2.1 The recognised social or Child Welfare agency sponsoring the application of the foreigner must also undertake while forwarding the application to the social or Child welfare agency in India, that it will ensure adoption of the child by the foreigner according to the law of his country within a period not exceeding two years and as soon as the adoption is effected, it will send one certified copy of the adoption order to the social and child welfare agency processing the application for adoption and from the child study Report, they would be able to gather information as to who are the biological parents of the child, if the biological parents are known. HELD: (1) The Tribunal was not justified in rejecting this claim of the Unions on the ground that the amount was of Rs.65,764. [14F] (2) The Tribunal did not accept this contention of the Unions. The last item relates to the claim made by the Unions that after distribution of bonus at 20% for the year 1964 65, there must have been a surplus and it. should have been set on for the next year, namely, 1965 66. [15G] (3) The further direction in the Award of the Tribunal regarding set on cannot be accepted. [15H] (4) The Tribunal had accepted the evidence that bon us at 20% could not have been declared for the year 1965 66 and in order to honour the declaration made by the Company, bonus was paid at that percentage. [15E] (5) The Tribunal accepted this contention of Union of India that the amount Of Rs. 65764 had not been accepted by the Income tax Officer, the Company can claim depreciation only in the sum of Rs. The Tribunal did neither accept this contention nor did accept this contention. [15F] (6) The Tribunal, however, did not accept the contention of the Union on the ground of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of the business and it was an expenditure allowable under section 37(1) of the Income tax Act. [15A] (7) The Tribunal has rejected this claim of Union of the appellant. The last Item relates to the claims made by the Union that after distribution, of bonus at 40% for the years 1964 65, the Tribunal had accepted this claim of Rs. 66,764 and in order for the accounting year 1965 66 on the basis of our judgment will be as follows Rs. Rs. 65754. [15B] (8) The further directions in the Award regarding set on can be accepted. The balance additional amount that the Company will have to pay by way of bonus to make up the 14.02%, as stated above, is the sum of Rupees. 65, 764 and in addition the bonus payable to the employees. The appellant was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes in 1954, and later as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1957, he was posted as a Joint Commercial Tax officer. The appellant was promoted to the post of Deputy Commissioner in 1954, after a lapse of 25 years. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Government retiring him from service. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the appellant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80 The appellant contended that the Government had accepted the views of the Full Board and dropped the charges making the following order on 29 11 1974: "As the preliminary enquiry disclosed a prima facie case of corruption, a detailed enquiry was taken up by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption. The Government accepted the report of the Directorate of vigilance and Anti Corruption and Anti Corruption, and dropped the charge making the following orders on 29 11 1975: "As there was no entry in the service book to his discredit or hinting even remotely that he had outlived his utility as a Govt. servant. If there was some entry, not wholly favourable to the appellant after his promotion, one might hark back to similar or like entries in the past, read them all in conjunction and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. But, with nothing of the sort, it is indeed odd to retire a Government servant a few months after promoting him to a Selection post. The Government, therefore, accepted the views and dropped the proceedings making the following. "As the enquiry was pending with the Vigilance and AntiCorruption Department in regard to the allegations against the appellant, the ultimate result of the enquiry which was that the charges should be dropped was nowhere noted in the personal file of the appellant. The Government accepting the views of both the Deputy Commissioner and dropping the charges made against the appellant was nowhere noted. The Government accept the views of https://hcservices.ecourts.gov.in/hcservices/ the Full Board of Revenue, and dropped charges making the Following order on 2911 1974: "The effect of the order of November 29, 1974 of the Government was to grant absolution to the appellant from the repercussions of, the note of the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax, made in 1969. If there is some entry, Not wholly favourable to him after his promotion the one might harkk back to similar and like entries in his past, read again all in conjunction with conclude that the period had arrived for Government servant to terminate Government service. " The appellant will be reinstated in service and paid the arrears of salary due to him under the rules. The appellant will also be reinstated in his service and paid arrears of salary payable to him under rules. " The Government accepted his views of the Deputy Commissioners and dropped the Charges making the following further order on 29 November 1974: " As the preliminary enquiry revealed a prima facie finding of corruption, the detailed enquiry was not substantiated in the enquiry made by the Directorate. The Government accordingly framed charges against the appellant. " The Board of Revenue (CT) was therefore requested to frame charges straightaway as for a major penalty against Thiru D. Ramaswami on the basis of allegations levelled against him. The Government also accepted the views expressed by the Full Board. The Government did not say that the previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored, once he is promoted. But, when there is nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, we see no justification for needless digging into the past. No. 1112 dated September 19, 1975, Commercial Taxes Religious Endowments Department, Government of Tamil Nadu is quashed.

The appellants were the owners of two buses, one in Andhra Pradesh and the other in Andhra Pradesh. The Corporation issued a notification under section 68 D of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, for nationalisation of the buses in the State of Andhra Pradesh. In the meantime the State Transport Undertaking issued a notification on April 1, 1962, under section 68D of the Act, for nationalisation and in the three schemes which were formulated in pursuance of this resolution the western half of Kurnool was selected as the area to be nationalised in the first instance. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was not in conformity with the requirements of section 68 C of the Act so long as the choice of the "area" in which and the routes in it to be run by the Corporation was made by them alone. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the scheme framed and approved by the Corporation did not originate from the Corporation, and that the schemes framed and approved were fully in conformity with section 68 C. Held, that the schemes were vitiated by non compliance with the requirements Of section 68 C and the Rules made thereunder, and the schemes framed thereunder, were fully in compliance with the provisions of section 68C. The scheme was not vitiated by noncompliance with the requirements prescribed by section 68 C, and the rules made thereunder, were to have effect notwithstanding anything in Ch. No doubt, in a State where there is no Regional Transport Authority at all, [vide e.g. proviso to section 44(1), but there is some other authority which functions as the Regional Transport Authority for the purposes of the Art, such an Authority might be that which would be comprehended by section 68F(1) but where as in Andhra Pradesh there is admit tedly a Regional Transport Authority, we cannot accede to the submission that such authority is deprived of the power to issue a permit by reason of section 68F (1) merely because the Regional Transport authority of that area cannot grant permits under Ch. No. doubt, in A. K. Gopalan vs The State of Madras, ; , followed.

The appellant was a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Act having its registered place of business at Calcutta. Under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, the appellant in order to claim exemption thereunder had to furnish declaration forms duly filled in and signed by registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. The appellant, it was said, made various attempts to get duplicate forms of declaration from the dealers but, on account of circumstances over which it had no 628 control and because of the unhelpful and hostile attitude of the Commercial Tax Officer within whose jurisdiction the said dealers functioned, it was not able to furnish the duplicate forms for all the declarations that were lost. On August 8, 1957, the appellant applied to the Commercial Tax officer under section 21A of the Act for summoning the dealers to produce the necessary documents in order to prove that they had issued the declaration forms to it, but the said officer did not issue the requisite summons to the parties concerned. On November 21, 1957, a notice was issued to the appellant to show cause why the goods should not be included in the list of declared goods. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that the said notice was invalid as it was not issued by the purchasing dealer. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the proviso to the said sub clause was only directory and, therefore, it would be enough and if it was substantially compiled with. HELD: (1) The proviso to the sub clause that the declaration form in the manner prescribed is the best evidence to prove that the sales to the registered dealers were for the purposes mentioned in the said sub clauses. [608 B] (2) The proviso is not mandatory but only directory and the rule is only directory and not mandatory. [609 C] (3) The proviso does not impose a condition on a dealer for claiming exemption. The proviso is only directory. The construction suggested by the learned counsel introduces an incongruity which shall be avoided. [610 E] (4) The proviso imposes a condition on the dealer for claiming the exemption. The object of section 5(1)(a)(i) of the Act and the rules made thereunder is self evident. Therefore, presumably to achieve the twofold object, namely, prevention of fraud and ' facilitating administrative efficiency, the exemption given is made subject to a condition that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration form in that manner prescribed under the section. That makes all the difference, for it is the proviso that imposes the condition. 27(2) made under the Orissa Act "a dealer shall produce a true declaration in writing by the purchasing registered dealer or by such responsible person as may be authorized in writing in this behalf by such dealer that the goods in question are specified in the purchasing dealer 's certificate of registration as being required for resale by him or in the execution of any contract." [610 F G] (5) The proviso, imposes a condition. 27A(2) makes under the Orissa Sales Tax Act "a registered dealer shall produce the true declaration in the manner specified under the section". That is the proviso which imposes the condition, which is made subject subject to a Condition that the person seeking the exemption shall produce a declaration form. That interpretation would be contrary to the plain terms of the clause.

The petitioners were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. The petitioners were released on bail. The State of Bihar filed an affidavit in response to the directions given by the High Court. The State filed an affidavit stating that the under trial prisoners whose particulars were given in the counter affidavit filed on 26th February, 1979 were periodically produced before the Magistrates in compliance with the proviso to section 167(2) and that the under trail prisoners whose particulars are given in the list filed on 26.2.1979 were periodically produced on 26th Feb. 1979. The State also filed an affidavit giving particulars of the under trial prisoner in 48 jails in the State of Bihar in addition to the particulars of the undertrial prisoners in 17 jails already submitted on 26th March, 1979. The affidavit stated that the under trials prisoners whose particulars had been given in the affidavit filed on 27th February,1979 were periodically remanded from time to time by the Magistrates as required by the proviso to Section 167(2). The State of West Bengal filed an affidavit on 26th April, 1979 stating that the Under trial prisoners whose names and particulars were given on 26th May, 1979 were repeatedly produced before the Magistrate in compliance with section 167(1) and that they were unable to engage a lawyer who would apprise them of their right to apply for bail and help them to secure release on bail by making a proper application to the Magistrate in that behalf. The State stated that the State should furnish to the Court the dates on which these under trial prisoners were remanded to judicial custody from time to lime by the Magistrates, so that they could be released on bail by taking a proper application for bail and opposing remand provided that no objection was raised to such lawyer on their behalf and if any application for bail is made, the Magistrates should dispose of the same in accordance with the broad outlines set out by us in our judgment dated 12th February, 1978. The State did not file any affidavit in reply to the affidavit filed by the State of West Bihar. The State was directed to furnish to the State of Jharkhand the dates on where these under trial prisoner were produced before the Courts or the Sessions Courts, as the case may be, and where such cases have been pending investigation for more than six months, the State of Haryana will furnish them a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application for bail, provided that no objections are raised to such advocate on their behalf, and if any such application for bail was made, the Magistrate should dispose of such of those cases as have been pending for more than 6 months, provided that the Magistrate or the Sessions Court, as the ease may be, should dispose of those cases in accordance with broad outlines laid down by us in this judgment dated 12.2.79. The State, however, filed an affidavit before the High Court stating that the State had not filed any affidavit in response thereto. The State contended that the State was under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The State is under a constitutional obligation to ensure speedy justice and whatever is required for this purpose have to be done through the State. [529G] 2. The State has to furnish to this Court within three weeks from today particulars as to the location of the courts of magistrates and courts of sessions in the State.

The appellant landlord gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent on December 31, 1951, under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The landlord made an application on April 7, 1953, under section 29(2) of the Act for obtaining possession. The landlord, however, made an application under article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court and contended that the provision of section 34(2 A) should have been taken into consideration by the Revenue Courts in deciding the application of the landlord under section 29 (2) and that the revenue courts were wrong in the view they had taken that sub section did not apply to the present proceedings. The High Court allowed the application of tenant relying on its previous Full Bench decision in Durlabbhai Fakirbhai Fakirabhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai, ; and held that as the tenancy had (1) 571 terminated and the right to obtain possession had accrued to the landlord after the coming into force of the Amending Act, the Amending Act applied and therefore the landlord, if he fails to satisfy the further conditions under the Amending Act would not be entitled to possession. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The right to terminate the tenancy by one year 's notice, which was given in this case in December 1951 before the Amending Act came into force, would not apply to notices given before the Amending Acts came into force. [571 E] (ii) The right of the landlord to terminate the tenant 's tenancy by one month 's notice was a right to terminate tenancy by one 's notice. But the date on which the right to terminate matures, that is, the date on the date of notice, the right to termination the tenancy, that is the date on when the tenancy actually terminates in consequence of the notice given to terminate, it. [571 G] (iii) The right conferred by sub section (2 A) on the right of the tenant to terminate the lease by one year is a right to the landlord to termination the tenant 'on the ground that the landlord bona fide requires the land for any of the purposes specified in sub section (1) then his right to terminate that tenancy shall be limited to an area which shall, after such termination, leave with the tenant half the area of the land leased.
