The assessee Company had two departments (1) for spinning of yarn from raw and waste wool and (2) for spinning and weaving of yarn from imported wool tops. ' The assessee Company had three departments (1), for spinning of cotton from raw and Waste wool and (3) for spinning, and weaving of cotton from imported wool. The assessee Company was a dealer in cotton yarn from raw cotton and waste wool. The Income tax Officer held that the agreement amounted to a joint venture for the distribution of profit between the assessee Company and the selling agents after the profits were ascertained. The Tribunal held that the assessee Company was not liable to deduct income tax on the amount paid to the selling agents. The High Court in reversing the order of the Tribunal mainly relied on certain materials which were not at all found by the Tribunal in its order nor were those materials mentioned in the statement of the case. The Tribunal also held that the cumulative effect of the interpretation of the various clauses of the agreement dated October 20, 1955 unmistakably revealed that in the garb of an agency the parties entered into a joint venture with a view to division of profits between the assessee company and the selling agent after being ascertained between themselves and that is why there was an express provision in the agreement by which the agents agreed to share losses which was a provision peculiar to the present transaction and was not at all covered by any authority cited before the Tribunal or the High Court, that itself was proof positive of the fact that the transaction amounted to a Joint venture resulting in division of profits and therefore the amount paid was not expenses incurred for the purpose of the business or for earning profits. The High court also held that there was a very thin line of distinction between a contract for payment of a share of profits simpliciter and a payment of remuneration which is deductible in truth from the profits divisible. The High ' Court also held that in the guise of an agency, the parties entered a joint venture and that was why there was a express provision in that agreement by which an agent agreed to share the losses which were to be deducted from the commission of the agents the agents become completely equated with the proprietors of the firm itself and therefore the contract of agency was really a sort of a sort of an agency to conceal the real intent and purpose the commercial venture. The High, Court, however, held that the mere fact that the agents agreed not to share the profits and the losses would not take the case of the assessee beyond the ambit of section 10(2)(xv) of the Act in order to show that the payments made to the agents were not expenses incurred in the character of trader or it was not laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose for earning profits, and that it was clearly pointed out in the judgment that there was an implied provision in the contract by which the agent agreed to pay the amounts in dispute. The High Courts also held that even if the payments were not legally deductible under section 10(1)(xv) the amount paid could not be claimed by the assessee Company as a deduction under 191 section 10(3)(xv) as it was not incurred for the purposes of the business. The High Curt held that the amount paid by the assessee company was not expenses for the purpose, of the business and that it could not be said that the payments were made to the selling agent were not expenses for that purpose. The High. Court also held in reversing the Tribunal 's order that the payments in question were not legally permissible under section 10 (2)(xv).

The assessee company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The assessee company was assessed to income tax for the year ending March 31, 1958. The Income tax Officer rejected the assessee 's claim for dividend on the ground that the accumulated profit would not include current profits for the purpose of section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Tribunal held that the accumulated profits would not include the current profits for that purpose. The assessee appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the assessee was entitled to apply to the High court for a reference of the questions of law which arose on its submissions negatived in appeal by the Appellate Tribunal. The High court held that the expression "accumulated profits" in section 2(7A)(e), could not be construed as including current profits. The Revenue appealed to this Court by certificate under article 136 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The expression "accompumulated profits", in section 2 (6A)(i) of the Income Tax Act. 1922, means profits which have accumulated prior to the accounting year of which the income profits and gains were being assessed, while current profit would mean the profits of the accounting year in which the income income profits and gain were being assessed. [950 A B] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs M. V. The Revenue, Madras, ; , referred to. The expression " Accumulated profits " in section 2 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, means the profits which have accrued prior to the assessment year of which income profits and profits were being assessed and while current profit could mean the profits which had accumulated prior to that accounting year of the income profits.

The respondents were the owners of certain lands in the district of Burdwan. The respondents claimed to have dealt with the properties as owners under assertion of an adverse title. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal the District Judge held that the documents on which the defendants claimed to have proceeded with the lands as owners under the assertion of an alleged adverse title were not proved to relate to the suit lands. The High Court held that the document was not proved to be a valid document. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the documents relied on by the defendants as containing assertions that they held under a Lakheraj grant were not proved, that the relationship subsisting between the parties was one of landlord and tenant, that the document in 1931 was correct, that the status of the Asthal had become extinguished by adverse possession for long over the statutory period. Held, that the documents were not shown to relate to a grant by the owner entitled to the land, but that the defendants could be said to have asserted a hostile title, and the suits were within time from that date. The documents relied on were not shown by the defendants to relate to their suit lands. Held, further, that the defendants were not trespassers, and that the documents could be said clearly to have been made by the Mahant of Asthal in favour of the predecessors of the defendants. The documents were not proved by the defendants. They were not shown as containing assertions in the plaint. The documents could not be said to relate to any grant by the owners of Asthal to the knowledge of the plaintiff prior to 1931, and that they were not shown in the plaint as containing assertions, that they held lands under a Lakhiraj grant.

The appellant was the owner of the land in question. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale of land admeasuring 45 acres 5 gunthas bearing Survey No. 25 situated in Sholapur Mouje Dongaon in Maharashtra State for a consideration of Rs. 42,000/ out of which Rs. 5,000/ were paid as earnest money and a further amount of Rs. 5.000/ was paid as earnest amount and a further sum of Rs. 10,000/ was also paid as earnest. The trial Court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to settle, decide or deal with any question arising in a suit for Specific performance of contract for sale was ousted. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The jurisdiction of the civil Court to settle or deal with a question arising in the suit for specific relief of sale of agricultural land governed by the provisions of the Tenancy Act would alone be barred under section 85. [682C] (2) The civil Court would be competent to entertain the suit. If there is an issue which has to be settled, decided or dealt with by the competent authority under the Tenancy Act, the jurisdiction of that Civil Court to decide or dealwith the same would be barred and it, will have to be referred to the competent authority. [683D] (3) The civil court would be competent, to entertain the suits. If there was an issue which had to be settled the jurisdiction of a civil court to settle, decided or deal with the same would not be ousted because the issue is not required to be settled or dealt with under the Tenancy Acts. [684E] (4) The civil courts would be competent under the Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act to settle, determine or deal with such issues under the Tenancy Laws. [685F] (5) The civil Courts would be competent in entertaining the suit. [686C] (6) The civil suit would be competent if the jurisdiction of Civil Court to deal with the issue arises in a properly constituted civil suit cognizable by the Civil Court. If there are an issue which arises in a duly constituted civil suit, the jurisdiction would be barred. [690F] (7) The civil jurisdiction of the High Court to settle and deal with any issue arising under the Tenancy laws would alone be ousted. [691F] (8) The civil and the civil court would have to take recourse to the provision contained in section 85A for reference of the issue to the competent authorities under the Tenancy Law. [692F] (9) The civil suits would be competent for entertain, an incidental or subsidiary issue which may arise with reference to provisions of the Land Tenancy Act.

The assessee company was carrying on the business of heavy engineering. The assessee company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling jute. The assessee was carrying on its business in jute. The company was carrying out its business in Jute. The assessee had been carrying on its trade in jute. In the course of its business the assessee company had been carrying out its trade in Jute. In the assessment year 1958 59, the assessee company claimed exemption under section 15C of the Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the assessee company was an industrial undertaking to which section 15C applied. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was an industrial company to which section15C applied. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner held that the two industrial undertakings were formed by reconstruction of the business already in existence and hence the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section15C of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on the above facts held that the steel Foundry and the Jute Mill Division were formed by the reconstruction of the assessee 's business already in exist ing the business already existing and hence the assesse was not entitled (1) 765 to exemption under s 15C(2) as rightly held by the High Court since they were formed by a reconstruction of the old business already in existed, namely, the business of Heavy engineering. The High Court in appeal held that the three industrial undertakings were not formed out of the reconstruction of its business already in existing existence, namely, that the business of the assessee company already in existence, namely the business of huge engineering. The Tribunal also held that the said two industrial undertakings cannot be said to be not formed out Of the already existing business of the assesse. The High court in appeal held against the assessee. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the two undertakings were not constituted out of the already existing and separate undertakings. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts were not right in answering the two questions in the negative and against the assessee '. [776D] 2. The fact that the assessee is carrying on the general business of heavy Engineering will not prevent him from setting up new industrial undertakings and from claiming benefit under section 15A if that section is otherwise applicable. [775E] 3. The fact of the assessee being carrying on the special business of heavy Engg engineering will not prevent the assessee from setting up a new industrial undertaking on account of some directions. The fact, that the articles produced by the two undertakings are used by the Boiler Division of the assessee will not affect the benefit of section 15C. [778F] 4. The fact is that the assessee has been carrying on the ordinary business of heavy art engineering will not preclude him from settingup new industrial undertakings. [782F] 5. The fact the assessee is carried on the general trade of heavy engineering will not affect his claim under section 15 C.

The inamdars were inamdars and were granted to office holders as remuneration for services to be rendered by them and were within the purview of section 44 B(2)(a)(i). The inamdars were granted to the temple for the performance of services connected therewith. The inamdars claimed title to the lands under a grant from the inamdars on the footing that the inamdars were entitled to the kudiwaram and the melwaram. The District Judge held that the inamdar was entitled to the Kudiwaram rights in the inam lands against the Government and thereby defeat the latter 's right to resume the inam lands. The High Court reversed this finding and held that the inams were personal inams burdened with services and the order of resumption was therefore illegal and a nullity. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The inamdars are entitled to the pudiwaram right against the Government. The inamdar is entitled to the Pudiwaram. [529 C] (ii) The inamdar has made an exchange, gift, sale or mortgage of the inam lands to any subordinate interest in the inams. The inam lands are resumable under section 44 B (2)(a) (i). The Government could, therefore resume the inam land made under section 44B (2) and dispossess the inamdars and the plaintiffs claiming as lessees under them. [530 D] (iii) The inam lands were resumable within section 44 B. The inam land was resumable. The inam resumed under section 44 A (2)(b)(i) was attracted if the holder of the inam has made an Exchange, gift, mortgage of the Inam or has granted a lease of it for a term exceeding five years. No. The District Collector held that the alienations were personal inams accompanied with services and that the order of resumed was therefore illegal.

The appellant Corporation was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. The Indore Municipality was governed by that Act. The Indore City Municipal Corporation Act, 1909, was repealed by the Indore Municipal Corporation Act (Act No. 4 of 1909) and the rules framed thereunder on the basis of the gross annual letting value of buildings. The Indore Municipal Corporation however purported to levy the house tax on the basis that the gross annual rent was less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The Municipal tax levied under the old Act and the rules made thereunder on the ground that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the basis Of gross annual letting Value less 10% Statutory allowance in lieu thereof. The Municipal Tax Officer, Indore, levied the house tax at the rate of 7% of the gross letting value at the rate applicable to the buildings and lands. The appellant Corporation challenged the levy of the house tax by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the Corporation was entitled to levy the tax at the rates of 7% and that it was not bound to deduct the 10% allowance provided by sec. 2(c) and therefore the rate of 8% of the net annual letting value at which the tax was levied was saved and secondly that under sec. 79(1) of the 1954 Act, the Corporation need not prepare a fresh assessment list every year, that it has to prepare a fresh list once in every 4 years, that the Corporation therefore can and in fact has adopted the said list for the two years in question and that being so, the list so adopted was in force during the years in question. HELD: (1) The Municipal tax is an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and the assessment list on the basis thereof is for each such official year. [132 D] (2) The Municipal Tax is an annual fee leviable for a specific official year and assessment list on that basis is for each of such official year and, the assessment list for each such officer is for each individual official year. The Municipal taxes are an annual tax and are therefore, inconsistent with the provisions of sec. 73 of the Act. [132 E F] (3) The Municipal taxes levied under the new Act and the Rules framed thereunder on that basis are obviously inconsistent with the provision of sec.73 of the Act and have to be adjusted in the light of the provisions of section 73 of the 1954. [132 G] (4) The Municipal Taxes are an annual fee and are not liable to pay any tax assessed on the gross annual rental value less 10% of the annual letting value. [132 F] (5) The Municipal Corporation is entitled to adopt the assessment list prepared for the year 1952 53 for the two assessment years, 1953 54 and 1954 55 under sec. 76(6) as conclusive evidence of the annual rent and the amount of tax assessed thereon and entitled the Corporation to collect the tax assessed thereon for at least 4 years even though the valuation or the annual letting Value thereof may have decreased for one reason or the other.

The assessee Company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. The Deputy Commissioner, however, relying on the Memorandum of Association, which allowed the assessee Company to manufacture and sell chemicals and on the Directors report, held that the assessee Company was liable to income tax on a profit of Rs. 1,15,259. An appeal was then filed before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal at Trivandrum and the assessee Company contended that the transaction of sale of the raw materials along with the business including machinery, plant and premises was a revenue sale and that the amount obtained was only by way of realisation sale and was not, therefore, liable to tax. The High Court held that the transaction was not during the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the business, and that the sum obtained was only in realisation of sale and was, therefore, not liable to tax under section 10(1)(iii) of the Income tax Act. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The transaction was not in the ordinary course of trade but was for the purpose for putting an end to the business, that is to say, the price without the chemicals and raw materials and the price with them. [357 B] (ii) The assessee Company was wound up at least in so far as its match manufacturing business was concerned. That the business of the Company was sold as a going concern, and was, in fact, worked by the assessee Company on behalf of the buyer till the entire consideration was paid, makes no difference because the agreement clearly indicated that the assessee company was keeping the factory going, not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf of its buyer. [337 C] (iii) The assessee company was carrying on a trading busi ness. That the assessee Company had been wound up at almost all in so far that its match manufacturing operations were concerned. That it was carrying on the trading busi cess. That it had not been able to establish that there was a profit other than what results from the appreciation of capital. [338 C] (iv) The assessee was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling chemicals, that in the past it bad sold chemicals and raw material and obtained a larger price, and that therefore the excess represented a capital appreciation and not a trading profit. [339 E] (v) The assessee had not been given a proper opportunity to explain the circumstances in which the excess represented the capital appreciation and the price was paid, make no difference because it was not a trading receipt. [335 D] (vi) The assessee 's case was, therefore decided on the finding of the special Commissioners, for which there was enough material in evidence. [336 E] (vii) The assessee could not reasonably infer that the chemicals and the raw materials were sold in the ordinary way of business or that the assessee was carrying business on a trading Busi ness, and that, therefore, the excess represented an capital appreciation and was not a realisation sale after the company was wound up, but had the characteristics of a trading sale.
